    Reason about every possible next step.

    TLA+ is a language for describing systems and asking precise questions about their behavior. This course follows Leslie Lamport's TLA+ Video Course lecture by lecture, then carries the same method into failure-prone architectures.

    Follow the route in the diagram. The top row starts from nothing and ends with your first real protocol. The second row runs right to left through commit protocols and into the question of what it means for one spec to implement another. The bottom row has no videos. It applies what you learned to concurrency, large models, failures, and application design, and it ends with review.

    TLA stands for Temporal Logic of Actions. A specification, or spec, is a precise description of what a system is allowed to do. It is not a program that serves requests. You decide what matters, how it can change, and what must stay true, and then a tool searches for a counterexample. The value is often finding that a design you can explain convincingly still allows a bad execution.

    The video in this lesson is Lamport's talk “Thinking Above the Code.” Watch it for motivation. No later lesson depends on its details, so you can return to it at any point. Its main example, Quicksort, is worked through at the end of this lesson as a lab, as code, and as a TLA+ spec.

    How to study with the videos

    Each lecture has one or more lessons here, in the lecture's order and with its examples. When a lecture spans several lessons, each lesson says which part of the lecture it covers. Its “While you watch” section tells you what to look for, where to stop and try the problem yourself, and what the lesson adds. Each video is meant to be viewed along with its web page on Lamport's course site. The videos and that site need internet; the lesson text and the labs work offline.

    1. Watch a segment, not a whole lecture. Lamport often tells you to stop the video and solve something. Do it.
    2. Predict. Before you click a step or open an answer, write down what you expect.
    3. Run it. Step the lab, or run the real tool once you have installed it.
    4. Break it. Weaken a condition or change a step, then predict the failure.
    5. Explain it. Close the lesson and rebuild the model or the argument from memory.

    The dashed arrow in the diagram is the most useful one: a surprise means your mental model and the system differ, so go back and predict again. In your next session, recall the previous lesson before continuing. Mark a lesson studied only when you can explain its exercise without looking. The Mac app saves completed lessons, notes, and reading position on this Mac. The standalone file saves in your browser when browser storage is available.

    A lab is not a verification. The interactive labs run small, purpose-built JavaScript models. They do not read TLA+ and they are not the model checker. Complete modules are printed so you can check them with the real tools, which you install in lesson 8.

    Scope and prerequisites

    You need basic programming intuition, not a mathematics degree. Each piece of notation is introduced when it is first needed. The lectures cover safety, liveness, and implementation. The later parts add concurrency, proof structure, model reduction, time, crash recovery, and consensus. This is a substantial foundation, not a complete language reference or a proof of any deployed system.

    A first example: an upload button

    Here is the kind of question the course teaches you to ask. A document-sharing app has an Upload button, and a designer says, “Disable the button while the upload is running.” That sentence hides several choices. Can the request succeed after the screen times out? Does Retry create another document?

    Each box in the diagram records only two things: where the upload is, and how many documents exist. The upper path is the one everyone pictures. On the lower path the server commits, the reply is lost, the screen times out, and the user retries. No single screen looks wrong, and the final box has two documents. Nothing about the button's appearance appears in the diagram, because the button is not what went wrong.

    Keep a prediction notebook with three lines for each claim: claim, suspected breaking path, evidence needed. For this app: “one upload creates at most one document; a lost reply followed by a retry might break it; inspect how the server recognizes a repeated request.” That is a concrete question for implementation, not a vague instruction to make uploads reliable. By the end of the lectures you will be able to write this as a spec and have a tool find the lower path for you.

    Predict: is disabling the Upload button enough to guarantee one document?

    No. It prevents one local interaction but says nothing about the lost reply and retry in the diagram. The server needs a way to connect a repeated request to the same result. The button can improve the experience, but the server has to enforce the rule.

    Quicksort, above the code

    The main example in Lamport's talk is Quicksort. Most programmers describe it as a recursive procedure: partition the array, then sort each half. That describes code. Lamport describes it one level up, without recursion:

    1. Keep a set U of index intervals that still need sorting. At the start it holds one interval, the whole array.
    2. Remove any interval from U. If it has one element, it is already sorted.
    3. Otherwise, partition it at some index p, so that every value in the left part is at most every value in the right part. Put both parts back in U.
    4. When U is empty, the array is sorted.

    The important word is “any.” The description doesn't say which interval to take next. A recursive program takes the newest one, so it is using a stack. A loop over a work queue takes the oldest one. Several threads could each take a different interval at the same time. All three are Quicksort, because each does something the description allows.

    Sort it yourself

    Each bar is one array element, with its index underneath. The brackets under the bars are the intervals in U, and a green bar is in its final place. Press an interval in the first row to choose it yourself. The next two buttons choose for you, the way a program would. U remembers the order in which intervals were added. Newest (stack) takes the interval added most recently, like taking the top plate from a stack. That is what the code below does with pop. Oldest (queue) takes the interval that has waited longest, like the front of a line, so the array is split one level at a time. A partition adds its left part first and then its right part, so the right part is always the newest. The dashed line shows where the last partition split its interval. This runs the JavaScript code printed below one step at a time; it is not TLC.

    Sort the array once with each button, then compare the two readouts. The steps come in a different order and the arrays in between differ, but both runs end with the same sorted array. Also notice when a bar turns green: only when its interval is down to one element, and after that it never moves.

    The iterative code

    This is the program the lab runs. The array todo plays the part of U, and pop makes it a stack. Change pop to shift and it becomes a queue, and it still sorts.

    function quicksort(a) {
  const todo = [[0, a.length - 1]];  // U: intervals still to sort
  while (todo.length > 0) {
    const [lo, hi] = todo.pop();     // choose one: here, the newest
    if (lo >= hi) continue;          // one element is already sorted
    const p = partition(a, lo, hi);
    todo.push([lo, p], [p + 1, hi]);
  }
  return a;
}

// Hoare's partition. Returns p with lo <= p < hi, and
// rearranges a[lo..hi] so every a[lo..p] <= every a[p+1..hi].
function partition(a, lo, hi) {
  const pivot = a[Math.floor((lo + hi) / 2)];
  let i = lo - 1, j = hi + 1;
  for (;;) {
    do i++; while (a[i] < pivot);
    do j--; while (a[j] > pivot);
    if (i >= j) return j;
    [a[i], a[j]] = [a[j], a[i]];
  }
}

    Hoare's partition is the hard part to get right, with its two indexes that cross. The description doesn't care how it works, only what it guarantees: p lies between lo and hi - 1, values outside lo..hi don't move, and every value up to p is at most every value after it.

    The same algorithm in TLA+

    Here is the description written as a TLA+ spec. For now, read it for its shape; Lectures 2 to 4 teach the notation. Init says the array may hold any values and that U holds the whole array. Partition is one step. It chooses any interval in U, then any p and any rearranged array B that meet the three conditions of a partition. Nothing in it mentions pivots, swaps, stacks, or recursion.

    ------------------------------ MODULE QuickSort ------------------------------
EXTENDS Integers, FiniteSets
CONSTANTS N, Values
Idx == 0..(N-1)
VARIABLES A, U       \* the array, and the set of intervals still to sort
vars == <<A, U>>

Count(B, v) == Cardinality({i \in Idx : B[i] = v})
IsPerm(B) == \A v \in Values : Count(B, v) = Count(A, v)
Sorted == \A i, j \in Idx : i < j => A[i] =< A[j]

Init == /\ A \in [Idx -> Values]
        /\ U = {<<0, N-1>>}

\* Pick ANY interval in U. The spec does not say which one.
Partition == \E I \in U :
    LET lo == I[1]
        hi == I[2]
    IN  IF lo < hi
        THEN \E p \in lo..(hi-1), B \in [Idx -> Values] :
               /\ \A i \in Idx \ (lo..hi) : B[i] = A[i]
               /\ IsPerm(B)
               /\ \A i \in lo..p, j \in (p+1)..hi : B[i] =< B[j]
               /\ A' = B
               /\ U' = (U \ {I}) \cup {<<lo, p>>, <<p+1, hi>>}
        ELSE /\ U' = U \ {I}
             /\ UNCHANGED A

Done == U = {} /\ UNCHANGED vars
Next == Partition \/ Done
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars /\ WF_vars(Partition)

SortedWhenDone == U = {} => Sorted
Terminates == <>(U = {})
==============================================================================

    The model checker reads a small configuration file that picks sizes for the constants and names what to check:

    CONSTANTS N = 4  Values = {1, 2, 3}
SPECIFICATION Spec
INVARIANT SortedWhenDone
PROPERTY Terminates
    In the codeIn the spec
    todoU
    todo.pop()\E I \in U, any interval
    if (lo >= hi) continuethe ELSE branch
    partition(a, lo, hi)any p and B that meet the conditions
    todo.push(…)U' = (U \ {I}) \cup {…}

    With 4 elements and values from 1 to 3, TLC tries all 81 starting arrays and every order of choosing intervals, 731 distinct states, in about a second. SortedWhenDone says the array is sorted once U is empty, and Terminates says U does become empty. That leaves a separate and smaller question: is every step of the code a step the spec allows? lesson 26 is about that question.

    Predict: a bug puts only the left part back, <<lo, p>>. Which property fails, and how long is the shortest failing behavior?

    SortedWhenDone fails, and TLC needs only three states. The array 1, 1, 1, 2 is partitioned at p = 0 into 1, 1, 2, 1. The bug drops the right part, the left part has one element, and U is empty while 2 still comes before 1. Terminates still holds, since a program that forgets work finishes sooner. Tests on arrays that are already sorted would all pass.

    Lecture 1: Introduction to TLA+

    Find the design error before there is code to debug.

    The upload example in lesson 1 went wrong in the design, not in any line of code. TLA+ exists to catch that kind of error, by letting you model a system above the code level and check the model.

    The diagram shows the argument of this lesson. A design error can sit in a system whose every function is correct. On the top route, you find it only if a test happens to hit the right circumstances, and the errors TLA+ aims at are the ones that are extremely hard to hit by testing. On the bottom route, you write the design down precisely and a tool checks it, so the dashed arrow takes you back to the design before you have written any code.

    What TLA+ is

    TLA+ is a language for high-level modeling of digital systems, and it comes with tools for checking those models. The tools you will hear about in the lecture are:

    • TLC, the model checker. A model checker explores the states a model can reach and tests your claims about them. This is the most important tool, and the one you will use.
    • TLAPS, the TLA+ proof system. Writing and checking proofs is a lot of work, and few engineers will use it.
    • The Toolbox, an IDE for writing specs and running the tools. lesson 8 also covers the VS Code extension.

    “Digital systems” includes algorithms, programs, and computer systems. “High-level” means at the design level, above the code. You can't generate code from a TLA+ spec, and that is a choice about what the language is for, as you will see below.

    TLA+ was designed for concurrent and distributed systems. Lamport's advice is direct: if you design such systems and care whether they work, use TLA+ or some other method to specify and check the design precisely. For other programming, he says plainly that he doesn't know exactly how useful it is. In his own small programs it sometimes helps and sometimes doesn't. His broader claim is that it gives most engineers a new way of thinking, which helps even when the language and tools don't apply.

    Abstraction is the skill you are learning

    Abstraction means simplifying by removing irrelevant details. Lamport calls it perhaps the most important part of engineering, since you can't get a complex system right unless you understand it, and you understand it only through abstraction. He credits his best-known work to this ability: stating important problems that details had hidden.

    In the diagram, a model keeps the left region and drops both right regions: the parts that matter less, and the lower-level details of how things are implemented. Choosing that boundary is the hard part. The former Intel engineer quoted in the lecture says the same thing: the difficulty in learning TLA+ is learning to think abstractly about the system, and doing so improves the design process.

    What engineers report

    The lecture gives two pieces of evidence. Treat them as reports from specific teams, not as promises.

    WhoWhat they reported
    Amazon Web Services, in the 2015 Communications of the ACM paperUsed on 10 large, complex systems when written (14 by some time in 2014, per Lamport), by 7 teams. It added significant value in each: subtle bugs they were sure they wouldn't otherwise have found, or the confidence to make aggressive optimizations. Engineers from entry level to principal got useful results in 2 to 3 weeks.
    A real-time operating system team led by Eric VerhulstThe TLA+ abstraction led to a much cleaner architecture. The code was about 10 times smaller than the previous version, which flew on the Rosetta spacecraft.

    The second result answers a question you may already have. If a spec doesn't produce code, why not spend the time improving the code? Because you don't get a factor of 10 from better coding. You get it from a cleaner architecture, and an architecture is a specification above the code level. That team described theirs as a TLA+ spec and debugged it with the tools. Don't expect a tenfold reduction yourself: it is one case.

    What you can check

    “Works right” has to become something a tool can test. The properties TLA+ can check are conditions on individual executions. A system satisfies such a property if and only if every possible execution does.

    Read the diagram one row at a time. “Doesn't produce a wrong answer” can be judged by looking at one row, and execution 3 fails it, so the system fails it. “99% of executions produce the right answer” can't be judged from any single row. It describes the collection, so TLA+ can't check it.

    Predict: can TLC check “95% of requests finish successfully”? What about “no request is charged twice”?

    The first is a statistic over many executions, so no. The second can be judged by examining one execution: did any request get charged twice in it? So yes, once you have modeled requests and charges. When a requirement is statistical, look for the per-execution rule underneath it.

    Which claim is the kind TLA+ can check?

    Lecture 1: Introduction to TLA+

    A system is a graph of possibilities.

    lesson 2 said TLA+ checks conditions on individual executions. To do that, an execution has to be something precise. Here it becomes a sequence of states, and a whole system becomes a state machine that allows many such sequences.

    The diagram shows two executions of the small C program you will meet below, drawn the way TLA+ sees them. Three words define that view: an execution is a sequence of discrete steps.

    Discrete, sequence, step

    Discrete. A digital system is a physical system whose continuous evolution we can abstract as separate events. Lamport's example is the first self-powered digital system, the escapement clock: its parts move continuously, but we can describe it as an abstract clock advancing in ticks. A computer running a program is the same kind of abstraction.

    Sequence. It may seem odd to describe a concurrent system, where several things happen at once, as one sequence. It is clearly possible, since a sequential program can simulate a concurrent system. As the course goes on, you will see that it also works well.

    Step. A state is an assignment of values to variables. A step is the change from one state to the next. A behavior is a sequence of states. So in the diagram, run 1 and run 2 are two behaviors, each with three states and two steps.

    State machines

    You want to describe all possible behaviors of a system, not just one. Programming languages, Turing machines, automata, and hardware description languages can all do that. TLA+ uses the abstraction underneath all of them, a state machine, which you describe by saying three things:

    1. What the variables are.
    2. Their possible initial values.
    3. The relation between their values in the current state and their possible values in the next state.

    A state machine halts if it reaches a state with no possible next state.

    A tiny example, and the problem it exposes

    int i;
void main()
{ i = someNumber();
  i = i + 1;
}

    Assume someNumber() returns an arbitrary number from 0 to 1000, possibly different on each execution. C initializes i to 0. The obvious model has one variable, i, with one initial value, 0. Now try to write item 2. What can follow i: 43?

    Follow the red state in the diagram. In run 1, the call returned 42 and the increment produced 43, so the program has finished: there is no next value. In run 2, the call returned 43, so the next value must be 44. The same current state needs two incompatible rules. So this program can't be described as a state machine with i alone.

    The missing part of the state says which statement runs next. It is called the control state, and we represent it with a second variable, pc, for program control. pc equal to "start" means the first assignment is next, "middle" means the second is next, and "done" means execution has finished.

    In the diagram, there are now two distinct states with i: 43, and each has its own rule. The relation can be stated, for now in English:

    if current value of pc equals "start"
  then next value of i in {0, 1, ..., 1000}
       next value of pc equals "middle"
  else if current value of pc equals "middle"
         then next value of i equals current value of i + 1
              next value of pc equals "done"
         else no next values

    That is awkward to read, and lesson 5 turns it into a formula. But notice what has already been gained. A program represents parts of its state differently because they are implemented differently: variables, control state, call stack, heap. A state machine represents every part the same way, as values of variables. Those implementation details are gone, and you have one simple abstraction.

    Why does the model with only variable i fail?

    Worked app example: a login screen

    The same idea applies far from C. Model a login screen with a variable phase, whose values are idle, submitting, signedIn, and failed, and a variable for the request being processed.

    From submitting, the diagram has two arrows. They are alternative next states, and any one behavior takes just one of them. To practice, draw the graph without code, put concrete values in each node, and name each arrow. Then invent a transition that should be impossible, like the dashed one from failed straight to signedIn. A graph is useful only if its rules exclude that arrow.

    Now suppose a developer stores both phase and isLoading. The combination signedIn with isLoading true becomes representable, although it should never occur. A spinner is derived from phase equal to submitting, so unless it can really vary on its own, leave it out of the model. A state with fewer independent variables is easier to reason about.

    Predict: are x = 1, y = 2 and x = 1, y = 3 the same state?

    No, if both x and y are variables of the model. If you deliberately leave y out, those two situations become one state. What you choose to model decides which differences exist. In the C example, adding pc did the reverse: it split one state into two.

    Predict: does a disabled Submit button mean the machine has no arrow from idle to submitting?

    Only if the button is the only trigger. If a programmatic retry or another event can start a login, the arrow exists regardless of the button. Model what can actually happen, not what one control suggests.

    Lecture 1: Introduction to TLA+

    Problem set 1: describe a system as states and steps.

    These problems practice Lecture 1: what a state, a step and a behavior are, which claims a single execution can settle, and how abstraction decides which variables a model keeps. They draw on How to study this course, Why think above the code and States, steps, and behaviors. You have no TLA+ syntax yet, so answer in English, lists of states, and drawings of state graphs.

    Write your answer down before you open a hint, and open the solution only after the checked question agrees with you. When a problem says “state,” it means an assignment of values to the variables you chose, exactly as in States, steps, and behaviors.

    Problem 1●○○Embedded control

    Which logs are behaviors of an elevator controller?

    Draws on Why think above the code and States, steps, and behaviors.

    A small building has one elevator serving floors 1 to 3. Its controller tracks two things: the floor the car is at, and the door, which is closed, opening, open or closing. The design document gives these rules:

    • At power-on the car is at floor 1 with the door closed.
    • The door goes closed → opening → open → closing → closed, one change at a time.
    • While the door is closing, the obstruction sensor can send it back to opening.
    • The car moves one floor up or down at a time, and only while the door is closed.

    Each change listed above is one step. The real controller also tracks motor current, the door's position in millimetres and several timers. This model leaves them out, which is the kind of abstraction Why think above the code described: they matter for building the controller, not for the question of which orders of events are possible.

    An engineer copied five sequences from the controller's logs into the figure. Each cell is one state, written as floor and door.

    1. Describe the state machine in the three parts States, steps, and behaviors uses: the variables, their initial values, and the relation between a state and its possible next states. Write the relation in English, one case per kind of step.
    2. For each sequence A to E, decide whether it is a behavior of this state machine. For each one that isn't, name the first state or step that breaks a rule, and the rule.
    3. How many different states can the controller reach? Does the state machine ever halt?
    4. A field report claims the car once moved one floor with its door open. Which arrow would the state graph need for that to be a behavior? Is it there, and what does that tell you about the report?

    Hint

    A behavior has to start in an initial state, and every consecutive pair of states has to be one allowed step. A step either changes the door along the cycle (or from closing back to opening) and leaves the floor alone, or changes the floor by exactly one while the door stays closed.

    Solution

    (a) The variables are floor and door. Initially floor is 1 and door is closed. The relation has two kinds of case. A door step keeps the floor and changes the door from closed to opening, opening to open, open to closing, closing to closed, or closing to opening. A move is possible only when the door is closed; it keeps the door closed and changes the floor to one more or one less, staying within 1 to 3.

    (b) A is a behavior: a full door cycle at floor 1, then a move to floor 2. C is a behavior too: the door starts closing, the sensor reopens it at state 5, and it opens. B breaks at the step from state 3 to state 4, where the floor changes while the door is opening. D breaks at its first step, from floor 1 to floor 3, which skips floor 2. E breaks before any step: its first state is floor 2, and the only initial state is floor 1 with the door closed. So 2 of the 5 are behaviors.

    (c) 12. There are 3 × 4 = 12 combinations of floor and door, and each can be reached: move to the floor with the door closed, then step the door to the value you want. The machine never halts, because every door value has at least one next door value, so every state has a next state. For an elevator that is correct: it should keep running. We checked this machine with TLC, which you install in Lecture 3; it found 12 distinct states.

    (d) An arrow from a state with the door open to a state on the next floor, still open. A move is allowed only when the door is closed, so no such arrow exists, and no behavior of this machine moves with the door open. If the report is true, the real elevator is not this state machine. Either the code does not follow the design, or the model left out something that matters, such as a maintenance override. The model doesn't tell you which, but it turns a vague report into a precise question to ask.

    Problem 2●●○Databases

    One state or a whole behavior? Claims about a transaction

    Draws on Why think above the code and States, steps, and behaviors.

    A relational database runs each transaction through a short lifecycle. After BEGIN the transaction is active. COMMIT makes its writes durable and visible to other sessions; ROLLBACK discards them. Postgres also has a failed status: if a statement inside a transaction block fails, the transaction becomes failed, every further statement is rejected with “current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block,” and, if no savepoints are in use, the only way out is to end the transaction, which rolls it back. This model leaves savepoints out.

    Model one transaction with two variables: status, one of active, failed, committed and aborted, and visible, yes when other sessions can see its writes. The figure shows the state machine.

    Your team wants to write down what the database promises. Someone collects these claims:

    1. The status is always one of active, failed, committed and aborted.
    2. If the status is committed, the writes are visible.
    3. If the writes are visible, the status is committed.
    4. Once a transaction is committed, its status never changes again.
    5. A transaction that was failed is never later committed.
    6. Every transaction eventually becomes committed or aborted.
    7. Fewer than 2% of transactions end aborted.
    1. Sort the claims into three groups: those you can judge by looking at each state of an execution on its own, those that need you to compare states across a whole behavior, and those that are not conditions on a single execution at all.
    2. Use the figure to explain why every behavior of this state machine satisfies claims 4 and 5.
    3. Which states halt? Is halting there a bug?
    4. Claim 7 matters to the operations team. Following the advice in Why think above the code, find a rule about single executions that sits underneath it, or explain why there isn't one.

    Why does every behavior of the figure satisfy claim 4?

    Hint

    Words like “once,” “never later” and “eventually” talk about time, so they need more than one state. A claim about a percentage of transactions talks about many executions; Why think above the code showed that kind with the 99% example.

    Solution

    (a) One state at a time: claims 1, 2 and 3. Each can be broken by a single state, for example status committed with visible no breaks claim 2, and status active with visible yes breaks claim 3. Whole behavior: claims 4, 5 and 6. No single state breaks claim 4; you need a committed state followed later by a different status. Claim 5 needs a failed state followed later by a committed one. Claim 6 needs the whole sequence, because it says something must happen eventually. Not a condition on one execution: claim 7. One execution can't show that 2% of transactions abort, so TLA+ can't check it.

    (b) A behavior moves only along arrows. No arrow leaves committed, so once a behavior reaches it, there is no later state with another status: claim 4 holds. For claim 5, the only arrow out of failed goes to aborted, and no arrow leaves aborted, so a behavior that passes through failed can never reach committed. The two claims are about behaviors, yet you proved them by looking at the arrows, one step at a time. That is the method this course builds on.

    (c) Committed and aborted have no next state, so the machine halts there. That is correct: the transaction is over. States, steps, and behaviors defined halting as reaching a state with no possible next state, and nothing about it is wrong in itself. Whether a stop is intended is something you decide about each system. Notice that active has no self-arrow either. This model doesn't say how long a transaction stays active, only which status comes next. Claim 6 is about something eventually happening, a kind of claim the course treats with care later on; this model leaves the question open.

    (d) A per-execution rule underneath claim 7 might be “a transaction aborts only after an error or an explicit ROLLBACK.” In this model that holds, because every arrow into aborted is labelled with one of them. The percentage itself depends on how often clients send errors and rollbacks, which is a statistic about the workload. It belongs in monitoring, not in the model.

    Problem 3●●○Design systems

    Choose the variables for a design-system Button

    Draws on How to study this course, Why think above the code and States, steps, and behaviors.

    Your design system's Button is used for every asynchronous action in the product: Save, Pay, Send invite. The page sets its disabled prop and can change it at any time. Its onClick handler returns a promise. While the promise is pending, the button shows a spinner. When the promise resolves, it shows a check mark for two seconds and then returns to its normal look. When it rejects, it shows a red outline, and the user can click again to retry. Its styles also have hover and pressed colours and a 150 ms fade between looks.

    A support ticket says a customer on a slow train connection double-clicked Pay and was charged twice. Before anyone changes code, the team wants a model of what the Button does. The figure shows the phases as one designer describes them.

    1. A teammate proposes four variables: phase (idle, loading, success or error), disabled (yes or no), hovered (yes or no) and spinnerVisible (yes or no). Which do you keep? For each one you drop, say whether it is redundant (its value is fixed by the others) or irrelevant to what a click can do. Where does the fade go?
    2. The teammate's model has 4 × 2 × 2 × 2 combinations of values. How many of them describe a screen the component can never show, given that the spinner is visible exactly when the phase is loading?
    3. With the variables you kept, suppose a second click while loading does start a second request. Write the step it causes. Can your model tell that state apart from the state before the click? If not, add the variable you need, and state “never two requests in flight” as a condition on a single state.
    4. Write one behavior, as a list of states, in which the page disables the button while a request is loading. What should happen when the response arrives?

    Hint

    States, steps, and behaviors dropped isLoading from the login screen because it was derived from the phase. Do the same test here for each variable: is it determined by the others, and does it change what can happen next? For (c), draw the dashed loop in the figure as a step between two states and compare the two states' values.

    Solution

    (a) Keep phase and disabled. disabled must stay because the page changes it independently of the phase, at any moment, including while loading. Drop spinnerVisible as redundant: it is just “phase is loading,” like isLoading in States, steps, and behaviors. Drop hovered as irrelevant: hover changes a colour, but no rule about clicks or requests depends on it. The pressed colour and the fade are irrelevant for the same reason, and they are also details of timing and rendering below the level of this model. If a future design made hover matter, for example a tooltip that blocks the click, you would add it back.

    (b) 16. There are 32 combinations. For each choice of phase, disabled and hovered, one of the two values of spinnerVisible matches the phase and the other doesn't. Keeping a redundant variable doubles the number of combinations and makes half of them impossible, which is a good reason to leave it out.

    (c) With only phase and disabled, the second click would be a step from (loading, no) to (loading, no). The two states are equal, so the model can't see the second request at all, and the double charge is invisible. Add inflight, the number of requests started and not yet finished. The click is then a step from (loading, no, 1) to (loading, no, 2), and the requirement is “in every state, inflight is 0 or 1.” That condition looks at one state, and the bad behavior idle, loading 1, loading 2 breaks it in its third state. This is the general lesson: if a requirement talks about something, the state must contain it. You now have three variables. The next problem set turns this model into formulas.

    (d) One such behavior: (idle, no, 0), (loading, no, 1), (loading, yes, 1), (success, yes, 0), (idle, yes, 0). Disabling stops new clicks; it doesn't cancel a request that has already been sent, so the response still arrives and the phase still changes. Whether a disabled button should show the check mark is a design decision. The model forces you to make it.

    Keep the upload example from How to study this course in mind. Even a Button that ignores clicks while loading can't prevent a double charge by itself: if the reply is lost and the user reloads and pays again, the server needs a way to recognise the repeat. The model of the Button shows what the component can promise and what it can't.

    Problem 4●●●CI/CD

    Two deploys, twenty interleavings, one stale release

    Synthesis. Draws on How to study this course, Why think above the code and States, steps, and behaviors.

    Your team's CI/CD pipeline deploys a service on every merge to the main branch. Each pipeline run does three steps, in order:

    1. test: run the test suite;
    2. read: read the version currently live from the deploy registry;
    3. write: if its own version is newer than the one it read, set the live version to its own.

    The check in step 3 exists so that an old build never replaces a newer one. Two merges land a minute apart: run A builds version 41, run B builds version 42, and version 40 is live. The team has an end-to-end test that starts two pipelines a minute apart and checks that 42 ends up live. It has passed 1,000 times in a row. The figure shows the order of steps it produces every time.

    Model the pair of runs as one state machine. Each numbered step of either run is one step of the machine. Each run does its own steps in order, but the two runs' steps can interleave, meaning they can mix in any order.

    1. Choose the variables. Each run needs its own control state, like pc in States, steps, and behaviors, and something else that the read step must leave behind for the write step.
    2. How many different interleavings of the six steps are there?
    3. In how many of them is 41 live after both runs finish? Describe exactly which interleavings they are.
    4. Write one bad behavior as a sequence of states. Then explain, using the two routes in Why think above the code, why 1,000 passing runs of the end-to-end test didn't find it.
    5. Write a prediction-notebook entry for the claim “after both runs finish, the newest version is live,” in the three lines How to study this course suggests. Is the claim a condition on a single execution?

    Hint

    Write an interleaving as a string such as AABBBA, where the k-th A is run A's k-th step. For (c), ask when A's write can change the live version to 41 at all, and what A must have read for its check to pass.

    Solution

    (a) Five variables: live, the live version; pcA and pcB, each saying which step that run does next (test, read, write or done); and readA and readB, the version each run read. The read values are easy to forget, but the write step's check uses them, so they are part of the state. Initially live is 40 and both runs are at test.

    (b) 20. Each run's steps stay in order, so an interleaving is fixed by choosing which 3 of the 6 positions hold A's steps, and there are 20 such choices.

    (c) 6. For 41 to end up live, A's write must change the live version, so A must have read something older than 41, which means 40. And nothing may change it afterwards, so B's write must come before A's write. If B's write came before A's read, A would read 42 and do nothing. So B's write falls between A's read and A's write, and A's write is last. That makes the last two steps B's write then A's write. The first four steps, A's test and read and B's test and read, can come in any order that keeps each run's steps in order: 6 ways, namely AABB, ABAB, ABBA, BAAB, BABA and BBAA. So 6 of the 20 interleavings are bad. We checked this with a small TLA+ model of the two runs: TLC finds a state where both runs are done and 41 is live.

    (d) The diagram shows ABABBA. Each column is a state, and each move to the next column is one step. In state 4 A has read 40, and B then reads 40 too. B's check passes and it writes 42. A's check compares 41 with the stale 40 it read, passes, and replaces 42 with 41. Every step did what its code says; the error is in the design, the gap between reading and writing. The end-to-end test takes the top route in the diagram of Why think above the code: it finds the error only if the timing happens to produce it. With A a minute ahead, A reads and writes seconds apart while B is still running its tests, so the test produces the interleaving in the first figure every time. A bad interleaving needs B to finish its read and write inside that short gap, for example when A's runner stalls between the two steps. That happens rarely in testing and eventually in production. The state machine contains all 20 interleavings equally, so a model checker doesn't depend on timing: TLC found a bad one in our model on its first run.

    (e) Claim: after both runs finish, the newest version is live. Suspected breaking path: the newer run reads and writes between the older run's read and write. Evidence needed: whether the registry can do the comparison and the write as one step, so that no other run's step can fall between them. Yes, the claim is a condition on a single execution: look at the last state of one behavior and check which version is live. That is the kind of property TLA+ checks.

    Lecture 2: State machines in TLA+

    The next-state relation is a formula, not a command.

    lesson 3 ended with an English description of the tiny program's state machine. It is neither precise nor practical. Rewriting it as math gives you something that is simply true or false for each pair of states.

    That is the destination, shown in the diagram: a formula, and two pairs of states it is true or false for. The rest of this lesson builds the formula and then explains these two verdicts.

    Why math?

    Asked what a specification language should look like, most programmers want something like their favorite programming language. TLA+ uses ordinary, simple math instead, and most programmers first find that a bad idea. The team behind the real-time operating system from lesson 2 started out biased toward a C-like language and saw the math as a hindrance. They ended up calling it a major benefit, because it forced them to reason more abstractly about the system.

    The initial values

    The initial values are i equal to 0 and pc equal to "start". The word “and” becomes a math operator, which is && in some programming languages and ∧ in math. In the ASCII you type, it is /\:

    (i = 0) /\ (pc = "start")

    Turning the relation into notation

    The English relation needs a handful of replacements:

    EnglishNotationNote
    current value of pcpcAn unprimed variable means its value in the current state.
    next value of pcpc'Read “pc prime”: its value in the next state.
    equals=Plain equality, as in 2 + 2 = 4.
    in\in“Is an element of,” written ∈ in math.
    {0, 1, ..., 1000}0..1000“...” is informal. .. is a precisely defined operator.
    the two lines of a then clause/\There is an implicit “and”: both must be true.
    no next valuesFALSESee below.

    The last row needs thought. “No next values” must become a formula that isn't true for any values of i, pc, i', and pc'. The simplest is the formula that is always false: FALSE. Most TLA+ keywords are uppercase, so the result, as you would type it in ASCII, is:

    IF pc = "start"
  THEN (i' \in 0..1000) /\
       (pc' = "middle")
  ELSE IF pc = "middle"
         THEN (i' = i + 1) /\
              (pc' = "done")
         ELSE FALSE

    How to read it

    The formula relates four values: i, pc, i', and pc'. It does not mean “if pc equals start, do the THEN part, otherwise do the ELSE part.” It means that if pc equals "start", the value of the whole formula equals the value of the THEN formula, and otherwise it equals the value of the ELSE formula.

    Use the tree to check the two pairs in the first diagram.

    The true pair: i = 17, pc = "start", i' = 534, pc' = "middle". The first test is true, so the tree goes to the first THEN formula. 534 is in 0..1000 and pc' is "middle", so both parts are true and the formula is true. You may have noticed that i = 17 with pc = "start" never occurs when the program runs, since i starts at 0. That doesn't matter here: the formula has a value for any four values you give it.

    The false pair: i = 534, pc = "middle", i' = 77, pc' = "done". The first test is false and the second is true, so the tree goes to the second THEN formula. pc' is right, but 77 does not equal 534 + 1, so the formula is false.

    Predict: what is the value for i = 5, pc = "middle", i' = 6, pc' = "middle"?

    False. The second test is true and i' = i + 1 holds, but pc' = "done" does not. An “and” needs both parts.

    Predict: what is the value for i = 43, pc = "done", i' = 44, pc' = "done"?

    False. Both tests are false, so the formula equals its last ELSE, which is FALSE. Any values of i' and pc' give the same answer when pc is "done", and that is what “no next values” means here.

    How many next states?

    Since the formula is just true or false for each pair, you can ask, for a given current state, how many next states make it true.

    In the diagram, the start state has 1001, and that is how someNumber() has been described. Nobody says how the number is chosen, only that i' is in the set. The middle state has exactly one. The done state has none, and that is how a state machine halts. Nondeterminism and termination need no special machinery, since both are just the shape of a formula.

    In this formula, what does the final ELSE FALSE do?

    You now have the complete description as two formulas: the initial-state formula and the next-state formula. There is a nicer way to write the second one, which comes next.

    While you watch

    This lesson covers Lecture 2 up to “The Complete Mathematical Description.” lesson 6 covers the rest, starting at “A nicer way to write the next-state formula.”

    • Look for: the slides that replace one English phrase at a time. The formula gets its shape from that sequence of small substitutions.
    • Pause before each of the two evaluated examples and work out the value yourself. The false example is the one to get right.
    • The lecture also shows the pretty-printed form, with ∧ and ∈, next to the ASCII. Both are the same formula. This course prints ASCII because it is what you type.
    • This lesson adds the decision tree and the count of next states.

    Lecture 2: State machines in TLA+

    List the cases instead of nesting them.

    The IF formula from lesson 5 works, but it won't scale. Using “or” and “and” as bulleted lists turns the same formula into a tree you can read at a glance, and that form is how nearly every spec in this course is written.

    From IF to “or”

    Call the two THEN formulas A and B. The IF formula is true in exactly two cases: pc = "start" and A are both true, or pc = "middle" and B are both true. So the same formula can be written with “or,” which is || in some programming languages, ∨ in math, and \/ in ASCII. The final FALSE is no longer needed, because when pc is "done" neither case holds.

    ((pc = "start")  /\ A)
\/ ((pc = "middle") /\ B)

    Now put A and B back, drop the parentheses that no longer help, and use the form TLA+ provides for lists. An extra /\ in front of the first item turns the items into a bulleted list, with a line per item. The list ends at the first token to the left of its bullets, so no closing parenthesis is needed. \/ works the same way:

    Next == \/ /\ pc = "start"
           /\ i' \in 0..1000
           /\ pc' = "middle"
        \/ /\ pc = "middle"
           /\ i' = i + 1
           /\ pc' = "done"

    This is what the tree at the top of the lesson shows. The outer \/ column is the root, with one branch for each case. Each /\ column is a node that requires all its lines. Indentation carries the structure, and widely separated matching parentheses are gone.

    The vocabulary so far

    ASCIIRead it asTrue when
    P /\ QP and QBoth are true. Such a formula is a conjunction.
    P \/ QP or QAt least one is true, possibly both.
    ~Pnot PP is false.
    P => QP implies QP is false, or Q is true.
    v'next value of vNot a truth value: it lets a formula talk about the next state.
    =equalsThe two sides have the same value.
    ==is defined to beGives a name to a formula.

    The lecture needs only /\ and \/. ~ and => complete the set you need before lesson 15, which adds quantifiers.

    It is still a formula

    The formula may look like commands, but it isn't. The order of lines carries no meaning, because \/ and /\ are commutative, meaning order makes no difference: swapping the two cases, or moving pc' = "middle" to the top of its list, yields an equivalent formula. The = means equality as in 2 + 2 = 4, while C's = means assignment, which isn't so simple.

    The C code may look simpler because it is familiar, but compare the two on what someNumber() stands for. In the formula, nondeterminism takes a single line: i' \in 0..1000. Common programming languages were not designed to express this. We need it because we can't predict the order in which things happen in a real system, and in the math it is easy.

    The complete spec

    A spec lives in a module. The module name matches the file name. EXTENDS Integers imports arithmetic operators such as + and ... VARIABLES declares the variables. Identifiers must be defined or declared before they are used. Init and Next are only conventional names, but use them.

    --------------- MODULE SimpleProgram ---------------
EXTENDS Integers
VARIABLES i, pc

Init == (pc = "start") /\ (i = 0)

Next == \/ /\ pc = "start"
           /\ i' \in 0..1000
           /\ pc' = "middle"
        \/ /\ pc = "middle"
           /\ i' = i + 1
           /\ pc' = "done"
====================================================

    You will run this module yourself in lesson 9.

    Decomposing with definitions

    A real next-state formula can run to hundreds or thousands of lines. Math has a simple way to split it up: definitions. This spec doesn't need splitting, but you can see the method by naming the two cases. You could call them Fred and Mary, but descriptive names are better:

    Pick == /\ pc = "start"
        /\ i' \in 0..1000
        /\ pc' = "middle"

Add1 == /\ pc = "middle"
        /\ i' = i + 1
        /\ pc' = "done"

Next == Pick \/ Add1

    This Next is completely equivalent to the earlier one. We checked with TLC, and all three versions, the IF form, the bulleted form, and this one, produce the same 2003 states. The diagram shows why the names help: they name kinds of step, so you can label every arrow in the state graph.

    Worked rules for a shopping cart

    A cart can be submitted only when it contains items, the customer has accepted the terms, and the goods are in stock. Define the rule before attaching any step to it, to separate “may this happen?” from “what changes if it does?” Here, items, termsAccepted, and inStock are variables.

    Eligible == /\ items > 0
            /\ termsAccepted

CanCheckout == /\ Eligible
               /\ inStock

    In the diagram, the cart has items and the terms are accepted, so Eligible is true. But inStock is false, so CanCheckout is false.

    The implication trap

    P => Q is true whenever P is false. Take the module this cart comes from, where ordered records that checkout happened, and the claim ordered => termsAccepted. It holds in the checked model, but note what that claim would do in a model where checkout never happens: it would hold there too, since ordered is always false. A check that passes because its left side never occurs is called vacuous. An implication doesn't make Q happen, and it doesn't show that P ever happens.

    Predict: with items = 2, termsAccepted = FALSE, inStock = TRUE, what are Eligible and CanCheckout?

    Both false. Eligible fails on the terms, and CanCheckout includes Eligible. Being in stock can't make up for a missing requirement in a conjunction.

    You swap the two \/ cases of Next and reorder the lines in each /\ list. What changes?

    While you watch

    This lesson covers Lecture 2 from “A nicer way to write the next-state formula” to the end. lesson 5 covers the earlier part.

    • Look for: the slide where the extra /\ appears and the parentheses vanish, and the rule for where a bulleted list ends.
    • Pause when the lecture compares the formula with the C code. Decide for yourself what each one says about someNumber().
    • Lamport says he prefers simple examples studied carefully over complex ones skimmed. Before moving on, rewrite Next from memory.
    • This lesson adds the tree view, ~ and =>, and the cart. Quantifiers come in lesson 15.

    Reference: Specifying Systems, chapter 1.

    Lecture 2: State machines in TLA+

    Problem set 2: write the next-state formula.

    These problems practice Lecture 2: an initial-state formula, a next-state formula with primed variables, evaluating a formula on a pair of states, and splitting Next into named cases joined by \/. They draw on From a program to a state machine and Writing Init and Next with logic, and on the models you built in Problem set 1.

    You run TLC in the next chapter, so for now check your formulas by evaluating them on pairs of states, as From a program to a state machine did. One consequence of reading Next as a formula matters in every problem. A case that says nothing about x' is true whatever the next value of x is, so it allows x to change arbitrarily. Until a later lesson gives a shorthand, write x' = x for each variable a case leaves alone. Some solutions also count states: a state that occurs in at least one behavior is called reachable.

    Problem 1●○○Networking

    An HTTP client's retry loop as Init and Next

    Draws on States, steps, and behaviors, From a program to a state machine and Writing Init and Next with logic.

    A mobile app's HTTP client makes up to three attempts to send a request, stopping at the first success. Simplified, its code is:

    bool ok = false;
int attempts = 0;
void fetchWithRetry()
{ while (!ok && attempts < 3) {   // test
    ok = send();                   // send
    attempts = attempts + 1;       // count
  }
}                                  // done

    send() returns true on success and false on failure, and any call can do either, just as someNumber() in States, steps, and behaviors could return any number. Model the program the way that lesson modeled the tiny C program, with three variables: attempts, ok, and pc, which is "test", "send", "count" or "done" according to which statement runs next. Testing the loop condition is one step. The figure shows the control flow you are writing down.

    1. Write Init.
    2. Write Next as Test \/ Exit \/ Send \/ Count, defining each case as a bulleted /\ list, one case per arrow in the figure. Each case must say what the next value of every variable is.
    3. Evaluate your Next on two pairs of states. First: attempts = 2, ok = FALSE, pc = "count" and attempts' = 3, ok' = FALSE, pc' = "test". Second: attempts = 3, ok = FALSE, pc = "test" and attempts' = 3, ok' = FALSE, pc' = "send".
    4. List every state in which the program can be when pc = "done".
    Which formula is the guard of Exit?

    Hint

    In Send, the next value of ok is TRUE or FALSE, and you have no set to put it in. “Or” is \/, so write two equalities joined by it, in parentheses. Exit applies when the while condition is false: negate it with ~.

    Solution 
    ------------------ MODULE PSl2_Retry ------------------
EXTENDS Integers
VARIABLES attempts, ok, pc

Init == /\ attempts = 0
        /\ ok = FALSE
        /\ pc = "test"

Test == /\ pc = "test"
        /\ ~ok
        /\ attempts < 3
        /\ pc' = "send"
        /\ attempts' = attempts
        /\ ok' = ok

Exit == /\ pc = "test"
        /\ (ok \/ ~(attempts < 3))
        /\ pc' = "done"
        /\ attempts' = attempts
        /\ ok' = ok

Send == /\ pc = "send"
        /\ (ok' = TRUE \/ ok' = FALSE)
        /\ pc' = "count"
        /\ attempts' = attempts

Count == /\ pc = "count"
         /\ attempts' = attempts + 1
         /\ pc' = "test"
         /\ ok' = ok

Next == Test \/ Exit \/ Send \/ Count

BudgetOK == attempts \in 0..3
DoneOK == pc = "done" => (ok \/ attempts = 3)
=======================================================

    The four cases match the four arrows. Send is where the nondeterminism lives: (ok' = TRUE \/ ok' = FALSE) plays the role that i' \in 0..1000 played for someNumber(). Exit's guard is the negation of the while condition, so in every "test" state exactly one of Test and Exit applies. BudgetOK and DoneOK are two claims about every reachable state that you will check with TLC in the next problem set.

    (c) The first pair satisfies Next through Count: pc is "count", 3 = 2 + 1, pc' is "test" and ok keeps its value. The second pair doesn't. Its pc is "test", so only Test or Exit could be true. Test needs attempts < 3, which is false, and Exit needs pc' = "done". The client has used its three attempts and can't send again.

    (d) 4 states: ok = TRUE with attempts equal to 1, 2 or 3, and ok = FALSE with attempts = 3. In each, no case of Next applies, so the program halts, as From a program to a state machine's tiny program did when pc was "done". We checked this module with TLC, which you install in the next chapter. It has 20 reachable states, and BudgetOK and DoneOK are true in all of them.

    Problem 2●●○Algorithms

    Binary search with git bisect: which steps does Next allow?

    Draws on From a program to a state machine and Writing Init and Next with logic.

    A performance regression slipped into one of 16 commits, numbered 1 to 16 in order. Commit 16 is known to be bad, the commit before commit 1 is known to be good, and once a commit is bad every later one is bad too. git bisect finds the first bad commit by binary search: you test a commit in the suspect range, mark it good or bad, and the range shrinks. Git checks out the middle commit for you, but you can test any commit you like, for example when the middle one doesn't build, and mark it with git bisect good <rev> or git bisect bad <rev>.

    This module models only the suspect range: the first bad commit is somewhere in lo..hi.

    ------------------ MODULE PSl2_Bisect ------------------
EXTENDS Integers
VARIABLES lo, hi

Init == /\ lo = 1
        /\ hi = 16

MarkBad == /\ lo < hi
           /\ hi' \in lo..(hi - 1)
           /\ lo' = lo

MarkGood == /\ lo < hi
            /\ lo' \in (lo + 1)..hi
            /\ hi' = hi

Next == MarkBad \/ MarkGood
========================================================

    In MarkBad, the tested commit is hi' and it was bad, so the range now ends there. In MarkGood, the tested commit is lo' - 1 and it was good, so the range now starts just after it. Neither case says which commit to test. Binary search tests the middle; this Next allows every choice, so it describes binary search along with every other way of bisecting. The figure shows one session.

    Pairlo, hilo', hi'
    a1, 161, 8
    b1, 169, 16
    c9, 169, 16
    d5, 86, 7
    e7, 77, 8
    f5, 85, 5
    g3, 44, 4
    1. For each pair in the table, decide whether it satisfies Next, and if it does, through which case. Say in words what the step means for the person bisecting.
    2. How many next states does the initial state have?
    3. An implementer writes MarkBad with hi' \in lo..hi instead. Which pair in the table does this version allow that the original doesn't? What does that step mean, and why could a program built on it loop forever?
    4. Next has no case that applies when lo = hi. What does it mean when the state machine halts?

    Hint

    Each case is a conjunction, so every line must be true. In MarkBad, lo must stay the same and hi' must be in lo..(hi - 1), which you can write out for the given lo and hi. A pair satisfies Next if either case is true.

    Solution

    (a) a: MarkBad; commit 8 was bad, so the first bad commit is in 1..8. b: MarkGood; commit 8 was good, so it is in 9..16. c: no. MarkBad needs hi' in 9..15 and MarkGood needs lo' in 10..16, and here neither end moved. d: no; both cases keep one end fixed, and here both moved. e: no; the guard lo < hi is false, since the answer is already known. f: MarkBad; commit 5 was bad, so commit 5 is the answer. g: MarkGood; commit 3 was good, so commit 4 is the answer. Four pairs satisfy Next.

    (b) 30: 15 from MarkBad, one for each hi' in 1..15, and 15 from MarkGood, one for each lo' in 2..16. Binary search would choose one of these 30; the spec describes them all, as i' \in 0..1000 described every value someNumber() might return.

    (c) Pair c. With hi' \in lo..hi, MarkBad allows hi' = hi: “test commit 16, find it bad.” Commit 16 was already known to be bad, so the step teaches nothing and leaves the state unchanged. It is the classic off-by-one in binary search. Code that computes the middle as (lo + hi + 1) / 2, rounding up, and sets hi = mid when the test is bad, picks mid = hi once lo + 1 = hi. If that commit is bad, nothing changes, and the loop repeats the same step forever. We ran both modules through TLC: each reaches the same 136 states, every range with 1 ≤ lo ≤ hi ≤ 16. The bug adds no new state, only a step from a state to itself, so you can't find it by asking which states are reachable. You find it by reading Next.

    (d) The state machine halts when lo = hi: the range holds one commit, which is the first bad one. Here halting is the intended end, as it was for the tiny program in From a program to a state machine.

    Problem 3●●○Databases

    Find the step a buggy connection pool allows

    Draws on From a program to a state machine and Writing Init and Next with logic.

    A web service talks to Postgres through a connection pool capped at 3 connections, because each Postgres connection is a separate server process and costs memory. The pool starts empty and opens connections only when needed. It counts idle connections (open, not in use) and busy ones (checked out by a request). Four things can happen:

    • Open: if fewer than 3 connections exist, the pool opens one; it starts idle.
    • Acquire: a request checks out an idle connection.
    • Release: a request returns its connection, which becomes idle.
    • Evict: the pool closes an idle connection that has been unused for too long.

    The figure shows part of the state graph the authors have in mind. A teammate wrote this module. PoolOK is the pool's promise: no count is negative, and there are never more than Max connections.

    ----------------- MODULE PSl2_PoolBug -----------------
EXTENDS Integers
VARIABLES idle, busy

Max == 3

Init == /\ idle = 0
        /\ busy = 0

Open    == /\ idle + busy < Max
           /\ idle' = idle + 1
           /\ busy' = busy

Acquire == /\ busy < Max
           /\ idle' = idle - 1
           /\ busy' = busy + 1

Release == /\ busy > 0
           /\ busy' = busy - 1
           /\ idle' = idle + 1

Evict   == /\ idle > 0
           /\ idle' = idle - 1
           /\ busy' = busy

Next == Open \/ Acquire \/ Release \/ Evict

PoolOK == /\ idle \in 0..Max
          /\ busy \in 0..Max
          /\ idle + busy \in 0..Max
=======================================================
    1. For each of the four cases, name its guard and say which variables change.
    2. Find a pair of states that satisfies this Next, where the first state satisfies PoolOK and the second doesn't. Start from the initial state.
    3. Which case is wrong? Describe the real bug it stands for in the pool's code, and fix the case.
    4. With your fix, argue case by case that if a state satisfies PoolOK, every next state allowed by Next does too.
    Which case is wrong?

    Hint

    A guard should test exactly what the change needs. A case that subtracts 1 from a count needs that count to be above 0 first. Compare each case's guard with the variable it decreases.

    Solution

    (a) Open: guard idle + busy < Max; idle goes up by 1. Acquire: guard busy < Max; idle goes down and busy up. Release: guard busy > 0; busy goes down and idle up. Evict: guard idle > 0; idle goes down.

    (b) idle = 0, busy = 0 and idle' = -1, busy' = 1. The initial state satisfies PoolOK. Acquire's guard busy < Max is true, so Acquire, and therefore Next, is true for this pair, and the second state has idle = -1. We ran the module through TLC: it reports PoolOK violated by exactly this two-state behavior.

    (c) Acquire checks whether the pool has room (busy < Max) when it should check whether an idle connection exists. In code, this is a pool that tests “not at capacity” before taking from the idle list, and on an empty list gets nothing, or a connection another request already holds. The fix:

    Acquire == /\ idle > 0
           /\ idle' = idle - 1
           /\ busy' = busy + 1

    When the pool is empty, a request now has to wait for Open first, as in the figure, where the only arrow out of the initial state is Open.

    (d) Suppose a state satisfies PoolOK. Open raises idle + busy by 1, but only when it is below Max, so it stays in 0..Max. Acquire and Release move one connection between the counts, so the total is unchanged, and each decreases a count only when its guard says that count is above 0. Evict lowers idle only when it is above 0, and lowers the total. So every case keeps every conjunct of PoolOK true. Arguing one step at a time like this, without listing behaviors, is how you will later show that a claim holds in every reachable state. TLC agrees: with the fix it finds 10 reachable states and no violation.

    Problem 4●●●Design systems

    The design-system Button as Init and Next

    Synthesis. Draws on Problem set 1 (the Button problem), How to study this course, States, steps, and behaviors, From a program to a state machine and Writing Init and Next with logic.

    In Problem set 1, problem 3, you chose variables for the design system's Button: phase, disabled, and inflight, the number of requests started and not yet finished. Now write its spec. The rules, as the design system's documentation should state them:

    • Initially the phase is idle and no request is in flight. The page may have set disabled either way.
    • Click: possible only when the button isn't disabled and the phase is idle or error. It starts a request and the phase becomes loading.
    • Resolve and Reject: the request of a loading button finishes, and the phase becomes success or error.
    • Reset: from success, back to idle (the two seconds are left out).
    • Toggle: the page flips disabled, at any time.

    The figure shows four sequences of states that people on the team wrote down while discussing the double-charge ticket.

    1. Write a module with Init and Next == Click \/ Resolve \/ Reject \/ Reset \/ Toggle. Use TRUE and FALSE for disabled.
    2. Check every step of A to D against your Next, and each first state against Init. For each sequence that is not a behavior, name the first step that fails and the case that would have to change to allow it.
    3. Define OneRequest (inflight is 0 or 1) and LoadingOK (if the phase is loading, exactly one request is in flight). Explain what LoadingOK would tell you in a model where Click could never happen.
    4. Sequence C is the double charge. Write the change to Click that would make C a behavior.

    Hint

    “Either way” in Init is a disjunction: (disabled = TRUE \/ disabled = FALSE). “Idle or error” in Click's guard is one too. Remember x' = x for every variable a case leaves alone: Toggle leaves two of them alone.

    Solution 
    ----------------- MODULE PSl2_Button -----------------
EXTENDS Integers
VARIABLES phase, disabled, inflight

Init == /\ phase = "idle"
        /\ (disabled = TRUE \/ disabled = FALSE)
        /\ inflight = 0

Click   == /\ ~disabled
           /\ (phase = "idle" \/ phase = "error")
           /\ phase' = "loading"
           /\ inflight' = inflight + 1
           /\ disabled' = disabled

Resolve == /\ phase = "loading"
           /\ phase' = "success"
           /\ inflight' = inflight - 1
           /\ disabled' = disabled

Reject  == /\ phase = "loading"
           /\ phase' = "error"
           /\ inflight' = inflight - 1
           /\ disabled' = disabled

Reset   == /\ phase = "success"
           /\ phase' = "idle"
           /\ inflight' = inflight
           /\ disabled' = disabled

Toggle  == /\ disabled' = ~disabled
           /\ phase' = phase
           /\ inflight' = inflight

Next == Click \/ Resolve \/ Reject \/ Reset \/ Toggle

OneRequest == inflight \in 0..1
LoadingOK  == (phase = "loading") => (inflight = 1)
======================================================

    (b) A is a behavior: Click, Reject, Click again from error (the retry), then Resolve. B is a behavior: Click, then Toggle while loading, then Resolve, then Reset. Nothing in Resolve or Reset depends on disabled, so the response still lands, as you predicted in Problem set 1. C fails at step 2: the phase stays loading while inflight goes from 1 to 2, which only Click could do, and Click requires idle or error. D fails at step 3: success to loading is again a Click, from a phase Click doesn't allow. To allow D you would change Click's guard; whether a click on the check mark should start a new request is a design decision the documentation must state.

    (c) Both definitions are in the module. LoadingOK is an implication, and Writing Init and Next with logic warned about it: if Click could never happen, the phase would never be loading, so LoadingOK would be true in every state without saying anything. Here it isn't vacuous, because A and B pass through loading states. We checked the module with TLC: it has 8 reachable states, 4 phases times 2 values of disabled, with inflight fixed by the phase, and OneRequest and LoadingOK hold in all of them.

    (d) Replace the phase condition so that it allows loading, for example /\ ~(phase = "success"). Then C's second step satisfies Click. We ran that variant through TLC as well: OneRequest fails in a three-state behavior, idle with 0, loading with 1, loading with 2, which is exactly C. The spec turns the support ticket into a one-line difference in a guard, and the design-system documentation can now say precisely what the Button guarantees: at most one request per Button at a time. As in Problem set 1, the server still has to recognise a repeated payment that arrives some other way, such as a retry after a lost reply.

    Lecture 3: Resources and tools

    Know where help lives, then install something that runs TLC.

    You can now read a complete module, so it is time to run one. This lesson gets the tools onto your machine and shows where to look when you are stuck. lesson 9 then uses them.

    The diagram is what you are installing. Your module goes to a parser, which checks that the text is legal TLA+. TLC then reads the module along with a model, a small set of choices about what to run: which formulas are Init and Next, and what to check. The red boxes are the two places errors come from, and they tell you different things. If the parser complains, TLC never ran.

    Where to look

    Lecture 3 opens with a tour of resources. Most of them start from the TLA+ home page, and most of the documentation is in PDF.

    • The Summary of TLA+ is a cheat sheet. Lamport says to download and print it, and that is good advice.
    • Specifying Systems, the TLA+ book, is a useful reference. It was written before the Toolbox existed, so it says nothing about the Toolbox.
    • The TLA+ Google group is where to find out what is happening in the community and to ask other users for help.

    The diagram gives the order for a problem: the install page's “If Something Goes Wrong” section first, then the group.

    Installing the tools

    The lecture installs the Toolbox, the IDE for creating specs and running tools on them. The steps it describes are to install Java if you don't have it, download a zip file and extract it, and install LaTeX, which the pretty-printer needs. The pretty-printer produces the typeset form you see on the slides, with ∧ and ∈. If you follow along in the videos, the Toolbox page has the current instructions.

    The current option is the official TLA+ VS Code extension. Follow its setup guide. You can also skip editors altogether: download tla2tools.jar from the official releases and run TLC from a terminal. The core tools currently require Java 11 or later.

    OptionWhere the model livesUse it when
    ToolboxForms on the Model Overview pageYou want your screen to match the lectures.
    VS Code extensionA .cfg file next to the moduleYou already work in VS Code.
    Command lineA .cfg file next to the moduleYou want repeatable runs. This course prints its commands in this form.

    Whichever you choose, the lectures' ideas are the same. When the Toolbox has you click “Add” under Invariants, a .cfg file has a line for it, as you'll see in the next few lessons. Here is the command form, for a module and config named Name:

    java -cp tla2tools.jar tlc2.TLC -config Name.cfg Name

    TLC checks a finite model. It can run many useful specs, but it is not a theorem prover, and a model whose states never run out, such as an unbounded counter, can't be fully searched. Keep the models small; every spec in the first lectures has few states.

    Predict: your run stopped because the machine ran out of memory, with no violation so far. Did your check pass?

    No. The search is incomplete, so you can report only that nothing was found in the part it reached. Shrink the model or add resources and rerun. “No error” counts only when exploration finished.

    The rest of the toolkit

    • Help pages. In the lecture, Lamport asks you to read the Toolbox's Getting Started help before the next video and to browse the other sections when you can. If you use the extension, read its documentation the same way.
    • TLAPS, from lesson 2, checks formal proofs written in TLA+. It can check proofs of real algorithms, but few engineers will use it. lesson 43 comes back to proof.
    • Unicode display. Most engineers prefer the ASCII form of their specs; Lamport says he uses the pretty-printed form only for publication. The lecture says a Unicode option was planned for those who want to see ∈ while editing. Check the current documentation for your editor, because the lecture can't tell you what exists today.
    The parser reports an error at line 12. What do you know about your spec's behavior?

    While you watch

    • Look for: where each resource sits on the home page. Website details may have changed since the recording, so search if a link has moved.
    • The lecture tells you to stop and install. Do it, either the Toolbox or the extension. Do not go on without a working TLC.

    Lecture 3: Resources and tools

    Run a spec, meet deadlock, then write your own.

    With TLC installed from lesson 8, you run the tiny program's spec exactly as the lecture does. TLC reports an error, and understanding why teaches you what TLC can and can't know. Then you write a small spec of your own and break it.

    Run SimpleProgram

    Create SimpleProgram.tla with the module from lesson 6, and next to it a config file, SimpleProgram.cfg. A config file is the text form of a model. These two lines name the formulas TLC should treat as the initial-state and next-state formulas:

    INIT Init
NEXT Next

    In the Toolbox, you create a model from the TLC Model Checker menu instead, and it fills these in for you. Run TLC. It stops with an error:

    Error: Deadlock reached.
Error: The behavior up to this point is:
State 1: <Initial predicate>
/\ i = 0
/\ pc = "start"
State 2: ...
/\ i = 0
/\ pc = "middle"
State 3: ...
/\ i = 1
/\ pc = "done"

    That output is a behavior, printed one state at a time. Which number it picks at State 2 can differ between runs. Follow it through the diagram: start, then middle, then done. The dashed red arrow is what TLC noticed: from pc = "done", no next state exists.

    Deadlock and termination

    Lamport's distinction is simple. Deadlock means execution stopped when it wasn't supposed to. Termination means it stopped when it was supposed to. Here the program is supposed to stop, so this is termination. But nothing in the spec says whether an execution should stop, so TLC can't tell them apart, and since most systems should not stop, it reports any stop as deadlock.

    When stopping is intended, turn the check off. In the Toolbox, it is the Deadlock checkbox on the Model Overview page. In a config file, add a line:

    CHECK_DEADLOCK FALSE

    Now TLC reports Model checking completed. No error has been found. and 2003 distinct states found. The diagram accounts for that number: 1 start state, 1001 middle states, and 1001 done states. Disable the check only when you know stopping is correct. Otherwise you are switching off a real alarm.

    Why does TLC report deadlock on a correct program?

    Your turn: a counter

    Write a spec without a C program to start from. This one describes a counter that starts at 0 and increments up to a bound. Save it as Counter.tla, since the module name and file name must match.

    ---------------- MODULE Counter ----------------
EXTENDS Integers
VARIABLE x

Max == 3

Init == x = 0

Next == /\ x < Max
        /\ x' = x + 1

Safe == x =< Max
================================================

    In ASCII, “less than or equal” is =<. The first line of Next has no prime, so it is a condition on the current state alone. A step can happen only when it is true. Such a condition is called a guard, and lesson 12 says more about it. Compare it with pc = "start" in SimpleProgram, which plays the same role.

    Safe is a formula you claim is always true. A state that occurs in some behavior is reachable, and a formula true in every reachable state is an invariant. A claimed invariant goes in the config, and TLC tests it in every state it finds:

    INIT Init
NEXT Next
INVARIANT Safe
CHECK_DEADLOCK FALSE

    TLC finishes with no error and 4 distinct states. As with SimpleProgram, the deadlock check has to be off, or TLC stops at x = 3, because this counter is designed to stop there.

    Explore the bounded model

    Changing Max in the lab is like editing the definition Max == 3. “Explore all states” does a breadth-first search of a tiny JavaScript model: all states one step away, then two, and so on. It is not TLC. Now tick the box to weaken the guard, and predict what the search will find before you press the button.

    The diagram compares the two guards. We ran the broken one, with x =< Max, through real TLC. It reports Invariant Safe is violated with a 5-state behavior, 0 through 4, which matches the bottom row. You can reason backward too: to reach the bad state x = 4, the predecessor must be x = 3, and the step must be allowed there. So the guard is the culprit, and you found that without reading a long trace.

    Retrieve: what are the two formulas TLC needs, and what is a third thing you can ask it to check?

    The initial-state formula and the next-state formula. On top of those you can name invariants. You can also decide whether a stop counts as deadlock. Later lessons add more, but this is the whole model so far.

    Transfer: a retry budget

    A file-upload client allows at most three attempts. Let attempts count those already started, not those remaining.

    Next == /\ attempts < 3
        /\ attempts' = attempts + 1

BudgetOK == attempts \in 0..3

    In the diagram, the guard reads the old value. At 2 it allows a step to 3, and at 3 it blocks the dashed arrow. That is why “allow three attempts” uses a strict comparison on attempts already used. Running this module through TLC gives 4 distinct states and no error. Writing the sentence out as a trace saves you from guessing whether the comparison should include equality.

    Now imagine resetting attempts to zero whenever the user taps Retry. Each session still passes this check, but one logical upload can now trigger unlimited attempts. If the requirement concerns one logical request, the count must belong to that request, and every way of resetting it must appear in Next.

    Exercise: instead count attempts remaining, initially 3. What would you write?
