    remaining > 0 /\ remaining' = remaining - 1 and the invariant remaining \in 0..3. Decide whether the first attempt consumes the budget. The variable's name can't settle that for you.

    While you watch

    This lesson covers the hands-on middle of Lecture 3: “Creating a spec,” “The pretty-printer,” and “Running TLC.” Those parts are a live demonstration, so do each thing as he does it and stop the video whenever you need to.

    • Look for: what TLC's results page shows, and the point where it reports deadlock.
    • Pause before the “Why does TLC report deadlock?” slide and try to answer the question yourself.
    • If you use the extension or the command line, your screen will differ. The results are the same: a deadlock error with the same kind of trace.
    • This lesson adds the config-file form, the count of 2003, and the counter, which is your first spec not taken from the lecture. The lecture introduces invariants in the next video, and lesson 13 uses them on a bigger model.

    Lecture 3: Resources and tools

    Problem set 3: run TLC and read what it tells you.

    These problems practice Lecture 3: writing a module and its config file, running TLC, reading “distinct states found,” checking invariants, reading an error trace backward, and telling deadlock from termination. They draw on The tools and where to learn more and Your first spec through TLC, and the last problem checks a model from Problem set 2.

    Every module here has been run through TLC, and every number in a checked answer is one TLC printed. Commands are in the command-line form from The tools and where to learn more, java -cp tla2tools.jar tlc2.TLC -config Name.cfg Name. In the Toolbox you enter the same things on the model's Overview page, and the VS Code extension reads the same .cfg file. Remember that the module name must match the file name.

    Problem 1●○○API gateway

    Does a fixed-window rate limiter keep its promise?

    Draws on Writing Init and Next with logic and Your first spec through TLC.

    An API gateway lets each client make 3 requests per minute. It uses a fixed window: a counter per client that resets when each minute starts on the clock, and a request is rejected when the counter is already at the limit. The product team has told the backend team: “a client never gets more than 3 requests through in any 60 seconds.”

    To see time inside a minute, the model splits each minute into two halves. half is 1 or 2, the half of the current minute it is now. a1 and a2 count the requests accepted in the first and second half of the current minute, and p2 counts those accepted in the second half of the previous minute. Here is the module without its accept steps:

    ----------------- MODULE PSl3_RateLimit -----------------
EXTENDS Integers
VARIABLES half, a1, a2, p2

Limit == 3

Init == /\ half = 1
        /\ a1 = 0
        /\ a2 = 0
        /\ p2 = 0

Tick == \/ /\ half = 1
           /\ half' = 2
           /\ a1' = a1
           /\ a2' = a2
           /\ p2' = p2
        \/ /\ half = 2
           /\ half' = 1
           /\ p2' = a2
           /\ a1' = 0
           /\ a2' = 0

\* AcceptFirst, AcceptSecond and Next: yours to write
=========================================================

    Tick moves time forward half a minute. At the end of a minute it saves the second half's count in p2 and resets the window. A rejected request changes nothing, so it needs no case. The figure shows which spans of time the counters cover.

    1. Write AcceptFirst and AcceptSecond: in the half it is now, a request is accepted when the window's total a1 + a2 is below Limit. Then define Next.
    2. Define WindowOK, “the current window never holds more than Limit accepted requests.” Save the module as PSl3_RateLimit.tla with a config PSl3_RateLimit.cfg containing INIT Init, NEXT Next and INVARIANT WindowOK, and run TLC. How many distinct states does it find? Why does it report no deadlock?
    3. The promise talks about any 60 seconds, including the span from the middle of the previous minute to the middle of this one. Define SlidingOK == p2 + a1 =< Limit, add a second INVARIANT line, and run again. Retell TLC's trace as a story with clock times.
    4. Is the gateway wrong, or the promise? Say what the fixed window really guarantees.

    Hint

    Each accept case needs three kinds of line: the guard (which half it is, and room in the window), the counter that grows, and x' = x for the other three variables. For the deadlock question, look for a case whose guard is true in every state.

    Solution 
    ----------------- MODULE PSl3_RateLimit -----------------
EXTENDS Integers
VARIABLES half, a1, a2, p2

Limit == 3

Init == /\ half = 1
        /\ a1 = 0
        /\ a2 = 0
        /\ p2 = 0

AcceptFirst  == /\ half = 1
                /\ a1 + a2 < Limit
                /\ a1' = a1 + 1
                /\ a2' = a2
                /\ p2' = p2
                /\ half' = half

AcceptSecond == /\ half = 2
                /\ a1 + a2 < Limit
                /\ a2' = a2 + 1
                /\ a1' = a1
                /\ p2' = p2
                /\ half' = half

Tick == \/ /\ half = 1
           /\ half' = 2
           /\ a1' = a1
           /\ a2' = a2
           /\ p2' = p2
        \/ /\ half = 2
           /\ half' = 1
           /\ p2' = a2
           /\ a1' = 0
           /\ a2' = 0

Next == AcceptFirst \/ AcceptSecond \/ Tick

WindowOK  == a1 + a2 =< Limit
SlidingOK == p2 + a1 =< Limit
=========================================================

    (b) TLC reports Model checking completed. No error has been found. and 56 distinct states found. You can account for the number: when half = 1, a2 is 0 and a1 and p2 each range over 0..3, giving 16 states; when half = 2, there are 10 pairs of a1 and a2 with a sum of at most 3, and 4 values of p2, giving 40. There is no deadlock because Tick has a case for each value of half, so some step is always possible. That is right for a model of time.

    (c) TLC reports Invariant SlidingOK is violated. with this 7-state trace:

    As a story: from 10:00:00 to 10:00:30 the client is quiet. At 10:00:40 and 10:00:50 it sends two requests, both accepted. At 10:01:00 the window resets. At 10:01:05 and 10:01:10 it sends two more, both accepted, since the new window is empty. That is 4 requests in 30 seconds, against a promise of 3 per 60 seconds. Four accepts and two ticks can't be done in fewer steps, so 7 states is the shortest possible behavior.

    (d) The gateway does what a fixed window does: at most Limit accepted requests per clock minute, which is WindowOK. Near a boundary a client can get up to twice the limit in a short span: 3 just before the minute and 3 just after. To see it, change the bound in SlidingOK to 5; TLC then prints a 9-state behavior ending with p2 = 3 and a1 = 3. Either the promise should say “per clock minute,” or the gateway needs an algorithm that tracks a moving 60 seconds, such as a sliding-window log of request times. Which to choose is a product decision; the model makes the difference precise.

    Problem 2●●○Concurrency

    Read a TLC trace backward to find a double release

    Draws on Writing Init and Next with logic and Your first spec through TLC.

    A thumbnail service runs image-resize jobs, at most 2 at a time because each job needs a lot of memory. A semaphore with 2 permits enforces this: a worker takes a permit before starting a job and gives it back when the job ends. The code that ends a job calls release() in its error handler, and again in its finally block, which also runs after an error. Java's java.util.concurrent.Semaphore, like many semaphores, does not require a release to match an earlier acquire, so an extra release simply adds a permit.

    The model counts running jobs and free permits; which worker runs which job is left out.

    ------------------ MODULE PSl3_Workers ------------------
EXTENDS Integers
VARIABLES running, permits

MaxJobs == 2

Init == /\ running = 0
        /\ permits = MaxJobs

Start  == /\ permits > 0
          /\ permits' = permits - 1
          /\ running' = running + 1

Finish == /\ running > 0
          /\ running' = running - 1
          /\ permits' = permits + 1

Fail   == /\ running > 0
          /\ running' = running - 1
          /\ permits' = permits + 2

Next == Start \/ Finish \/ Fail

AtMostTwo == running =< MaxJobs
=========================================================

    A teammate ran TLC with INIT Init, NEXT Next and INVARIANT AtMostTwo and got:

    Error: Invariant AtMostTwo is violated.
Error: The behavior up to this point is:
State 1: <Initial predicate>
/\ permits = 2
/\ running = 0

State 2: <Start line 10, col 11 to line 12, col 35 of module PSl3_Workers>
/\ permits = 1
/\ running = 1

State 3: <Start line 10, col 11 to line 12, col 35 of module PSl3_Workers>
/\ permits = 0
/\ running = 2

State 4: <Fail line 18, col 11 to line 20, col 35 of module PSl3_Workers>
/\ permits = 2
/\ running = 1

State 5: <Start line 10, col 11 to line 12, col 35 of module PSl3_Workers>
/\ permits = 1
/\ running = 2

State 6: <Start line 10, col 11 to line 12, col 35 of module PSl3_Workers>
/\ permits = 0
/\ running = 3
    1. Which state violates AtMostTwo? Now read the trace backward, as Your first spec through TLC did for the counter: for each step, ask whether the step itself was allowed and sensible. Which step first went wrong?
    2. Find a formula over permits and running that is true in states 1 to 3 and false from state 4 on. Why is it a sharper invariant for this design than AtMostTwo?
    3. Fix Fail, add your formula as a second invariant, and run TLC. How many distinct states does it find?
    4. If you run TLC with several worker threads, using its -workers option, it may print a different trace of the same length. Is that a different bug?
    Which case of Next is wrong?

    Hint

    The state where the invariant fails is where the damage shows, not where it was done. Steps 4 to 5 and 5 to 6 are Start, and each had a permit available. So where did the extra permit come from?

    Solution

    (a) State 6, with 3 jobs running. Going backward: step 5 to 6 is Start with permits = 1, so its guard was true. Step 4 to 5 is Start with 2 permits, also allowed. But state 4 is already wrong: one job is running and 2 permits are free, so the semaphore will admit 2 more. Step 3 to 4 is Fail: one job ended and 2 permits came back. That is the error handler and the finally block each calling release().

    (b) permits + running = MaxJobs. Each permit is either free or held by a running job, and this formula says exactly that. It fails at state 4, the moment the bookkeeping goes wrong, while AtMostTwo fails only two steps later when the extra permit happens to be used. An invariant that states why the design works catches errors closer to their cause.

    (c) With Fail releasing one permit, TLC reports no error and 3 distinct states. Deadlock checking was on, and none was reported: from every state, either a job can start or one can end.

    ------------------ MODULE PSl3_WorkersFixed ------------------
EXTENDS Integers
VARIABLES running, permits

MaxJobs == 2

Init == /\ running = 0
        /\ permits = MaxJobs

Start  == /\ permits > 0
          /\ permits' = permits - 1
          /\ running' = running + 1

Finish == /\ running > 0
          /\ running' = running - 1
          /\ permits' = permits + 1

Fail   == /\ running > 0
          /\ running' = running - 1
          /\ permits' = permits + 1

Next == Start \/ Finish \/ Fail

AtMostTwo == running =< MaxJobs
PermitsOK == permits + running = MaxJobs
=========================================================

    Fail and Finish are now the same formula. Keep both if you want the trace to say which way a job ended. In the code, the fix is to release only in the finally block.

    (d) No. With one worker thread, TLC searches in a fixed order and printed the trace above. With several threads, our run printed Start, Fail, Start, Start, Start: the extra permit appears after the first job fails instead of the second. Both traces have 6 states and the same Fail step, so they show the same bug. Read any trace for the step that breaks the design's reasoning, not for its exact order.

    Problem 3●●○Algorithms

    Euclid's algorithm: termination, deadlock, and a loop that never ends

    Draws on From a program to a state machine, Writing Init and Next with logic and Your first spec through TLC.

    Euclid's algorithm finds the greatest common divisor (GCD) of two positive integers, the largest number that divides both. In its original form it uses only subtraction: while the two numbers differ, subtract the smaller from the larger. When they are equal, that value is the GCD of the numbers you started with. The GCD of 34 and 21 is 1.

    ------------------ MODULE PSl3_Euclid ------------------
EXTENDS Integers
VARIABLES x, y

M == 34
N == 21

Init == /\ x = M
        /\ y = N

SubY == /\ y < x
        /\ x' = x - y
        /\ y' = y

SubX == /\ x < y
        /\ y' = y - x
        /\ x' = x

Next == SubY \/ SubX

Positive == x > 0 /\ y > 0
Answer   == (x = y) => (x = 1)
========================================================

    As with Max in Your first spec through TLC, the inputs are definitions; to try other inputs, edit them.

    1. Run TLC with a config containing only INIT Init and NEXT Next. It reports a deadlock. Look at the last state of the trace: is it a deadlock or a termination, in Lamport's sense?
    2. Add CHECK_DEADLOCK FALSE, INVARIANT Positive and INVARIANT Answer, and run again. How many distinct states does TLC find? Why is it the same as the number of states in the trace from (a)?
    3. Answer is an implication. In which states is it true only because x = y is false? If a bug kept the algorithm from ever reaching x = y, what would TLC report about Answer?
    4. A colleague changes SubY's guard to y =< x, “to handle equal numbers.” Predict, then run TLC twice: once with INVARIANT Positive (and deadlock checking on), and once with only INIT and NEXT. Explain each result.
    5. Change the inputs to 12 and 18, and Answer to x = 6. Run again.
    What does TLC's deadlock report in (a) mean?

    Hint

    For (d), work out by hand what happens at x = 1, y = 1 with the new guard, and then at the state after it. Which case applies there, and what next state does it produce?

    Solution

    (a) TLC prints Error: Deadlock reached. and a trace of 8 states, shortened here:

    State 1: <Initial predicate>
/\ x = 34
/\ y = 21
State 2: <SubY line 11, col 9 to line 13, col 17 of module PSl3_Euclid>
/\ x = 13
/\ y = 21
...
State 8: <SubY line 11, col 9 to line 13, col 17 of module PSl3_Euclid>
/\ x = 1
/\ y = 1

    It is termination: the algorithm is supposed to stop when x = y, and x holds the GCD, 1. As Your first spec through TLC explained, nothing in the spec says stopping is intended, so TLC reports it. Here the report is even useful: it shows you where and how the algorithm stops.

    (b) No error, and 8 distinct states. The guards y < x and x < y can't both be true, so every state has at most one next state. With one initial state, the reachable states form a single path, drawn above, and the deadlock trace in (a) was that whole path.

    (c) In states 1 to 7, where x and y differ, Answer is true because its left side is false. It says something only in state 8. If a bug kept the algorithm from ever reaching x = y, Answer would be true in every state and TLC would report no error: this is the vacuous check from Writing Init and Next with logic. Answer says the result is right if the algorithm stops; it does not say the algorithm stops.

    (d) With INVARIANT Positive, TLC reports Invariant Positive is violated in state 9, x = 0, y = 1: at x = 1, y = 1, the guard 1 =< 1 is true, so SubY subtracts. With only INIT and NEXT, TLC reports Model checking completed. No error has been found. and 9 distinct states. There is no deadlock now, because at x = 0, y = 1, SubX applies (0 < 1) and produces y' = 1 - 0 = 1, the same state again. The algorithm subtracts zero forever. So “no deadlock” here is bad news: the deadlock check finds states with no next step, and this bug creates a state whose only next step goes nowhere. Saying “the algorithm eventually stops” is a different kind of property, which the course reaches later. For now, notice that Positive caught the bug, and the deadlock report you got in (a) was a sign of health.

    (e) The path is (12, 18), (12, 6), (6, 6): TLC finds 3 distinct states and no error, and Answer holds with 6.

    Problem 4●●●Networking

    Model-check the retry loop, then lose a response

    Synthesis. Draws on Problem set 2 (the retry loop), How to study this course, States, steps, and behaviors, Writing Init and Next with logic and Your first spec through TLC.

    In Problem set 2, problem 1, you wrote the HTTP client's retry loop as Init and Next. Now check it, and then make it more realistic.

    1. Save the solution module of that problem as PSl2_Retry.tla, with a config containing INIT Init and NEXT Next, and run TLC. It reports a deadlock. Read the last state of the trace: deadlock or termination?
    2. CHECK_DEADLOCK FALSE would silence this, but it would also silence a real hang added later. Instead, add a case to Next that allows the finished program to take a step that changes nothing: 
      Done == /\ pc = "done"
        /\ pc' = pc
        /\ attempts' = attempts
        /\ ok' = ok
      Run again with deadlock checking on and with INVARIANT BudgetOK and INVARIANT DoneOK. How many distinct states does TLC find, and what does a deadlock report now mean?
    3. Now model the network. send() becomes a request followed by a wait for the response, which may be "ok", "err", or lost. Add a variable resp, initially "none", add resp' = resp to every case that doesn't set it, and replace Send with these three cases: 
      Send == /\ pc = "send"
        /\ (resp' = "ok" \/ resp' = "err" \/ resp' = "lost")
        /\ pc' = "wait"
        /\ attempts' = attempts
        /\ ok' = ok

GotOk  == /\ pc = "wait"
          /\ resp = "ok"
          /\ ok' = TRUE
          /\ pc' = "count"
          /\ attempts' = attempts
          /\ resp' = resp

GotErr == /\ pc = "wait"
          /\ resp = "err"
          /\ ok' = FALSE
          /\ pc' = "count"
          /\ attempts' = attempts
          /\ resp' = resp
      Run with deadlock checking on and INVARIANT BudgetOK. What does TLC report?
    4. Is that report a real deadlock? Which line of real client code does it correspond to? Add a case Timeout that fixes it, and run again.
    5. The timeout counts a lost response as a failure and tries again. Using the upload example in How to study this course, say what can go wrong on the server. What did this model leave out that hides the problem?

    Hint

    For (c), look at the figure: from wait, which values of resp have a case that leaves? For (d), a hang that the user sees as a spinner forever is exactly what an HTTP timeout is for.

    Solution

    (a) In our run the trace ended in the state attempts = 1, ok = TRUE, pc = "done": the first send succeeded and the loop exited. Your trace may end in another of the four done states. Either way, it is termination: the program is supposed to stop there.

    (b) No error, and 20 distinct states, the same 20 as in Problem set 2. Done adds a step from each finished state to itself, so no state is left without a next state, and no new states appear. Now a deadlock report can only mean the program got stuck somewhere other than "done". This is a common way to separate the two: say in the spec that stopping at the end is intended, and leave deadlock checking on for everything else.

    (c) TLC reports a deadlock with a 3-state trace:

    Error: Deadlock reached.
Error: The behavior up to this point is:
State 1: <Initial predicate>
/\ resp = "none"
/\ attempts = 0
/\ ok = FALSE
/\ pc = "test"

State 2: <Test line 10, col 9 to line 16, col 23 of module PSl3_RetryNet>
/\ resp = "none"
/\ attempts = 0
/\ ok = FALSE
/\ pc = "send"

State 3: <Send line 25, col 9 to line 29, col 19 of module PSl3_RetryNet>
/\ resp = "lost"
/\ attempts = 0
/\ ok = FALSE
/\ pc = "wait"

    In the figure, the red box marks these states: pc is "wait", the response was lost, and no case of Next applies.

    (d) Yes, this one is real. The client waits for a response that will never come, which in code is an HTTP call with no timeout. Some popular HTTP libraries wait indefinitely unless you set a timeout, so this hang happens in production: the user sees a spinner forever. The fix is a case for the lost response:

    ----------------- MODULE PSl3_RetryNetFixed -----------------
EXTENDS Integers
VARIABLES attempts, ok, pc, resp

Init == /\ attempts = 0
        /\ ok = FALSE
        /\ pc = "test"
        /\ resp = "none"

Test == /\ pc = "test"
        /\ ~ok
        /\ attempts < 3
        /\ pc' = "send"
        /\ attempts' = attempts
        /\ ok' = ok
        /\ resp' = resp

Exit == /\ pc = "test"
        /\ (ok \/ ~(attempts < 3))
        /\ pc' = "done"
        /\ attempts' = attempts
        /\ ok' = ok
        /\ resp' = resp

Send == /\ pc = "send"
        /\ (resp' = "ok" \/ resp' = "err" \/ resp' = "lost")
        /\ pc' = "wait"
        /\ attempts' = attempts
        /\ ok' = ok

GotOk  == /\ pc = "wait"
          /\ resp = "ok"
          /\ ok' = TRUE
          /\ pc' = "count"
          /\ attempts' = attempts
          /\ resp' = resp

GotErr == /\ pc = "wait"
          /\ resp = "err"
          /\ ok' = FALSE
          /\ pc' = "count"
          /\ attempts' = attempts
          /\ resp' = resp

Timeout == /\ pc = "wait"
           /\ resp = "lost"
           /\ ok' = FALSE
           /\ pc' = "count"
           /\ attempts' = attempts
           /\ resp' = resp

Count == /\ pc = "count"
         /\ attempts' = attempts + 1
         /\ pc' = "test"
         /\ ok' = ok
         /\ resp' = resp

Done == /\ pc = "done"
        /\ pc' = pc
        /\ attempts' = attempts
        /\ ok' = ok
        /\ resp' = resp

Next == Test \/ Exit \/ Send \/ GotOk \/ GotErr \/ Timeout \/ Count \/ Done

BudgetOK == attempts \in 0..3
========================================================

    TLC now reports no error and 38 distinct states, with deadlock checking on. That is evidence that the only place the client stops is "done", which you could not have learned with CHECK_DEADLOCK FALSE.

    (e) A lost response does not mean a lost request. In the upload example of How to study this course, the server committed the document and only the reply was lost; retrying created a second document. Here, a timeout after a request that the server did process leads to a second request, and if the request was “charge this card” or “create this order,” it happens twice. The model hides this because it has no server: it records only what the client sees. To check “at most one order per click,” the state would need the server's side too, such as the number of orders created, plus a way for the server to recognise a repeated request. Later lessons build that kind of model.

    Lecture 4: Die Hard

    Start a spec by writing one correct behavior.

    The counter in lesson 9 had one variable and one kind of step. Now for a real puzzle. To disarm a bomb, the heroes of the 1995 film Die Hard 3 must put exactly 4 gallons of water in a jug, and they have only a 3-gallon jug, a 5-gallon jug, and a faucet.

    The jugs have no markings, and it must be exactly 4 gallons, not 3.99 or 4.01. Before any formula, Lamport recommends the step in the diagram: write the start of one correct behavior, informally. Follow it from the left. They fill the small jug, pour it into the big one, fill the small jug again, and pour again. The big jug fills up and leaves 1 gallon in the small jug. Then they empty the big jug on the ground, and so on. It doesn't solve the puzzle. It isn't meant to.

    What one behavior teaches you

    That single behavior answers the two questions that begin every spec.

    What are the variables? small and big, the number of gallons in each jug.

    What is a step? Filling a jug is one step, with no state in between.

    The red states in the bottom row do not exist in this model. Real water passes through 1 and 2 gallons, of course, but that doesn't matter to the problem, and this is the simplest abstraction that does the job. There is a related choice: pouring 4 gallons straight into the big jug is physically possible, but they would need to be very lucky to get exactly 4. So the model allows only behaviors where they always know how much water each jug holds. Real specs are written for a purpose, usually to eliminate some particular kinds of error. Here, the kind that gets you blown up.

    Beginning the module

    ------------------------------ MODULE DieHard ------------------------------
EXTENDS Integers

VARIABLES small, big

TypeOK == /\ small \in 0..3
          /\ big   \in 0..5

Init == /\ big   = 0
        /\ small = 0

    TLA+ has no type declarations. Type correctness means that all variables have sensible values, and it is a good idea to define a formula that says so. Lamport calls it TypeOK. It helps a reader understand the spec, and TLC can check that it is always true. The definition isn't part of the spec: removing it changes nothing about which behaviors are allowed. Init says both jugs start empty.

    The next-state formula is a list of kinds of step

    The next-state formula describes all permitted steps. It is usually written as one formula or another, each allowing a different kind of step. The behavior above has three kinds of step, and two jugs give each of them two versions:

    Next == \/ FillSmall
        \/ FillBig
        \/ EmptySmall
        \/ EmptyBig
        \/ SmallToBig
        \/ BigToSmall

    Names must be defined before they are used, so the definitions of these six go above Next in the module. lesson 12 writes them. You already know enough of what they mean to explore.

    Every step in a behavior comes from this choice. In the diagram, the state with 3 gallons in each jug has six options. Four change the state. SmallToBig leads to small 1 and big 5, because only 2 gallons fit. FillSmall and BigToSmall are also allowed but change nothing, since the small jug is already full.

    Pour it yourself

    Save the heroes by hand. Each button is one line of Next. Each circle is a reachable state, labeled small,big; the green-ringed circles have big = 4. Dashed arrows show where a step could go from the current state, and solid ones show your path. Small dots mark combinations that can't be reached. This is a small JavaScript model of the rules, not TLC.

    Try to reach a green ring before reading on. Notice two things. Every circle you can reach has a jug that is empty or full, which is why the dots are in the middle of the grid. And you are doing by hand what TLC does in lesson 13.

    Predict: can the state with small 2 and big 2 ever occur?

    No. It is a dot in the lab. Each of the six kinds of step leaves at least one jug empty or full: filling and emptying do so directly, and a pour stops when the source is empty or the destination is full. Since small 2 and big 2 has neither jug empty or full, no step can produce it.

    What did writing one informal behavior give us?

    While you watch

    This lesson covers Lecture 4 up to the definition of Next. lesson 12 continues with FillSmall and the pours, and lesson 13 covers “Saving our heroes” to the end.

    • Look for: the struck-out partial fill, and the reason for ruling out the lucky pour. Both are abstraction decisions, and neither is forced by physics.
    • Pause when the informal behavior is complete. Extend it by hand for a few more steps before the lecture moves on.
    • This lesson adds the fan-out from one state and the stepping lab, which the lecture doesn't have. Use the lab between this video segment and the next.

    Lecture 4: Die Hard

    A step formula must describe the whole next state.

    lesson 11 left Next as six names. Writing their definitions exposes the most common beginner's mistake in TLA+, and it fixes what you need to say about every variable in every step.

    A formula like the six in Next, which relates a current state to a next state and describes one kind of step, is called an action. Start with FillSmall. Most people first write this:

    FillSmall == small' = 3
    Predict: why is that wrong? Decide before opening this. The diagram above is a clue.

    If you didn't see it, you are reading it as a command that sets small to 3. It is a formula, true for some steps and false for others. It is true for any step where small is 3 in the second state, whatever big does. In the diagram, that includes the two red arrows, where big becomes √7 or the string "abc".

    Frames: say what stays the same

    The correct definition also says big doesn't change:

    FillSmall == /\ small' = 3
             /\ big'   = big

FillBig == /\ big'   = 5
           /\ small' = small

    A line like big' = big is called a frame condition. Most engineers feel it shouldn't be needed. Lamport's answer is that “unchanged unless mentioned” would take you out of simple math and into the more complicated world of programming languages. In math, a formula that doesn't mention big' says nothing about it.

    TLC enforces this in practice. We removed the frame line and ran the spec:

    Error: Successor state is not completely specified by action FillSmall
of the next-state relation. The following variable is not defined: big.

    Keep the two facts separate. Mathematically, omission permits any value. In TLC, omission usually produces this error. In neither case does it preserve the old value.

    Exercise: write EmptySmall and EmptyBig.

    EmptySmall == /\ small' = 0 /\ big' = big and EmptyBig == /\ big' = 0 /\ small' = small, each written as a two-line bulleted list. Each one has a line for each variable.

    Pouring has two cases

    Now SmallToBig. There are two cases, and the behavior from lesson 11 contains both.

    In the top row of the diagram, the big jug has room for all the water in the small one, so all of it moves and the small jug is empty. In the bottom row there isn't enough room, so the big jug ends up full and some water stays behind. Which case applies depends only on the total, so an IF formula fits:

    SmallToBig == IF big + small =< 5
                THEN /\ big'   = big + small
                     /\ small' = 0
                ELSE ...

    Stop and solve this. Write the ELSE part of SmallToBig, and then all of BigToSmall. Write them down. As in the lecture, you will check your answer with TLC after saving the heroes, so the full definitions wait until lesson 13. You can test your arithmetic against the lab in lesson 11.

    All the lines in a list describe the same pair of states, so nothing happens first. In big' = big + small, both unprimed values are from the current state. This is what lets one step swap two values:

    With x = 2 and y = 9, what next state does x' = y /\ y' = x allow?

    Predict: does x' = x + 1 /\ x' = x + 2 increment x twice?

    No. No integer equals both x + 1 and x + 2, so no next state satisfies the formula and this action never happens. Conjunction combines conditions. It doesn't sequence assignments.

    Guards, and why the jugs have none

    You saw a guard in lesson 9: a line with no primes, which an action needs to be true of the current state. x < Max is one. An action is enabled in a state when some next state satisfies it, so a false guard disables the action.

    The jug actions have no guards. Every one of the six is enabled in every state, which is why the lab never greys out a button, and why TLC will never report deadlock for this spec. The IF in SmallToBig is not a guard, since it doesn't disable anything. It chooses between two descriptions of the next state, and both are possible to satisfy.

    The matrix is a mechanical check for the frame of every action: one row per action, one column per variable, no blanks. A blank cell is a question you haven't answered. A later lecture introduces UNCHANGED, a shorthand for frame lines, once specs have more variables. For now, write each one out.

    Worked action: sending a chat message

    A chat composer stores a draft, a count of pending messages, the last text sent, and the selected conversation. Sending should record the draft, clear it, and leave the selected conversation alone. /= means “not equal.”

    Send == /\ draft /= ""
        /\ pending' = pending + 1
        /\ lastSent' = draft
        /\ draft' = ""
        /\ selected' = selected

    The first line is a guard that rejects an empty draft. lastSent' = draft uses the old draft, even though the same action clears it, as the diagram shows. If you instead cleared the draft in one action and recorded it in a later one, the later action would see an empty draft unless you saved a copy. That model needs an extra variable. Where you draw the boundary of an action says whether capture and clearing are one indivisible operation or two visible steps.

    Predict: Send specifies draft' but says nothing about pending'. Is pending preserved?

    No. Nothing constrains its next value, and TLC would report that the successor state isn't completely specified, just as it did for FillSmall. Add the increment you want or an explicit pending' = pending.

    While you watch

    This lesson covers Lecture 4 from the definition of FillSmall through “Pouring between jugs.”

    • Look for: the three example steps that the wrong FillSmall allows. They are the three arrows in the first diagram.
    • Pause where the lecture says to figure out why the definition is wrong, and again where it asks you to finish the pours. Really do the second one on paper.
    • This lesson adds the frame matrix, guards, the swap, and the chat example. The lecture's own spec has no guards; you will see them in the transaction commit lecture too.

    Lecture 4: Die Hard

    Claim the puzzle is unsolvable, and TLC shows you the solution.

    You have the jugs' variables from lesson 11 and their actions from lesson 12. Now run them. The trick for saving the heroes is one line: tell TLC that the big jug never holds 4 gallons, and let it prove you wrong.

    Run the module

    Save the module as DieHard.tla. It contains complete definitions of SmallToBig and BigToSmall, so keep your own solutions from lesson 12 handy and don't study these until you have seen the error trace.

    The complete DieHard module (open to copy; contains the pour solutions) 
    ------------------------------ MODULE DieHard ------------------------------
EXTENDS Integers

VARIABLES small, big

TypeOK == /\ small \in 0..3
          /\ big   \in 0..5

Init == /\ big   = 0
        /\ small = 0

FillSmall == /\ small' = 3
             /\ big'   = big

FillBig == /\ big'   = 5
           /\ small' = small

EmptySmall == /\ small' = 0
              /\ big'   = big

EmptyBig == /\ big'   = 0
            /\ small' = small

SmallToBig == IF big + small =< 5
                THEN /\ big'   = big + small
                     /\ small' = 0
                ELSE /\ big'   = 5
                     /\ small' = small - (5 - big)

BigToSmall == IF big + small =< 3
                THEN /\ big'   = 0
                     /\ small' = big + small
                ELSE /\ big'   = small - (3 - big)
                     /\ small' = 3

Next == \/ FillSmall
        \/ FillBig
        \/ EmptySmall
        \/ EmptyBig
        \/ SmallToBig
        \/ BigToSmall

NotSolved == big /= 4
=============================================================================

    First run it with only INIT Init and NEXT Next in the config. TLC reports no error and 16 distinct states. No error means little here, because you asked it to check nothing. It shows that TLC could run the spec. The 16 are the filled cells in the grid above, the states reachable in some behavior, the same circles you saw in the lab.

    Next, check type correctness by adding INVARIANT TypeOK. Remember from lesson 9 that an invariant must hold in every reachable state. Still no error, so every filled cell has values in range.

    Saving our heroes

    The 4 gallons must be in the big jug, since the small one holds only 3. So claim that it never happens. “Not equal” is /= or # in ASCII.

    INIT Init
NEXT Next
INVARIANT TypeOK
INVARIANT NotSolved

    In the Toolbox, you can type big /= 4 directly under Invariants. A config file needs a named formula, which is why the module defines NotSolved. Run it, and TLC reports Invariant NotSolved is violated, along with this behavior:

    That is the answer, in 7 states: fill the big jug; pour into the small one, leaving 2; empty the small one; pour the 2 across; fill the big jug again; and top up the small one, which holds 2 and takes exactly 1. That leaves 4. Each state in TLC's output names its action, as in State 3: <BigToSmall ...>, which is the label above each arrow in the diagram. In the Toolbox, double-clicking an action in the trace jumps to the part of Next that allowed it.

    Run with one worker for the shortest trace. With -workers 1, TLC searches in strict breadth-first order, and we got the lecture's 7-state trace in each run. With several workers, states may be processed out of order. One of our runs reported a longer, 9-state trace ending at small 0, big 4. That trace is valid, but it isn't the shortest.

    Predict: there are two red cells in the grid. Why does the lecture's trace end at small 3, big 4 and not small 0, big 4?

    TLC searches breadth-first, so with one worker it finds a nearest violation first. Small 3, big 4 is 7 states from the start. Small 0, big 4 is further: at best you empty the small jug after reaching small 3, big 4, which takes 8 states. The 9-state trace in the callout got there by a different route.

    Reading SmallToBig and BigToSmall

    Now compare your definitions. Look at the ELSE of SmallToBig. The big jug is filled, so the amount poured is 5 - big, and that is what comes out of the small jug. Someone new to TLA+ might say this is wrong, since big was set to 5 on the line above. But you know better from lesson 6: /\ is commutative, and all these values of big are from the current state.

    A warning follows. = is commutative too, so small' = 0 and 0 = small' are equivalent formulas, and the specs are equivalent. TLAPS treats them the same, but TLC does not. We ran the flipped version, and it stopped with:

    In evaluation, the identifier small is either undefined or not an operator.

    TLC can almost always handle the ways engineers naturally write specs, and later lectures explain why. For now, follow the lecture's rule: use a primed variable v' only in formulas of the form v' = ... or v' \in ..., where the right side has no primes.

    Finding your own mistakes

    The diagram shows what catches what, from left to right. We made each of the lecture's mistakes and ran it:

    MistakeCaught byWhat you see
    Delete the + in big + smallParserA parse error: Encountered "small" at line 24, column 22
    Misspell an identifier as biggParserUnknown operator: `bigg'.
    Change 5 to "5" in the comparisonTLC, while runningThe second argument of <= should be an integer, with the behavior so far
    Claim big /= 4TLC, checking invariantsThe trace above

    Execution errors come with a position, so go there first; you can read the rest of the report later if you are curious.

    Check your definitions

    Comment out the module's two pour definitions by placing (* and *) around them, and add your own. Fix what the parser finds, then run TLC. Your definitions are probably correct if TLC finds no execution errors, no violation of TypeOK, and a violation of big /= 4. To be sure, remove NotSolved and run again with only TypeOK, since the search stops at the first violation. If it all passes, try writing the definitions a different way. You learn most from your mistakes.

    With no invariants listed, TLC reports no error and 16 states. What does that show?

    A good experiment can fail. The lecture's test expects a violation of big /= 4. A check you expect to fail shows that your setup reaches the interesting states. If a deliberately false claim passes, investigate the setup before you trust anything else.

    Transfer: ask for a path through a product

    The trick works on any “can this happen?” question. Here is the whole cart module from lesson 6, now with a Checkout action that you can read after lesson 12. It starts with both unknowns free: \in lets a variable begin with either value of a set, so there are 4 initial states.

    ---------------- MODULE Cart ----------------
EXTENDS Integers
VARIABLES items, termsAccepted, inStock, ordered

Init == /\ items = 2
        /\ termsAccepted \in {TRUE, FALSE}
        /\ inStock \in {TRUE, FALSE}
        /\ ordered = FALSE

Eligible == /\ items > 0
            /\ termsAccepted

CanCheckout == /\ Eligible
               /\ inStock

Checkout == /\ CanCheckout
            /\ ~ordered
            /\ ordered' = TRUE
            /\ items' = items
            /\ termsAccepted' = termsAccepted
            /\ inStock' = inStock

Next == Checkout

OrderOK == ordered => termsAccepted
NeverOrdered == ~ordered
=============================================

    With INVARIANT OrderOK and the deadlock check off, TLC finds no error in 5 distinct states. Now claim INVARIANT NeverOrdered. TLC reports a violation with a 2-state trace: a cart with the terms accepted and goods in stock, then Checkout. You now have a concrete example of a successful order, and evidence that the implication in that lesson wasn't vacuous. To reach a harder state, you state that it is unreachable and let TLC produce the steps.

    While you watch

    This lesson covers Lecture 4 from “Saving our heroes” to the end.

    • Look for: the Toolbox's error window, and the double-click that jumps from a trace step to its formula.
    • Pause before the trace appears and predict its length, using your experience from the lab.
    • The lecture types the spec into the Toolbox. If you use a config file, each click corresponds to a line as shown above.
    • This lesson adds the grid, the note on worker count, and the transfer to the cart. The lecture then leaves Hollywood for transaction commit, in lesson 15 and lesson 16.

    Lecture 4: Die Hard

    Problem set 4: write the steps, then let TLC search.

    These problems practice what Lecture 4 taught: actions with guards and complete frames, and the trick of claiming that a goal is never reached so that TLC hands you the steps. They also lean on running TLC and reading its results, from lesson 9, and the last one reuses Euclid's algorithm from Problem set 3.

    Write every frame line out in full: UNCHANGED arrives with Lecture 6. When a problem asks for the length of a trace, run TLC with one worker (-workers 1), as lesson 13 recommends, so that its breadth-first search returns a shortest one.

    Problem 1●○○Design systems

    The modal that leaves the page frozen

    Draws on Actions, guards, and frames, Die Hard: make TLC solve it and Your first spec through TLC.

    Your design system ships a Modal dialog component. While it is open, it keeps keyboard focus inside the dialog and locks page scrolling, so the page behind it doesn't move. It closes in two ways: the close button, or the Escape key. A bug report arrives: after someone closes a dialog with Escape, the page no longer scrolls. You write the component as a state machine with three variables. CloseButton was written carefully. PressEscape was added later by copying its first three lines.

    ------------------------------ MODULE PSl4_Modal ------------------------------
VARIABLES open, focus, scrollLocked

TypeOK == /\ open \in {TRUE, FALSE}
          /\ focus \in {"page", "dialog"}
          /\ scrollLocked \in {TRUE, FALSE}

Init == /\ open = FALSE
        /\ focus = "page"
        /\ scrollLocked = FALSE

OpenDialog == /\ ~open
              /\ open' = TRUE
              /\ focus' = "dialog"
              /\ scrollLocked' = TRUE

CloseButton == /\ open
               /\ open' = FALSE
               /\ focus' = "page"
               /\ scrollLocked' = FALSE

PressEscape == /\ open
               /\ open' = FALSE
               /\ focus' = "page"

Next == OpenDialog \/ CloseButton \/ PressEscape

LockMatches == scrollLocked = open
FocusInside == open => focus = "dialog"
=============================================================================

    The config lists INIT Init, NEXT Next, and the invariants TypeOK, LockMatches and FocusInside.

    1. Before running anything: as a formula, what does PressEscape say about scrollLocked'? Which next states does it allow? The dashed arrow down in the diagram is your clue.
    2. Run TLC. What does it report, and after which action?
    3. A teammate makes the error go away by adding /\ scrollLocked' = scrollLocked to PressEscape. Run TLC again. What does it report now, and how long is the trace?
    4. Write the correct PressEscape. Then draw the frame matrix from lesson 12 for the three actions: one row per action, one column per variable, and the value each action gives each variable. How many distinct states does TLC find with your fix?
    What does TLC report for the module as written?

    Hint

    A frame line is a decision about what a step does, not boilerplate. Ask what pressing Escape should do to the scroll lock, then compare with what CloseButton does.

    Solution

    (a) PressEscape doesn't mention scrollLocked', so as a formula it allows any value at all: TRUE, FALSE, 42, or "abc". It doesn't keep the old value.

    (b) TLC stops with the error you met in lesson 12:

    Error: Successor state is not completely specified by action PressEscape
of the next-state relation. The following variable is not defined: scrollLocked.
State 1: <Initial predicate>      open = FALSE, focus = "page",   scrollLocked = FALSE
State 2: <OpenDialog ...>         open = TRUE,  focus = "dialog", scrollLocked = TRUE
State 3: <PressEscape ...>        open = FALSE, focus = "page",   scrollLocked = null

    (We put each state on one line.) The null is how TLC prints the value it couldn't determine.

    (c) With the copied frame line, the spec is complete and wrong. TLC reports Invariant LockMatches is violated with a 3-state trace: the initial state, OpenDialog, then PressEscape, which ends with the dialog closed and scrollLocked = TRUE. That is the red box in the diagram, and it is exactly the bug report. The error in (b) was TLC pointing at the problem. Silencing it with the first frame line that parses turned it into the bug.

    (d) Escape should do what the close button does:

    PressEscape == /\ open
               /\ open' = FALSE
               /\ focus' = "page"
               /\ scrollLocked' = FALSE
    Actionopen'focus'scrollLocked'
    OpenDialogTRUE"dialog"TRUE
    CloseButtonFALSE"page"FALSE
    PressEscapeFALSE"page"FALSE

    With this fix (module PSl4_ModalFixed), TLC finds no error and 2 distinct states: closed and open. Two of the three cells in the bug's row of the matrix were right. The blank one was where the bug lived. In component code the same gap appears when one close path calls the cleanup and another doesn't. Many teams avoid it by routing every way of closing through one function. In the spec, the matrix makes the gap visible.

    Problem 2●●○Databases

    Rename a column without downtime

    Draws on Actions, guards, and frames, Die Hard: make TLC solve it and Your first spec through TLC.

    Your team must rename users.email to users.email_address in a production Postgres database. A plain rename would break every running server that still queries email. So you use the expand and contract pattern: add the new column, deploy app v2 that writes both columns, backfill old rows, deploy v3 that reads the new column, deploy v4 that writes only the new column, and drop the old column. Each step has a precondition in the runbook. In the model below, each precondition is a guard.

    missing means some row has no value in email_address. It starts TRUE: no existing row has one. SignUp is a user registering while v1 is live, which writes only email.

    The module (open to copy) 
    --------------------------- MODULE PSl4_Migration ---------------------------
EXTENDS Integers

VARIABLES schema,      \* columns that exist: "old", "both", or "new"
          app,         \* deployed app version, 1..4
          backfilled,  \* the backfill job has finished
          missing      \* some row has no value in email_address

TypeOK == /\ schema \in {"old", "both", "new"}
          /\ app \in 1..4
          /\ backfilled \in {TRUE, FALSE}
          /\ missing \in {TRUE, FALSE}

Init == /\ schema = "old"
        /\ app = 1
        /\ backfilled = FALSE
        /\ missing = TRUE

OldExists == schema \in {"old", "both"}
NewExists == schema \in {"both", "new"}

\* v1 reads and writes email; v2 writes both; v3 reads email_address;
\* v4 writes only email_address.
WritesOld == app \in {1, 2, 3}
WritesNew == app \in {2, 3, 4}
ReadsNew  == app \in {3, 4}

AddColumn == /\ schema = "old"
             /\ schema' = "both"
             /\ app' = app
             /\ backfilled' = backfilled
             /\ missing' = missing

DeployV2 == /\ app = 1
            /\ NewExists
            /\ app' = 2
            /\ schema' = schema
            /\ backfilled' = backfilled
            /\ missing' = missing

Backfill == /\ ~backfilled
            /\ app = 2
            /\ backfilled' = TRUE
            /\ missing' = FALSE
            /\ schema' = schema
            /\ app' = app

DeployV3 == /\ app = 2
            /\ backfilled
            /\ app' = 3
            /\ schema' = schema
            /\ backfilled' = backfilled
            /\ missing' = missing

DeployV4 == /\ app = 3
            /\ app' = 4
            /\ schema' = schema
            /\ backfilled' = backfilled
            /\ missing' = missing

DropOld == /\ schema = "both"
           /\ app = 4
           /\ schema' = "new"
           /\ app' = app
           /\ backfilled' = backfilled
           /\ missing' = missing

\* A user signs up while v1 is live: the new row gets only email.
SignUp == /\ app = 1
          /\ missing' = TRUE
          /\ schema' = schema
          /\ app' = app
          /\ backfilled' = backfilled

Next == \/ AddColumn \/ DeployV2 \/ Backfill \/ DeployV3
        \/ DeployV4 \/ DropOld \/ SignUp

WritesOK == /\ (WritesOld => OldExists)
            /\ (WritesNew => NewExists)
ReadsOK == IF ReadsNew THEN NewExists /\ ~missing ELSE OldExists
NotDone == ~(schema = "new" /\ app = 4)
=============================================================================

    The config:

    INIT Init
NEXT Next
INVARIANT TypeOK
INVARIANT WritesOK
INVARIANT ReadsOK
CHECK_DEADLOCK FALSE
    1. For each of the guards NewExists in DeployV2, app = 2 in Backfill, backfilled in DeployV3, and app = 4 in DropOld, say which invariant would fail without it, and in which situation.
    2. Run TLC with the config. How many distinct states does it find? Why must the deadlock check be off here, and is the stop it would report a deadlock or termination?
    3. Add INVARIANT NotDone. What does TLC's trace give you?
    4. The backfill takes hours on a big table, so a teammate wants to start it as soon as the column exists. Change the guard app = 2 in Backfill to NewExists and run again. Which invariant fails, and why?

    Hint

    For (a), delete one guard at a time and run TLC. That's faster than arguing, and the trace tells you the situation. For (d), look at which action can set missing back to TRUE, and when it is enabled.

    Solution

    (a) Without NewExists, v2 could go live before the column exists, so it would write to a column that isn't there: WritesOK. Without app = 2, the backfill could run while v1 still writes only email: that is part (d), and ReadsOK fails later. Without backfilled, v3 would read email_address while old rows have no value there: ReadsOK. Without app = 4, you could drop email while v1, v2 or v3 still writes it: WritesOK.

    (b) No error, 7 distinct states. The guards leave exactly one runbook step enabled at a time, so the state graph is a single line. SignUp adds nothing, because while v1 is live missing is already TRUE. After DropOld, no action is enabled. The migration is supposed to end there, so this is termination, as in lesson 9. With the check on, TLC reports Deadlock reached at that final state.

    (c) TLC reports Invariant NotDone is violated with a 7-state trace: AddColumn, DeployV2, Backfill, DeployV3, DeployV4, DropOld. That is the runbook, in an order every guard allows. It also shows the guards don't block each other: a runbook whose preconditions can never all be met would have no such trace.

    (d) TLC reports Invariant ReadsOK is violated:

    The backfill copies every row that exists at the time, and the guard NewExists allows it while v1 is live. A user signs up, and v1 writes the new row's email only. The backfill already ran, so nothing ever copies that row. v2 and v3 deploy, and v3 reads email_address, which is empty for that user. In production the user would look like they had no email address. The step the trace exposes is SignUp, and you probably never thought of it as part of the migration. The guard app = 2 says the backfill starts only once every new row gets both columns, which closes that gap.

    Two limits of this model are worth knowing. It deploys each version to every server in one step, while a real rolling deploy runs two versions side by side for a while. And it has one kind of write; updates and deletes of existing rows need the same reasoning. Both would be good extensions once you have more notation.

    Problem 3●●○Algorithms

    Tower of Hanoi: let breadth-first search find the shortest solution

    Draws on Die Hard: model the jugs, Actions, guards, and frames and Die Hard: make TLC solve it.

    The Tower of Hanoi is the textbook example of recursion. Disks of different sizes sit on peg 1, largest at the bottom. You must move them all to peg 3, one disk at a time, never putting a disk on a smaller one. The recursive algorithm moves n − 1 disks out of the way, moves the largest, then moves the n − 1 back on top, for 2n − 1 moves. A colleague reviewing your course notes asks whether any solution is shorter. Rather than prove it, let TLC look at every possibility for 3 disks.

    Use one variable per disk: d1 (smallest), d2, d3 (largest), each holding the number of the peg the disk is on. You don't need to record the order of disks on a peg, because the rules force it: it is always by size.

    1. Write the module: TypeOK, Init, and one action per disk, MoveD1, MoveD2, MoveD3. A disk can move only if no smaller disk is on its peg, and only to a peg with no smaller disk. Remember the frame lines.
    2. Write NotSolved, the claim that the disks never all reach peg 3, and run TLC with one worker. How many states are in the trace? Compare it with the recursive algorithm's moves.
    3. Remove NotSolved and run again. How many distinct states are there, and why exactly that many?
    4. Add a fourth disk. Predict both numbers before you run TLC, then check.

    Hint

    If a and b are two different pegs among 1, 2 and 3, the third one is 6 - a - b. When can d2 move, and where can it go? The smallest disk is always on top and has two choices: use d1' \in with an IF that gives the set of the other two pegs.

    Solution

    (a)

    ------------------------------ MODULE PSl4_Hanoi ------------------------------
EXTENDS Integers

\* d1 is the smallest disk, d3 the largest. Each holds the peg (1, 2 or 3)
\* the disk is on. On any peg, the disks sit in size order.
VARIABLES d1, d2, d3

TypeOK == /\ d1 \in 1..3
          /\ d2 \in 1..3
          /\ d3 \in 1..3

Init == /\ d1 = 1
        /\ d2 = 1
        /\ d3 = 1

\* The smallest disk is always on top, and can go to either other peg.
MoveD1 == /\ d1' \in IF d1 = 1 THEN {2, 3}
                     ELSE IF d1 = 2 THEN {1, 3}
                     ELSE {1, 2}
          /\ d2' = d2
          /\ d3' = d3

\* d2 is on top if d1 isn't on its peg. It can't go onto d1, so it goes to
\* the one remaining peg. Pegs are 1, 2, 3, so the third one is 6 - d1 - d2.
MoveD2 == /\ d1 /= d2
          /\ d2' = 6 - d1 - d2
          /\ d1' = d1
          /\ d3' = d3

\* d3 can move only when d1 and d2 are both on the same other peg.
MoveD3 == /\ d1 = d2
          /\ d1 /= d3
          /\ d3' = 6 - d1 - d3
          /\ d1' = d1
          /\ d2' = d2

Next == MoveD1 \/ MoveD2 \/ MoveD3

NotSolved == ~(d1 = 3 /\ d2 = 3 /\ d3 = 3)
=============================================================================

    The guards come from the rules. d2 is on top of its peg exactly when d1 isn't there. It can't go onto d1, so its only legal target is the third peg, 6 - d1 - d2. d3 can move only when both smaller disks are off its peg and off the target, which means they are together on the remaining peg: d1 = d2 and d1 /= d3.

    (b) With INVARIANT NotSolved and one worker, TLC reports the violation with an 8-state trace: 7 moves. The diagram shows it, one column per state. It is the recursive algorithm's sequence exactly. The smallest disk moves on every other step, and the largest moves once, in the middle. Breadth-first search examined all states 1 move away, then 2, and so on, so no solution with 6 or fewer moves exists. For 3 disks, that answers your colleague.

    (c) Without NotSolved, there is no error and 27 distinct states. Every way of giving three disks a peg each is a legal position, and every legal position is reachable. The state graph is connected.

    (d) MoveD4 needs d1 = d2, d2 = d3 and d1 /= d4, and every other action gains the frame line d4' = d4 (module PSl4_Hanoi4). TLC finds a 16-state trace (15 moves, which is 24 − 1) and 81 = 34 distinct states. A check on 3 and 4 disks is not a proof for every n, of course. It is strong evidence for a claim that has a short proof by induction.

    Problem 4 · Synthesis●●●Algorithms

    A dosing station that can't measure 3 litres

    Draws on Die Hard: make TLC solve it, Your first spec through TLC, Writing Init and Next with logic, and the Euclid's GCD problem in Problem set 3.

    A lab automation rig measures liquid with two fixed chambers and no level sensors: a 4-litre chamber and a 6-litre chamber. It can fill a chamber from the supply, drain a chamber, or pump from one chamber into the other until the source is empty or the destination is full. These are the Die Hard jugs in steel. A new recipe needs exactly 3 litres, and the controls engineer asks you whether any sequence of operations produces it.

    Recall Euclid's algorithm from Problem set 3: replacing the larger of two numbers by their difference doesn't change their greatest common divisor, so it ends at gcd of the starting pair. Here gcd(4, 6) = 2.

    1. Generalize the DieHard module. Define the capacities as Small == 4 and Big == 6, the way Counter defined Max == 3, and use those names everywhere, including in the pours.
    2. Claim NoThree: neither chamber ever holds 3. Run TLC. How many distinct states does it find, and what does the result mean? Before you trust it, show that your setup can find a violation by claiming NoTwo == big /= 2.
    3. Explain the result with the gcd. Write it as an invariant Even and check it.
    4. The vendor offers a 5-litre chamber instead of the 4-litre one. Predict what changes, then change one definition and check. How many states are in the shortest trace to 3 litres?

    TLC reports no violation of NoThree. What makes that a trustworthy answer?

    Hint

    Look at what each of the six actions does to the amounts: each one sets a chamber to 0 or to its capacity, or moves water from one chamber to the other. If both amounts are even before a step, can either be odd after it?

    Solution

    (a)

    ------------------------------- MODULE PSl4_Dosing -------------------------------
EXTENDS Integers

Small == 4    \* litres the small chamber holds
Big   == 6    \* litres the big chamber holds

VARIABLES small, big

TypeOK == /\ small \in 0..Small
          /\ big   \in 0..Big

Init == /\ small = 0
        /\ big   = 0

FillSmall == /\ small' = Small
             /\ big'   = big

FillBig == /\ big'   = Big
           /\ small' = small

EmptySmall == /\ small' = 0
              /\ big'   = big

EmptyBig == /\ big'   = 0
            /\ small' = small

SmallToBig == IF big + small =< Big
                THEN /\ big'   = big + small
                     /\ small' = 0
                ELSE /\ big'   = Big
                     /\ small' = small - (Big - big)

BigToSmall == IF big + small =< Small
                THEN /\ big'   = 0
                     /\ small' = big + small
                ELSE /\ big'   = big - (Small - small)
                     /\ small' = Small

Next == \/ FillSmall  \/ FillBig
        \/ EmptySmall \/ EmptyBig
        \/ SmallToBig \/ BigToSmall

NoThree == /\ small /= 3
           /\ big   /= 3
NoTwo   == big /= 2
Even    == /\ small \in {0, 2, 4}
           /\ big   \in {0, 2, 4, 6}
=============================================================================

    (b) With INVARIANT TypeOK and INVARIANT NoThree, TLC reports no error and 10 distinct states, the filled cells of the grid. Because the model is finite and TLC examined every reachable state, “no error” here means that no sequence of operations ever puts 3 litres in either chamber. That is a real answer only if the check could have failed. Claiming NoTwo shows it could: TLC reports a violation with a 3-state trace, FillBig then BigToSmall, which leaves 2 litres in the big chamber. This is the experiment-that-fails test from lesson 13, used in reverse to trust a success.

    (c) Each action sets a chamber to 0, to 4, or to 6, all even, or moves water between chambers so that the total stays the same and one chamber ends empty or full. Start with two even amounts, and every one of these steps leaves two even amounts. So Even is an invariant, and TLC confirms it: no error, 10 states. It is the same argument as Euclid's: a step that only adds or subtracts multiples of 2 can't produce an odd number. In general, every amount you can measure is a multiple of gcd(Small, Big). Euclid's algorithm computes exactly that number by repeated subtraction, much as the pumps subtract one chamber from the other.

    (d) gcd(5, 6) = 1, so the argument no longer rules 3 out. Set Small == 5 (module PSl4_Dosing56) and TLC reports NoThree violated with a 9-state trace: fill 5, pump into 6, fill 5, pump until 6 is full (4 left), drain 6, pump the 4 across, fill 5, pump until 6 is full, which leaves 3 in the 5-litre chamber. Without NoThree, TLC finds 22 distinct states. So the engineer's answer is: not with these chambers; with a 5-litre chamber, yes, in 8 operations.

    Notice what each chapter contributed. The state machine view turned a machine into variables and steps. TLC's exhaustive search made “impossible” a checkable claim. The invariant from Problem set 3 explains why it's impossible, and tells you which chamber sizes would work before you run anything.

    Lecture 5: Transaction commit

    Three pieces of math describe a whole group of processes.

    Die Hard had two jugs, so naming each one was easy. The next spec has a set of processes whose size you don't fix in advance. To write about all of them at once you need sets, functions, and the quantifiers "there exists" and "for all".

    The diagram is one function, rmState. Each resource manager on the left has exactly one solid arrow to a value on the right. That is the whole idea of a function, and the dashed arrow is the only change that one step of the next spec will make.

    While you watch

    Lecture 5 teaches this notation in passing, while reading the TCommit spec. This lesson collects it so you can recognize it there; lesson 16 then covers the spec itself. Watch for two pauses: Lamport asks why rmState'[r] = "prepared" is wrong, and later asks you to look at what a formula says rather than what you think it should say. Stop and answer before going on. This lesson adds quantifier order and the empty-set cases.

    Sets

    A set is a collection with no order and no duplicates: it either contains a value or it doesn't. So {"r1", "r2", "r1"} and {"r2", "r1"} are the same set. You write membership as e \in S, and 1..3 is the set {1, 2, 3}.

    In TLA+ every value is a set, even 42 and "abc", but the language doesn't say what their elements are. TLC reports an error if asked to evaluate 42 \in "abc". A module can therefore say CONSTANT RM and use RM as a set without declaring a type. A constant has the same value throughout every behavior, and you give it a value when you run TLC.

    Functions are what programmers call arrays

    ProgrammingMath and TLA+
    arrayfunction
    index setdomain
    f[e]f[e] (math writes f(e))

    A function's domain can be any set, including one of strings or an infinite one. There are two expressions to tell apart:

    sqr == [i \in 1..42 |-> i^2]     \* one function; sqr[3] = 9, DOMAIN sqr = 1..42
[RM -> {"working", "prepared"}]   \* a set: all functions from RM to those values

    |-> builds one function. -> builds the set of all functions with that domain and those possible values. DOMAIN f gives the domain. (^ comes from the Integers module.)

    In the diagram, the outer box is the value of [{"r1", "r2"} -> {"a", "b"}]. The highlighted inner box is the single function [r \in {"r1", "r2"} |-> "a"], which is one element of it. A type invariant such as rmState \in [RM -> ...] uses the outer form, and an initial state uses the inner one.

    Changing one entry

    A next-state formula can't say only that r's entry changes. Compare the middle and right columns.

    rmState'[r2] = "prepared" says what the new value at r2 is. About every other resource manager it says nothing, which is why the middle column is full of question marks. You must give the whole new function:

    rmState' = [s \in RM |-> IF s = r THEN "prepared" ELSE rmState[s]]
rmState' = [rmState EXCEPT ![r] = "prepared"]     \* the same thing, shorter

    In the EXCEPT form, the ! means nothing. It's just syntax. EXCEPT doesn't modify anything: it is an expression for a new function, and rmState itself keeps its value in the current state.

    Quantifiers

    \E r \in RM : P(r) says there exists some r in RM for which P(r) is true. \A r \in RM : P(r) says P(r) is true for all r in RM. Over a finite set they are just a long "or" and a long "and":

    Read the diagram from the top. One TRUE row makes the "or" true, and one FALSE row makes the "and" false. A few rules follow from this:

    • The bound name is local. \E xyz \in RM : ...xyz... means the same as \E r \in RM : ...r..., provided xyz isn't already declared or defined. TLA+ doesn't let you redefine a name that already has a meaning.
    • Abbreviation. \A r1, r2 \in RM : P abbreviates \A r1 \in RM : \A r2 \in RM : P.
    • Not and not-equal. ~P is "not P", and x # y is "x doesn't equal y".
    • Empty set. \A r \in {} : P is always true, since there is no counterexample, and \E r \in {} : P is always false.
    • Scope. A quantifier reaches as far as it can: to a closing bracket, or to the end of its /\ or \/ list item. Parentheses end it sooner.
    \A x \in S : x = 1
    /\ \A x \in T : x = 2     \* illegal: this is inside the first \A, so x is redeclared

    The parser rejects that with a multiply-defined symbol error.

    Quantifier order changes the meaning

    A cart holds a book and a mug. Compare two claims about shipping them.

    \A i \in Items : \E w \in Warehouses : i \in CanShip[w]   \* true
\E w \in Warehouses : \A i \in Items : i \in CanShip[w]   \* false

    The first says each item has some warehouse, and different items may have different ones (the left of the diagram). The second says one warehouse handles everything, and the dashed arrow on the right is why it fails. When you read a nested formula, invent a tiny example like this one.

    Predict: which of the formulas in this lesson changes meaning if RM is empty?

    With no resource managers, every \A r \in RM formula is true and every \E r \in RM formula is false. A check that "all RMs are prepared" passes trivially. That's why a claim such as "the cart can be checked out" needs its own "the cart isn't empty" condition: \A alone can't say so.

    Worked example: a group chat

    A chat has members and a read position for each member. Those are two concepts, so they get two shapes: a set for membership, a function for positions.

    Members   == {"Ada", "Ben"}
lastRead  == [p \in Members |-> 0]
lastRead2 == [lastRead EXCEPT !["Ada"] = 2]     \* Ada 2, Ben still 0
lastRead2 \in [Members -> 0..3]                 \* true
\A p \in Members : lastRead2[p] <= 3            \* true

    Because lastRead maps each person to a number, Ada and Ben can't accidentally share one cursor. Adding Cara to Members would leave the function's domain out of date, so both must change in one step. An ordered message history would need a sequence, which comes later with lesson 30. Every formula in this lesson was checked by TLC as an assumption in a small module.

    Which expression is a set of functions?

    What is wrong with using rmState'[r] = "prepared" as the whole effect of a step?

    Reference: Specifying Systems, chapters 1 and 6.

    Lecture 5: Transaction commit

    Say what a wedding must accomplish, and leave out the minister.

    You now have the notation for talking about a set of processes. Lecture 5 uses it on a problem from databases, transaction commit, which is simple enough to specify in about twenty lines. The spec describes only the outcome that must be reached, not any protocol for reaching it.

    The diagram is the state machine of one participant, and it is nearly the whole problem. A participant starts out working, can prepare or abort, and from prepared can commit or abort. Committed and aborted have no outgoing arrows, so those decisions are final.

    While you watch

    Lamport, following Jim Gray, starts with a wedding: bride, groom, and minister. Ask yourself what the minister is for. Then follow the walk through module TCommit, whose notation you met in lesson 15. Pause where he says to stop the video. The lecture runs TLC from the Toolbox; the same run works in the VS Code extension, the current option, and this lesson shows it as a .cfg file. This lesson adds a graph of every reachable state for two participants and a broken variant of the spec.

    From a wedding to a transaction

    At a wedding, each of two people starts unsure, and either may say no. It must end with both believing they are committed or both believing it was aborted. The minister helps make this happen, but he is part of how the wedding works, not part of what it must accomplish. So the spec leaves him out.

    Now allow any number of participants, and you have transaction commit. A database transaction is carried out by processes called resource managers (RMs). The unsure state is traditionally called working. The rules are:

    • The transaction can commit only if all RMs are prepared to commit.
    • It must abort if any RM wants to abort.
    • All RMs must agree on the result.

    The spec

    ------------------------------- MODULE TCommit ------------------------------
CONSTANT RM              \* The set of resource managers
VARIABLE rmState         \* rmState[r] is the state of RM r
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
TCTypeOK == rmState \in [RM -> {"working", "prepared", "committed", "aborted"}]

TCInit == rmState = [r \in RM |-> "working"]

canCommit == \A r \in RM : rmState[r] \in {"prepared", "committed"}

notCommitted == \A r \in RM : rmState[r] # "committed"
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
Prepare(r) == /\ rmState[r] = "working"
              /\ rmState' = [rmState EXCEPT ![r] = "prepared"]

Decide(r) == \/ /\ rmState[r] = "prepared"
                /\ canCommit
                /\ rmState' = [rmState EXCEPT ![r] = "committed"]
             \/ /\ rmState[r] \in {"working", "prepared"}
                /\ notCommitted
                /\ rmState' = [rmState EXCEPT ![r] = "aborted"]

TCNext == \E r \in RM : Prepare(r) \/ Decide(r)
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
TCConsistent == \A r1, r2 \in RM : ~ /\ rmState[r1] = "aborted"
                                     /\ rmState[r2] = "committed"
=============================================================================

    The "TC" prefix on names such as TCTypeOK is there because a later module uses this one alongside its own definitions. Prepare(r) is the top arrow of the diagram. Decide(r) has two cases: the branch to committed needs canCommit (every RM prepared or committed), and the branch to aborted needs notCommitted (no RM committed). TCNext says some RM takes one of those steps.

    canCommit and notCommitted are only names. You could paste their definitions into Decide, renaming the bound variable to s to avoid clashing with r, and the meaning would stay the same. You could also split Decide into two actions. There are many ways to decompose a next-state formula, and definitions are how you make it readable.

    One Decide(r) step reads the state of every RM. No programming language gives you that in a single step, and it doesn't matter: this says what commit must achieve, not how. lesson 18 covers the how.

    Every reachable state, for two RMs

    Each box is a state of two RMs: r1's state, then r2's, abbreviated w, p, c, a. Right and left arrows are r1 moving, and up and down arrows are r2 moving. The curved arrows are a prepared RM aborting. Start at the accent box and follow the guards. The commit arrows only appear once the other RM is prepared or committed. Once one RM commits, the arrows to aborted disappear, because notCommitted is false. The two red boxes have no arrows into them, which is exactly what TCConsistent claims. TLC agrees: with two RMs it finds 12 distinct states, the 12 non-red boxes.

    Check it with TLC

    INIT TCInit
NEXT TCNext
CONSTANT RM = {"r1", "r2", "r3"}
INVARIANT TCTypeOK
INVARIANT TCConsistent
CHECK_DEADLOCK FALSE

    Since the initial and next-state formulas aren't called Init and Next, you name them. A constant needs a value, and Lamport's three strings are as good as any; he'd normally start with a smaller model, but this spec is simple. A correct behavior ends when all RMs have finished, so you turn deadlock checking off.

    Result of this run: no error, 94 states generated, 34 distinct states.

    Be suspicious of success. Look at the state count: is it plausible? Look at the coverage report, which counts how often each part of the next-state formula produced a new state. A count of zero usually means an error in the spec.

    Predict: delete notCommitted from the abort branch of Decide. What does TLC find?

    It reports that TCConsistent is violated, with a 6-state trace. All three RMs prepare, r1 commits, and r2 then aborts. The trace is the bottom half of the next diagram.

    The top three rows are a behavior of the real spec. The bottom three are what TLC printed for the broken one. They are identical until the last column shown for the bad run, where r2 aborts even though r1 has committed. The guard you deleted is the only thing preventing it.

    Comments and layout

    \* starts an end-of-line comment, and (* ... *) encloses any other comment. A line of dashes between statements is decoration.

    Why does TCommit have no minister or coordinator?

    Lecture page and specs: The TLA+ Video Course.

    Lecture 5: Transaction commit

    Problem set 5: say it about every process at once.

    Lecture 5 gave you sets, functions and quantifiers, and the TCommit spec, which uses them to describe any number of participants. These problems use that notation on replicas, pods, services and servers. They still rely on guards, frames and the never-reached claim from Problem set 4, and on TLC's reports from lesson 9.

    UNCHANGED and records come with Lecture 6, so frames are still written out as v' = v. A function-valued variable that a step changes with EXCEPT needs no other frame. For trace lengths, run TLC with -workers 1.

    Problem 1●○○Databases

    A failover tool reads the replica map

    Draws on Sets, functions, and quantifiers, The transaction commit spec and Your first spec through TLC.

    A Postgres primary streams its write-ahead log to three replicas. A failover tool keeps two functions with the same domain: status, modeled loosely on the state column of Postgres's pg_stat_replication view, and lag, each replica's last reported replay lag in seconds. When the primary dies, the tool promotes a candidate: a streaming replica with the smallest lag.

    Evaluate these by hand, before using TLC. Each is TRUE or FALSE.

    E1 == \A r \in Replicas : status[r] = "streaming" => lag[r] =< 5
E2 == \E r \in Replicas : \A s \in Replicas : lag[r] =< lag[s]
E3 == \A s \in Replicas : \E r \in Replicas : lag[r] < lag[s]
E4 == \A r \in Replicas : lag[r] =< 5
E5 == \A r \in {} : lag[r] > 100

    Then look at the tool's rule, as the module below writes it. Next is one event: db1 crashes.

    ----------------------------- MODULE PSl5_Failover -----------------------------
EXTENDS Integers

Replicas == {"db1", "db2", "db3"}

\* Replay lag in seconds, as last reported.
lag == [r \in Replicas |-> IF r = "db1" THEN 0
                           ELSE IF r = "db2" THEN 4
                           ELSE 90]

VARIABLE status

Init == status = [r \in Replicas |-> IF r = "db3" THEN "catchup"
                                     ELSE "streaming"]

\* db1 crashes. Its last reported lag stays in the table.
Next == status' = [status EXCEPT !["db1"] = "down"]

Candidate(r) == /\ status[r] = "streaming"
                /\ \A s \in Replicas : lag[r] =< lag[s]

SomeCandidate == \E r \in Replicas : Candidate(r)
=============================================================================

    The config is INIT Init, NEXT Next, INVARIANT SomeCandidate.

    1. Give the values of E1 to E5, with a one-line reason each.
    2. How many elements does [Replicas -> {"streaming", "catchup", "down"}] have? Write a type invariant for status using it.
    3. Which replicas satisfy Candidate in the initial state? Run TLC. What does it report, and why?
    4. Fix Candidate so that only streaming replicas are compared, and check it again.
    Which of E2 and E3 is true?

    Hint

    Over a finite set, \A is a long “and” and \E a long “or”. Write them out for db1, db2 and db3. For the bug, ask which replicas the \A s in Candidate compares against after the crash.

    Solution

    (a) E1 is TRUE: the streaming replicas are db1 and db2, with lags 0 and 4. For db3 the left side of => is false, so its case is true. E2 is TRUE: take r = db1. E3 is FALSE: for s = db1, no lag is below 0. E4 is FALSE because of db3's 90. Compare it with E1, where the implication excused db3. E5 is TRUE, like every \A over the empty set.

    (b) 27, since each replica independently gets one of three values. The type invariant is status \in [Replicas -> {"streaming", "catchup", "down"}].
