    (c) Initially only db1 is a candidate: it is streaming and its lag of 0 is no larger than anybody's. TLC reports Invariant SomeCandidate is violated in a 2-state trace:

    State 1: <Initial predicate>
status = [db1 |-> "streaming", db2 |-> "streaming", db3 |-> "catchup"]

State 2: <Next ...>
status = [db1 |-> "down", db2 |-> "streaming", db3 |-> "catchup"]

    TLC prints a function whose domain is a set of strings in this bracket form, the notation for records, which Lecture 6 introduces. After the crash, db2 is the obvious choice, but Candidate("db2") still compares its lag with db1's last reported 0 and fails. The dead replica's old number blocks every live one. A failover tool with this rule would refuse to promote anything in exactly the situation it exists for.

    (d) Restrict the comparison to streaming replicas:

    Candidate(r) == /\ status[r] = "streaming"
                /\ \A s \in Replicas : status[s] = "streaming" => lag[r] =< lag[s]

    With this definition (module PSl5_FailoverFixed), TLC reports no error in 2 distinct states: db1 is the candidate before the crash and db2 after it. The fix uses the same pattern as E1, an implication inside \A that excuses the elements you don't care about. (The fixed rule still has a gap: if no replica is streaming, there is no candidate, and maybe that's what you want.)

    Problem 2●●○Infrastructure

    A rolling update that takes down two pods

    Draws on Sets, functions, and quantifiers, The transaction commit spec and Die Hard: make TLC solve it.

    A Kubernetes Deployment can replace pods one at a time: with maxSurge: 0 and maxUnavailable: 1, its rolling update keeps at most one replica unavailable, and a new pod counts as available only once it passes its readiness probe. Your team runs a stateful service whose pods need a custom drain step, so it wrote its own rollout script with the same goal: with three replicas, at least two serve traffic at every moment. Each pod goes from v1 to stopping, to starting, to v2, and serves only in v1 and v2. The script's rule for stopping a pod is “only if no other pod is stopping”.

    ------------------------------ MODULE PSl5_Rollout ------------------------------
CONSTANT Pod             \* the Deployment's replicas
VARIABLE pod             \* pod[p] is the state of replica p

TypeOK == pod \in [Pod -> {"v1", "stopping", "starting", "v2"}]

Init == pod = [p \in Pod |-> "v1"]

Serving(p) == pod[p] \in {"v1", "v2"}

\* The controller replaces one old pod. The guard is its availability rule.
Stop(p) == /\ pod[p] = "v1"
           /\ \A q \in Pod : pod[q] /= "stopping"
           /\ pod' = [pod EXCEPT ![p] = "stopping"]

\* The old container has exited; the new one is scheduled.
Start(p) == /\ pod[p] = "stopping"
            /\ pod' = [pod EXCEPT ![p] = "starting"]

\* The new container passes its readiness probe.
Ready(p) == /\ pod[p] = "starting"
            /\ pod' = [pod EXCEPT ![p] = "v2"]

Next == \E p \in Pod : Stop(p) \/ Start(p) \/ Ready(p)
=============================================================================
    1. Add the invariant AtMostOneDown: at most one pod is out of service. You don't have a way to count elements of a set yet, so say it with quantifiers.
    2. Run TLC with CONSTANT Pod = {"p1", "p2", "p3"}, INVARIANT TypeOK, INVARIANT AtMostOneDown and CHECK_DEADLOCK FALSE. Explain the trace. Why is the deadlock check off?
    3. Fix the guard of Stop. How many distinct states does TLC find now, and why that number?
    4. Use the trick from lesson 13 to make TLC show you a complete rollout. How many steps does it take?
    Which formula says “at least two of the three pods serve”?

    Hint

    “At most one” means: if two pods are both down, they are the same pod. For the fix, ask what the rule should look at: whether a pod is stopping, or whether it is serving.

    Solution

    (a) If two pods are both out of service, they are the same pod:

    AtMostOneDown == \A p, q \in Pod : (~Serving(p) /\ ~Serving(q)) => p = q

    (b) TLC reports Invariant AtMostOneDown is violated:

    p1 is stopped and its replacement is starting. That pod is not stopping, so the script's guard \A q \in Pod : pod[q] /= "stopping" is true and p2 stops too. For as long as p1's new container takes to pass its probe, only p3 serves. The rule checked the wrong state: “stopping” is one way of being out of service, not the only one. The deadlock check is off because a finished rollout, with every pod on v2, has no next step, and that stop is intended.

    (c) Make the guard the property you want: stop a pod only if every pod is serving.

    Stop(p) == /\ pod[p] = "v1"
           /\ \A q \in Pod : Serving(q)
           /\ pod' = [pod EXCEPT ![p] = "stopping"]

    TLC finds no error and 32 distinct states: the 8 where every pod is v1 or v2, plus the 24 where exactly one pod is stopping or starting. Counting reachable states by hand and matching TLC's number is a good check that the model allows what you think it allows, as lesson 16 advised.

    (d) Claim NotRolledOut == ~(\A p \in Pod : pod[p] = "v2") as an invariant. TLC reports it violated with a 10-state trace: Stop, Start and Ready for p1, then the same for p2, then p3. That is 9 steps, 3 per pod, done strictly one pod at a time, which is what the rule promised. Kubernetes' maxSurge exists to speed this up by starting new pods before old ones stop. Modeling it would need a variable number of pods.

    Problem 3●●○Microservices

    All services move to schema v2, or none do

    Draws on The transaction commit spec, Sets, functions, and quantifiers and Die Hard: make TLC solve it.

    Three services, orders, billing and shipping, publish and consume OrderPlaced events on a shared topic. Version 2 of the event schema renames a field. A service on v1 code can't parse a v2 event, so the platform team sets two rules. First, nobody may emit v2 until every service has deployed a reader that understands both versions. Second, any team may back out, and if one does, nobody ever emits v2.

    So each service goes through four states: "v1", "ready" (reads both, still emits v1), "v2" (emits v2), and "pinned" (backed out: stays on v1 for good). This should look familiar.

    1. Write the module, with CONSTANT Svc and one variable st, a function from services to states. Write the actions GetReady(s), Switch(s) and Cancel(s), and two invariants: Agreement (no service on v2 while another is pinned) and ReadersReady (if any service is on v2, every service is ready or on v2).
    2. Run TLC with the three services as strings. How many distinct states does it find? Why is that number familiar?
    3. A teammate argues that the switch guard is too strict, since a service only needs “nobody has backed out”. Replace the guard of Switch(s) by \A t \in Svc : st[t] # "pinned" and run again.

    With the teammate's guard, which invariant does TLC report violated?

    Hint

    Match each state to one of TCommit's. Which TCommit formula says “everyone is ready”, and which one says “nobody has gone ahead”?

    Solution

    (a) In the diagram, each state carries its TCommit name. The module:

    ---------------------------- MODULE PSl5_Schema ----------------------------
CONSTANT Svc             \* services that produce and consume OrderPlaced events
VARIABLE st              \* st[s] is where service s is in the upgrade

TypeOK == st \in [Svc -> {"v1", "ready", "v2", "pinned"}]

Init == st = [s \in Svc |-> "v1"]

canSwitch == \A s \in Svc : st[s] \in {"ready", "v2"}

noneSwitched == \A s \in Svc : st[s] # "v2"

\* Deploy code that can read both v1 and v2 events; still emit v1.
GetReady(s) == /\ st[s] = "v1"
               /\ st' = [st EXCEPT ![s] = "ready"]

\* Start emitting v2 events.
Switch(s) == /\ st[s] = "ready"
             /\ canSwitch
             /\ st' = [st EXCEPT ![s] = "v2"]

\* Give up on v2 and stay on v1 for good.
Cancel(s) == /\ st[s] \in {"v1", "ready"}
             /\ noneSwitched
             /\ st' = [st EXCEPT ![s] = "pinned"]

Next == \E s \in Svc : GetReady(s) \/ Switch(s) \/ Cancel(s)

Agreement == \A s, t \in Svc : ~ /\ st[s] = "v2"
                                 /\ st[t] = "pinned"

ReadersReady == (\E s \in Svc : st[s] = "v2")
                  => \A t \in Svc : st[t] \in {"ready", "v2"}
=============================================================================

    (b) With CONSTANT Svc = {"orders", "billing", "shipping"}, the two invariants and CHECK_DEADLOCK FALSE, TLC finds no error and 34 distinct states. That is TCommit's count for three RMs, and not by coincidence. Rename v1, ready, v2 and pinned to working, prepared, committed and aborted, and this module is TCommit with Decide split into its two branches. A schema rollout and a database commit are the same problem: a group must reach one decision, anyone may veto before it is made, and nobody may act on it early.

    (c) With the weaker guard (module PSl5_SchemaEager), TLC reports Invariant ReadersReady is violated after 3 states: orders gets ready, then switches while billing and shipping are still on v1. Their consumers would choke on the first v2 event. Agreement alone doesn't catch this. Run with only Agreement and TLC finds no error, in 46 distinct states. Once orders is on v2, nobody can cancel, so the services do end up agreeing, after an outage.

    This is why TCommit's commit branch requires canCommit. For a database it means that no RM commits until every RM has promised it can. Here it means that nobody emits v2 before everyone can read it. The consistency invariant TCConsistent doesn't state that requirement, which is why you want ReadersReady written down and checked too.

    Problem 4 · Synthesis●●●Databases

    Distributed cron: every job at most once

    Draws on Sets, functions, and quantifiers, The transaction commit spec, Your first spec through TLC, and the migration problem in Problem set 4.

    Two application servers run the same crontab, so that the nightly jobs still run if one server is down. There are two jobs: backup, and report, which reads the backup. Neither may run twice in a night. Each server, for each job, reads the job's row in a shared jobs table. If owner is empty, it writes its own name and runs the job; otherwise it skips. A report must wait until some server has run the backup.

    The module (open to copy) 
    ------------------------------ MODULE PSl5_Cron ------------------------------
CONSTANT Node                   \* servers that each run the same crontab
VARIABLES pc,                   \* pc[n][j]: where node n is with job j tonight
          owner                 \* owner[j]: the node in the jobs table, or "none"

Jobs == {"backup", "report"}

TypeOK == /\ pc \in [Node -> [Jobs -> {"idle", "seen", "ran", "skipped"}]]
          /\ \A j \in Jobs : owner[j] = "none" \/ owner[j] \in Node

Init == /\ pc = [n \in Node |-> [j \in Jobs |-> "idle"]]
        /\ owner = [j \in Jobs |-> "none"]

\* pc with node n's entry for job j set to v
Set(n, j, v) == [pc EXCEPT ![n] = [pc[n] EXCEPT ![j] = v]]

\* The report reads the backup, so it may start only after a backup ran.
Ready(j) == j = "report" => \E n \in Node : pc[n]["backup"] = "ran"

\* SELECT owner FROM jobs WHERE name = j  -- and see "none"
Check(n, j) == /\ pc[n][j] = "idle"
               /\ owner[j] = "none"
               /\ Ready(j)
               /\ pc' = Set(n, j, "seen")
               /\ owner' = owner

\* UPDATE jobs SET owner = n WHERE name = j; then run the job
Run(n, j) == /\ pc[n][j] = "seen"
             /\ owner' = [owner EXCEPT ![j] = n]
             /\ pc' = Set(n, j, "ran")

\* Someone else has it.
Skip(n, j) == /\ pc[n][j] = "idle"
              /\ owner[j] # "none"
              /\ pc' = Set(n, j, "skipped")
              /\ owner' = owner

Next == \E n \in Node : \E j \in Jobs : Check(n, j) \/ Run(n, j) \/ Skip(n, j)

AtMostOnce == \A j \in Jobs : \A n, m \in Node :
                (pc[n][j] = "ran" /\ pc[m][j] = "ran") => n = m
=============================================================================

    The config:

    INIT Init
NEXT Next
CONSTANT Node = {"n1", "n2"}
INVARIANT TypeOK
INVARIANT AtMostOnce
CHECK_DEADLOCK FALSE

    pc is a function whose values are functions: pc[n] is node n's function from jobs to states, and pc[n][j] is one entry. Set(n, j, v) builds the new pc by applying EXCEPT at both levels.

    1. Read AtMostOnce aloud. Why does it end in n = m rather than n # m?
    2. Run TLC. Explain the trace in terms of SQL statements.
    3. Replace Check and Run by a single action Claim(n, j) that models one conditional UPDATE jobs SET owner = n WHERE name = j AND owner IS NULL: it succeeds and runs the job only if owner is still empty. Check AtMostOnce.
    4. The Ready guard plays the role the runbook guards played in the migration problem of Problem set 4. Use the same never-reached claim to make TLC produce a night's schedule in which both jobs run.
    5. Run your fixed module with the deadlock check on. Is the stop TLC reports a deadlock or termination? Add an action that tells TLC which stops are intended, so that the check can stay on.

    With the deadlock check on, TLC reports “Deadlock reached” for the fixed module. What is it?

    Hint

    For (c), the check and the write must be one step, so the guard owner[j] = "none" and the change owner' = [owner EXCEPT ![j] = n] belong to the same action. For (e), an action whose guard says “everyone is finished” and whose frame keeps every variable the same is enabled exactly in the intended final states.

    Solution

    (a) “For every job, for any two nodes: if both ran it, they are the same node.” With n # m it would say that both ran it only if they are different nodes, and the case n = m would make it false in any state where some node ran the job. The \A n, m includes the pairs where n and m are equal. That is what makes “at most one” come out right.

    (b) TLC reports Invariant AtMostOnce is violated with a 5-state trace:

    Both servers ran SELECT owner and saw it empty before either wrote. n1's UPDATE doesn't change what n2 already read, and n2's UPDATE overwrites the owner with its own name. The backup runs twice, and the table even says n2 owns it. This is check-then-act: the decision is based on a value that may be stale by the time the action happens.

    (c) Make the check part of the write:

    --------------------------- MODULE PSl5_CronClaim ---------------------------
CONSTANT Node                   \* servers that each run the same crontab
VARIABLES pc,                   \* pc[n][j]: where node n is with job j tonight
          owner                 \* owner[j]: the node in the jobs table, or "none"

Jobs == {"backup", "report"}

TypeOK == /\ pc \in [Node -> [Jobs -> {"idle", "ran", "skipped"}]]
          /\ \A j \in Jobs : owner[j] = "none" \/ owner[j] \in Node

Init == /\ pc = [n \in Node |-> [j \in Jobs |-> "idle"]]
        /\ owner = [j \in Jobs |-> "none"]

Set(n, j, v) == [pc EXCEPT ![n] = [pc[n] EXCEPT ![j] = v]]

Ready(j) == j = "report" => \E n \in Node : pc[n]["backup"] = "ran"

\* UPDATE jobs SET owner = n WHERE name = j AND owner IS NULL
\* One statement: the check and the write are one step.
Claim(n, j) == /\ pc[n][j] = "idle"
               /\ owner[j] = "none"
               /\ Ready(j)
               /\ owner' = [owner EXCEPT ![j] = n]
               /\ pc' = Set(n, j, "ran")

Skip(n, j) == /\ pc[n][j] = "idle"
              /\ owner[j] # "none"
              /\ pc' = Set(n, j, "skipped")
              /\ owner' = owner

Next == \E n \in Node : \E j \in Jobs : Claim(n, j) \/ Skip(n, j)

AtMostOnce == \A j \in Jobs : \A n, m \in Node :
                (pc[n][j] = "ran" /\ pc[m][j] = "ran") => n = m

NotAllRan == ~(\A j \in Jobs : \E n \in Node : pc[n][j] = "ran")

AllFinished == \A n \in Node : \A j \in Jobs : pc[n][j] \in {"ran", "skipped"}

\* An intended stop: every node is done for the night. Nothing changes.
Finished == /\ AllFinished
            /\ pc' = pc
            /\ owner' = owner

NextOrDone == Next \/ Finished
=============================================================================

    The module also holds the definitions for parts (d) and (e). With the config of (b), TLC finds no error and 21 distinct states. The model now says the check and the write are one step, so it is your job to make that true in the system too. A single UPDATE … WHERE owner IS NULL does it in Postgres at the default isolation level, read committed: when two such statements hit the same row, the second waits for the first to commit, then re-checks its WHERE clause against the new row and updates nothing. The server then sees that zero rows changed, and skips the job.

    (d) Claim NotAllRan, which says that it never happens that every job has run somewhere. TLC reports it violated with a 3-state trace: Claim("n1", "backup"), then Claim("n1", "report"). The report comes second because Ready disables it until a backup has run, exactly as app = 2 forced the backfill after v2 in the migration runbook. The guard is the dependency, and TLC's trace is a schedule that respects it.

    (e) With the deadlock check on, TLC reports Deadlock reached after a 5-state trace that ends with n1 having run both jobs and n2 having skipped both. Nothing is left to do, so this is termination, as with the counter in lesson 9. Rather than turn the check off, the module defines Finished, which is enabled only when every entry of pc is "ran" or "skipped" and changes nothing, and NextOrDone == Next \/ Finished. With NEXT NextOrDone and the deadlock check on, TLC finds no error in 21 states. That shows something the earlier run couldn't: every state with no further step is a finished night. If Ready could block the report forever, this run would report the deadlock.

    The pieces came from four chapters: functions and quantifiers for “at most once across nodes”, TCommit's style of guard that reads every process, the runbook guard and never-reached claim from Problem set 4, and the deadlock-or-termination question from Lecture 3.

    Lecture 6: Two-phase commit

    Two-phase commit puts the minister back, as a process with messages.

    TCommit let one step read every RM's state. Lecture 6 replaces that impossible step with a protocol: a transaction manager (TM) collects "prepared" messages and then announces the result. First you need one more data type, the record, because messages are records.

    This is a real run of the spec below, printed by TLC with two RMs, and it has 8 states. An RM's "prepared" message and its change of state happen in one step. The TM commits only once tmPrepared holds every RM.

    While you watch

    Lecture 6 opens with records, then reruns the wedding with texting. Notice that he drops the minister's "are you prepared?" message because TCommit doesn't need it. When he describes each remaining action, stop the video and write the definition yourself, as he asks. Later, compare your version by rerunning TLC. This lesson adds a trace in which an RM aborts, and the commit-lab below. How the spec models messages gets its own treatment in lesson 19.

    Records

    r == [prof |-> "Fred", num |-> 42]     \* r.prof = "Fred", r.num = 42
[prof : {"Fred", "Ted"}, num : 0..99]   \* the set of all such records
[r EXCEPT !.prof = "Red"]               \* same as r except field prof

    A record is like a C struct, except that field order doesn't matter. It is really a function whose domain is a set of strings: r.prof abbreviates r["prof"], and !.prof abbreviates !["prof"]. So you already know how they behave.

    The spec

    ------------------------------- MODULE TwoPhase -----------------------------
CONSTANT RM              \* The set of resource managers
VARIABLES
  rmState,               \* rmState[r] is the state of RM r
  tmState,               \* "init" or "done"
  tmPrepared,            \* the RMs the TM knows are prepared
  msgs                   \* every message ever sent
vars == <<rmState, tmState, tmPrepared, msgs>>

Messages == [type : {"Prepared"}, rm : RM] \cup [type : {"Commit", "Abort"}]

TPTypeOK ==
  /\ rmState \in [RM -> {"working", "prepared", "committed", "aborted"}]
  /\ tmState \in {"init", "done"}
  /\ tmPrepared \subseteq RM
  /\ msgs \subseteq Messages

TPInit ==
  /\ rmState = [r \in RM |-> "working"]
  /\ tmState = "init"
  /\ tmPrepared = {}
  /\ msgs = {}
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
TMRcvPrepared(r) ==
  /\ tmState = "init"
  /\ [type |-> "Prepared", rm |-> r] \in msgs
  /\ tmPrepared' = tmPrepared \cup {r}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<rmState, tmState, msgs>>

TMCommit ==
  /\ tmState = "init"
  /\ tmPrepared = RM
  /\ tmState' = "done"
  /\ msgs' = msgs \cup {[type |-> "Commit"]}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<rmState, tmPrepared>>

TMAbort ==
  /\ tmState = "init"
  /\ tmState' = "done"
  /\ msgs' = msgs \cup {[type |-> "Abort"]}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<rmState, tmPrepared>>

RMPrepare(r) ==
  /\ rmState[r] = "working"
  /\ rmState' = [rmState EXCEPT ![r] = "prepared"]
  /\ msgs' = msgs \cup {[type |-> "Prepared", rm |-> r]}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<tmState, tmPrepared>>

RMChooseToAbort(r) ==
  /\ rmState[r] = "working"
  /\ rmState' = [rmState EXCEPT ![r] = "aborted"]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<tmState, tmPrepared, msgs>>

RMRcvCommitMsg(r) ==
  /\ [type |-> "Commit"] \in msgs
  /\ rmState' = [rmState EXCEPT ![r] = "committed"]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<tmState, tmPrepared, msgs>>

RMRcvAbortMsg(r) ==
  /\ [type |-> "Abort"] \in msgs
  /\ rmState' = [rmState EXCEPT ![r] = "aborted"]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<tmState, tmPrepared, msgs>>
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
TPNext ==
  \/ TMCommit \/ TMAbort
  \/ \E r \in RM : TMRcvPrepared(r) \/ RMPrepare(r) \/ RMChooseToAbort(r)
                     \/ RMRcvCommitMsg(r) \/ RMRcvAbortMsg(r)
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
INSTANCE TCommit
=============================================================================

    Three pieces of notation are new:

    • S \cup T (or \union) is the set of elements in S or T or both.
    • S \subseteq T says every element of S is in T.
    • UNCHANGED <<a, b>> says each listed variable keeps its value. <<a, b>> is an ordered tuple; vars names the tuple of all four variables.

    msgs holds every message ever sent. A Prepared record goes from r to the TM. A Commit or Abort record goes from the TM to all RMs. The formulas with no primes at the start of an action are its enabling conditions: conditions on the first state of a step. Put them first. That is easier to read, and TLC often can't handle the action otherwise. Finally, INSTANCE TCommit imports TCommit's definitions, including TCConsistent, applied to this module's rmState.

    A trace where an RM aborts

    r2 aborts on its own, shown as a note because no message is sent. In a real system it would tell the TM, but that is an optimization the spec omits. r1 is prepared and can't abort itself; it has to wait to hear from the TM. Nothing makes the TM wait, because TMAbort is enabled whenever tmState = "init".

    This order is one of many. TLC, asked for any run with this outcome, returned a 5-state trace with TMAbort as the very first step, before anyone had done anything. That is also allowed. The diagram shows the order you would expect in practice, and the guards permit both.

    Check it with TLC

    INIT TPInit
NEXT TPNext
CONSTANT RM = {"r1", "r2", "r3"}
INVARIANT TPTypeOK
INVARIANT TCConsistent
CHECK_DEADLOCK FALSE

    Result: no error, 288 distinct states (1146 generated), the same count the lecture reports. The lecture uses that number as a test of your own definitions: paste one in, rerun, and if TLC finds no error and again 288 states, it's probably correct.

    Symmetry and model values

    All RMs play the same role. Swap r1 and r3 everywhere in a reachable state, as in the diagram, and you get another reachable state. Swap them in a whole behavior and you get another allowed behavior, so TLC needn't check both. A set with this property is a symmetry set. To use one, make its elements model values: special values not equal to anything else, written as bare identifiers. In the Toolbox you tick "Symmetry set". In a .cfg file you need a small wrapper module:

    ---- MODULE MCTwoPhase ----
EXTENDS TwoPhase, TLC
CONSTANTS r1, r2, r3
RMs == {r1, r2, r3}
Sym == Permutations(RMs)
====
    INIT TPInit
NEXT TPNext
CONSTANTS r1 = r1
          r2 = r2
          r3 = r3
          RM <- RMs
SYMMETRY Sym
INVARIANT TPTypeOK
INVARIANT TCConsistent
CHECK_DEADLOCK FALSE

    RM <- RMs replaces the constant by the module's definition RMs. Permutations comes from the TLC module. Result: no error, 80 distinct states examined, out of the same 288 reachable ones. Be careful: TLC may miss errors if you declare a symmetry set falsely. For now it's safe if the model values aren't used elsewhere; lesson 22 gives the full rule.

    Is it correct?

    The run above also checks TCConsistent: one RM can't commit while another aborts. TwoPhase actually does more than keep that invariant: it implements TCommit. That claim needs its own definition, given in lesson 26.

    Explore the TM's decision

    In the lab, "coordinator" is the common industry name for the TM, and participants A and B are RMs. It is an educational model, not TLC: it leaves out msgs and tmPrepared, treating "prepared" as instantly known. Prepare both RMs and crash the coordinator. No commit can happen, and nothing lets a prepared RM move. Agreement isn't violated, but the transaction is stuck, which is the starting point of lesson 22.

    Predict: both RMs are prepared and the TM has gone silent. Is it safe for an RM to abort on its own?

    No. The TM may already have sent Commit, and the other RM may have received it. Not having heard is no evidence that no decision exists. The spec gives a prepared RM no way to leave that state except by receiving a message.

    Worked architecture: reserve a seat and charge a wallet

    A purchase spans an inventory RM and a wallet RM. Preparing means each one promises it can honor a commit and holds what it needs: the seat, the funds. That promise is what makes prepared different from "looks available".

    Trace a hard run with the first diagram. Both prepare; the TM sends Commit; inventory receives it and marks the seat sold, and the wallet hasn't heard yet. For a while one RM is committed and another prepared. TCConsistent allows this, because it forbids only committed alongside aborted. If the wallet then gave up and aborted on a timeout, that would be the forbidden state: a seat sold and no money taken.

    In this spec, what lets the TM commit?

    Compare with the official specifications and Lamport's lecture page.

    Lecture 6: Two-phase commit

    A network can be one set that only grows.

    In TwoPhase, sending adds a record to msgs, and receiving removes nothing. That choice looks odd, and it's the most reusable modeling idea in lecture 6. This lesson explains why it works, then uses it to model loss, delay, and duplicates without new machinery.

    Follow both rows left to right. The top row is the obvious model: msgs is what's in transit, and receiving takes a message out. In the last column r1 has consumed the only Commit, so r2 can never get it. The bottom row is the lecture's: msgs is everything ever sent, and both RMs can read the same record.

    While you watch

    Find the part of lecture 6 titled "Sending Messages", and "A Simpler Method" right after it. Then stop at his explanation of TMRcvPrepared and predict what a second receipt of the same message does. Everything after the lecture's two points (one message, many readers; one reader, many receipts) is what this lesson adds.

    What the spec needs from the network

    A spec should describe only what the algorithm requires of message passing. Two-phase commit needs no ordering between messages, so a set is enough. Lamport compares two methods:

    • Simple: msgs is the set of messages in transit. Receiving removes one.
    • Simpler: msgs is the set of all messages ever sent. A receive action merely requires the message to be there.

    Here is what TLC finds for both, with three RMs, plus a repaired version of the first.

    Model of msgsDistinct statesCan all three RMs commit?
    Ever sent (the lecture's TwoPhase)288Yes
    In transit, one Commit record265No: ~\A r : committed holds as an invariant
    In transit, one addressed copy per RM415Yes: TLC finds the run, 11 states long

    The second row is a warning: TLC reports no error on TCConsistent, yet the model can't do its job. It's the kind of success to be suspicious of. The third row works, but it adds a to field and more states. It also says each copy is received at most once, which real networks don't promise.

    Receiving twice is harmless, here

    Since a message stays in msgs, TMRcvPrepared(r) stays enabled after it runs. A later step does tmPrepared' = tmPrepared \cup {r} with r already in the set. A set can't contain two copies of r, so nothing changes. A step that leaves every variable unchanged is a stuttering step, and it makes no difference; lesson 25 explains why such steps are always allowed. This matters because a real process can receive one message twice.

    The set is doing real work. In the diagram, the top row is TwoPhase, and the bottom row is a variant where the TM keeps a count instead and commits when the count reaches the number of RMs. TLC finds a TCConsistent violation in a 7-state trace, with two RMs: r1 prepares, the TM counts r1's message twice, commits, r1 commits, and r2, still working, aborts on its own. A message read twice made one vote look like two.

    Predict: does the grow-only set break when the TM's rule is "commit once I've seen any Prepared from r1 and r2"?

    No, and it's exactly what TMCommit with tmPrepared = RM says. A rule about which messages exist is automatically immune to duplicates. A rule about how many receipts happened isn't.

    Extending the model: the network's freedoms

    Nothing in msgs forces a process to act on a message. That one fact covers most of what a network can do, as long as you're checking safety (what can happen, not what must).

    Network behaviorIn the grow-only model
    DelayThe message sits in msgs while other steps happen
    ReorderingAny message in the set may be read next
    Duplicate deliveryThe receive action can run again
    LossThe receive action never runs for that message
    Timeout and retryA new message or attempt; nothing proves the first was lost

    A permanently lossy channel still satisfies every safety property, because nothing happens. Saying that something must eventually be delivered is a liveness assumption, the subject of lesson 29. And if an algorithm needs ordering, a set is too weak and you'd use a sequence, as lesson 30 does.

    Worked trace: the uncertain checkout response

    A checkout client sends request r7. The server creates an order, but the reply is lost, and the browser times out.

    At the X in the diagram the client knows nothing and the server has an order. A timeout only shows no reply arrived in time; it doesn't show the server did nothing. The dashed retry is what makes a double order possible. Here's the model. Attempts are records with both the logical request and the transport attempt:

    ------------------------------ MODULE CheckoutRetry ---------------------------
EXTENDS Integers
CONSTANTS Attempt,          \* the attempts the client may send for request r7
          KeyField          \* the message field the server deduplicates on
VARIABLES
  msgs,                     \* every attempt ever sent; never shrinks
  applied,                  \* what the server has recorded as already done
  orders,                   \* orders the server created
  replied,                  \* the server has sent a reply
  client                    \* "waiting" or "knows"
vars == <<msgs, applied, orders, replied, client>>

CInit == /\ msgs = {} /\ applied = {} /\ orders = 0
         /\ replied = FALSE /\ client = "waiting"

\* First try, or a retry after a timeout. Nothing forces a reply to come first.
Send(a) == /\ client = "waiting"
           /\ [req |-> "r7", try |-> a] \notin msgs
           /\ msgs' = msgs \cup {[req |-> "r7", try |-> a]}
           /\ UNCHANGED <<applied, orders, replied, client>>

\* The client learns the result only if it reads a reply.
Hear == /\ replied
        /\ client' = "knows"
        /\ UNCHANGED <<msgs, applied, orders, replied>>

\* Creates an order unless this message's key is recorded. Delivery leaves m
\* in msgs, so m can be delivered again; one never delivered has been lost.
Deliver ==
  \E m \in msgs :
    /\ m[KeyField] \notin applied
    /\ orders < 2
    /\ orders' = orders + 1
    /\ applied' = applied \cup {m[KeyField]}
    /\ replied' = TRUE
    /\ UNCHANGED <<msgs, client>>

\* A repeat of work already done: just send the reply again.
Repeat ==
  \E m \in msgs :
    /\ m[KeyField] \in applied
    /\ replied' = TRUE
    /\ UNCHANGED <<msgs, applied, orders, client>>

CNext == \/ \E a \in Attempt : Send(a)
         \/ Deliver \/ Repeat \/ Hear

OneOrder == orders <= 1
KnowsTruth == client = "knows" => orders >= 1
=============================================================================
    INIT CInit
NEXT CNext
CONSTANTS Attempt = {"e1", "e2"}
          KeyField = "req"
INVARIANT OneOrder
INVARIANT KnowsTruth
CHECK_DEADLOCK FALSE

    The constant KeyField picks what the server deduplicates on. m[KeyField] works because a record is a function. With KeyField = "req", TLC reports no error, 10 distinct states. With KeyField = "try", OneOrder is violated in 5 states: send e1, send e2, deliver each, two orders. The retry looks like a new purchase because its transport identity is new.

    Predict: the client gives every retry a fresh request ID. Is it protected?

    No. That is the "try" run again: a fresh ID makes each retry a distinct purchase. The ID has to survive the ambiguous response, so it must belong to the customer's intent, not to the attempt.

    In TwoPhase, how is a lost message represented?

    Lecture 6: Two-phase commit

    Problem set 6: what a commit protocol promises, and what it doesn't.

    Lecture 6 turned TCommit into a protocol: records as messages, a grow-only set of messages as the network, and UNCHANGED for frames. These problems change TwoPhase the way real teams do, adding a business rule, a crash, a side effect, and see what breaks. They reuse functions and quantifiers from Sets, functions, and quantifiers, the agreement spec of Problem set 5, and TLC's deadlock check from lesson 9.

    Most modules here are the lesson's TwoPhase with a few lines changed, and they end with INSTANCE TCommit, so keep TCommit.tla from lesson 16 in the same folder. For trace lengths, run TLC with -workers 1.

    Problem 1●○○Travel booking

    A trip where the car is optional

    Draws on Two-phase commit and records, The transaction commit spec and Sets, functions, and quantifiers.

    A travel site sells trips: a flight, a hotel and a rental car, each booked in a different supplier's system. The booking service runs two-phase commit exactly as the TwoPhase spec in lesson 18 describes. It is the TM, and the three suppliers are RMs. Preparing means a supplier holds the seat, room or car. A product manager asks for a change: “The car is optional. If the car supplier can't confirm, book the trip without it.” A developer implements it with one line in TMCommit:

    TMCommit ==
  /\ tmState = "init"
  /\ {"flight", "hotel"} \subseteq tmPrepared   \* the car is optional
  /\ tmState' = "done"
  /\ msgs' = msgs \cup {[type |-> "Commit"]}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<rmState, tmPrepared>>

    Everything else is the lesson's TwoPhase, renamed PSl6_Booking. The config uses CONSTANT RM = {"flight", "hotel", "car"}, the invariants TPTypeOK and TCConsistent, and CHECK_DEADLOCK FALSE.

    1. Run the unchanged TwoPhase with these three RMs first. What do you expect for the state count, and why?
    2. Make the change and run TLC. Explain the trace.
    3. Add this invariant, which says that an RM commits only after it prepared, and run again with it as the only invariant besides TPTypeOK. What does TLC find? Why does the lesson's TwoPhase get away with no guard in RMRcvCommitMsg? 
      CommitAfterPrepare == \A r \in RM : rmState[r] = "committed"
                         => [type |-> "Prepared", rm |-> r] \in msgs
    4. Propose a design that meets the product manager's request and keeps TCConsistent true.

    Why can RMRcvCommitMsg in the lesson's spec omit a guard on rmState[r]?

    Hint

    Once the Commit message is in msgs, what can the car do while it is still working? Look at the guards of RMChooseToAbort and RMRcvCommitMsg.

    Solution

    (a) No error and 288 distinct states, the lesson's count. The RMs' names don't matter, only how many there are.

    (b) TLC reports Invariant TCConsistent is violated with an 8-state trace:

    The flight and hotel prepare and the TM records both. That is enough for the new guard, so the TM commits, and the flight receives Commit. The car never prepared, so RMChooseToAbort("car") is still enabled, and it aborts. One RM committed and another aborted, which TCommit forbids. In business terms this might even be the outcome the product manager wanted. But the spec claimed all or nothing for three RMs, and the code now does something else. The problem is the mismatch.

    (c) TLC reports Invariant CommitAfterPrepare is violated with a 7-state trace that ends in RMRcvCommitMsg("car"): the car, still working, receives Commit and becomes committed without ever having held a car. In the lesson's spec the invariant holds (TLC: no error, 288 states, module PSl6_BookingOrig), because a Commit message can only exist once every RM is in tmPrepared. RMRcvCommitMsg relies on TMCommit's guard. Change that guard and every receive action becomes wrong too, even though nobody touched it.

    (d) Make the transaction say what the business means. Run two-phase commit over RM = {"flight", "hotel"}, the parts that must succeed together. TLC: no error in 56 states. Then book the car as a separate step after the trip commits, and if that fails, tell the customer. If the car really must be all-or-nothing with the rest, it has to stay an RM, and the trip aborts when the car can't be held. Either way the spec and the code agree on which RMs share a fate.

    Problem 2●●○Databases

    Postgres prepared transactions and a dead coordinator

    Draws on Two-phase commit and records, Messages, failures, and retries and Your first spec through TLC.

    An app server writes an order to one Postgres database and a payment to another, using Postgres's own two-phase commit. On each database it runs PREPARE TRANSACTION 'tx42', then COMMIT PREPARED 'tx42' on both, or ROLLBACK PREPARED 'tx42'. A prepared transaction is stored on disk, survives a database restart, and keeps every lock it holds until one of those two commands arrives. If the app server's session drops before PREPARE TRANSACTION, Postgres rolls the transaction back. Meanwhile a nightly report session wants to update a row the payment locked.

    The model is TwoPhase with the app server as the TM and three changes. The TM can crash and stay down (TMCrash), and an RM can prepare only while the TM is up. A report variable models the waiting session. A Finished action marks the intended end, so that the deadlock check can stay on. A constant DBA picks what a database administrator may do by hand while the app server is down.

    The module (open to copy) 
    ---------------------------- MODULE PSl6_Prepared ----------------------------
CONSTANTS RM,            \* the Postgres databases in the transaction
          DBA            \* the DBA's rule: "never", "blind", or "checklog"
VARIABLES
  rmState,               \* rmState[r] is the state of r's transaction
  tmState,               \* the app server: "init", "done", or "down"
  tmPrepared,            \* the databases the app server knows are prepared
  msgs,                  \* every message ever sent
  report                 \* a session on "payments" blocked on a row lock
vars == <<rmState, tmState, tmPrepared, msgs, report>>

Messages == [type : {"Prepared"}, rm : RM] \cup [type : {"Commit", "Abort"}]

TypeOK ==
  /\ rmState \in [RM -> {"working", "prepared", "committed", "aborted"}]
  /\ tmState \in {"init", "done", "down"}
  /\ tmPrepared \subseteq RM
  /\ msgs \subseteq Messages
  /\ report \in {"waiting", "done"}

Init ==
  /\ rmState = [r \in RM |-> "working"]
  /\ tmState = "init"
  /\ tmPrepared = {}
  /\ msgs = {}
  /\ report = "waiting"
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
TMRcvPrepared(r) ==
  /\ tmState = "init"
  /\ [type |-> "Prepared", rm |-> r] \in msgs
  /\ tmPrepared' = tmPrepared \cup {r}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<rmState, tmState, msgs, report>>

TMCommit ==                                  \* COMMIT PREPARED on each database
  /\ tmState = "init"
  /\ tmPrepared = RM
  /\ tmState' = "done"
  /\ msgs' = msgs \cup {[type |-> "Commit"]}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<rmState, tmPrepared, report>>

TMAbort ==                                   \* ROLLBACK PREPARED on each database
  /\ tmState = "init"
  /\ tmState' = "done"
  /\ msgs' = msgs \cup {[type |-> "Abort"]}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<rmState, tmPrepared, report>>

TMCrash ==                                   \* the app server dies and stays down
  /\ tmState # "down"
  /\ tmState' = "down"
  /\ UNCHANGED <<rmState, tmPrepared, msgs, report>>

RMPrepare(r) ==                \* the app server's PREPARE TRANSACTION succeeds
  /\ tmState = "init"
  /\ rmState[r] = "working"
  /\ rmState' = [rmState EXCEPT ![r] = "prepared"]
  /\ msgs' = msgs \cup {[type |-> "Prepared", rm |-> r]}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<tmState, tmPrepared, report>>

RMChooseToAbort(r) ==          \* an error, or the app server's session is lost
  /\ rmState[r] = "working"
  /\ rmState' = [rmState EXCEPT ![r] = "aborted"]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<tmState, tmPrepared, msgs, report>>

RMRcvCommitMsg(r) ==
  /\ [type |-> "Commit"] \in msgs
  /\ rmState' = [rmState EXCEPT ![r] = "committed"]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<tmState, tmPrepared, msgs, report>>

RMRcvAbortMsg(r) ==
  /\ [type |-> "Abort"] \in msgs
  /\ rmState' = [rmState EXCEPT ![r] = "aborted"]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<tmState, tmPrepared, msgs, report>>

\* The report's UPDATE waits for the row lock until the transaction ends.
ReportRuns ==
  /\ report = "waiting"
  /\ rmState["payments"] \in {"committed", "aborted"}
  /\ report' = "done"
  /\ UNCHANGED <<rmState, tmState, tmPrepared, msgs>>

\* ROLLBACK PREPARED by hand while the app server is down. "blind": anything
\* still prepared. "checklog": only if the app server's log has no Commit.
DBARollback(r) ==
  /\ \/ DBA = "blind"
     \/ DBA = "checklog" /\ [type |-> "Commit"] \notin msgs
  /\ tmState = "down"
  /\ rmState[r] = "prepared"
  /\ rmState' = [rmState EXCEPT ![r] = "aborted"]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<tmState, tmPrepared, msgs, report>>

\* An intended stop: every transaction has ended and the report has run.
Finished ==
  /\ \A r \in RM : rmState[r] \in {"committed", "aborted"}
  /\ report = "done"
  /\ UNCHANGED vars
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
Next ==
  \/ TMCommit \/ TMAbort \/ TMCrash \/ ReportRuns \/ Finished
  \/ \E r \in RM : \/ TMRcvPrepared(r) \/ RMPrepare(r) \/ RMChooseToAbort(r)
                   \/ RMRcvCommitMsg(r) \/ RMRcvAbortMsg(r) \/ DBARollback(r)
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
INSTANCE TCommit
=============================================================================

    The config, with the deadlock check on:

    INIT Init
NEXT Next
CONSTANTS RM = {"orders", "payments"}
          DBA = "never"
INVARIANT TypeOK
INVARIANT TCConsistent
    1. Why is Finished needed for the deadlock check to mean anything here? (Compare the terminating counter in lesson 9.)
    2. Run TLC with DBA = "never". What does it report? Describe the final state in Postgres terms: what holds locks, and who waits?
    3. The on-call DBA's runbook says: “If the app server is down, run ROLLBACK PREPARED on anything still prepared.” Run with DBA = "blind". What breaks, and why can't the payments database alone tell the DBA what to do?
    4. Run with DBA = "checklog", where the DBA rolls back only if the app server's log contains no Commit decision. What does TLC report?

    Hint

    In TwoPhase, after the TM decides, RMRcvCommitMsg or RMRcvAbortMsg stays enabled forever, so TLC never sees a stop. Here, which states have no enabled action? For (c), remember that a message in msgs may never be received: that is how the model says it was lost.

    Solution

    (a) A run in which both transactions end and the report finishes is supposed to stop. Without Finished, TLC would report that intended stop as a deadlock, and you would have to turn the check off, which also hides the stops you care about. Finished is enabled exactly in the good final states and changes nothing, so any deadlock TLC reports is a state where work is left undone.

    (b) TLC reports Deadlock reached with a 4-state trace:

    Both databases prepared, and then the app server died before deciding. Each database holds a prepared tx42 with its row locks. Nothing in Postgres will resolve it: the protocol gives a prepared participant no step of its own. The report's UPDATE waits on the payment row, indefinitely. Postgres's documentation warns against leaving transactions prepared for long, because they also stop VACUUM from reclaiming storage. You can list them in the pg_prepared_xacts view. This is the blocking problem the lab in lesson 18 showed, now as a TLC trace.

    (c) TLC reports Invariant TCConsistent is violated with a 9-state trace. Both databases prepare, the app server commits and sends Commit, then crashes. Orders receives Commit and commits. Payments never gets its Commit (in the model, that message is never received), and the DBA, following the runbook, rolls it back. An order with no payment. From inside the payments database, “prepared and the coordinator is down” looks the same whether or not a Commit decision exists. The information the DBA needs is the decision, and that lives in the coordinator's log, not in this database.

    (d) No error and 194 distinct states, and no deadlock. If the log has no Commit, nobody can have committed, so a rollback is safe. If it does, the Commit message stays in msgs, and receiving it models the DBA running COMMIT PREPARED. Resolving a prepared transaction by hand is safe only with the decision in hand. Real transaction managers write their decision to durable storage before sending it, so that they, or a person, can finish the job after a crash.

    Problem 3●●○Messaging

    Receipt emails over an at-least-once queue

    Draws on Messages, failures, and retries, Two-phase commit and records and Sets, functions, and quantifiers.

    After an order commits, the order service publishes a “send receipt” message to a queue, and an email worker consumes it. The queue behaves like Amazon SQS standard queues: delivery is at least once, ordering is best effort, and a message that isn't acknowledged within its visibility timeout is delivered again. The model below uses the grow-only msgs from lesson 19. The constant Mode picks how the worker handles a delivery. emailed is the worker's table of orders it has emailed.

    The module (open to copy) 
    ----------------------------- MODULE PSl6_Receipts -----------------------------
EXTENDS Integers
CONSTANT Mode            \* how the email worker handles a delivery:
                         \* "naive", "atomic", or "twostep"
Orders == {"o1", "o2"}   \* o1 is placed before o2
Receipt(o) == [type |-> "receipt", order |-> o]
VARIABLES
  msgs,                  \* every message ever published to the queue
  sent,                  \* sent[o]: receipt emails sent for order o
  emailed                \* orders the worker's table records as emailed
vars == <<msgs, sent, emailed>>

TypeOK == /\ msgs \subseteq [type : {"receipt"}, order : Orders]
          /\ sent \in [Orders -> 0..2]
          /\ emailed \subseteq Orders

Init == /\ msgs = {}
        /\ sent = [o \in Orders |-> 0]
        /\ emailed = {}

\* The order service publishes after each order commits, o1 first.
Publish(o) == /\ Receipt(o) \notin msgs
              /\ o = "o2" => Receipt("o1") \in msgs
              /\ msgs' = msgs \cup {Receipt(o)}
              /\ UNCHANGED <<sent, emailed>>

SendEmail(o) == sent' = [sent EXCEPT ![o] = sent[o] + 1]

\* The queue hands o's receipt message to the worker (again, possibly).
Deliver(o) ==
  /\ Receipt(o) \in msgs
  /\ sent[o] < 2                          \* keeps the model finite
  /\ \/ /\ Mode = "naive"
        /\ SendEmail(o)
        /\ UNCHANGED emailed
     \/ /\ Mode = "atomic"                \* check, send, record: one step
        /\ o \notin emailed
        /\ SendEmail(o)
        /\ emailed' = emailed \cup {o}
     \/ /\ Mode = "twostep"               \* check and send; record later
        /\ o \notin emailed
        /\ SendEmail(o)
        /\ UNCHANGED emailed
  /\ UNCHANGED msgs

\* twostep only: the worker writes "emailed" after the provider accepts.
Record(o) == /\ Mode = "twostep"
             /\ sent[o] > 0
             /\ o \notin emailed
             /\ emailed' = emailed \cup {o}
             /\ UNCHANGED <<msgs, sent>>

Next == \E o \in Orders : Publish(o) \/ Deliver(o) \/ Record(o)

OneEmail == \A o \in Orders : sent[o] =< 1
InOrder  == sent["o2"] > 0 => sent["o1"] > 0
=============================================================================

    The config for the first run:

    INIT Init
NEXT Next
CONSTANT Mode = "naive"
INVARIANT TypeOK
INVARIANT OneEmail
CHECK_DEADLOCK FALSE

    Notice what is not in the module: no action duplicates, delays or reorders messages. Deliver(o) only requires the message to be in msgs.

    1. Run with Mode = "naive". Where in the module does the duplicate come from?
    2. Run with Mode = "atomic". What does TLC report? What does putting the check, the email and the record in one step claim about the real worker?
    3. Run with Mode = "twostep", the honest version: the worker checks the table, calls the email API, and records the order afterwards. What happens?
    4. With Mode = "atomic", add INVARIANT InOrder. What does TLC find? Does a receipt service need to care?

    Which of these can't happen in this model of the queue?

    Hint

    Look for what removes a message from msgs, or disables Deliver(o) once it has run. In "twostep", which action has to happen between the two deliveries to prevent the second email?

    Solution

    (a) TLC reports Invariant OneEmail is violated with a 4-state trace: Publish("o1"), Deliver("o1"), Deliver("o1"). Nothing removes a message from msgs, so Deliver("o1") stays enabled. That is the lesson's point about one reader and many receipts, with an effect, an email, that isn't harmless to repeat. You got duplicate delivery without writing a line for it.

    (b) No error, 7 distinct states. The second delivery finds "o1" \in emailed and is disabled. But the step claims that checking the table, calling the email API, and writing the table happen as one indivisible event. A database transaction can make the check and the write atomic. It can't include a call to an external email service.

    (c) TLC reports OneEmail violated, again in 4 states: Publish, then Deliver("o1") twice, before Record("o1") ever runs.

    In SQS terms, the worker took longer than the visibility timeout, or crashed after sending and before recording, and the queue handed the message to another delivery. Your table can make duplicates rarer. It can't rule them out, because the gap between the external effect and the record is real. The usual way out is to give the email provider an idempotency key such as the order id and let it deduplicate, or to accept that a customer may occasionally get two receipts. Which one is right is a product decision, and the model has made it a visible one.

    (d) TLC reports InOrder violated with a 4-state trace: Publish("o1"), Publish("o2"), Deliver("o2"). The set model includes reordering for free, which matches the queue's best-effort ordering. Receipts don't need order, so you'd delete the invariant. A consumer that applies successive updates to the same record would care. It would need a sequence and an ordered channel, which the course models with the alternating bit protocol in Lecture 9.

    Problem 4 · Synthesis●●●Databases

    Reserving stock in two warehouses

    Draws on Two-phase commit and records, Messages, failures, and retries, Sets, functions, and quantifiers, Actions, guards, and frames, and the schema-agreement problem in Problem set 5.

    An online shop fulfils an order from two warehouses, east and west, one unit from each. Each warehouse's inventory database is an RM in two-phase commit, and the order service is the TM. Preparing reserves a unit: it leaves the shelf count and is held for this order. Committing ships the held unit. Aborting must cancel the reservation and put the unit back. A developer adds a stock variable to TwoPhase, with these changes:

    RMPrepare(r) ==
  /\ rmState[r] = "working"
  /\ stock[r] > 0
  /\ rmState' = [rmState EXCEPT ![r] = "prepared"]
  /\ stock' = [stock EXCEPT ![r] = stock[r] - 1]
  /\ msgs' = msgs \cup {[type |-> "Prepared", rm |-> r]}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<tmState, tmPrepared>>

RMRcvAbortMsg(r) ==
  /\ [type |-> "Abort"] \in msgs
  /\ rmState' = [rmState EXCEPT ![r] = "aborted"]
  /\ stock' = [stock EXCEPT ![r] = stock[r] + 1]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<tmState, tmPrepared, msgs>>

    Every other action has stock in its UNCHANGED list, TypeOK requires stock \in [RM -> 0..Stock0] with Stock0 == 1, and the module ends with INSTANCE TCommit. The fixed module is in the solution; the developer's version differs only in RMRcvAbortMsg.

    1. Write Conservation: for every warehouse, the units on the shelf plus the units held or shipped for this order equal Stock0. A helper Held(w), which is 1 when w is prepared or committed and 0 otherwise, makes it short.
    2. Run TLC with CONSTANT RM = {"east", "west"}, listing INVARIANT Conservation first, then TypeOK and TCConsistent, with CHECK_DEADLOCK FALSE. Explain the trace.
    3. Compare with the schema-agreement problem in Problem set 5, where Agreement and ReadersReady were the requirements. Does TCConsistent catch this bug?
    4. A reviewer suggests releasing stock only if rmState[r] # "working". Try it. Then write a fix that works, and check it with two and with three warehouses.

    Does TCConsistent catch the bug?

    Hint

    Which RMs can receive an Abort message? In TwoPhase, receiving the same message twice was harmless because setting rmState[r] to "aborted" again changes nothing. Is stock[r] + 1 like that? The release should depend on what this particular step undoes.

    Solution

    (a)

    Held(w) == IF rmState[w] \in {"prepared", "committed"} THEN 1 ELSE 0

Conservation == \A w \in RM : stock[w] + Held(w) = Stock0

    (b) TLC reports Invariant Conservation is violated with a 3-state trace: TMAbort, then RMRcvAbortMsg("east") while east is still working. East never reserved anything, but the release adds a unit, so its shelf shows 2. TLC checks the invariants in the order the config lists them. With TypeOK listed first it reports TypeOK violated in the same 3 states, since 2 isn't in 0..Stock0. In TwoPhase, an Abort can reach any RM, prepared or not, and any number of times. Those receives were safe only because they had no effect beyond setting rmState.

    (c) No. TCConsistent mentions only rmState, and this change never affects rmState. With shelf counts bounded at 4, TLC confirms it: no error in 245 states. The decision was abort and nobody committed, so agreement holds, and the inventory is wrong anyway. In the schema problem of Problem set 5, agreement wasn't enough either, and ReadersReady was the requirement that mattered. Here it is Conservation. A commit protocol guarantees agreement on the decision, and the effects you attach to the decision need their own invariant.

    (d) The reviewer's guard isn't enough. TLC finds a 4-state trace: TMAbort, east aborts on its own with RMChooseToAbort, then receives Abort and releases a unit it never reserved.

    A duplicate delivery to a prepared warehouse is a third route: prepare, TM aborts, receive Abort (correct release), receive it again (second release). The fix releases exactly when this step undoes a reservation, that is, when the RM is prepared:

    ------------------------------ MODULE PSl6_StockFixed ------------------------------
EXTENDS Integers
CONSTANT RM              \* the warehouses; the order needs one unit from each
Stock0 == 1              \* units each warehouse has on the shelf at the start
VARIABLES rmState, tmState, tmPrepared, msgs,
          stock          \* stock[w]: units on the shelf at w, not reserved
vars == <<rmState, tmState, tmPrepared, msgs, stock>>

Messages == [type : {"Prepared"}, rm : RM] \cup [type : {"Commit", "Abort"}]

TypeOK ==
  /\ rmState \in [RM -> {"working", "prepared", "committed", "aborted"}]
  /\ tmState \in {"init", "done"}
  /\ tmPrepared \subseteq RM
  /\ msgs \subseteq Messages
  /\ stock \in [RM -> 0..Stock0]

Init ==
  /\ rmState = [r \in RM |-> "working"]
  /\ tmState = "init"
  /\ tmPrepared = {}
  /\ msgs = {}
  /\ stock = [r \in RM |-> Stock0]
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
TMRcvPrepared(r) ==
  /\ tmState = "init"
  /\ [type |-> "Prepared", rm |-> r] \in msgs
  /\ tmPrepared' = tmPrepared \cup {r}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<rmState, tmState, msgs, stock>>

TMCommit ==
  /\ tmState = "init"
  /\ tmPrepared = RM
  /\ tmState' = "done"
  /\ msgs' = msgs \cup {[type |-> "Commit"]}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<rmState, tmPrepared, stock>>

TMAbort ==
  /\ tmState = "init"
  /\ tmState' = "done"
  /\ msgs' = msgs \cup {[type |-> "Abort"]}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<rmState, tmPrepared, stock>>

\* Prepare = reserve: take a unit off the shelf and hold it for this order.
RMPrepare(r) ==
  /\ rmState[r] = "working"
  /\ stock[r] > 0
  /\ rmState' = [rmState EXCEPT ![r] = "prepared"]
  /\ stock' = [stock EXCEPT ![r] = stock[r] - 1]
  /\ msgs' = msgs \cup {[type |-> "Prepared", rm |-> r]}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<tmState, tmPrepared>>

RMChooseToAbort(r) ==
  /\ rmState[r] = "working"
  /\ rmState' = [rmState EXCEPT ![r] = "aborted"]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<tmState, tmPrepared, msgs, stock>>

\* Commit = ship the held unit. The shelf count doesn't change.
RMRcvCommitMsg(r) ==
  /\ [type |-> "Commit"] \in msgs
  /\ rmState' = [rmState EXCEPT ![r] = "committed"]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<tmState, tmPrepared, msgs, stock>>

\* Abort = cancel the reservation and put the unit back on the shelf.
RMRcvAbortMsg(r) ==
  /\ [type |-> "Abort"] \in msgs
  /\ rmState' = [rmState EXCEPT ![r] = "aborted"]
  /\ stock' = IF rmState[r] = "prepared"
                THEN [stock EXCEPT ![r] = stock[r] + 1]
                ELSE stock
  /\ UNCHANGED <<tmState, tmPrepared, msgs>>
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
Next ==
  \/ TMCommit \/ TMAbort
  \/ \E r \in RM : TMRcvPrepared(r) \/ RMPrepare(r) \/ RMChooseToAbort(r)
                     \/ RMRcvCommitMsg(r) \/ RMRcvAbortMsg(r)
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
INSTANCE TCommit

Held(w) == IF rmState[w] \in {"prepared", "committed"} THEN 1 ELSE 0

\* Every unit is on the shelf, or held or shipped for this order.
Conservation == \A w \in RM : stock[w] + Held(w) = Stock0
=============================================================================

    TLC finds no error: 56 distinct states with two warehouses and 288 with three. These are exactly TwoPhase's counts for two and three RMs. In the fixed model, stock[w] always equals Stock0 - Held(w), which is what Conservation says, so the extra variable adds no states. When adding a variable doesn't change the count, it is a function of the others, and it is worth asking whether you need to store it at all. The general lesson: an effect attached to a receive action must be idempotent, because the network may deliver the message to any RM, any number of times.

    Lecture 7: Paxos commit

    Two majorities always share someone, and that's where evidence survives.

    Two-phase commit depends on one TM remembering the decision. The fix in lecture 7 is to spread that memory over several processes and count on overlapping groups. This lesson teaches the set operators the lecture uses, and the quorum idea, on a simpler example: copies of a stored value.

    Two sets of acceptors, each a majority of three. \cap is the part in both, and in the diagram that's a2. An acceptor is just a process whose job is to record votes; lesson 22 says what they vote on. Whichever two majorities you pick, some acceptor is in both.

    While you watch

    The lecture gets to these operators while it reads module PaxosCommit, so here they come first. Listen for the ASSUME statement and the conjunct about Majority, which is the most important line in this lesson. He also defines Ballot \ {0} and two set constructors. This lesson adds the storage example and the read and write set lab, which aren't in the lecture; the algorithm itself is in lesson 22.

    The set operators

    ExpressionMeaningExample that TLC evaluated as true
    S \cap TElements in both (also \intersect){"a1","a2"} \cap {"a2","a3"} = {"a2"}
    S \ TElements of S not in T(10..20) \ (1..14) = 15..20
    SUBSET SThe set of all subsets of SSUBSET {"a","b"} = { {}, {"a"}, {"b"}, {"a","b"} }
    {v \in S : P}The elements of S satisfying P{n \in 1..6 : n > 4} = {5, 6}
    {e : v \in S}All values of e as v ranges over S{n^2 : n \in 1..3} = {1, 4, 9}
    Cardinality(S)Number of elements, from module FiniteSetsCardinality(SUBSET {"a1","a2","a3"}) = 8

    Don't confuse SUBSET S, a set of sets, with T \subseteq S, a true-or-false statement from lesson 18. Nat, from module Integers, is the set of natural numbers. The two constructors look alike: if the colon has a set on the left, it filters; if on the right, it maps.

    Why majorities overlap

    With the set operators you can state the property directly, rather than counting:

    Majority == {Q \in SUBSET Acceptor : Cardinality(Q) = 2}   \* with 3 acceptors
\A MS1, MS2 \in Majority : MS1 \cap MS2 # {}               \* the property that matters

    Each row of the diagram is one set in Majority, and each column an acceptor. Pick any two green rows: some column is filled in both. Now look at the red row, {a3}. It shares no column with {a1, a2}. A set of "majorities" containing it fails the property even though every row looks like a reasonable group. Paxos Commit assumes only the property, not a count. You will see TLC break that assumption on purpose.

    The general rule for N replicas: if a read set has R members and a write set has W, then R + W > N forces overlap, because R + W elements can't fit into N places without sharing one. That is a statement about sets and nothing more.

    Worked architecture: a replicated product price

    A price is stored on replicas A, B, and C, all at version 7. A write of version 8 counts as acknowledged once 2 replicas (W = 2) store it. A read afterward asks R replicas and keeps the newer version it hears.

    ----------------------------- MODULE PriceQuorum ----------------------------
EXTENDS Integers, FiniteSets
CONSTANTS Replica, W, R          \* write-set size and read-set size
VARIABLES stored, acked, result  \* result: what a read returned (0 = none yet)
vars == <<stored, acked, result>>

WriteSets == {Q \in SUBSET Replica : Cardinality(Q) = W}
ReadSets  == {Q \in SUBSET Replica : Cardinality(Q) = R}

PInit == /\ stored = [n \in Replica |-> 7]
         /\ acked = FALSE
         /\ result = 0

Store(n) == /\ stored' = [stored EXCEPT ![n] = 8]
            /\ UNCHANGED <<acked, result>>

Ack == /\ \E Q \in WriteSets : \A n \in Q : stored[n] = 8
       /\ acked' = TRUE
       /\ UNCHANGED <<stored, result>>

\* A read after the ack hears from one read set and keeps the newer version.
Read == /\ acked
        /\ result = 0
        /\ \E Q \in ReadSets :
             result' = IF \E n \in Q : stored[n] = 8 THEN 8 ELSE 7
        /\ UNCHANGED <<stored, acked>>

PNext == Ack \/ Read \/ \E n \in Replica : Store(n)

SeesAckedWrite == result \in {0, 8}
=============================================================================
    INIT PInit
NEXT PNext
CONSTANTS Replica = {"A", "B", "C"}
          W = 2
          R = 2
INVARIANT SeesAckedWrite
CHECK_DEADLOCK FALSE

    With R = 2: no error, 16 distinct states. With R = 1: SeesAckedWrite is violated in a 5-state trace.

    In that trace (the diagram) version 8 reaches C and A, the write is acknowledged, and a read asks only B. Nothing has failed. No machine lost data or broke a local rule, and the client still reads the old price. With R = 2, any read set contains A or C, as the last column shows.

    Find the worst-case intersection

    Predict: N = 5, R = 2, W = 3. Can a read miss every written replica?

    Yes. Write to {A, B, C}; read from {D, E}. Their intersection is empty, and TLC confirms such a pair exists. With R = 3, it confirms that every pair of size-3 sets intersects.

    The model is deliberately easy: one writer, one write, and a version order given in advance. Overlap gives you a place to find evidence. It doesn't say how to interpret it. With two concurrent writers, "the newer version" needs a definition, and overlap alone doesn't supply one. Likewise, if a replica acknowledges before storing durably, its restart can erase what the overlap was counting on.

    From stored prices to votes

    Replace the pieces. The write set becomes a majority of acceptors that voted for an outcome. The read becomes a new leader asking a majority what they've voted for, because it suspects that the old leader died. Every majority it asks contains someone who voted, so if an outcome was already decided, the new leader can find out. That one sentence is the core of lesson 22: the leader can take over without the old leader's memory, because the memory was in the overlap.

    What does Paxos Commit's Majority assumption require?

    Predict: R + W > N, so is every read correct, whatever else happens?

    No. You still need to know which versions replies represent, how a read chooses, how concurrent writes are ordered, when a write completes, and what survives a crash. Intersection is a place to look; it isn't an answer.

    Read a precise memory specification in Specifying Systems, and compare with the official examples.

    Lecture 7: Paxos commit

    Paxos Commit keeps the decision alive when the transaction manager doesn't.

    In two-phase commit, one process holds the decision. If it stops, prepared RMs wait forever. Lecture 7 opens with that problem, shows why the obvious fix is wrong, and then reads the spec of Paxos Commit: a real algorithm by Jim Gray and Leslie Lamport, and a tour of the last TLA+ constructs you need.

    This is a TLC trace of TwoPhase plus one TMCrash action, with two RMs. It takes 4 states to reach the bottom of the diagram. There, r1 and r2 are prepared, and the only actions that move a prepared RM need a Commit or Abort message that only the TM can send. Checking the property "once blocked, no step changes anything" gives no error over 112 distinct states. TCConsistent holds as well: nothing is wrong except that nothing happens.

    While you watch

    Lamport states plainly that the lecture is about TLA+ and that the paper explains the algorithm, so he goes through the operators and doesn't explain the protocol. This lesson does the reverse order: first the idea, with diagrams, then the operators. Follow the spec alongside him at the Phase2a definition. Pause at the model values and decide whether Acceptor can be a symmetry set before he answers. lesson 23 covers one Paxos instance by itself.

    The fix that fails

    The textbook answer is a backup TM that takes over when the primary fails. It's simple to build and to test. Then one day the primary decides to commit and pauses. The backup concludes the primary has died.

    This run came from TwoPhase plus a BackupAbort action, with two RMs: TLC reports a TCConsistent violation in a 9-state trace, drawn above. The backup can't distinguish slow from dead, and both TMs' messages are valid. Testing won't easily catch this, because it needs a rare pause. Finding it needs a spec.

    The idea: several acceptors remember each RM's vote

    Paxos Commit replaces the TM's one memory with a set of acceptors, with the overlap property from lesson 21. It runs one separate decision, called an instance, per RM, whose outcome is either "prepared" or "aborted". The field ins in each message says which RM's instance it belongs to.

    A leader is any process that believes it's in charge. The spec doesn't care who it is, or how many there are; several may act at once. Here's the normal case, for one RM's instance.

    r1 votes by sending a phase2a message in ballot 0, the ballot number reserved for the RM itself. Each acceptor records its vote and announces it in phase2b. Once a majority voted the same value in the same ballot, that value is chosen. a3 was slow and it didn't matter. When every instance has chosen "prepared", a leader may send Commit; if any chose "aborted", it may send Abort. No single process has to survive.

    What a new ballot does

    If an RM's vote seems stuck, a leader starts a higher ballot (Phase1a). An acceptor receiving that message promises to ignore lower ballots by raising mbal, and reports its last vote (Phase1b). Having heard from a majority, the leader sends one value (Phase2a):

    • If anyone reported a vote, it sends the value from the highest ballot reported.
    • If nobody did, it sends "aborted". An RM with no recorded vote can't be assumed prepared.

    On the left, a1 and a2 voted "prepared" in ballot 0, so it's chosen. A leader in ballot 1 hears from a2 and a3. The overlap is a2, whose report forces the leader to send "prepared" too. So the old result survives without the old leader. On the right, no such acceptor exists, and the leader hears nothing: this is the experiment at the end of this lesson.

    The spec's new constructs

    Maximum(S) == IF S = {} THEN -1
                        ELSE CHOOSE n \in S : \A m \in S : n >= m

    CHOOSE. CHOOSE v \in S : P is some value v in S satisfying P. If there are several, TLA+ doesn't say which; if none, its value is unspecified and TLC reports an error. It isn't random. Like any expression, it equals itself, so TLC gets the same answer every time. Hence x' \in 1..99 allows 99 next values and x' = CHOOSE i \in 1..99 : TRUE allows just one. Use it when exactly one v qualifies, as in Maximum, or when the larger expression doesn't depend on which you get. Here's the second kind:

    Phase2a(bal, r) ==
  /\ ~\E m \in msgs : /\ m.type = "phase2a"
                      /\ m.bal = bal
                      /\ m.ins = r
  /\ \E MS \in Majority :
       LET mset == {m \in msgs : /\ m.type = "phase1b"
                                 /\ m.ins = r
                                 /\ m.mbal = bal
                                 /\ m.acc \in MS}
           maxbal == Maximum({m.bal : m \in mset})
           val == IF maxbal = -1
                    THEN "aborted"
                    ELSE (CHOOSE m \in mset : m.bal = maxbal).val
       IN  /\ \A ac \in MS : \E m \in mset : m.acc = ac
           /\ Send([type |-> "phase2a", ins |-> r, bal |-> bal, val |-> val])
  /\ UNCHANGED <<rmState, aState>>

    LET-IN makes definitions local to one expression. mset filters and {m.bal : m \in mset} maps, the two constructors from lesson 21. Several messages in mset may have the top ballot, so CHOOSE may have several choices, but the lecture points out that in any reachable state they all have the same val. Lamport calls this the most subtle part of the algorithm.

    Nested EXCEPT. The acceptor state is aState[r][a], a record per acceptor per instance, with fields mbal, bal, and val.

    aState' = [aState EXCEPT ![m.ins][acc].mbal = m.bal,
                         ![m.ins][acc].bal  = m.bal,
                         ![m.ins][acc].val  = m.val]

    Read it as three programming assignments to aState[m.ins][acc]'s fields. The first form abbreviates nested EXCEPTs, one per level. Lamport's advice is to remember the idiom rather than decode it.

    Show the complete module that was checked
    ----------------------------- MODULE PaxosCommit ----------------------------
EXTENDS Integers

Maximum(S) == IF S = {} THEN -1
                        ELSE CHOOSE n \in S : \A m \in S : n >= m

CONSTANTS RM,        \* The set of resource managers
          Acceptor,  \* The set of acceptors
          Majority,  \* The sets of acceptors that count as a majority
          Ballot     \* The set of ballot numbers

ASSUME /\ Ballot \subseteq Nat
       /\ 0 \in Ballot
       /\ Majority \subseteq SUBSET Acceptor
       /\ \A MS1, MS2 \in Majority : MS1 \cap MS2 # {}

Messages ==
  [type : {"phase1a"}, ins : RM, bal : Ballot \ {0}]
    \cup
  [type : {"phase1b"}, ins : RM, mbal : Ballot, bal : Ballot \cup {-1},
   val : {"prepared", "aborted", "none"}, acc : Acceptor]
    \cup
  [type : {"phase2a"}, ins : RM, bal : Ballot, val : {"prepared", "aborted"}]
    \cup
  [type : {"phase2b"}, acc : Acceptor, ins : RM, bal : Ballot,
   val : {"prepared", "aborted"}]
    \cup
  [type : {"Commit", "Abort"}]
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
VARIABLES rmState, aState, msgs

PCTypeOK ==
  /\ rmState \in [RM -> {"working", "prepared", "committed", "aborted"}]
  /\ aState \in [RM -> [Acceptor -> [mbal : Ballot,
                                     bal  : Ballot \cup {-1},
                                     val  : {"prepared", "aborted", "none"}]]]
  /\ msgs \subseteq Messages

PCInit ==
  /\ rmState = [r \in RM |-> "working"]
  /\ aState = [r \in RM |->
                 [ac \in Acceptor |-> [mbal |-> 0, bal |-> -1, val |-> "none"]]]
  /\ msgs = {}

Send(m) == msgs' = msgs \cup {m}
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Resource manager actions. RMs vote by sending a ballot 0 phase 2a message.
RMPrepare(r) ==
  /\ rmState[r] = "working"
  /\ rmState' = [rmState EXCEPT ![r] = "prepared"]
  /\ Send([type |-> "phase2a", ins |-> r, bal |-> 0, val |-> "prepared"])
  /\ UNCHANGED aState

RMChooseToAbort(r) ==
  /\ rmState[r] = "working"
  /\ rmState' = [rmState EXCEPT ![r] = "aborted"]
  /\ Send([type |-> "phase2a", ins |-> r, bal |-> 0, val |-> "aborted"])
  /\ UNCHANGED aState

RMRcvCommitMsg(r) ==
  /\ [type |-> "Commit"] \in msgs
  /\ rmState' = [rmState EXCEPT ![r] = "committed"]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<aState, msgs>>

RMRcvAbortMsg(r) ==
  /\ [type |-> "Abort"] \in msgs
  /\ rmState' = [rmState EXCEPT ![r] = "aborted"]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<aState, msgs>>
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Leader actions: any process that believes it is the leader may do these.
Phase1a(bal, r) ==
  /\ Send([type |-> "phase1a", ins |-> r, bal |-> bal])
  /\ UNCHANGED <<rmState, aState>>

Phase2a(bal, r) ==
  /\ ~\E m \in msgs : /\ m.type = "phase2a"
                      /\ m.bal = bal
                      /\ m.ins = r
  /\ \E MS \in Majority :
       LET mset == {m \in msgs : /\ m.type = "phase1b"
                                 /\ m.ins = r
                                 /\ m.mbal = bal
                                 /\ m.acc \in MS}
           maxbal == Maximum({m.bal : m \in mset})
           val == IF maxbal = -1
                    THEN "aborted"
                    ELSE (CHOOSE m \in mset : m.bal = maxbal).val
       IN  /\ \A ac \in MS : \E m \in mset : m.acc = ac
           /\ Send([type |-> "phase2a", ins |-> r, bal |-> bal, val |-> val])
  /\ UNCHANGED <<rmState, aState>>

PCDecide ==
  /\ LET Decided(r, v) ==
           \E b \in Ballot, MS \in Majority :
             \A ac \in MS : [type |-> "phase2b", ins |-> r,
                             bal |-> b, val |-> v, acc |-> ac] \in msgs
     IN  \/ /\ \A r \in RM : Decided(r, "prepared")
            /\ Send([type |-> "Commit"])
         \/ /\ \E r \in RM : Decided(r, "aborted")
            /\ Send([type |-> "Abort"])
  /\ UNCHANGED <<rmState, aState>>
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Acceptor actions.
Phase1b(acc) ==
  \E m \in msgs :
    /\ m.type = "phase1a"
    /\ aState[m.ins][acc].mbal < m.bal
    /\ aState' = [aState EXCEPT ![m.ins][acc].mbal = m.bal]
    /\ Send([type |-> "phase1b", ins |-> m.ins, mbal |-> m.bal,
             bal |-> aState[m.ins][acc].bal, val |-> aState[m.ins][acc].val,
             acc |-> acc])
    /\ UNCHANGED rmState

Phase2b(acc) ==
  /\ \E m \in msgs :
       /\ m.type = "phase2a"
       /\ aState[m.ins][acc].mbal <= m.bal
       /\ aState' = [aState EXCEPT ![m.ins][acc].mbal = m.bal,
                                   ![m.ins][acc].bal  = m.bal,
                                   ![m.ins][acc].val  = m.val]
       /\ Send([type |-> "phase2b", ins |-> m.ins, bal |-> m.bal,
                val |-> m.val, acc |-> acc])
  /\ UNCHANGED rmState
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
PCNext ==
  \/ \E r \in RM : \/ RMPrepare(r) \/ RMChooseToAbort(r)
                   \/ RMRcvCommitMsg(r) \/ RMRcvAbortMsg(r)
  \/ \E bal \in Ballot \ {0}, r \in RM : Phase1a(bal, r) \/ Phase2a(bal, r)
  \/ PCDecide
  \/ \E acc \in Acceptor : Phase1b(acc) \/ Phase2b(acc)
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
TC == INSTANCE TCommit
TCConsistent == TC!TCConsistent
=============================================================================

    This was adapted from the official example to the lecture's names and its Maximum. The lecture imports with INSTANCE; here TC == INSTANCE TCommit keeps TCommit's Decide from clashing, so the leader's action is called PCDecide.

    Check a small model

    The lecture's model is the smallest that could reveal a non-trivial error:

    ---- MODULE MCPaxosCommit ----
EXTENDS PaxosCommit, TLC
CONSTANTS a1, a2, a3, r1, r2
Acceptors == {a1, a2, a3}
RMs == {r1, r2}
Majorities == {{a1, a2}, {a1, a3}, {a2, a3}}
Sym == Permutations(Acceptors) \cup Permutations(RMs)
====
    INIT PCInit
NEXT PCNext
CONSTANTS a1 = a1
          a2 = a2
          a3 = a3
          r1 = r1
          r2 = r2
          Acceptor <- Acceptors
          RM <- RMs
          Majority <- Majorities
          Ballot = {0, 1}
SYMMETRY Sym
INVARIANT PCTypeOK
INVARIANT TCConsistent
CHECK_DEADLOCK FALSE

    Can Acceptor be a symmetry set when a1, a2, a3 appear in the value of Majority? Yes, because that expression is symmetric: swap a1 and a3, and you get the same set. This is the rule promised in lesson 18: elements of a symmetry set may be used in another constant's value only if that expression is symmetric in them, and those elements, or any constant assigned them, must not appear in a CHOOSE. The CHOOSEs here range over messages and numbers, not over RM or Acceptor.
