    Result: no error, 119,992 distinct states (1,545,109 generated), with PCTypeOK and TCConsistent invariant, in line with the lecture's figure. Time and space grow exponentially with model size. Lamport says one more ballot makes it vastly bigger; that model wasn't re-run here.

    What good is such a small model?

    Break the overlap: delete a2 from the last element, so Majority is { {a1, a2}, {a1, a3}, {a3} }. It's no longer symmetric, so Acceptor stops being a symmetry set. Comment out the conjunct in ASSUME, since TLC would otherwise reject it. TLC reports TCConsistent violated, with a 14-state trace, as in the lecture.

    StatesTLC's actionsWhat happened
    2–3RMPrepare(r1), RMPrepare(r2)Both RMs vote prepared in ballot 0
    4–6Phase1a(1,r1), Phase1b(a1), Phase1b(a2)A leader polls {a1, a2} for r1; no one has voted
    7Phase2a(1,r1)So it sends "aborted" in ballot 1
    8–9Phase2b(a3) twicea3 votes r1 prepared (ballot 0), then aborted (ballot 1)
    10–11PCDecide, RMRcvAbortMsg(r1){a3} "chose" aborted for r1: Abort sent, r1 aborts
    12–14Phase2b(a3), PCDecide, RMRcvCommitMsg(r2)a3's vote for r2 means both instances "chose" prepared: Commit sent, r2 commits

    Every phase2b message stays in msgs, so a3's old vote for r1 still counts. A leader that consulted {a1, a2} couldn't see a3, which is the right panel of the overlap diagram. Even a very small model catches a real error in a real algorithm.

    Predict: does Paxos Commit still block if a majority of acceptors stops?

    Yes. No new ballot can complete, so an undecided instance stays undecided. What improves is the failure it tolerates: any process can act as leader, and any single acceptor can fail, with three acceptors. Safety never relied on anyone being up; the checked model allows steps simply never to happen.

    Why can a new leader safely take over in Paxos Commit but not a backup TM in two-phase commit?

    Read the algorithm: Consensus on Transaction Commit, Jim Gray and Leslie Lamport, ACM TODS 31(1), 2006, linked from the lecture page. The official module is in the examples repository.

    Lecture 7: Paxos commit

    Inside Paxos Commit is one small agreement problem.

    You've seen Paxos Commit run one decision per RM. Each of those decisions is an instance of consensus: a group chooses one value, and two different values are never chosen. This lesson separates consensus from commit, then breaks its key rule so you can see why the rule exists.

    Read the diagram from the left. Each RM has its own instance with its own acceptor votes. Commit is a small rule on top of the results: all "prepared" gives Commit, and any "aborted" gives Abort. Everything difficult is in the instances, so you can study one of them alone.

    While you watch

    Lecture 7 doesn't teach Paxos as such; Lamport leaves it to the paper. Go back to his remark that the CHOOSE in Phase2a can have several choices that all have the same m.val, and try to explain it. This lesson's experiment gives you the means to. Everything about one instance and Raft here is added to the lecture.

    One instance

    The module below cuts PaxosCommit down: no RMs and no ins field. Values are just "X" and "Y", and with no reports a leader may propose either. Ballots start at 1 since no RM owns ballot 0. Its contract is:

    Chosen(v) == \E b \in Ballot, MS \in Majority :
               \A a \in MS : [type |-> "2b", bal |-> b, val |-> v, acc |-> a] \in msgs
Agreement == \A v, w \in Value : Chosen(v) /\ Chosen(w) => v = w

    Chosen is derived from the votes in msgs, so no process has to know it. A value can be chosen while everyone is still unaware. A model where nothing is ever chosen also satisfies Agreement, so progress needs separate assumptions.

    Show the complete module
    ----------------------------- MODULE OneDecree ------------------------------
\* One Paxos consensus instance, cut out of PaxosCommit: the ins field and the
\* RMs are gone, and with no earlier evidence a leader may propose any value.
EXTENDS Integers
Maximum(S) == IF S = {} THEN -1
                        ELSE CHOOSE n \in S : \A m \in S : n >= m
CONSTANTS Value, Acceptor, Majority, Ballot
ASSUME /\ Ballot \subseteq Nat \ {0}
       /\ \A MS1, MS2 \in Majority : MS1 \cap MS2 # {}
VARIABLES aState, msgs
vars == <<aState, msgs>>

Init == /\ aState = [a \in Acceptor |-> [mbal |-> 0, bal |-> -1, val |-> "none"]]
        /\ msgs = {}
Send(m) == msgs' = msgs \cup {m}

Phase1a(b) == /\ Send([type |-> "1a", bal |-> b])
              /\ UNCHANGED aState

Phase1b(a) ==
  \E m \in msgs :
    /\ m.type = "1a"
    /\ aState[a].mbal < m.bal
    /\ aState' = [aState EXCEPT ![a].mbal = m.bal]
    /\ Send([type |-> "1b", mbal |-> m.bal, bal |-> aState[a].bal,
             val |-> aState[a].val, acc |-> a])

Reports(b, MS) == {m \in msgs : /\ m.type = "1b" /\ m.mbal = b /\ m.acc \in MS}
FromAll(b, MS) == \A a \in MS : \E m \in Reports(b, MS) : m.acc = a
NotUsed(b) == ~\E m \in msgs : m.type = "2a" /\ m.bal = b

\* The rule that matters: repeat the value of the highest ballot reported.
Phase2a(b) ==
  /\ NotUsed(b)
  /\ \E MS \in Majority, v \in Value :
       LET maxbal == Maximum({m.bal : m \in Reports(b, MS)})
       IN  /\ FromAll(b, MS)
           /\ \/ maxbal = -1
              \/ \E m \in Reports(b, MS) : m.bal = maxbal /\ m.val = v
           /\ Send([type |-> "2a", bal |-> b, val |-> v])
  /\ UNCHANGED aState

\* The broken version: same quorum, but the reports are ignored.
Phase2aForget(b) ==
  /\ NotUsed(b)
  /\ \E MS \in Majority, v \in Value :
       /\ FromAll(b, MS)
       /\ Send([type |-> "2a", bal |-> b, val |-> v])
  /\ UNCHANGED aState

Phase2b(a) ==
  \E m \in msgs :
    /\ m.type = "2a"
    /\ aState[a].mbal <= m.bal
    /\ aState' = [aState EXCEPT ![a].mbal = m.bal,
                                ![a].bal  = m.bal,
                                ![a].val  = m.val]
    /\ Send([type |-> "2b", bal |-> m.bal, val |-> m.val, acc |-> a])

Next == \/ \E b \in Ballot : Phase1a(b) \/ Phase2a(b)
        \/ \E a \in Acceptor : Phase1b(a) \/ Phase2b(a)
NextForget == \/ \E b \in Ballot : Phase1a(b) \/ Phase2aForget(b)
              \/ \E a \in Acceptor : Phase1b(a) \/ Phase2b(a)

Chosen(v) == \E b \in Ballot, MS \in Majority :
               \A a \in MS : [type |-> "2b", bal |-> b, val |-> v, acc |-> a] \in msgs
Agreement == \A v, w \in Value : Chosen(v) /\ Chosen(w) => v = w
OneValuePerBallot == \A m1, m2 \in msgs :
  (m1.type = "2b" /\ m2.type = "2b" /\ m1.bal = m2.bal) => m1.val = m2.val
=============================================================================
    INIT Init
NEXT Next
CONSTANTS Value = {"X", "Y"}
          Acceptor = {"A", "B", "C"}
          Majority = {{"A", "B"}, {"A", "C"}, {"B", "C"}}
          Ballot = {1, 2}
INVARIANT Agreement
INVARIANT OneValuePerBallot
CHECK_DEADLOCK FALSE

    With three acceptors, two values, and ballots {1, 2}, TLC reports no error, 3921 distinct states. That run also checks OneValuePerBallot: all votes in one ballot have the same value. The NotUsed guard allows just one 2a message per ballot, and acceptors repeat only what it says. That's why the CHOOSE Lamport points at can't matter. Messages with the same highest ballot agree.

    Worked failure: a new ballot forgets the old vote

    Now replace Phase2a with Phase2aForget, which still needs reports from a majority but ignores what they say:

    Phase2aForget(b) ==
  /\ NotUsed(b)
  /\ \E MS \in Majority, v \in Value :
       /\ FromAll(b, MS)
       /\ Send([type |-> "2a", bal |-> b, val |-> v])
  /\ UNCHANGED aState

    TLC reports Agreement violated in a 13-state trace. These are its last few states, showing each acceptor's last vote.

    By state 12, A and B voted Y in ballot 2, so Y is chosen. In the last column, C votes X in ballot 1: B's X vote in ballot 1 is still in msgs, so {B, C} also chose X. In state 9 B reported "I voted X in ballot 1" to the ballot 2 leader. That report was the warning, and the broken rule ignored it. The real rule would have made ballot 2 propose X, and then both ballots agree.

    Quorum overlap was present the whole time: {A, B} and {B, C} share B. So overlap alone doesn't save you. It creates a place where evidence can pass between ballots, and the protocol must also obey it. This is the point lesson 21 ended on: a place to look isn't yet an answer.

    Predict: if B restarts and forgets its promise and last vote, is overlap still enough?

    No. B would report no vote, and the leader of ballot 2 may then propose Y, the same failure by a different path. The spec has no action that loses aState, which is an assumption: those fields must survive a restart. A recovery action in your model must keep exactly what this argument relies on.

    From one value to a log

    Paxos Commit runs a fixed set of instances, one per RM. A replicated service needs an ordered list of operations, so it runs one consensus decision per log position. Replicas apply chosen operations in order.

    In the diagram, a column is one decision. S3 lags behind but it holds no conflicting value in any filled column. Agreement per position is what a replicated log needs, and new questions come with it: who proposes, what happens to entries no majority has, and what can be discarded.

    Raft is a widely used protocol for replicated logs. It separates leader election, log replication, and safety. A term plays a role like a ballot; it isn't a wall-clock time. To study it, follow one committed entry across a leader crash and an election, and ask what prevents an elected leader from lacking that entry. "A majority elected it" is not the whole answer: Raft restricts which logs can win. Use its published spec rather than reconstructing it from a diagram.

    Why is quorum intersection useful in consensus?

    Primary sources: Paxos Made Simple and the extended Raft paper. Formal models are in the official examples.

    Lecture 7: Paxos commit

    Problem set 7: count on the overlap.

    Four problems on quorums, consensus and Paxos Commit. You'll use the set operators and the overlap property from lecture 7 to find a stale read and to choose where cluster members live. Then you'll break a leader election by losing one field in a restart, and compare Paxos Commit with the two-phase commit booking from Problem set 6. Every problem ends in a TLC run.

    Each module below is complete and was checked with TLC exactly as shown. Type it in yourself or copy it into a file of the same name. Counts like "distinct states" only match if your module is identical, so use those numbers to test your copy.

    Problem 1●○○Databases

    Find the stale read in a Dynamo-style store

    Draws on Set operations and quorums, Paxos Commit: surviving the coordinator and Your first spec through TLC.

    A shopping-cart service keeps each cart in a key-value store built on the design of Amazon's Dynamo paper. Every key lives on N replicas. A write counts as successful once W replicas have stored it, and a read asks R replicas and returns the newest version it hears. The team runs N = 5 with W = 3. To cut read latency, someone proposes R = 2: "three of the five replicas have every acknowledged write, so asking two will nearly always find one." Customers then report carts that lose the item they just added.

    The module models one key. Every replica starts at version 1, a client writes version 2, and once the write is acknowledged a single read happens. Maximum is the definition from Paxos Commit.

    ---------------------------- MODULE PSl7_Quorum -----------------------------
\* One key of a Dynamo-style store with replication factor N = |Replica|.
\* Every replica holds version 1. A client writes version 2: the coordinator
\* stores it replica by replica and reports success once W replicas have it.
\* A later read asks R replicas and returns the highest version it hears.
EXTENDS Integers, FiniteSets
CONSTANTS Replica, W, R
VARIABLES version,   \* version[n]: the version replica n stores
          acked,     \* the coordinator has told the client "write succeeded"
          seen       \* what the read returned (0 = no read yet)
vars == <<version, acked, seen>>

Maximum(S) == IF S = {} THEN -1
                        ELSE CHOOSE n \in S : \A m \in S : n >= m
WriteSets == {Q \in SUBSET Replica : Cardinality(Q) = W}
ReadSets  == {Q \in SUBSET Replica : Cardinality(Q) = R}

Init == /\ version = [n \in Replica |-> 1]
        /\ acked = FALSE
        /\ seen = 0

Store(n) == /\ version[n] = 1
            /\ version' = [version EXCEPT ![n] = 2]
            /\ UNCHANGED <<acked, seen>>

Ack == /\ ~acked
       /\ \E Q \in WriteSets : \A n \in Q : version[n] = 2
       /\ acked' = TRUE
       /\ UNCHANGED <<version, seen>>

Read == /\ acked
        /\ seen = 0
        /\ \E Q \in ReadSets : seen' = Maximum({version[n] : n \in Q})
        /\ UNCHANGED <<version, acked>>

Next == Ack \/ Read \/ \E n \in Replica : Store(n)

ReadsLatest == seen \in {0, 2}
Overlap == \A Wq \in WriteSets, Rq \in ReadSets : Wq \cap Rq # {}
=============================================================================
    INIT Init
NEXT Next
CONSTANTS Replica = {"A", "B", "C", "D", "E"}
          W = 3
          R = 2
INVARIANT ReadsLatest
CHECK_DEADLOCK FALSE
    1. Before running anything, use the R + W > N rule to say which values of R from 1 to 5 make every read set meet every write set.
    2. Run TLC with R = 1, R = 2 and R = 3. For each, report whether ReadsLatest holds, and for failures, the length of the trace and which replicas the read asked.
    3. Add the line ASSUME Overlap after the definition of Overlap, and run it with R = 2 and with R = 3. What changes in TLC's output, and why does it appear before any state is explored?
    4. Say in one sentence why Read takes the maximum of the versions it hears instead of the version of whichever replica answers first.

    Keep R = 3, but change the read to \E n \in Q : seen' = version[n]: it returns the version of any one replica it asked. Does ReadsLatest still hold?

    Hint

    A read set of size R and a write set of size W must share an element when R + W elements can't fit into N places without repeating one. For task 3, remember that a constant formula doesn't depend on any state.

    Solution

    1. R + W > N means R + 3 > 5, so R ≥ 3. R = 3, 4 and 5 force overlap; R = 1 and R = 2 don't. With R = 2 the write set {A, C, D} and the read set {B, E} are disjoint.

    2. R = 1 and R = 2 both violate ReadsLatest with a 6-state trace. In the R = 2 run, the trace went Store("A"), Store("C"), Store("D"), Ack, Read, ending with seen = 1. The read set must have been {B, E}, the only pair whose maximum is 1 there, as the diagram shows. Your run may store a different three replicas first. R = 3 gives no error, with 64 distinct states. That count is easy to check by hand: 32 version maps before the ack, then for each of the 16 maps with at least three 2s, one state before the read and one after it, which returns 2.

    3. With R = 2 TLC stops at once with "Assumption … is false" and explores no states. With R = 3 the assumption holds, and the run is the same as before. Overlap mentions no variable, so it is a constant formula, and TLC evaluates assumptions before it computes the initial states. That's why Paxos Commit puts its Majority condition in an ASSUME: a bad configuration is rejected before any behavior is checked.

    4. The overlap only promises that some replica asked has version 2. The read has to recognize that replica among its answers, and taking the highest version is how it does that. The quiz shows the same read with no such rule failing at R = 3. Real stores also need versions that order concurrent writes, which this one-writer model avoids.

    The team's "nearly always" was correct as a probability and wrong as a guarantee. TLC doesn't weigh how likely a behavior is: it reports the one bad read that is allowed.

    Problem 2●○○Infrastructure

    Place five cluster members across data centres

    Draws on Set operations and quorums, From Paxos Commit to Paxos and Raft and Sets, functions, and quantifiers.

    Your company's configuration store is a five-member cluster that uses Raft, like etcd. A write needs a quorum of three members. The cluster must keep accepting writes when a whole data centre (DC) goes dark. The infrastructure team has three proposals:

    • Two DCs, three members in one and two in the other.
    • Three DCs, with two, two and one members.
    • Save a machine: four members in two DCs, two in each, with a quorum of just two "so either DC can carry on alone."

    In the module below DCs is a set of sets: each element is the set of members in one DC. The single variable lost is the DC that has gone dark, and Init lets TLC try every choice. Because Next changes nothing, each state is one "what if". The cfg shows the first proposal.

    --------------------------- MODULE PSl7_Placement ---------------------------
\* Where to put the members of a quorum-based cluster. DCs is a set of sets:
\* each element is the set of nodes in one data centre. The variable lost is
\* the one data centre that has gone dark; Init lets TLC try each in turn.
EXTENDS Integers, FiniteSets
CONSTANTS Node, DCs, QSize
ASSUME \A d1, d2 \in DCs : d1 # d2 => d1 \cap d2 = {}   \* no node in two DCs
ASSUME \A n \in Node : \E d \in DCs : n \in d           \* every node placed
VARIABLE lost
Quorum == {Q \in SUBSET Node : Cardinality(Q) >= QSize}
\* The property Paxos and Raft rely on, checked before any state is explored.
QuorumsOverlap == \A Q1, Q2 \in Quorum : Q1 \cap Q2 # {}
ASSUME QuorumsOverlap

Init == lost \in DCs
Next == UNCHANGED lost

\* Some quorum is made only of nodes outside the lost data centre.
QuorumSurvives == \E Q \in Quorum : Q \cap lost = {}
=============================================================================
    INIT Init
NEXT Next
CONSTANTS Node = {"n1", "n2", "n3", "n4", "n5"}
          DCs = {{"n1", "n2", "n3"}, {"n4", "n5"}}
          QSize = 3
INVARIANT QuorumSurvives
CHECK_DEADLOCK FALSE
    1. By hand: how many elements does Quorum have for five members with QSize = 3? Check your count by adding ASSUME Cardinality(Quorum) = n, with your n, at the end of the module: TLC rejects a false assumption before it explores anything.
    2. Run all three proposals (for the third, use four members and QSize = 2, then QSize = 3). For each run, write down what TLC reports and which DC, if any, is fatal to lose.
    3. The third proposal can't be fixed by choosing a quorum size. Explain why in terms of the two properties the module checks.
    4. Find a layout of six members in three DCs, and a QSize, that passes both checks. Run it.

    With the 2 + 2 + 1 layout and quorum 3, how many DCs can be lost at the same time without stopping writes?

    Hint

    QuorumSurvives asks for a quorum disjoint from the lost DC. QuorumsOverlap asks every two quorums to share a member. A quorum that fits inside one DC of the 2 + 2 layout satisfies the first and is exactly what breaks the second.

    Solution

    1. 10 + 5 + 1 = 16. With ASSUME Cardinality(Quorum) = 16 TLC runs as before; with 15 it reports the assumption false.

    2. Results of the runs:

    LayoutQSizeTLC says
    3 + 23QuorumSurvives violated by the initial state lost = {"n1", "n2", "n3"}
    2 + 2 + 13No error, 3 distinct states
    2 + 22Assumption QuorumsOverlap is false
    2 + 23QuorumSurvives violated by lost = {"n1", "n2"}
    2 + 2 + 24No error, 3 distinct states (22 quorums)

    In the 3 + 2 layout, losing the small DC is fine, but losing the large one leaves two members. The diagram shows both.

    3. If either DC alone must be able to write, a quorum has to fit inside each DC. But then {n1, n2} and {n3, n4} are both quorums and share nobody: during a network split, each side could elect its own leader, which is the property Paxos and Raft assume can't happen. If quorums must overlap, a quorum needs at least three of the four members, and neither DC has three. With two DCs of equal size you can't have both properties, whatever QSize you choose.

    4. Three DCs of two members each with QSize = 4: two quorums of four out of six share at least two members, and losing any DC leaves exactly four. TLC reports no error. Notice that a fourth member and a third DC improve nothing by themselves. What matters is that no single DC holds more than N − QSize members, the number a quorum system can do without.

    Problem 3●●○Algorithms

    Two leaders in one term

    Draws on From Paxos Commit to Paxos and Raft, Set operations and quorums, Messages, failures, and retries and Two-phase commit and records.

    A team is writing its own Raft-style leader election for a job scheduler. A server that hears nothing from a leader times out, moves to a higher term, votes for itself, and asks the others for votes. A server grants at most one vote per term. A candidate that collects votes from a majority becomes leader of that term. As in From Paxos Commit to Paxos and Raft, a term plays the role of a ballot.

    To keep the hot path fast, the implementation writes term to disk but keeps votedFor only in memory. After a deploy, the logs show two servers both acting as leader of term 1, both accepting jobs.

    The module records votes as messages in a set that only grows, as in two-phase commit, and keeps the history leaders so that an invariant can talk about every election ever won. Logs are left out, so this checks only the election.

    --------------------------- MODULE PSl7_Election ----------------------------
\* Leader election in the style of Raft, with votes as messages. Logs are
\* left out. A server that times out moves to a higher term, votes for
\* itself and asks for votes; it is leader of a term once a majority voted
\* for it in that term. Restart models a crash and reboot.
EXTENDS Integers
CONSTANTS Server, Majority, Term
ASSUME \A MS1, MS2 \in Majority : MS1 \cap MS2 # {}
None == "none"
VARIABLES term,      \* term[s]: the highest term s has seen
          votedFor,  \* votedFor[s]: whom s voted for in term[s], or None
          msgs,      \* every message ever sent
          leaders    \* every [srv, term] pair that has won an election
vars == <<term, votedFor, msgs, leaders>>

Init == /\ term = [s \in Server |-> 0]
        /\ votedFor = [s \in Server |-> None]
        /\ msgs = {}
        /\ leaders = {}

Timeout(s, t) ==
  /\ t > term[s]
  /\ term' = [term EXCEPT ![s] = t]
  /\ votedFor' = [votedFor EXCEPT ![s] = s]
  /\ msgs' = msgs \cup {[type |-> "request", term |-> t, from |-> s],
                        [type |-> "vote", term |-> t, from |-> s, to |-> s]}
  /\ UNCHANGED leaders

\* s grants its vote for term m.term at most once, unless it forgot.
Grant(s) ==
  \E m \in msgs :
    /\ m.type = "request"
    /\ \/ m.term > term[s]
       \/ m.term = term[s] /\ votedFor[s] \in {None, m.from}
    /\ term' = [term EXCEPT ![s] = m.term]
    /\ votedFor' = [votedFor EXCEPT ![s] = m.from]
    /\ msgs' = msgs \cup {[type |-> "vote", term |-> m.term, from |-> s, to |-> m.from]}
    /\ UNCHANGED leaders

BecomeLeader(s) ==
  /\ \E MS \in Majority :
       \A v \in MS : [type |-> "vote", term |-> term[s], from |-> v, to |-> s] \in msgs
  /\ leaders' = leaders \cup {[srv |-> s, term |-> term[s]]}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<term, votedFor, msgs>>

\* The process restarts. term is on disk; votedFor was kept only in memory.
Restart(s) ==
  /\ votedFor' = [votedFor EXCEPT ![s] = None]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<term, msgs, leaders>>

Next == \E s \in Server : \/ \E t \in Term : Timeout(s, t)
                          \/ Grant(s) \/ BecomeLeader(s) \/ Restart(s)
\* Both fields on disk: a restart then changes nothing in this model.
NextDurable == \E s \in Server : \/ \E t \in Term : Timeout(s, t)
                                 \/ Grant(s) \/ BecomeLeader(s)

OneLeaderPerTerm == \A l1, l2 \in leaders : l1.term = l2.term => l1.srv = l2.srv
=============================================================================
    INIT Init
NEXT Next
CONSTANTS Server = {"s1", "s2", "s3"}
          Majority = {{"s1", "s2"}, {"s1", "s3"}, {"s2", "s3"}}
          Term = {1, 2}
INVARIANT OneLeaderPerTerm
CHECK_DEADLOCK FALSE
    1. Without TLC: suppose two different servers won term t. Use the ASSUME to show that some server sent a vote for each of them in term t. What in Grant is supposed to prevent that?
    2. Run TLC with Next. Report the length of the trace and the server whose two votes in term 1 let both candidates win.
    3. Run it again with NEXT NextDurable, which models keeping both fields on disk. Report TLC's result.
    4. Would keeping votedFor on disk and forgetting term on restart be safe? Decide by reading Grant, then answer the quiz.

    Restart keeps votedFor but resets term to 0. Is OneLeaderPerTerm safe?

    Hint

    Two winners in term t means two sets of vote messages, each from a set in Majority. Any two such sets share a server. That server sent two votes in term t to different candidates. Look for the step after which Grant's guard no longer remembers the first one.

    Solution

    1. If s and s' both won term t, there are majorities MS and MS' whose members all sent term-t votes to s and to s' respectively. The ASSUME says MS ∩ MS' contains some server v, so v voted for both. In term term[v] = t, Grant allows a vote only when votedFor[v] is None or the same candidate. So two votes in one term can happen only if votedFor[v] went back to None while term[v] stayed t. Restart does exactly that.

    2. TLC reports OneLeaderPerTerm violated after 8 states. The run here printed:

    State 2: <Timeout("s1",1)>    \* s1 votes for itself in term 1
State 3: <Restart("s1")>      \* votedFor["s1"] = "none", term["s1"] = 1
State 4: <Timeout("s2",1)>    \* s2 votes for itself in term 1
State 5: <Grant("s1")>        \* s1 votes for s2 in term 1
State 6: <BecomeLeader("s2")> \* leaders = {[term |-> 1, srv |-> "s2"]}
State 7: <Grant("s3")>        \* s3 votes for s1 in term 1
State 8: <BecomeLeader("s1")> \* leaders = {[term |-> 1, srv |-> "s1"],
                               \*            [term |-> 1, srv |-> "s2"]}

    The server that voted twice is s1. Its first vote was for itself, sent in state 2 and still in msgs. In your run the servers may be named differently, but the shape is the same: the double voter sits in the overlap of the two majorities. The overlap was there all along. What failed is that the server in it forgot what it had said, which is the restart warning from From Paxos Commit to Paxos and Raft in another form.

    3. No error: 1444 distinct states. The overlap argument from task 1 now goes through.

    4. No. A server whose term drops to 0 treats any term-1 request as newer, and the first disjunct of Grant lets it vote without looking at votedFor. A vote record means something only together with the term it belongs to. That's why Raft requires both to reach stable storage before a server answers a vote request.

    Problem 4●●●Databases

    Synthesis: book the trip with Paxos Commit

    Draws on Paxos Commit: surviving the coordinator, Two-phase commit and records, The transaction commit spec and Problem set 6.

    Return to the travel booking of Problem set 6: one transaction reserves a flight, a hotel room and a rental car, each held by its own resource manager (RM), coordinated with two-phase commit. Last month the coordinator's machine died after all three RMs had prepared. Each RM held its reservation and waited. Nobody could release the seat without risking a car booked for a trip with no flight. An engineer proposes Paxos Commit with three acceptors. Your job is to state precisely which failures each protocol survives, with a TLC run for each claim.

    The first module is TwoPhase with RM = {flight, hotel, car} plus a crash: after Crash the TM never takes another step.

    -------------------------- MODULE PSl7_TwoPCBooking -------------------------
\* Two-phase commit for the booking, plus a coordinator crash: after Crash
\* the TM takes no step ever again. RMs are unchanged from TwoPhase.
EXTENDS TwoPhase
VARIABLE tmUp
CInit == TPInit /\ tmUp = TRUE
Crash == /\ tmUp
         /\ tmUp' = FALSE
         /\ UNCHANGED vars
CNext == \/ Crash
         \/ /\ tmUp
            /\ \/ TMCommit \/ TMAbort
               \/ \E r \in RM : TMRcvPrepared(r)
            /\ UNCHANGED tmUp
         \/ /\ \E r \in RM : \/ RMPrepare(r) \/ RMChooseToAbort(r)
                             \/ RMRcvCommitMsg(r) \/ RMRcvAbortMsg(r)
            /\ UNCHANGED tmUp
NeverDecided == [type |-> "Commit"] \notin msgs /\ [type |-> "Abort"] \notin msgs
\* Everyone has voted yes and nobody can ever learn the outcome.
InDoubt == ~tmUp /\ NeverDecided /\ \A r \in RM : rmState[r] = "prepared"
NotInDoubt == ~InDoubt
=============================================================================
    INIT CInit
NEXT CNext
CONSTANT RM = {"flight", "hotel", "car"}
INVARIANT TCConsistent
INVARIANT NotInDoubt
CHECK_DEADLOCK FALSE

    The second module extends PaxosCommit, unchanged from the lecture. Only acceptors in Up take steps. Both claims at the bottom should fail when the protocol can still make progress: a counterexample to NeverAllCommitted is a run that commits the trip.

    ------------------------- MODULE PSl7_PaxosBooking --------------------------
\* Paxos Commit for the booking, with some acceptors crashed for good.
\* Only acceptors in Up ever take a step; the others stay silent forever.
\* Leader actions need no "up" flag: any live process may act as leader.
EXTENDS PaxosCommit
CONSTANT Up
ASSUME Up \subseteq Acceptor

UpNext ==
  \/ \E r \in RM : \/ RMPrepare(r) \/ RMChooseToAbort(r)
                   \/ RMRcvCommitMsg(r) \/ RMRcvAbortMsg(r)
  \/ \E bal \in Ballot \ {0}, r \in RM : Phase1a(bal, r) \/ Phase2a(bal, r)
  \/ PCDecide
  \/ \E acc \in Up : Phase1b(acc) \/ Phase2b(acc)

\* Claims that FAIL exactly when the protocol can still make progress:
NeverAllCommitted == \E r \in RM : rmState[r] # "committed"
NeverDecided == [type |-> "Commit"] \notin msgs /\ [type |-> "Abort"] \notin msgs
=============================================================================
    INIT PCInit
NEXT UpNext
CONSTANTS RM = {"flight", "hotel", "car"}
          Acceptor = {"a1", "a2", "a3"}
          Majority = {{"a1", "a2"}, {"a1", "a3"}, {"a2", "a3"}}
          Ballot = {0, 1}
          Up = {"a1", "a2"}
INVARIANT TCConsistent
INVARIANT NeverAllCommitted
CHECK_DEADLOCK FALSE
    1. Run PSl7_TwoPCBooking. Using the guards of TwoPhase, explain why no step can change rmState once InDoubt holds.
    2. Run PSl7_PaxosBooking as shown, with a3 crashed. Does the trip commit? Which acceptors' phase 2b messages does PCDecide rely on?
    3. Now crash two acceptors: Up = {"a1"}, with INVARIANT NeverDecided instead of NeverAllCommitted. What does TLC report, and what does it mean?
    4. Run Paxos Commit with a single acceptor: Acceptor = {"tm"}, Majority = {{"tm"}}, and Up = {}, checking NeverDecided. Compare it with task 1.
    5. Fill in the table: for each failure, does two-phase commit, and does Paxos Commit with three acceptors, still reach a decision? The failures are: an RM crashes before voting, the TM crashes before deciding, one acceptor crashes, two acceptors crash.

    In every run of this problem, TCConsistent held. What do the crashes cost?

    Hint

    For task 1, list every action and the first conjunct that is false in the InDoubt state. For task 2, Decided(r, v) in PCDecide needs phase 2b messages from every acceptor of one set in Majority, and only one of those sets avoids a3.

    Solution

    1. TLC reports NotInDoubt violated after 5 states: the TM crashes, then flight, hotel and car prepare (your trace may crash the TM later). In that state the TM actions are disabled by tmUp = FALSE. RMPrepare and RMChooseToAbort need "working". RMRcvCommitMsg and RMRcvAbortMsg need a decision message, and only the TM sends those. Crash isn't enabled either, and it never touches rmState anyway. All three reservations stay held forever.

    2. Yes. TLC reports NeverAllCommitted violated with a 14-state trace: the three RMPrepare steps, three Phase2b("a1") steps, three Phase2b("a2") steps, PCDecide, and three RMRcvCommitMsg steps. PCDecide uses the majority {a1, a2} for all three instances. a3 never did anything, and nobody had to notice that it was gone. (Even this run explores more than 170,000 distinct states before it stops, which is why the lecture's model has two RMs.)

    3. No error, 3375 distinct states: with a1 alone, no Commit or Abort is ever sent. No majority can form, so no instance can choose a value, and leaders' ballots can't complete either. Paxos Commit blocks too, but only when a majority of acceptors is gone.

    4. No error, 216 distinct states: nothing is ever decided. A single acceptor is a single memory, which is what the TM was in two-phase commit. If it's down, every prepared RM waits, exactly as in task 1. Paxos Commit with three acceptors spreads that memory over three processes and needs any two of them.

    5.

    FailureTwo-phase commitPaxos Commit, 3 acceptors
    An RM crashes before votingDecides: TMAbort is always enabled while tmState = "init"Decides: a leader runs ballot 1 for that RM's instance, hears no vote, and proposes "aborted"
    TM crashes before decidingBlocks (task 1)There is no single TM: any process may run Phase1a, Phase2a and PCDecide
    One acceptor crashes(no acceptors)Decides (task 2)
    Two acceptors crash(no acceptors)Blocks (task 3)

    Both protocols keep TCConsistent in every case, because no step depends on anyone being up. What changes is who you need alive to finish. The price is more messages and more state. In general, with 2F + 1 acceptors the live ones still contain a majority after F crashes, which is the numeric question above.

    Lecture 8: Implementation

    A whole specification can be one formula.

    So far you have handed TLC two formulas: an initial one and a next-state one, as you did for TwoPhase in lesson 18. A single formula can say both, if it is true or false of a whole behavior. To write it you first sort expressions by how much of a behavior they need, then add one operator, always.

    Implication, briefly

    Everything in this lesson and the next is stated with =>, read "implies." P => Q means: if P is true then Q is true, and otherwise we know nothing. Mathematically, "we know nothing" is the value TRUE, so it equals IF P THEN Q ELSE TRUE.

    PQP => Q~Q => ~P
    TRUETRUETRUETRUE
    TRUEFALSEFALSEFALSE
    FALSETRUETRUETRUE
    FALSEFALSETRUETRUE

    The last two columns match, so P => Q equals ~Q => ~P. "If it's raining the ground is wet" therefore means the same as "if the ground is not wet it's not raining." That sounds wrong because in speech if suggests a cause. In math, implication asserts only that two truths go together.

    Four kinds of expression

    Here an expression is complete: after expanding definitions it contains only built-in operators, numbers and strings, declared constants and variables, and identifiers bound inside it. \E v \in Nat : x' = x + v is complete. Its part x' = x + v is not, because v is bound outside that part. A formula is a Boolean-valued expression. The figure sorts expressions from the inside out.

    • Constant. No declared variables, no ', no UNCHANGED. An ASSUME must be a constant formula.
    • State. May also contain declared variables, so it has a value on a state. If a state gives v the set Nat and w the value -42, then v \cup {w} has the value Nat \cup {-42} there.
    • Action. May also contain ' and UNCHANGED, so it has a value on a step. If s gives p the value 42 and t gives q the value 24, then p - q' has the value 18 on the step from s to t. An action formula is simply called an action.
    • Temporal. New here. It has a value on a behavior. TLA+ has only Boolean ones.

    Each level is a special case of the next. A state expression is an action expression whose value depends only on the first state of the step. You may also prime any state expression, not just a variable: e' on a step is the value of e in the second state. So UNCHANGED <<x, y, z>> is <<x, y, z>>' = <<x, y, z>>, which is (x' = x) /\ (y' = y) /\ (z' = z).

    From two formulas to one

    TPSpec should be true on a behavior exactly when TPInit holds on the first state and TPNext holds on every step. The figure shows both duties on a real TLC trace. The first duty needs nothing new, because a state formula counts as a temporal formula that is true on a behavior when it is true on the first state. The second needs the always operator, typed []. []TPNext is true on a behavior when TPNext is true on every step.

    That suggests TPSpec == TPInit /\ []TPNext. It is almost right. The definition at the end of module TwoPhase is:

    TPSpec == TPInit /\ [][TPNext]_<<rmState, tmState, tmPrepared, msgs>>

    Applied to a state formula, always needs no brackets or subscript: []TPTypeOK means TPTypeOK holds on every state, because its value on each step depends only on that step's first state.

    The subscript allows stuttering

    [TPNext]_vars abbreviates TPNext \/ UNCHANGED vars, where vars is the tuple of the spec's variables. A step that leaves all of them unchanged is a stuttering step. So the formula says every step is a TPNext step or changes nothing. In the figure, the two stutter columns are allowed and the red one is not.

    Why a spec should allow steps that do nothing is the subject of lesson 26. For now, take the two facts it implies. A formula of this form can never require anything to happen, and it can never be violated by a pause.

    Predict: TPSpec has variables rmState, tmState, tmPrepared, msgs. Is a step that changes only tmPrepared always allowed?

    No. It is not stuttering, because tmPrepared changed. It is allowed only if it is a TPNext step, namely TMRcvPrepared(r) for a resource manager whose Prepared message is in msgs while tmState is "init".

    Stuttering is not deadlock

    A deadlock report from TLC is about Next only: a reachable state with no Next successor. Take SimpleProgram from lesson 5. TLC reports "Deadlock reached" at pc = "done", as the solid arrows in the figure predict. The dashed loops don't count, even though the formula allows them.

    You can silence that report by writing the loop into the next-state formula: Next \/ UNCHANGED vars. TLC then finishes with no error, with 2003 distinct states. Nothing got better, the program still stops there, and a blocked protocol patched this way looks healthy. Likewise, a livelock is endless Next steps with no useful progress, and neither report catches it. Properties that do catch it arrive in lesson 29.

    Theorems, and checking them

    THEOREM TF asserts that temporal formula TF is true on every possible behavior, not just behaviors of some spec. So implication is the way to talk about a spec:

    THEOREM TPSpec => []TPTypeOK

    For every behavior, if it satisfies TPSpec, then TPTypeOK holds on all its states. That is what "TPTypeOK is an invariant of TPSpec" means. TLC does not read theorems; they tell your reader what you expect. To check this one, name TPSpec as the behavior spec and []TPTypeOK as a property. In the Toolbox that is the Properties list. With the VS Code extension or the command line, a .cfg file says the same, and a property must be a defined name, so a small wrapper module adds AlwaysTypeOK == []TPTypeOK:

    SPECIFICATION TPSpec
CONSTANT RM = {r1, r2, r3}
INVARIANT TPTypeOK
PROPERTY AlwaysTypeOK

    On this configuration TLC finds no error: 1146 states generated, 288 distinct, depth 11. Since this is an invariance property, the INVARIANT line alone would be enough. The two lines are the same assertion written at two levels.

    A behavior starts with tmState = "ouch", so it does not satisfy TPSpec. Is TPSpec => []TPTypeOK true on it?

    While you watch

    • Look for how often the lecture reduces a new idea to substitution or to a definition. Pause at the implication example and substitute the other three pairs of values yourself.
    • Lamport asks you to ignore the subscript for now. This lesson has already said what it abbreviates; the next part of the lecture and the next lesson say why it must be there.
    • The lecture's phrase is "module-closed" and "module-complete" for what this page just calls a complete expression. The lecture's check uses the Toolbox; the .cfg above is the same check.

    Lamport's TLA+ Video Course, lecture 8.

    Lecture 8: Implementation

    To implement a spec is to imply it.

    The previous lesson made each spec a formula. Two-phase commit was supposed to implement transaction commit, and now that claim has a one-line statement: every behavior satisfying TPSpec also satisfies TCSpec. The surprise is what must be true of states and steps for that line to make sense.

    The theorem

    Module TCommit has one variable, so its spec has a simpler subscript: TCSpec == TCInit /\ [][TCNext]_rmState. At the end of module TwoPhase, INSTANCE imports every definition from TCommit, and a theorem follows:

    INSTANCE TCommit

THEOREM TPSpec => TCSpec

    Checking it follows the recipe you just learned: behavior spec on the left, property on the right.

    SPECIFICATION TPSpec
CONSTANT RM = {r1, r2, r3}
PROPERTY TCSpec

    TLC finds no error, with 288 distinct states: the same states as before, since only the question changed.

    How can that formula even make sense?

    TPSpec talks about four variables and TCSpec about one. The theorem looks like apples implying oranges. The answer is a fact held back until now: a state does not assign values only to the variables of your module. It assigns a value to every possible variable, infinitely many of them.

    So one state may have Mozart = <<-37, {14}>> and tmState = "ouch" alongside rmState. TCInit is true on it if rmState maps each element of RM to "working", whatever else is there. A behavior of TCSpec may even have tmPrepared changing wildly from state to state, since TCSpec is silent on it.

    This feels odd only if you read a spec as a program. It is a formula. x + y = 7 does not claim there is no variable z. A useful picture: a spec describes a history of the universe in which the system and its environment behave correctly. It mentions the parts it depends on (msgs might stand for a real transport underneath the protocol), and says nothing about the rest.

    Why stuttering has to be there

    Both formulas now apply to the same behaviors. But how can the implication be true? TMAbort leaves rmState unchanged, while every TCNext step changes it. So a TMAbort step is not a TCNext step.

    The subscript from lesson 25 is the answer. TCSpec requires only that every step satisfies TCNext or leaves rmState unchanged, and TMAbort does the second. In the first figure, each stutter cell is exactly that.

    Predict: narrow what counts as stuttering, so only a step that leaves all four TwoPhase variables unchanged is excused. Property: [][TCNext]_<<rmState, tmState, tmPrepared, msgs>>. What does TLC find?

    An error, immediately. TLC reports the action property violated after two states, with a TMAbort step, as the figure below shows. The property is the formula you would effectively have if specs could not stutter on variables they don't mention.

    Without stuttering, TPSpec would also forbid the Timbuktu Starbucks customer count from changing except when the protocol took a step. That is one reason all TLA+ specs allow it. The most important reason is the theorem itself: because of stuttering, implementation is simply implication. There is no separate notion of implementing to define.

    A check that can fail

    A theorem that TLC confirms tells you more if you've seen it fail. In a copy of TwoPhase, delete one line from TMCommit, the conjunct tmPrepared = RM, so the manager can commit without hearing from anyone. Then check PROPERTY TCSpec again with two resource managers.

    TLC reports the action property on the [][TCNext]_rmState part of TCSpec as violated, with the three-state trace above. The buggy step changes only tmState and msgs, so TCSpec lets it pass as stuttering. Only when r1 acts on the message does rmState do something no TCNext step allows, because Decide commits only from "prepared". A violation in the high-level view may show up later than its cause.

    Should TCSpec => TPSpec also hold?

    Termination, and stopping too soon

    Return to SimpleProgram: Init /\ [][Next]_<<pc, i>>. Its formula allows stuttering between real steps, and after the last one, forever. That is how TLA+ represents a terminating execution: a behavior ending in infinitely many stuttering steps. The universe keeps going after your system finishes. As a result, all behaviors are infinite, and finite ones never need separate treatment.

    Look at the bottom row. It also satisfies the formula: it takes one step, then stutters forever. Everything you've written so far allows the system to stop at any time. These specs say what a system may do, not what it must do. That is not a defect to patch inside the next-state formula. They are very different requirements and should be stated separately, by conjoining a further temporal formula L:

    Init /\ [][Next]_vars /\ L

    Writing L is the main business of the next lecture, starting at lesson 29. It is the tiny part of a spec. The may part is much larger, usually more important, and already enough for useful specs.

    Predict: TLC checks TPSpec => TCSpec and finds no error. Does that show two-phase commit ever commits anything?

    No. A behavior that stutters forever from the initial state satisfies both formulas. The theorem says each step TwoPhase takes is one TCommit permits. Nothing here says a step must be taken.

    While you watch

    • Lamport warns that this will feel strange, and compares it to learning the earth is round. Notice exactly which two facts do the work: states assign all variables, and all specs allow stuttering.
    • Pause where he asks you to add TCSpec as a property in your TwoPhase model, and run it. The bug above is something to try afterwards; it is not in the lecture.
    • Watch how a single behavior gets redrawn several times. First it has hidden variables, then stuttering steps, and then an infinite tail.

    Lamport's TLA+ Video Course, lecture 8.

    Lecture 8: Implementation

    Problem set 8: a spec is a formula, and implementing it is implying it.

    Four problems on lecture 8: stuttering, reading formulas that are true or false of whole behaviors, and checking that one spec implements another with PROPERTY. The last problem asks whether the two-phase commit booking from Problem set 6 and Problem set 7 still implements all-or-nothing agreement once operators get a manual override.

    As before, every module shown was checked with TLC exactly as printed. When a problem uses TwoPhase, put the TwoPhase and TCommit modules from the lessons in the same folder.

    Problem 1●○○Infrastructure

    Add minutes to the dashboard clock

    Draws on Temporal formulas and stuttering, What it means to implement a spec and Paxos Commit: surviving the coordinator.

    An operations dashboard has a tile showing the current hour. The on-call team's alerting rules ("page only between 8 and 20") were written and reviewed against this tiny spec of the tile:

    --------------------------- MODULE PSl8_HourClock ---------------------------
\* The "current hour" tile on an ops dashboard: a 24-hour clock.
EXTENDS Integers
VARIABLE hr
HInit == hr \in 0..23
HNext == hr' = IF hr = 23 THEN 0 ELSE hr + 1
HSpec == HInit /\ [][HNext]_hr
=============================================================================

    A redesign shows hours and minutes. The designer asks whether the alert rules must be reviewed again. They don't need to be if the new tile still satisfies the old spec, that is, if Spec => HourSpec. The new module imports the old one with a named INSTANCE, as PaxosCommit did with TCommit. It also includes the daylight-saving jump that product wants next quarter.

    --------------------------- MODULE PSl8_Dashboard ---------------------------
\* The redesigned tile shows hours and minutes. Does it still satisfy the
\* hour-clock spec that the alerting rules were written against?
EXTENDS Integers
VARIABLES hr, min
vars == <<hr, min>>
Init == hr \in 0..23 /\ min \in 0..59
Tick == /\ min' = IF min = 59 THEN 0 ELSE min + 1
        /\ hr' = IF min = 59 THEN (IF hr = 23 THEN 0 ELSE hr + 1) ELSE hr
\* Daylight saving time starts: the local clock jumps from 01:59 to 03:00.
SpringForward == /\ hr = 1 /\ min = 59
                 /\ hr' = 3 /\ min' = 0
Spec == Init /\ [][Tick]_vars
DSTSpec == Init /\ [][Tick \/ SpringForward]_vars

H == INSTANCE PSl8_HourClock
HourSpec == H!HSpec
\* The same claim with stuttering allowed only when hr AND min are unchanged.
HourSpecNoStutter == H!HInit /\ [][H!HNext]_vars
=============================================================================
    SPECIFICATION Spec
PROPERTY HourSpec
    1. Take the behavior 13:58, 13:59, 14:00, 14:01. For each of its three steps, say whether it is an HNext step, a stuttering step of HSpec, or neither.
    2. Run the cfg as shown. Report TLC's result and the number of distinct states, and explain that number.
    3. Change the property to HourSpecNoStutter. What does TLC report, and how long is the trace?
    4. Change the specification to DSTSpec and the property back to HourSpec. Which step does TLC reject, and what should the team do about the alert rules?

    A behavior goes 10:05, then 10:37, then 11:02. Does it satisfy HourSpec?

    Hint

    [HNext]_hr is HNext \/ UNCHANGED hr. A step that changes only min satisfies the second disjunct. HourSpecNoStutter excuses a step only when <<hr, min>> is unchanged.

    Solution

    1. 13:58 → 13:59 leaves hr unchanged, so it's a stuttering step of HSpec. 13:59 → 14:00 is an HNext step. 14:00 → 14:01 is stuttering again. The diagram marks each one.

    2. No error, 1440 distinct states. Every state of the dashboard is reachable, as Init allows all 24 × 60. So Spec => HourSpec holds on this model: whatever the alert rules relied on about the hour tile is still true.

    3. TLC reports the action property violated after 2 states, on the first Tick it tries (in this run, 0:04 → 0:05). Nearly every tick changes min but not hr. If stuttering meant "nothing changes at all", the hour spec would forbid the minutes from moving, and no clock with a finer display could ever implement it. That's the reason every spec allows steps that leave its own variables unchanged.

    4. TLC reports the action property of HourSpec violated after 2 states: from 01:59, SpringForward sets hr to 3. That's neither hr' = hr + 1 nor stuttering. Any alert rule that assumed every hour is visited (for example "the 02:00 batch job always runs") must be reviewed, and that rule really does break on such a night. The spec found the one change that matters and accepted the rest.

    Problem 2●○○Design system

    Read temporal formulas on a confirm dialog

    Draws on Temporal formulas and stuttering, What it means to implement a spec and States, steps, and behaviors.

    A design system has a ConfirmDialog component: the user opens it, then confirms or cancels. Confirm runs an async request. While the request is in flight, the dialog shows a spinner, and the form must not come back. If the request fails, an error is shown with Retry and Cancel. The component team writes the contract as a spec, then writes a few properties that QA asked for as temporal formulas:

    ---------------------------- MODULE PSl8_Dialog -----------------------------
\* A design-system confirm dialog whose Confirm button runs an async request.
VARIABLE dialog
Status == {"closed", "open", "submitting", "error"}
Init == dialog = "closed"
Open    == dialog = "closed"     /\ dialog' = "open"
Cancel  == dialog \in {"open", "error"} /\ dialog' = "closed"
Confirm == dialog = "open"       /\ dialog' = "submitting"
Succeed == dialog = "submitting" /\ dialog' = "closed"
Fail    == dialog = "submitting" /\ dialog' = "error"
Retry   == dialog = "error"      /\ dialog' = "submitting"
Next == Open \/ Cancel \/ Confirm \/ Succeed \/ Fail \/ Retry
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_dialog

TypeOK == dialog \in Status
AlwaysTypeOK == []TypeOK
\* While a request is in flight the form never reappears.
NoReopenWhileBusy == [][dialog = "submitting" => dialog' # "open"]_dialog
\* An error is shown only right after a request.
ErrorOnlyAfterSubmit == [][dialog' = "error" => dialog = "submitting"]_dialog
\* Once closed, the dialog stays closed (a wrong claim, for comparison).
ClosedIsFinal == [][dialog = "closed" => dialog' = "closed"]_dialog
=============================================================================

    Here are four behaviors taken from bug reports and tests. Each one continues by stuttering forever after its last state.

    1. For each of B1 to B4, decide whether it satisfies Spec, AlwaysTypeOK and NoReopenWhileBusy.
    2. Is the formula Spec => NoReopenWhileBusy true on B2? On B3?
    3. Check the contract with TLC using the cfg below. Then add PROPERTY ClosedIsFinal and run it again. Report both results.
    SPECIFICATION Spec
INVARIANT TypeOK
PROPERTY NoReopenWhileBusy
PROPERTY ErrorOnlyAfterSubmit

    B2 violates NoReopenWhileBusy. What is the value of Spec => NoReopenWhileBusy on B2?

    Hint

    A state formula such as Init, used as a temporal formula, is about the first state only. [][A]_dialog is about every step, and a step where dialog doesn't change satisfies it whatever A says.

    Solution

    1.

    BehaviorSpecAlwaysTypeOKNoReopenWhileBusy
    B1TRUETRUETRUE
    B2FALSE: submitting → open is no action of NextTRUEFALSE: that same step
    B3FALSE: Init fails on the first stateTRUETRUE
    B4TRUE: every step is stutteringTRUETRUE

    B3 shows that a property can hold on a behavior the spec rejects. Only B2 breaks the rule QA cares about, and it's the real double-submit bug: a failed request should go to "error", not reopen the form. These values were confirmed by replaying each behavior in TLC.

    2. TRUE on B2 and TRUE on B3. Neither satisfies Spec, so the implication asserts nothing about them. The implication fails only on a behavior that satisfies Spec and breaks the property. TLC's run in task 3 shows there is none.

    3. No error, 4 distinct states, with TypeOK invariant and both action properties holding. With ClosedIsFinal added, TLC reports it violated after 2 states: closed → open by Open. That's a step of Spec that changes dialog away from "closed", which is exactly what the property forbids. Having a deliberately wrong property fail is a cheap check that TLC is reading your properties the way you meant them.

    Problem 3●●○Databases

    Does the cache implement the store?

    Draws on What it means to implement a spec, Temporal formulas and stuttering, Sets, functions, and quantifiers and Paxos Commit: surviving the coordinator.

    Clients of a key-value store see two operations: put a value, and get the current value of a key. The platform team's spec of what clients may observe records in out what the last get returned:

    ------------------------------ MODULE PSl8_KV -------------------------------
\* What clients of the key-value store may observe. out is the value the
\* most recent Get returned ("none" before the first Get).
CONSTANTS Key, Val
VARIABLES store, out
KVInit == /\ store \in [Key -> Val]
          /\ out = "none"
Put(k, v) == /\ store' = [store EXCEPT ![k] = v]
             /\ out' = out
Get(k) == /\ out' = store[k]
          /\ store' = store
KVNext == \E k \in Key : Get(k) \/ \E v \in Val : Put(k, v)
KVSpec == KVInit /\ [][KVNext]_<<store, out>>
=============================================================================

    To cut database load, the team puts a cache in front of the store. Reads use the cached copy if there is one. Writes are write-through: the database and the cache change together. Fill and Evict are background work. A refactor accidentally replaced Put with PutNoInvalidate, which writes the database and leaves the cache alone.

    ----------------------------- MODULE PSl8_Cache -----------------------------
\* The same store with a cache in front of it. cache[k] is "miss" or a copy.
CONSTANTS Key, Val
VARIABLES store, out, cache
vars == <<store, out, cache>>
Init == /\ store \in [Key -> Val]
        /\ out = "none"
        /\ cache = [k \in Key |-> "miss"]
\* Write-through: the database and the cache change in one step.
Put(k, v) == /\ store' = [store EXCEPT ![k] = v]
             /\ cache' = [cache EXCEPT ![k] = v]
             /\ out' = out
\* The bug: write to the database and forget the cached copy.
PutNoInvalidate(k, v) == /\ store' = [store EXCEPT ![k] = v]
                         /\ UNCHANGED <<cache, out>>
Fill(k)  == /\ cache[k] = "miss"
            /\ cache' = [cache EXCEPT ![k] = store[k]]
            /\ UNCHANGED <<store, out>>
Evict(k) == /\ cache[k] # "miss"
            /\ cache' = [cache EXCEPT ![k] = "miss"]
            /\ UNCHANGED <<store, out>>
Get(k) == /\ out' = IF cache[k] = "miss" THEN store[k] ELSE cache[k]
          /\ UNCHANGED <<store, cache>>
Next == \E k \in Key : \/ Get(k) \/ Fill(k) \/ Evict(k)
                       \/ \E v \in Val : Put(k, v)
BugNext == \E k \in Key : \/ Get(k) \/ Fill(k) \/ Evict(k)
                          \/ \E v \in Val : PutNoInvalidate(k, v)
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars
BugSpec == Init /\ [][BugNext]_vars

KV == INSTANCE PSl8_KV
KVSpec == KV!KVSpec
THEOREM Spec => KVSpec
=============================================================================
    SPECIFICATION Spec
CONSTANTS Key = {"k1", "k2"}
          Val = {"v1", "v2"}
PROPERTY KVSpec
    1. For each action of Next (Put, Get, Fill, Evict), say whether its steps are KVNext steps or stuttering steps of KVSpec.
    2. Run the cfg as shown and report the result.
    3. Change the specification to BugSpec. Report the trace, and for each step in it say what KVSpec makes of it.
    4. Another team builds a write-back cache: Put writes only the cache, and a later Flush copies it to the database. Without running it, predict whether TLC would accept PROPERTY KVSpec for that design. Does the answer mean the write-back cache is wrong?

    To KVSpec, an Evict step is

    Hint

    KVSpec sees only store and out. A Get step is a KVNext step only if the new out equals store[k]. When can cache[k] differ from store[k]?

    Solution

    1. Put(k, v) is a KV!Put(k, v) step: store changes the same way and out is unchanged. Fill and Evict change only cache, so they're stuttering steps. Get(k) sets out to the cached copy or to store[k]. It's a KV!Get(k) step as long as every cached copy equals the stored value, which holds in every reachable state of Spec, because Put updates both.

    2. No error, 48 distinct states: 4 stores × 4 consistent caches (each key missing or equal to the store) × 3 values of out.

    3. TLC reports the action property of KVSpec violated after 4 states:

    Fill("k1") copies "v2": stuttering. PutNoInvalidate("k1","v1") sets the store to "v1": a KV!Put step, still fine. Get("k1") returns the cached "v2" while store["k1"] is "v1", so out changes to a value KV!Get doesn't allow. The bug happens in step 2, and the client sees it in step 3. That's typical: the high-level spec flags a problem only when it becomes observable.

    4. TLC would reject it. A write-back Put leaves store and out unchanged, so KVSpec treats it as stuttering. The next Get returns the new value while store still holds the old one, and that's not a KV!Get step. A hidden run of this design gives exactly that 3-state trace. But the design may be perfectly correct: what a client observes as "the store" is the cached value when it is dirty, not the database row. The check failed because the implementation's variable store isn't the right thing to compare with the spec's store. Lecture 10 shows how to state that comparison with an expression in place of a variable of the same name.

    Problem 4●●●Databases

    Synthesis: the operator's rollback button

    Draws on What it means to implement a spec, Two-phase commit and records, The transaction commit spec, Problem set 5, Problem set 6 and Problem set 7.

    The trip booking (flight, hotel, car) still runs two-phase commit. After the coordinator outage in Problem set 7, operations wrote a runbook step: "If a reservation has been prepared for more than ten minutes, roll it back by hand." Some transaction managers offer exactly this escape hatch for in-doubt participants, often called a heuristic decision. Your job is to check it against all-or-nothing agreement, written in the style of TCommit as in Problem set 5, and now as one formula.

    --------------------------- MODULE PSl8_Agreement ---------------------------
\* All-or-nothing agreement, TCommit with its spec written as one formula.
CONSTANT RM
VARIABLE rmState
AInit == rmState = [r \in RM |-> "working"]
canCommit == \A r \in RM : rmState[r] \in {"prepared", "committed"}
notCommitted == \A r \in RM : rmState[r] # "committed"
Prepare(r) == /\ rmState[r] = "working"
              /\ rmState' = [rmState EXCEPT ![r] = "prepared"]
Decide(r) == \/ /\ rmState[r] = "prepared"
                /\ canCommit
                /\ rmState' = [rmState EXCEPT ![r] = "committed"]
             \/ /\ rmState[r] \in {"working", "prepared"}
                /\ notCommitted
                /\ rmState' = [rmState EXCEPT ![r] = "aborted"]
ANext == \E r \in RM : Prepare(r) \/ Decide(r)
ASpec == AInit /\ [][ANext]_rmState
=============================================================================

    The booking module extends the lesson's TwoPhase. It defines its spec as a formula and adds the operator's action. Because PSl8_Agreement has the same variable rmState and constant RM, INSTANCE matches them by name.

    ---------------------------- MODULE PSl8_Booking ----------------------------
\* Two-phase commit for the trip booking, plus the operator's escape hatch:
\* a participant stuck in "prepared" can be forced to roll back by hand.
EXTENDS TwoPhase
BookSpec == TPInit /\ [][TPNext]_vars

HeuristicAbort(r) == /\ rmState[r] = "prepared"
                     /\ rmState' = [rmState EXCEPT ![r] = "aborted"]
                     /\ UNCHANGED <<tmState, tmPrepared, msgs>>
OpsNext == TPNext \/ \E r \in RM : HeuristicAbort(r)
OpsSpec == TPInit /\ [][OpsNext]_vars

AG == INSTANCE PSl8_Agreement
Agreement == AG!ASpec
THEOREM BookSpec => Agreement
=============================================================================
    SPECIFICATION BookSpec
CONSTANT RM = {"flight", "hotel", "car"}
PROPERTY Agreement
    1. Run the cfg as shown. Report the result, and say one thing the theorem guarantees and one thing it doesn't.
    2. Without TLC: all three RMs are prepared and nothing has been decided. Is a HeuristicAbort("flight") step from there an ANext step?
    3. Change the specification to OpsSpec. Report the trace length and the first step that is neither an ANext step nor stuttering for Agreement.
    4. A reviewer suggests a guard: allow HeuristicAbort only while no Commit message has been sent. Would that make OpsSpec implement Agreement? What guard would, and who can check it?

    Which step does Agreement reject in TLC's trace?

    Hint

    Write out Decide(r)'s abort branch and evaluate it on the state in task 2. For task 4, ask whether the TM could still send Commit after the guard was checked. What has the TM already recorded?

    Solution

    1. No error, 288 distinct states: BookSpec => Agreement holds on this model. It guarantees that every step the protocol takes changes rmState in a way agreement allows. It doesn't guarantee that anything is ever decided. A behavior that stutters forever satisfies both sides, and the coordinator crash of Problem set 7 is still possible.

    2. Yes. The abort branch of Decide("flight") needs rmState["flight"] \in {"working", "prepared"} and notCommitted, and both hold. Taken alone, the operator's step looks like a legal abort.

    3. TLC reports the action property of Agreement violated after 10 states. The run here:

    States 2 to 5: hotel and flight prepare and the TM records both. State 6: HeuristicAbort("flight"), an allowed abort. States 7 to 9: car prepares, the TM records it, and TMCommit sends Commit, because tmPrepared = RM no matter what flight did afterwards. That's stuttering for Agreement. State 10: RMRcvCommitMsg("flight") moves flight from aborted to committed. TwoPhase's receive action has no guard on the RM's state, since in the real protocol a prepared RM can't have aborted. Your run may end instead with hotel or car committing while flight is aborted. Either way, the step that breaks the high-level spec is a commit receipt, three steps after the cause.

    4. No. TLC rejects the guarded version too, again in 10 states. The TM recorded flight's Prepared before the operator acted, and nothing tells it to forget. The only safe guard is that the TM has decided Abort, and then the heuristic is just RMRcvAbortMsg. In other words, the decision has to be made at the coordinator, which is the process that's down. The check shows why the runbook step is dangerous: once you allow it, all-or-nothing is no longer a property of the system, and any mixed outcome has to be found and repaired by hand.

    Lecture 9: Alternating bit protocol

    First say what a channel should accomplish.

    You now have two ways to read a spec: as what a system may do, and as a formula another spec can imply. The next lessons use one small protocol for sending data across a channel that loses messages. Before seeing how it works, you write what it should achieve, and that takes one more data structure: sequences.

    Finite sequences

    A finite sequence is another name for a tuple, and programmers would call it a list. <<-3, "xyz", {0, 2}>> has length 3. A sequence of length N is simply a function with domain 1..N, so <<-3, "xyz", {0, 2}>>[2] is "xyz", and [i \in 1..N |-> i^2] is the sequence of the first N squares. The standard module Sequences defines the operators. These values come from TLC, using the evaluation trick described below:

    ExpressionValue
    Head(<<"Fred", "Mary", "Ted">>)"Fred"
    Tail(<<"Fred", "Mary", "Ted">>)<<"Mary", "Ted">>
    Append(<<3, 2, 1>>, "a")<<3, 2, 1, "a">>
    <<3, 2, 1>> \o <<"a", "b">><<3, 2, 1, "a", "b">>
    Len(<<3, 2, 1>>)3
    1..0, the domain of <<>>{}

    Seq(S) is the set of all finite sequences with elements in S. It is infinite: Seq({3}) contains <<>>, <<3>>, <<3, 3>>, and so on. Sequences are the last commonly used data type you need.

    The protocol will need to delete a message from the middle of a channel. No built-in does this, so define it, by writing a function on a shorter domain and working out what each position holds:

    Remove(i, seq) ==
  [j \in 1..(Len(seq) - 1) |-> IF j < i THEN seq[j] ELSE seq[j + 1]]

    A definition like that deserves a test, and there's no need for a behavior to run one. In the Toolbox, type an expression into a model's results page and TLC computes it. In a plain module, write ASSUME PrintT(Remove(3, <<1, 2, 3, 4>>)) after EXTENDS TLC, and TLC prints <<1, 2, 4>> while checking assumptions.

    The Cartesian product

    S \X T is the set of all pairs <<a, b>> with a in S and b in T. So (1..3) \X {"a", "b"} has six elements. Keep the parentheses. Without them it parses as 1..(3 \X {"a", "b"}), and TLC stops with an error. S \X T \X U is the obvious set of triples.

    What must the protocol accomplish?

    Sender A sends a sequence of data items to receiver B. An obvious model uses two variables, AVar and BVar. A sets AVar to the string it wants to send. Then B sets BVar equal to it. Watching that, you would see Fred, Mary, Ted, Ann. But suppose A meant to send Mary twice. Nothing would change, and a value can't have been sent if nothing changed.

    So something must change when a value is sent again. The lecture lets each variable be a pair: the value, and one bit that flips every time A chooses a value. The top figure sends Fred, Mary, Mary this way. The spec is short:

    ------------------------------- MODULE ABSpec -------------------------------
EXTENDS Integers
CONSTANT Data
VARIABLES AVar, BVar

TypeOK == /\ AVar \in Data \X {0, 1}
          /\ BVar \in Data \X {0, 1}

vars == <<AVar, BVar>>

Init == /\ AVar \in Data \X {1}
        /\ BVar = AVar

A == /\ AVar = BVar
     /\ \E d \in Data : AVar' = <<d, 1 - AVar[2]>>
     /\ BVar' = BVar

B == /\ AVar # BVar
     /\ BVar' = AVar
     /\ AVar' = AVar

Next == A \/ B

Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars

Inv == (AVar[2] = BVar[2]) => (AVar = BVar)

FairSpec == Spec /\ WF_vars(Next)
=============================================================================

    The last line uses WF, which lesson 29 explains; ignore it for now. 1 - AVar[2] complements the bit. A step of A needs the two variables equal, because B must have received the last value. A step of B needs them unequal and copies. There's no channel, no message, and no retransmission here, since those belong to how, not what.

    Check it

    Type correctness alone doesn't make a spec right. To find errors, check formulas that ought to be invariants. Here that is Inv: if the bits agree, the pairs agree. Make sure you see why before running it. The bits differ exactly between an A step and the following B step.

    SPECIFICATION Spec
CONSTANT Data = {d1, d2, d3}
INVARIANT TypeOK
INVARIANT Inv

    d1, d2, d3 are model values, as you used for RM. TLC finds no error: 39 states generated, 24 distinct, depth 4.

    Predict: where do the 24 states come from?

    There are 3 × 2 = 6 possible pairs. When the variables agree there is one state per pair, giving 6. When they differ, the bits must differ, by Inv, so AVar is any of 6 pairs and BVar any of the 3 pairs with the other bit, giving 18. And 6 + 18 = 24.

    A has just set AVar to <<"Mary", 1>> and B has not copied it. Can A now replace it with <<"Ted", 0>>?

    Like every spec so far, Spec says only what may happen. A behavior may stop right after A sets AVar, so nothing is ever received. lesson 29 fixes that.

    While you watch

    • This lesson covers the first half of the lecture's first part: sequences, the product, ABSpec, and the type and Inv checks. The second half goes with lesson 29.
    • Pause at Remove and try to fill in the dots yourself before he reveals the definition. Pause again at the animation with Mary sent twice, and say what you'd add to make it visible.
    • He downloads ABSpec, makes a model with a few model values, and has you run it. Do so, in the Toolbox as he shows or in VS Code with the configuration above.

    Lamport's TLA+ Video Course, lecture 9.

    Lecture 9: Alternating bit protocol

    "May happen" is not "will happen."

    ABSpec's Spec allows a value to be sent and then never received, because a behavior may stutter forever, as you saw in lesson 26. This lesson adds what a system must do. You write the requirement as a temporal formula, then add fairness conditions that make it true.

    Safety and liveness

    A safety formula says what may happen. If a behavior violates it, the violation occurs at some particular point, and nothing later can undo it. Init /\ [][Next]_vars is one: it fails on a bad first state or on a step that is neither Next nor stuttering. A liveness formula says what must happen, and no point in a behavior can violate it, because the rest of the behavior could always make it true. Remember that a behavior here is any infinite sequence of states, not just one allowed by some spec.

    The figure's second row uses a new operator. <>P, read eventually P, says P is true on some state. It equals ~[]~P; convince yourself of that. For a sequential program, the one liveness property is termination: <>Terminated. Concurrent systems have many others, written with these forms:

    FormulaMeaning
    <>PP holds at some state.
    []<>PP holds infinitely often.
    <>[]PThere comes a point after which P always holds.
    P ~> QP leads to Q, which abbreviates [](P => <>Q). Whenever P holds, Q holds then or later.

    For the channel, we'd like every value being sent to be received. The lecture gives this formula to copy; here it has a name, defined in a small wrapper module that extends ABSpec:

    Delivered == \A v \in Data \X {0, 1} : (AVar = v) ~> (BVar = v)

    Eventually is not a deadline. It has no time bound at all. Also, with changing requests, the predicate must identify which request. Here the pair v plays that role, while an imprecise "some request completed" could be satisfied by an old one.

    Enabled, and weak fairness

    Action A is enabled in state s when some state t makes s → t an A step. A conjunct with no primes is an enabling condition, so ABSpec's A is enabled when AVar = BVar and Data is non-empty.

    Weak fairness of A says: if A ever remains continuously enabled, an A step must eventually occur. Equivalently, A cannot stay enabled forever without another A step. It is written WF_vars(A), in ASCII exactly like that, and read "WF of A". It is a liveness property, because an A step or a state where A is disabled can always make it true.

    Strong fairness, SF_vars(A), is stronger: if A is repeatedly enabled, even with gaps, an A step must eventually occur. The difference is the flicker shown in run 2 below.

    Inspect repeating schedules

    Predict: Serve is enabled every other step and never runs. Does weak fairness reject the behavior?

    No. It never stays enabled continuously forever. Strong fairness rejects that particular infinite behavior. Whether strong fairness is a justified system assumption is a separate question.

    What the subscript means

    WF_vars(A) is weak fairness of the action A /\ (vars' # vars), a non-stuttering A step. It makes no sense to require a stuttering step, since nobody could tell whether it happened.

    Adding liveness to a spec

    A spec with liveness has the form Init /\ [][Next]_vars /\ Fairness. Fairness is a conjunction of WF and SF formulas, each on a subaction of Next, meaning every step of it is a Next step. Now you can read the last line of ABSpec:

    FairSpec == Spec /\ WF_vars(Next)

    Behaviors must keep taking Next steps while Next is enabled. The safety part never reaches a state where it isn't, so A keeps sending and B keeps receiving forever. A second possible spec says something weaker, using WF_vars(B) alone: every sent value is received, but the sender may stop. Here are the checks, with Data = {d1, d2, d3}. All explore the same 24 states; only the question differs. FairAB abbreviates Spec /\ WF_vars(A) /\ WF_vars(B).

    SPECIFICATIONPROPERTYTLC says
    SpecDeliveredViolated. A step, then stuttering.
    FairSpecDeliveredNo error.
    Spec /\ WF_vars(B)DeliveredNo error.
    Spec /\ WF_vars(B)FairABViolated. Stuttering from the first state: the sender stops.
    FairSpecFairABNo error.
    FairABFairSpecNo error.

    The last two rows solve the lecture's exercise by checking both directions: weak fairness of Next and of A and B separately are equivalent here. A liveness check must not use a symmetry set, a TLC reduction some models use. These don't.

    Why is weak fairness enough for action B of ABSpec?

    Worked architecture: a background upload worker

    A mobile app has accepted upload U. The worker can Send(U) whenever the device is online and U is pending. Take a behavior where the phone keeps reconnecting and disconnecting before U is selected. As the figure shows, the upload was enabled many times, and weak fairness still doesn't require it to run.

    For Pending(U) ~> Uploaded(U), decide what the environment promises. If the device eventually stays online, Send(U) becomes continuously enabled and weak fairness suffices. Strong fairness would let recurring opportunities suffice, but background execution limits on the platform may make that assumption false. And sending still isn't delivery: a separate assumption is needed if the network can drop every attempt.

    Fairness also needs the right granularity. With uploads U and V pending, WF_vars(SendAny) can be satisfied by sending V forever while U waits. Attach fairness per request, such as \A p \in Processes : WF_vars(Serve(p)). Never add fairness merely to silence a counterexample. Fairness is not a scheduler, a response-time bound, or a delivery guarantee. It states what you assume, and permanent partitions can make the assumption false.

    Predict: a worker is weakly fair, but every request is dropped. Does "pending leads to delivered" follow?

    No. Worker scheduling and network delivery are different actions with different assumptions. A correct argument must connect retries, eventual delivery, acknowledgement, and durable completion instead of jumping from "worker runs" to "request succeeds".

    While you watch
