    • Pause at the eventually exercise. Then, at the two fair specs, explain to yourself why the sender may stop in one but not the other.
    • The upload worker is not in the lecture.

    Temporal properties and Lamport's lecture 9.

    Lecture 9: Alternating bit protocol

    Keep resending until the right bit comes back.

    lesson 28 said what should happen and lesson 29 said it must. Now comes how. Sender A and receiver B talk over two channels that can lose messages, and all they have to work with is the one bit from ABSpec. You'll check that the protocol implements its spec, then see weak fairness fail on a real counterexample and strong fairness repair it.

    How it works

    A repeatedly sends its current AVar on channel AtoB, since any copy might be lost. B repeatedly sends the bit of BVar on channel BtoA, as an acknowledgement. Then the bits do all the work:

    • When B receives a message whose bit differs from its own, it's a new value, so B sets BVar to it. A message with the same bit is one B already has.
    • When A receives a bit equal to its own, its current value has been acknowledged, so it chooses a new value and flips its bit. A different bit is a stale ack for the previous value.

    Step the protocol yourself

    You are the scheduler and the network. This is an educational model, not TLC. Click a message to lose it. A channel holds at most 3 messages here, as in the lecture's model.

    AtoB
    BtoA

    Try this in the lab. Send, lose the message, and send again, watching the high-level view stay at stuttering until one copy gets through. Then tick the box, send acks, and receive them with nothing delivered.

    The specification

    Module AB has nothing new except sequence operators. A send appends to a channel, a receive takes the head, and LoseMsg uses Remove to delete any message.

    --------------------------------- MODULE AB ---------------------------------
EXTENDS Integers, Sequences

CONSTANT Data

Remove(i, seq) ==
  [j \in 1..(Len(seq) - 1) |-> IF j < i THEN seq[j] ELSE seq[j + 1]]

VARIABLES AVar, BVar, AtoB, BtoA

vars == <<AVar, BVar, AtoB, BtoA>>

TypeOK == /\ AVar \in Data \X {0, 1}
          /\ BVar \in Data \X {0, 1}
          /\ AtoB \in Seq(Data \X {0, 1})
          /\ BtoA \in Seq({0, 1})

Init == /\ AVar \in Data \X {1}
        /\ BVar = AVar
        /\ AtoB = <<>>
        /\ BtoA = <<>>

ASnd == /\ AtoB' = Append(AtoB, AVar)
        /\ UNCHANGED <<AVar, BtoA, BVar>>

ARcv == /\ BtoA # <<>>
        /\ IF Head(BtoA) = AVar[2]
             THEN \E d \in Data : AVar' = <<d, 1 - AVar[2]>>
             ELSE AVar' = AVar
        /\ BtoA' = Tail(BtoA)
        /\ UNCHANGED <<AtoB, BVar>>

BSnd == /\ BtoA' = Append(BtoA, BVar[2])
        /\ UNCHANGED <<AVar, BVar, AtoB>>

BRcv == /\ AtoB # <<>>
        /\ IF Head(AtoB)[2] # BVar[2]
             THEN BVar' = Head(AtoB)
             ELSE BVar' = BVar
        /\ AtoB' = Tail(AtoB)
        /\ UNCHANGED <<AVar, BtoA>>

LoseMsg == /\ \/ /\ \E i \in 1..Len(AtoB) : AtoB' = Remove(i, AtoB)
                 /\ BtoA' = BtoA
              \/ /\ \E i \in 1..Len(BtoA) : BtoA' = Remove(i, BtoA)
                 /\ AtoB' = AtoB
           /\ UNCHANGED <<AVar, BVar>>

Next == ASnd \/ ARcv \/ BSnd \/ BRcv \/ LoseMsg

Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars

ABS == INSTANCE ABSpec

THEOREM Spec => ABS!Spec

FairSpec == Spec /\ SF_vars(ARcv) /\ SF_vars(BRcv)
                 /\ WF_vars(ASnd) /\ WF_vars(BSnd)

THEOREM FairSpec => ABS!FairSpec
=============================================================================

    The new line is ABS == INSTANCE ABSpec. A plain INSTANCE ABSpec is illegal here, because it would import a second Spec; TLC reports multiple definitions. Naming the instance imports everything with a prefix, so ABS!Spec is ABSpec's formula. The variables AVar and BVar carry over by name. This is the theorem pattern from lesson 26 again.

    Checking safety needs a bound

    A and B can send faster than messages are received or lost, so channels can grow without limit. There are infinitely many reachable states, and TLC would run forever. You could change the spec, but you shouldn't have to change a spec to check it. Instead, give TLC a state constraint:

    Bound == (Len(AtoB) <= 2) /\ (Len(BtoA) <= 2)

    Normally TLC takes an unexplored state, computes its successors, and repeats. With a constraint, it first tests the state, and if the test fails it doesn't go on from there. That is a limit on what was checked, so say so when reporting a result. A cfg can't name ABS!Spec directly, so a small wrapper module extends AB and defines HighSafety == ABS!Spec. The Toolbox accepts ABS!Spec in its property list.

    SPECIFICATION Spec
CONSTANT Data = {d1, d2}
CONSTRAINT Bound
INVARIANT TypeOK
PROPERTY HighSafety

    TLC finds no error: 1286 states generated, 216 distinct, depth 13. With the lecture's model, three data values and channel length at most 3, it finds no error in 960 distinct states.

    Predict: delete the bit test from ARcv, so any ack makes A choose a new value. And separately, delete the test from BRcv, so B always copies the head. Which breaks?

    Only the first. With A broken, TLC reports ABS!Spec violated in five states, shown below. With B broken, this model still gives no error, with the same 216 states. Channels are first-in first-out, so on this model a message carrying B's own bit always equals BVar, and copying it changes nothing. The test that does the work on this model is the one at A. B's test only says, in the spec's terms, when nothing new arrived.

    Liveness: which fairness?

    The complete spec should imply ABS!FairSpec, with messages that keep getting sent and received. Try the natural candidates, always with the same 216-state model:

    Added to SpecChecked againstTLC says
    nothingDeliveredViolated: stops after a value is sent, then stutters.
    WF_vars(Next)ABS!FairSpecViolated: BSnd, LoseMsg, forever.
    WF on all four, no LoseMsgABS!FairSpecViolated: the loop below.
    FairSpec as printedABS!FairSpec and DeliveredNo error.

    WF_vars(Next) is too weak, because Next keeps being satisfied by something useless. So each of the four real actions needs its own requirement. There is none on LoseMsg, since nothing requires messages to be lost. Weak fairness on all four looks plausible, and here is what TLC found:

    Read the fairness conditions against it. ASnd, BSnd and BRcv steps keep occurring. ARcv is enabled in State 3 and disabled again in State 4, so it's never continuously enabled and weak fairness asks nothing of it. Your run may find a different loop; the lecture shows one where messages in both directions get lost. Both have the same cause: LoseMsg keeps disabling a receive.

    Strong fairness from lesson 29 closes the gap. BSnd is always enabled, so weak fairness makes B keep sending. Each send enables ARcv, so ARcv is repeatedly enabled, and SF_vars(ARcv) requires it to happen, however often loss disables it. The argument from A to B is symmetric. Strong fairness doesn't stop losses. It says that if you keep sending, something eventually gets through, which is the assumption a lossy channel has to meet to be usable at all.

    Why is weak fairness enough for ASnd and BSnd?

    What good is eventually?

    Something that happens a million years from now is no use, and you could never observe strong fairness failing. But a spec is a compromise between accuracy and simplicity. Requiring receipt within 4.7 ms would mean specifying delivery times, loss rates, and retransmission rates. And if a message is never received, it isn't received in 4.7 ms. So for systems without hard real-time requirements, liveness checking finds errors that prevent things from happening. Timeouts that exist only so that something eventually happens can be plain actions with weak fairness and no clocks. A failed liveness check can also reveal a safety part that's too strict.

    While you watch

    • Stop before he runs TLC and predict why the model won't finish. Then change the two SF to WF as he asks and run it.
    • His TLC run may produce a different trace from the one above. Check any trace you get the way he does, condition by condition.
    • The lab, the five-state bug, and the BRcv experiment are additions; the rest follows the lecture's order.

    Lamport's TLA+ Video Course, lecture 9.

    Lecture 9: Alternating bit protocol

    Problem set 9: say what must happen, and what it assumes.

    Four problems on lecture 9: liveness properties, weak and strong fairness, and the alternating bit protocol. Each one asks TLC whether something eventually happens and then asks you why the answer depends on the fairness you assumed. The last problem returns to the trip booking of Problem set 6, Problem set 7 and Problem set 8, now over a network that loses messages.

    Every module shown was checked with TLC exactly as printed. Liveness counterexamples aren't unique: TLC may show you a different loop from the one described here, so check yours condition by condition, as The alternating bit protocol does. None of these models uses a symmetry set, since liveness checking must not.

    Problem 1●○○Infrastructure

    Will every background job run?

    Draws on Liveness and fairness, The high-level spec of a channel and The alternating bit protocol.

    A web app pushes slow work (sending receipts, resizing images) onto a background-job queue with a single worker. Support asks for a guarantee: every job that is submitted is eventually processed. The worker also sends a heartbeat to the scheduler, so a monitor can tell it's alive. Last week a customer's receipt never went out, although the job sat in the queue and the worker's heartbeat stayed green on the monitor the whole time. The module below has no deadlines, because "eventually" has none.

    ---------------------------- MODULE PSl9_JobQueue ---------------------------
\* A background-job queue with one worker. Each job is submitted once.
\* While running, the worker also sends heartbeats to the scheduler.
EXTENDS Integers, Sequences
CONSTANT Job
VARIABLES queue, submitted, done, beat
vars == <<queue, submitted, done, beat>>
Init == /\ queue = <<>>
        /\ submitted = {}
        /\ done = {}
        /\ beat = 0
Submit(j) == /\ j \notin submitted
             /\ submitted' = submitted \cup {j}
             /\ queue' = Append(queue, j)
             /\ UNCHANGED <<done, beat>>
Process == /\ queue # <<>>
           /\ done' = done \cup {Head(queue)}
           /\ queue' = Tail(queue)
           /\ UNCHANGED <<submitted, beat>>
Heartbeat == /\ beat' = 1 - beat
             /\ UNCHANGED <<queue, submitted, done>>
Next == Process \/ Heartbeat \/ \E j \in Job : Submit(j)
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars
FairNext == Spec /\ WF_vars(Next)
FairWorker == Spec /\ WF_vars(Process)

EveryJobProcessed == \A j \in Job : (j \in submitted) ~> (j \in done)
=============================================================================
    SPECIFICATION FairWorker
CONSTANT Job = {"j1", "j2", "j3"}
PROPERTY EveryJobProcessed
    1. Run TLC with SPECIFICATION Spec. What does the counterexample end with, and why is it allowed?
    2. Run it with FairNext. Describe the loop TLC reports, and explain why it satisfies WF_vars(Next).
    3. Run it with FairWorker, as in the cfg shown. Report the result.
    4. Nothing is fair about Submit. Should it be? Say what WF_vars(\E j \in Job : Submit(j)) would claim about the users of the app.

    Why is weak fairness enough for Process?

    Hint

    WF_vars(Next) needs Next steps to keep happening while Next is enabled. Is there any state where some Next step is not possible? Which action is always enabled?

    Solution

    1. TLC reports EveryJobProcessed violated. In this run, some jobs are submitted and processed, and the trace ends with j1 still in the queue followed by "Stuttering". Spec says only what may happen, so a behavior may stop at any point. TLC even warns that the stuttering counterexample may come from a missing fairness condition.

    2. TLC again reports a violation, this time ending in a loop. In the run here, j1 is submitted and processed, j3 and j2 are submitted, and then states 5 and 6 alternate by Heartbeat steps forever while j3 and j2 wait in the queue. Every step is a Next step, so WF_vars(Next) is satisfied. It requires only that Next steps keep happening, not that any particular one does. This is the same weakness The alternating bit protocol found in WF_vars(Next) for the alternating bit protocol.

    3. No error, 76 distinct states. In a state where some job is in the queue, Process is enabled and stays enabled until it runs, so weak fairness forces a Process step. The queue is first-in first-out, so a submitted job reaches the head after the jobs before it have been processed.

    4. No. That condition would say that users keep submitting jobs as long as some job hasn't been submitted, which is a claim about the environment, not the system, and it's false. Fairness belongs on actions the system promises to take. The property is already conditional: it talks only about jobs that are submitted.

    Problem 2●●○Databases

    A migration that never gets its lock

    Draws on Liveness and fairness, The alternating bit protocol and Sets, functions, and quantifiers.

    A database's lock manager lets many queries hold a table lock in shared mode, while a schema migration (ALTER TABLE) needs it exclusively. The first version grants a shared lock whenever no writer holds the table. On a busy table the migration has been waiting for an hour. The team's first idea is "make the scheduler fairer". The module below lets you test that idea. Queries release the lock eventually (weak fairness on every release), and the three specs differ only in the fairness of WriteAcquire and in one guard.

    ---------------------------- MODULE PSl9_RWLock -----------------------------
\* A table lock: queries take it shared, a schema migration takes it
\* exclusive. writer is "idle", "waiting" or "writing".
CONSTANT Reader
VARIABLES readers, writer
vars == <<readers, writer>>
Init == readers = {} /\ writer = "idle"

ReadAcquire(r) == /\ r \notin readers
                  /\ writer # "writing"
                  /\ readers' = readers \cup {r}
                  /\ writer' = writer
\* The fix: a waiting writer also blocks new readers.
ReadAcquireQueued(r) == writer = "idle" /\ ReadAcquire(r)
ReadRelease(r) == /\ r \in readers
                  /\ readers' = readers \ {r}
                  /\ writer' = writer
Request      == writer = "idle"    /\ writer' = "waiting" /\ readers' = readers
WriteAcquire == /\ writer = "waiting"
                /\ readers = {}
                /\ writer' = "writing"
                /\ readers' = readers
WriteRelease == writer = "writing" /\ writer' = "idle"    /\ readers' = readers

Next   == Request \/ WriteAcquire \/ WriteRelease
          \/ \E r \in Reader : ReadAcquire(r) \/ ReadRelease(r)
QNext  == Request \/ WriteAcquire \/ WriteRelease
          \/ \E r \in Reader : ReadAcquireQueued(r) \/ ReadRelease(r)

Releases == WF_vars(WriteRelease) /\ \A r \in Reader : WF_vars(ReadRelease(r))
WFSpec  == Init /\ [][Next]_vars  /\ Releases /\ WF_vars(WriteAcquire)
SFSpec  == Init /\ [][Next]_vars  /\ Releases /\ SF_vars(WriteAcquire)
QWFSpec == Init /\ [][QNext]_vars /\ Releases /\ WF_vars(WriteAcquire)

WriterProgress == (writer = "waiting") ~> (writer = "writing")
=============================================================================
    SPECIFICATION WFSpec
CONSTANT Reader = {"q1", "q2"}
PROPERTY WriterProgress
    1. Run WFSpec with Reader = {"q1", "q2"}. Is WriteAcquire ever enabled in the loop TLC reports? Why doesn't weak fairness force it?
    2. Run SFSpec, first with Reader = {"q1"}, then with two readers. Explain why strong fairness helps with one reader and not with two.
    3. Run QWFSpec with two readers. What changed, and why is weak fairness enough now?
    4. PostgreSQL behaves like the fixed version: once a statement is waiting for an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, later requests that conflict with it, even a plain SELECT's ACCESS SHARE, wait behind it. What does the fix cost while a long query holds the table, and why do migration guides recommend setting lock_timeout?

    The migration starves under SFSpec with two queries. What has to change?

    Hint

    Write down, for each state of the loop, whether readers = {}. Weak fairness needs an action enabled continuously; strong fairness needs it enabled infinitely often. Neither says anything about an action that is never enabled.

    Solution

    1. TLC reports WriterProgress violated. In this run the writer requests the lock, then q2 acquires and releases forever. WriteAcquire is enabled in the states where readers = {} and disabled whenever q2 holds the lock. It is never continuously enabled, so weak fairness asks nothing of it. That's the flicker from Liveness and fairness.

    2. With one query, SFSpec gives no error (5 distinct states). Each release by q1 makes the table free, so WriteAcquire is enabled infinitely often, and strong fairness forces it to happen. With two queries TLC again reports a violation:

    q1 and q2 overlap, so one of them always holds the lock. readers is never empty, WriteAcquire is never enabled, and strong fairness, which talks only about enabled actions, doesn't apply. Each query still releases the lock infinitely often, so the release fairness holds too. No scheduler policy fixes this, because it isn't a scheduling problem.

    3. No error (9 distinct states). ReadAcquireQueued refuses new shared locks while the writer is waiting. The current holders release because of their weak fairness, readers becomes empty and stays empty, and WriteAcquire is then continuously enabled, so weak fairness is enough. The fix changed the protocol, not the fairness.

    4. While the migration waits behind one long-running query, every new query on that table waits behind the migration. To users, a slow report plus a migration looks like a table outage. Setting lock_timeout limits how long the migration waits in the queue: if it can't get the lock quickly, it fails and is retried later, and the other queries proceed. That's the same trade-off as the model: whoever waits blocks those behind it.

    Problem 3●●○Networking

    The alternating bit protocol over a link that reorders

    Draws on The alternating bit protocol, The high-level spec of a channel and Messages, failures, and retries.

    A battery-powered temperature sensor (A) sends readings to a gateway (B) using the alternating bit protocol, the way the firmware team learned it. On the test bench, over a serial link that delivers in order, everything works. In the field the link is UDP, and UDP datagrams can be lost, duplicated, and delivered out of order. Now and then, the dashboard shows an old reading as new.

    The module is the lesson's AB with one change: when Reorder is TRUE, a receiver may take any message in its channel, not just the head. PSl9_LinkSpec is ABSpec from The high-level spec of a channel, unchanged except for its name.

    ----------------------------- MODULE PSl9_Sensor ----------------------------
\* The alternating bit protocol between a sensor (A) and a gateway (B).
\* As module AB, except a receiver may take ANY message in its channel when
\* Reorder is TRUE, as over UDP. With Reorder = FALSE it is exactly AB.
EXTENDS Integers, Sequences
CONSTANTS Data, Reorder
Remove(i, seq) ==
  [j \in 1..(Len(seq) - 1) |-> IF j < i THEN seq[j] ELSE seq[j + 1]]
VARIABLES AVar, BVar, AtoB, BtoA
vars == <<AVar, BVar, AtoB, BtoA>>
TypeOK == /\ AVar \in Data \X {0, 1}
          /\ BVar \in Data \X {0, 1}
          /\ AtoB \in Seq(Data \X {0, 1})
          /\ BtoA \in Seq({0, 1})
Init == /\ AVar \in Data \X {1}
        /\ BVar = AVar
        /\ AtoB = <<>>
        /\ BtoA = <<>>
\* The positions a receiver may take a message from.
Pick(ch) == IF Reorder THEN 1..Len(ch) ELSE 1..1

ASnd == /\ AtoB' = Append(AtoB, AVar)
        /\ UNCHANGED <<AVar, BtoA, BVar>>
ARcv == /\ BtoA # <<>>
        /\ \E i \in Pick(BtoA) :
             /\ IF BtoA[i] = AVar[2]
                  THEN \E d \in Data : AVar' = <<d, 1 - AVar[2]>>
                  ELSE AVar' = AVar
             /\ BtoA' = Remove(i, BtoA)
        /\ UNCHANGED <<AtoB, BVar>>
BSnd == /\ BtoA' = Append(BtoA, BVar[2])
        /\ UNCHANGED <<AVar, BVar, AtoB>>
BRcv == /\ AtoB # <<>>
        /\ \E i \in Pick(AtoB) :
             /\ IF AtoB[i][2] # BVar[2]
                  THEN BVar' = AtoB[i]
                  ELSE BVar' = BVar
             /\ AtoB' = Remove(i, AtoB)
        /\ UNCHANGED <<AVar, BtoA>>
LoseMsg == /\ \/ /\ \E i \in 1..Len(AtoB) : AtoB' = Remove(i, AtoB)
                 /\ BtoA' = BtoA
              \/ /\ \E i \in 1..Len(BtoA) : BtoA' = Remove(i, BtoA)
                 /\ AtoB' = AtoB
           /\ UNCHANGED <<AVar, BVar>>
Next == ASnd \/ ARcv \/ BSnd \/ BRcv \/ LoseMsg
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars

ABS == INSTANCE PSl9_LinkSpec
HighSafety == ABS!Spec
Bound == (Len(AtoB) <= 2) /\ (Len(BtoA) <= 2)
=============================================================================
    SPECIFICATION Spec
CONSTANTS Data = {d1, d2}
          Reorder = TRUE
CONSTRAINT Bound
INVARIANT TypeOK
PROPERTY HighSafety
    1. Run it with Reorder = FALSE and check that you get the lesson's result.
    2. Run it with Reorder = TRUE, as shown. Report the length of the trace, and say which message is delivered out of order.
    3. In The alternating bit protocol, deleting B's bit test changed nothing on the in-order model. Which test does the reordered trace defeat, and why does a single bit not suffice?
    4. Describe a change to the messages that would let B tell a stale copy from a new value. What makes it hard to check with TLC on a finite model?

    Why is the last step of the trace not allowed by ABS!Spec?

    Hint

    A keeps sending its current value, so old copies can stay in AtoB after the value has been acknowledged. With one bit, "different from my bit" means "new" only if nothing older than the previous value can still arrive.

    Solution

    1. No error, 216 distinct states, the same as module AB in The alternating bit protocol. With Reorder = FALSE, Pick is 1..1, so each receive takes the head, exactly as before.

    2. TLC reports the action property of PSl9_LinkSpec violated after 7 states:

    B acknowledges with bit 1 (state 2). A sends <<d1, 1>>, a copy of the value B already has (state 3), then receives the ack, picks the new value <<d1, 0>> (state 4), and sends it (state 5). B takes the newer message first, out of order (state 6). Then it takes the old <<d1, 1>>, sees a bit different from its own, and accepts it as new (state 7). The data happens to be d1 both times, but B has gone back to a stale copy of the previous value and treated it as a new one. With different readings, the dashboard shows an old reading as new, as in the field.

    3. B's test: "the bit differs from mine, so this is new". On a first-in first-out channel, the old copies of the previous value were ahead of the new value in the channel, so by the time B accepts the new value they have been received or lost. With reordering, an old copy can arrive after the new value. Because the bit only alternates, a copy of the previous value carries the same bit as the next new value, so B can't tell them apart. One bit distinguishes a value only from its immediate neighbours.

    4. Number each value with a counter instead of a bit, and have B accept only the number after the last one it accepted. That is the idea behind sequence numbers in protocols such as TCP. The counter grows without bound, so a TLC model needs another constraint on it, and you must say that the result holds only within that bound, just as with channel lengths in The alternating bit protocol. A counter that wraps around has the same weakness, if an old copy can survive until the counter comes back to its number.

    Problem 4●●●Databases

    Synthesis: does every booking eventually decide?

    Draws on Liveness and fairness, The alternating bit protocol, Messages, failures, and retries, Two-phase commit and records, Problem set 6, Problem set 7 and Problem set 8.

    The trip booking from Problem set 6 (flight, hotel and car RMs, one TM, two-phase commit) is moving to a network that loses messages. Problem set 8 showed that its steps keep agreement, and Problem set 7 showed how a coordinator crash blocks it. Product now asks the liveness question: does every reservation eventually end up committed or aborted, so that held seats, rooms and cars are always released?

    In the module below, net holds messages in flight. Receiving or losing a message removes it, unlike msgs in TwoPhase. Messages are addressed to one RM, and the TM may abort at any time while undecided, which models a timeout. RMResend and TMResend are retries. Because net is a set of finitely many possible messages, the channel is bounded without a state constraint.

    -------------------------- MODULE PSl9_BookingLive --------------------------
\* Two-phase commit for the trip booking over a network that loses messages.
\* net holds the messages in flight: receiving or losing one removes it, so
\* a lost message is gone unless someone sends it again. net is a set, so it
\* never holds more than the finitely many different messages.
CONSTANT RM
VARIABLES rmState, tmState, tmPrepared, net
vars == <<rmState, tmState, tmPrepared, net>>
Prep(r) == [type |-> "Prepared", rm |-> r]
Dec(r)  == [type |-> IF tmState = "commit" THEN "Commit" ELSE "Abort", rm |-> r]

Init == /\ rmState = [r \in RM |-> "working"]
        /\ tmState = "init"          \* then "commit" or "abort"
        /\ tmPrepared = {}
        /\ net = {}
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
RMPrepare(r) == /\ rmState[r] = "working"
                /\ rmState' = [rmState EXCEPT ![r] = "prepared"]
                /\ net' = net \cup {Prep(r)}
                /\ UNCHANGED <<tmState, tmPrepared>>
RMChooseToAbort(r) == /\ rmState[r] = "working"
                      /\ rmState' = [rmState EXCEPT ![r] = "aborted"]
                      /\ UNCHANGED <<tmState, tmPrepared, net>>
RMRcvCommit(r) == /\ [type |-> "Commit", rm |-> r] \in net
                  /\ rmState' = [rmState EXCEPT ![r] = "committed"]
                  /\ net' = net \ {[type |-> "Commit", rm |-> r]}
                  /\ UNCHANGED <<tmState, tmPrepared>>
RMRcvAbort(r) == /\ [type |-> "Abort", rm |-> r] \in net
                 /\ rmState' = [rmState EXCEPT ![r] = "aborted"]
                 /\ net' = net \ {[type |-> "Abort", rm |-> r]}
                 /\ UNCHANGED <<tmState, tmPrepared>>
TMRcvPrepared(r) == /\ tmState = "init"
                    /\ Prep(r) \in net
                    /\ tmPrepared' = tmPrepared \cup {r}
                    /\ net' = net \ {Prep(r)}
                    /\ UNCHANGED <<rmState, tmState>>
\* The TM decides and sends one copy of the decision to every RM.
TMDecide ==
  /\ tmState = "init"
  /\ \/ /\ tmPrepared = RM
        /\ tmState' = "commit"
        /\ net' = net \cup {[type |-> "Commit", rm |-> r] : r \in RM}
     \/ /\ tmState' = "abort"                 \* e.g. after a timeout
        /\ net' = net \cup {[type |-> "Abort", rm |-> r] : r \in RM}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<rmState, tmPrepared>>
Lose == \E m \in net : /\ net' = net \ {m}
                       /\ UNCHANGED <<rmState, tmState, tmPrepared>>
\* Retries.
RMResend(r) == /\ rmState[r] = "prepared"
               /\ net' = net \cup {Prep(r)}
               /\ UNCHANGED <<rmState, tmState, tmPrepared>>
TMResend(r) == /\ tmState # "init"
               /\ net' = net \cup {Dec(r)}
               /\ UNCHANGED <<rmState, tmState, tmPrepared>>
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
Core == \/ TMDecide \/ Lose
        \/ \E r \in RM : \/ RMPrepare(r) \/ RMChooseToAbort(r)
                         \/ RMRcvCommit(r) \/ RMRcvAbort(r) \/ TMRcvPrepared(r)
Next          == Core \/ \E r \in RM : RMResend(r) \/ TMResend(r)
NoTMRetryNext == Core \/ \E r \in RM : RMResend(r)
NoRMRetryNext == Core \/ \E r \in RM : TMResend(r)

Base == /\ WF_vars(TMDecide)
        /\ \A r \in RM : WF_vars(RMPrepare(r) \/ RMChooseToAbort(r))
WFRcv == \A r \in RM : /\ WF_vars(TMRcvPrepared(r))
                       /\ WF_vars(RMRcvCommit(r) \/ RMRcvAbort(r))
SFRcv == \A r \in RM : /\ SF_vars(TMRcvPrepared(r))
                       /\ SF_vars(RMRcvCommit(r) \/ RMRcvAbort(r))
RMRetry == \A r \in RM : WF_vars(RMResend(r))
TMRetry == \A r \in RM : WF_vars(TMResend(r))

WFSpec        == Init /\ [][Next]_vars /\ Base /\ WFRcv /\ RMRetry /\ TMRetry
SFSpec        == Init /\ [][Next]_vars /\ Base /\ SFRcv /\ RMRetry /\ TMRetry
NoTMRetrySpec == Init /\ [][NoTMRetryNext]_vars /\ Base /\ SFRcv /\ RMRetry
NoRMRetrySpec == Init /\ [][NoRMRetryNext]_vars /\ Base /\ SFRcv /\ TMRetry

Decided(r) == rmState[r] \in {"committed", "aborted"}
EveryoneDecides == \A r \in RM : <>Decided(r)
Consistent == \A r1, r2 \in RM : ~(rmState[r1] = "aborted" /\ rmState[r2] = "committed")
=============================================================================
    SPECIFICATION SFSpec
CONSTANT RM = {"flight", "hotel", "car"}
INVARIANT Consistent
PROPERTY EveryoneDecides
CHECK_DEADLOCK FALSE
    1. Run WFSpec. Describe the loop in TLC's counterexample, and name the fairness condition that the loop escapes and why.
    2. Run SFSpec, as in the cfg shown. Report the result and connect it to the argument in The alternating bit protocol.
    3. Run NoTMRetrySpec and NoRMRetrySpec. One retry is essential and the other isn't. Which, and why?
    4. Add the coordinator crash of Problem set 7: after Crash, no TM action is enabled. Can any fairness condition on the TM's actions bring back EveryoneDecides? Answer, then check the quiz.

    With the crash added, can fairness alone restore EveryoneDecides?

    Hint

    Every loop TLC can report under WFSpec must satisfy each WF condition. Look for a receive action that the loop keeps enabling with a retry and then disabling with Lose. For task 3, ask what the TM does if a Prepared message never arrives.

    Solution

    1. TLC reports EveryoneDecides violated, with a loop. In the run here the TM has decided abort, flight and car have aborted, and hotel is still prepared. Inside the loop, TMResend("hotel") puts an Abort for hotel into net, other steps follow, and Lose removes it before hotel takes it, again and again:

    RMRcvAbort("hotel") is enabled for a while each time around and then disabled by Lose, so it is never continuously enabled. WF_vars(RMRcvCommit("hotel") \/ RMRcvAbort("hotel")) therefore asks nothing of it. The retries still happen as their weak fairness requires, so every condition of WFSpec holds on this behavior.

    2. No error, 6560 distinct states. Retries make each receive action enabled infinitely often, and strong fairness on receives then forces it to happen. This is the argument for SF_vars(ARcv) and SF_vars(BRcv) in The alternating bit protocol: strong fairness doesn't stop losses, it says that a message sent again and again eventually gets through.

    3. NoTMRetrySpec is violated: in the run here the TM aborts, Abort messages for flight and hotel are lost, and those two RMs stay prepared forever. Nothing would ever send them the decision again. NoRMRetrySpec gives no error (2933 distinct states). A lost Prepared message can't block anyone, because the TM may abort while it is undecided, and weak fairness on TMDecide makes it decide. Losing a vote costs a commit that could have happened. It doesn't cost liveness. The retry that matters is the one that carries the decision, because a prepared RM can't leave that state on its own, as Two-phase commit and records showed.

    4. No, as the quiz explains: a hidden run that adds Crash to SFSpec reports EveryoneDecides violated, ending with hotel prepared and the TM down. Fairness is an assumption about steps that can happen. It can't make a stopped process act. The booking can only be live if the decision survives the TM, either in a log that a restarted TM reads back, or in Paxos Commit's acceptors from Problem set 7, which needs a majority of them to keep working.

    Lecture 10: Implementation with refinement

    Implication runs out when the variables differ.

    Implementation as implication, from lesson 26, worked because every variable of the high-level spec also appeared in the low-level one. TwoPhase had rmState, and AB has AVar and BVar. This lesson builds a protocol where that fails for an obvious pair of specs, and collects the two tools needed to repair it, recursion and substitution, in time for lesson 33.

    Recursive definitions

    Suppose you want an operator that removes every "X" from a sequence of strings. There's no single formula for the position of each element, as there was for Remove. Define it in terms of itself on a shorter sequence, and declare first that you are doing so:

    RECURSIVE RemoveX(_)
RemoveX(seq) == IF seq = <<>>
                  THEN <<>>
                  ELSE IF Head(seq) = "X"
                         THEN RemoveX(Tail(seq))
                         ELSE <<Head(seq)>> \o RemoveX(Tail(seq))

    The _ marks one argument. If you've used a functional language, this will feel natural. Otherwise, reach for it where a program would use a loop. TLC evaluates RemoveX(<<"Tom", "X", "Dick", "Harry", "X">>) to <<"Tom", "Dick", "Harry">>.

    Substitution, and when it's allowed

    For this lecture only, write f WITH v <- e for f with expression e substituted for symbol v. This is not TLA+ notation. For example, (y^3 - y) WITH y <- x + 2 is (x + 2)^3 - (x + 2). Ordinary math has a basic law, which the lecture calls the Simple Substitution Law:

    THEOREM (v = e) => (f = (f WITH v <- e))

    It holds for declared constants and constant expressions, the only things ordinary math has. It fails for declared variables. Take f to be y', v to be y, and e to be x + 2. The law then says (y = x + 2) => (y' = (x + 2)'): if y = x + 2 holds in the first state, it holds in the second. Run 1 in the figure refutes that. Adding always gives the Temporal Substitution Law, which holds when v is a variable and e a state expression:

    THEOREM [](v = e) => (f = (f WITH v <- e))

    It generalizes to several variables at once, f WITH v1 <- e1, v2 <- e2. The substitutions are simultaneous, not one after the other. You'll use this general form in lesson 33.

    Predict: is the simple law true when v is a constant and e a constant expression, even with no always?

    Yes. Their values don't depend on the state, so v = e is true on the first state exactly when it's true on all of them. [](v = e) says the same as v = e, and the temporal law reduces to the ordinary one.

    The AB2 protocol

    AB2 is AB with one change. Messages are detectably corrupted instead of lost. A corrupted message is represented by a constant Bad, assumed unequal to any real message, and the action that hurts messages replaces them in place:

    CONSTANTS Data, Bad

ASSUME Bad \notin (Data \X {0, 1}) \cup {0, 1}

VARIABLES AVar, BVar, AtoB2, BtoA2

TypeOK == /\ AVar \in Data \X {0, 1}
          /\ BVar \in Data \X {0, 1}
          /\ AtoB2 \in Seq((Data \X {0, 1}) \cup {Bad})
          /\ BtoA2 \in Seq({0, 1, Bad})

BRcv == /\ AtoB2 # <<>>
        /\ IF (Head(AtoB2) # Bad) /\ (Head(AtoB2)[2] # BVar[2])
             THEN BVar' = Head(AtoB2)
             ELSE BVar' = BVar
        /\ AtoB2' = Tail(AtoB2)
        /\ UNCHANGED <<AVar, BtoA2>>

CorruptMsg == /\ \/ /\ \E i \in 1..Len(AtoB2) :
                         AtoB2' = [AtoB2 EXCEPT ![i] = Bad]
                    /\ BtoA2' = BtoA2
                 \/ /\ \E i \in 1..Len(BtoA2) :
                         BtoA2' = [BtoA2 EXCEPT ![i] = Bad]
                    /\ AtoB2' = AtoB2
              /\ UNCHANGED <<AVar, BVar>>

    Init, ASnd, and BSnd only rename the channels. ARcv needs no change beyond that: Bad isn't 0 or 1, so the test Head(BtoA2) = AVar[2] is false and A ignores it. BRcv gets a new conjunct, because Head(AtoB2)[2] means nothing when the head is Bad. Next has CorruptMsg where AB had LoseMsg.

    A value for Bad

    The obvious model sets Bad to the string "Bad". TLC stops while evaluating the assumption:

    Attempted to check equality of integer 0 with non-integer:
"Bad"

    You think "Bad" differs from 0, but the semantics of TLA+ don't say so, and TLC won't guess. The answer is a model value, which TLC assumes unequal to any value you'd expect it to differ from. In a cfg file that's CONSTANT Bad = Bad, and the Toolbox has a model value option for it.

    Which theorem can AB2 state with what you know so far?

    Checking AB2 against ABSpec

    As in lesson 30, the model needs data values and a state constraint. The lecture uses three values and channel lengths below 4. A smaller instance shows the same thing quickly:

    SPECIFICATION Spec
CONSTANT Data = {d1, d2}
CONSTANT Bad = Bad
CONSTRAINT Bound
INVARIANT TypeOK
PROPERTY HighSafety

    With Bound limiting both channels to length 2, and HighSafety naming ABS!Spec in a wrapper module, TLC finds no error: 6926 states generated, 1008 distinct, depth 16.

    Liveness needs something imaginary

    Copy AB's FairSpec onto AB2 and check it against ABS!FairSpec. TLC reports a violation:

    Strong fairness can't help, since ARcv steps do occur. Each one just receives Bad. Lamport says he believes fairness on subactions of Next can't guarantee that any message is received before it's corrupted. So the safety spec has to change. The idea is that sending a message also decides whether it may ever be corrupted.

    These flags are imaginary variables: not meant to be implemented, used only to state fairness. Choosing in advance doesn't change what AB2's own variables can do, so ignoring AtoBgood and BtoAgood, SpecP and Spec allow the same behaviors. Lamport's module AB2P extends AB2 this way. What follows is this course's own version, written to test the idea, and it may differ from his download. Corruption requires a false flag, and weak fairness applies to the receives and to sending a good message:

    FairSpecP == SpecP /\ WF_varsP(ARcvP) /\ WF_varsP(BRcvP)
                   /\ WF_varsP(SndA(TRUE)) /\ WF_varsP(SndB(TRUE))

    On the same bound, TLC finds no error against ABS!FairSpec and against AB2's Spec, with 4212 distinct states. Requiring only that some message keeps being sent, whether good or not, brings the violation back.

    Predict: AB needed strong fairness on its receives. Why does weak fairness suffice for ARcvP and BRcvP here?

    Corruption doesn't remove messages. Once a channel is non-empty, only a receive can empty it, so the receive stays continuously enabled, and there's no flicker for strong fairness to handle.

    The question from the top of the page is still open: AB2 clearly behaves like AB, yet AtoB and BtoA don't exist in it. lesson 33 says what "implements" means in that case.

    While you watch

    • This is the first part of the lecture. Run the model with the string "Bad" first, so you see the error he describes, then change to a model value.
    • Pause at the TypeOK line for AtoB2 when he asks you to, and read the set out loud.
    • He leaves AB2P for you to read. His version is the reference.

    Lamport's TLA+ Video Course, lecture 10.

    Lecture 10: Implementation with refinement

    A refinement mapping says how one state stands in for another.

    lesson 32 ended with AB2 behaving like AB although it has no AtoB or BtoA. Ordinary implication can't say so. The fix is small: write down how the missing variables are computed from the ones that exist. That expression is a refinement mapping, and it's the general meaning of implementation.

    What "AB2 implements AB" means

    The claim is stronger than the one you checked last lesson. AB2 doesn't just implement ABSpec. It implements the AB protocol, with each CorruptMsg step implementing a LoseMsg step. Losing a message may feel like something the environment does, not the protocol. But specs say nothing about who performs a step; that is an interpretation we put on the formula.

    Here's the meaning. Take any behavior of AB2 and change each state as in the figure, deleting Bad from each channel. The result must be a behavior of AB.

    The top half of this figure shows it on one behavior. A corrupting step maps to a LoseMsg step, since a message disappears from the mapped channel. An ARcv that consumes Bad maps to stuttering, because the mapped state doesn't change. This is the same idea as TMAbort in lesson 26.

    From meaning to something checkable

    To make it a formula, invent a spec SpecH whose states also contain AtoB and BtoA, always equal to the cleaned channels. Module AB2H defines it:

    SpecH == /\ AB2!Spec
         /\ [] /\ AtoB = RemoveBad(AtoB2)
               /\ BtoA = RemoveBad(BtoA2)

    RemoveBad is RemoveX from last lesson, with Bad in place of "X". Here AtoB and BtoA are imaginary variables, with no effect on what the other four can do. So THEOREM SpecH => AB!Spec says just what we want. But TLC can't check it, because SpecH doesn't have the standard form of an initial formula and [][Next]_vars. You could rewrite it, and module AB2H does so as SpecHH. The lecture instead takes a longer path that teaches more.

    Follow the figure from the top. SpecH implies the always formula, so by the Temporal Substitution Law, AB!Spec may be replaced by its substituted version. That version no longer mentions AtoB or BtoA, so the always conjunct of SpecH has nothing left to do, and it goes. SpecH has now vanished. Only AB2!Spec remains on the left, and inside module AB2 that's plain Spec, which TLC can handle.

    INSTANCE ... WITH

    One problem remains: WITH so far is lecture notation, not TLA+. But the real INSTANCE statement has a WITH clause. After expanding definitions, formula Spec of AB contains only operators and AB's declared symbols, Data, AVar, BVar, AtoB, BtoA. To import it elsewhere, you give an expression for each. Omitting one means "the symbol of the same name," which is what every INSTANCE so far has done without saying so. So these lines go at the end of AB2:

    RECURSIVE RemoveBad(_)
RemoveBad(seq) == IF seq = <<>>
                    THEN <<>>
                    ELSE IF Head(seq) = Bad
                           THEN RemoveBad(Tail(seq))
                           ELSE <<Head(seq)>> \o RemoveBad(Tail(seq))

AB == INSTANCE AB WITH AtoB <- RemoveBad(AtoB2),
                       BtoA <- RemoveBad(BtoA2)

THEOREM Spec => AB!Spec

    These substitutions are the refinement mapping, and AB2 implements AB under it. Check it like any other implementation, with a model whose behavior spec is Spec and whose property is AB!Spec. With Data = {d1, d2}, Bad a model value, and channels of length at most 2, TLC finds no error: 6926 states generated, 1008 distinct, depth 16.

    Predict: map AtoB <- AtoB2 and BtoA <- BtoA2, keeping the Bad slots. What does TLC say?

    It reports the action property of AB violated after three states: BSnd, then CorruptMsg. That is the bottom half of the figure above. A mapped channel containing Bad changes in a way that no AB action allows, because LoseMsg removes a message and doesn't rewrite one.

    A mapping that discards information fails too. Map both channels to <<>>, and TLC finds the violation in three states: BSnd, then an ARcv in which A chooses a new value while the mapped channel is empty. No AB step could do that.

    What implementation means, in general

    If Spec2 doesn't contain all the variables of Spec1, then Spec2 can implement Spec1 only under a refinement mapping that assigns expressions of Spec2 to the missing variables. This is the usual case. Even a variable they share may be mapped to something other than itself.

    So what does it mean for a program to implement a TLA+ spec? That you could, in principle, write a spec of the program which implements the spec under a suitable mapping. In practice that spec would be far too long. But you can still explain informally how the spec's variables are represented by the program's state. Writing it down, perhaps as comments in the code, explains what the program does, and can expose errors in it.

    Why can't Spec of AB implement Spec of AB2 under a plain refinement mapping?

    Imaginary variables

    You've now seen two uses: AtoBgood and BtoAgood to state liveness, and AtoB and BtoA to explain implementation. Adding imaginary variables to a spec means the new and old specs allow the same behaviors if you ignore those variables. They need not describe real state, they aren't meant to be implemented, and if their values can be computed from the original variables, you don't need them, as this lesson's mapping shows. But they may be necessary. As the quiz above shows, AB can implement AB2 only with added variables recording where lost messages were. They are usually called auxiliary variables, and the lecture points to the paper Auxiliary Variables in TLA+.

    Extension: choosing a mapping in a real product

    This section goes beyond the lecture and isn't model-checked. A document editor shows "ca". The user types "t" and immediately sees "cat". A request goes out, the server durably commits it, and an acknowledgement comes back. The draft on screen, the durable log, and what the client knows are three different states. Which belongs in the abstract contract is your first decision.

    Suppose the abstract object promises durable edits, with one variable savedText. Map it to the result of applying the durable log in order. In the figure, only the commit is an abstract edit. If the server commits but the reply is lost, a retry must not insert a second "t", so requests need identities, and the mapped text should stay "cat", not "catt". Mapping savedText to the draft instead describes a different contract, speculative display. A later rejection could then remove the "t", which a durable-only abstract spec forbids. That's a failed mapping, not necessarily an editor bug.

    Linearizability is a related but specific contract, and a generic refinement check doesn't give it to you automatically. It gives each completed operation one point between its invocation and response, with a legal sequential order that respects the real-time order of non-overlapping operations. To check for it, the abstract interface must include invocations, responses, and the treatment of pending operations. With several editors, refining to one sequential text object promises more than replicas eventually converging.

    Transfer exercise: an editor shows "Saved" before the server commits. Which property exposes the problem?

    Represent the status change as an acknowledgement event and require that each acknowledged operation is durable under the modeled failures. Crash after showing "Saved" and before committing. If recovery loses the edit, the client-visible durability contract fails, however good the optimistic draft looked.

    While you watch

    • Lamport warns the path is long and may not always seem to be heading anywhere. The chain figure above is the map. Stop at each step and find your place on it.
    • He writes WITH with a left arrow in lecture notation, then shows the real INSTANCE form. Notice when the first becomes the second.
    • This is the last lecture. His closing list of what's left (more TLA+, Toolbox features, PlusCal) is where the rest of this course goes, starting with lesson 36. The checks with wrong mappings and the editor extension are additions.

    Lecture 10: Implementation with refinement

    Problem set 10: say what stands for what.

    Four refinement problems. Each gives you an implementation with more machinery than its spec, such as shards, files on disk, replicas or an optimistic screen. You write the refinement mapping, check it with TLC, and decide what a failed check means. You'll use RECURSIVE and INSTANCE … WITH from lecture 10. The last problem adds the message sets of lecture 6 and the fairness of lecture 9.

    Every module below was checked with TLC exactly as shown. To check a refinement, do what lesson 33 did: put the implementation's Spec under SPECIFICATION, and the instantiated abstract spec under PROPERTY. Keep the abstract module in the same folder, because INSTANCE looks for it there. Counts like "distinct states" only match if your copy is identical.

    Problem 1●○○Infrastructure

    A sharded like counter is still a counter

    Draws on Refinement mappings, The general meaning of implementation and What it means to implement a spec.

    A social app keeps the like count of each post in one database row. A popular post turns that row into a hot spot: every like is an update of the same row, and concurrent updates of one row wait for each other. The team splits the counter into shards. Each like increments one shard, chosen at random, and the page shows the sum of the shards. The product promise is unchanged: the number on the page goes up by one per like and never goes down.

    That promise is this spec:

    ---------------- MODULE PSl10_Counter ----------------
EXTENDS Naturals
VARIABLE count
Init == count = 0
Inc == count' = count + 1
Spec == Init /\ [][Inc]_count
======================================================

    Here is the implementation. MaxPerShard only keeps the model finite.

    ---------------- MODULE PSl10_Sharded ----------------
EXTENDS Naturals
CONSTANTS Shards, MaxPerShard
VARIABLE shard
Init == shard = [s \in Shards |-> 0]
Inc(s) == /\ shard[s] < MaxPerShard
          /\ shard' = [shard EXCEPT ![s] = shard[s] + 1]
Next == \E s \in Shards : Inc(s)
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_shard
======================================================
    SPECIFICATION Spec
CONSTANTS Shards = {s1, s2, s3}
          MaxPerShard = 2
PROPERTY CounterSpec
CHECK_DEADLOCK FALSE
    1. Add a recursive operator SumOver(f, S), the sum of f[s] over all s in a finite set S. Then add the refinement mapping as an instance C of PSl10_Counter, define CounterSpec == C!Spec, and run the model above.
    2. To keep reads cheap, a job periodically folds a shard into a stored base value: it adds the shard's count to base and resets the shard to 0. Add a base variable and a Fold(s) action, map count to base plus the shard sum, and check again. You'll need a state constraint, because shards can now refill forever.
    3. The shards are moved to an in-memory cache without persistence. Model a cache restart as Restart(s), which sets one shard back to 0. What does TLC report?
    4. A teammate maps count <- shard[Home], where Home is the shard their app server writes to. TLC finds no error. Why is that result worthless as evidence for the product promise?

    Under the mapping count <- base + sum of shards, what abstract step does a Fold(s) step with shard[s] = 3 correspond to?

    Hint

    Write SumOver like RemoveX in lesson 32: an empty set sums to 0, and otherwise pick one element with CHOOSE, add its value, and recurse on the rest. For the restart, ask what happens to the mapped count, and whether any step of PSl10_Counter can do that.

    Solution

    (a) The completed module. TLC finds no error, with 55 states generated and 27 distinct states.

    ---------------- MODULE PSl10_Sharded ----------------
EXTENDS Naturals
CONSTANTS Shards, MaxPerShard
VARIABLE shard
Init == shard = [s \in Shards |-> 0]
Inc(s) == /\ shard[s] < MaxPerShard
          /\ shard' = [shard EXCEPT ![s] = shard[s] + 1]
Next == \E s \in Shards : Inc(s)
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_shard

RECURSIVE SumOver(_, _)
SumOver(f, S) == IF S = {} THEN 0
                 ELSE LET s == CHOOSE x \in S : TRUE
                      IN  f[s] + SumOver(f, S \ {s})
Total == SumOver(shard, Shards)

C == INSTANCE PSl10_Counter WITH count <- Total
THEOREM Spec => C!Spec
CounterSpec == C!Spec
======================================================

    The cfg line CHECK_DEADLOCK FALSE matters here: once every shard reaches MaxPerShard no step is enabled, which is the end of the model, not a bug. CHOOSE is safe in SumOver because addition doesn't care which element comes first. Every Inc(s) raises the sum by exactly one, so it is an Inc step of the counter.

    (b) With a base value and a fold:

    ---------------- MODULE PSl10_ShardedFold ----------------
EXTENDS Naturals
CONSTANTS Shards, MaxPerShard
VARIABLES shard, base
vars == <<shard, base>>
Init == /\ shard = [s \in Shards |-> 0]
        /\ base = 0
Inc(s) == /\ shard[s] < MaxPerShard
          /\ shard' = [shard EXCEPT ![s] = shard[s] + 1]
          /\ UNCHANGED base
Fold(s) == /\ shard[s] > 0
           /\ base' = base + shard[s]
           /\ shard' = [shard EXCEPT ![s] = 0]
Next == \E s \in Shards : Inc(s) \/ Fold(s)
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars

RECURSIVE SumOver(_, _)
SumOver(f, S) == IF S = {} THEN 0
                 ELSE LET s == CHOOSE x \in S : TRUE
                      IN  f[s] + SumOver(f, S \ {s})
Total == base + SumOver(shard, Shards)
Bound == Total <= 4

C == INSTANCE PSl10_Counter WITH count <- Total
CounterSpec == C!Spec
==========================================================
    SPECIFICATION Spec
CONSTANTS Shards = {s1, s2, s3}
          MaxPerShard = 2
CONSTRAINT Bound
PROPERTY CounterSpec
CHECK_DEADLOCK FALSE

    TLC finds no error: 220 states generated, 55 distinct. A fold changes the implementation's state but not the mapped count, so it maps to stuttering, as the quiz says. This is the same move as TMAbort in lesson 26 and as the ARcv of a corrupted message in lesson 33: internal work is invisible in the abstract spec.

    (c) Add Restart(s) == shard[s] > 0 /\ shard' = [shard EXCEPT ![s] = 0] as a disjunct of Next (module PSl10_ShardedRestart). TLC reports that the action property of PSl10_Counter is violated, with three states: shards all 0; Inc(s1), so the count is 1; Restart(s1), so the count is 0 again. The figure shows a longer behavior of the same module. The count fell, and the abstract spec only allows count' = count + 1 or no change. The product consequence is that a like disappears from the page. A cache restart that forgets data is exactly a step the contract forbids, so the shards need persistence, or a recovery step that restores them.

    (d) With Home = s1, TLC finds no error (27 distinct states). Every step either raises shard[s1] by one or leaves it alone, so every step is an Inc or a stutter. The check is correct; the claim is just weak. Under this mapping the abstract "count" ignores two thirds of the likes. A refinement theorem is only as meaningful as its mapping: the mapping says what the implementation's state means, and here it means the wrong thing. TLC can tell you a mapping works, but not that it is the one your users read.

    Problem 2●●○Databases

    An LSM tree implements a map

    Draws on Refinement mappings, The general meaning of implementation, The high-level spec of a channel and Sets, functions, and quantifiers.

    Storage engines such as LevelDB and RocksDB are log-structured merge trees. A write goes into an in-memory table, the memtable. When the memtable is big enough, it is flushed to disk as an immutable file. Compaction later merges files, keeping the newer value of each key. A read checks the memtable first, then the files from newest to oldest. The application sees none of this. It sees a map from keys to values:

    ---------------- MODULE PSl10_KV ----------------
CONSTANTS Keys, Vals, NoVal
VARIABLE store
Init == store = [k \in Keys |-> NoVal]
Put(k, v) == store' = [store EXCEPT ![k] = v]
Next == \E k \in Keys, v \in Vals : Put(k, v)
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_store
=================================================

    The engine, with tables[1] the oldest file and at most MaxTables files:

    ---------------- MODULE PSl10_LSM ----------------
EXTENDS Naturals, Sequences
CONSTANTS Keys, Vals, NoVal, MaxTables
VARIABLES mem, tables
vars == <<mem, tables>>
Empty == [k \in Keys |-> NoVal]
Init == /\ mem = Empty
        /\ tables = <<>>              \* tables[1] is the oldest
Put(k, v) == /\ mem' = [mem EXCEPT ![k] = v]
             /\ UNCHANGED tables
Flush == /\ mem # Empty
         /\ Len(tables) < MaxTables
         /\ tables' = Append(tables, mem)
         /\ mem' = Empty
Merge(older, newer) ==
    [k \in Keys |-> IF newer[k] # NoVal THEN newer[k] ELSE older[k]]
Compact == /\ Len(tables) >= 2
           /\ tables' = <<Merge(tables[1], tables[2])>> \o Tail(Tail(tables))
           /\ UNCHANGED mem
Next == \/ \E k \in Keys, v \in Vals : Put(k, v)
        \/ Flush
        \/ Compact
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars
==================================================
    SPECIFICATION Spec
CONSTANTS Keys = {k1, k2}
          Vals = {v1, v2}
          NoVal = NoVal
          MaxTables = 2
PROPERTY KVSpec
CHECK_DEADLOCK FALSE
    1. Write Get(k), the value a read returns, using a recursive helper that searches the files from newest to oldest. Then add the mapping KV == INSTANCE PSl10_KV WITH store <- … and KVSpec == KV!Spec, and check it.
    2. Which actions of the engine map to stuttering? Say why for each.
    3. A refactoring swaps the arguments of Merge in Compact, so the older file wins. Check the buggy engine with Keys = {k1, k2}, and then with Keys = {k1}.
    4. Explain the difference between the two runs. What does it say about how strong PSl10_KV is as a contract?

    With Keys = {k1}, what does TLC report for the buggy compaction?

    Hint

    Give the helper the index of the file to look at: Find(k, i) looks in tables[i] and, if the key isn't there, in tables[i - 1]. Start it at Len(tables); index 0 means "not found". For (d), ask which steps of PSl10_KV could explain a one-key rollback.

    Solution

    (a) The added definitions:

    RECURSIVE Find(_, _)
Find(k, i) == IF i = 0 THEN NoVal
              ELSE IF tables[i][k] # NoVal THEN tables[i][k]
              ELSE Find(k, i - 1)
Get(k) == IF mem[k] # NoVal THEN mem[k] ELSE Find(k, Len(tables))

KV == INSTANCE PSl10_KV WITH store <- [k \in Keys |-> Get(k)]
THEOREM Spec => KV!Spec
KVSpec == KV!Spec

    TLC finds no error: 3277 states generated, 657 distinct.

    (b) Flush and Compact map to stuttering. A flush moves the memtable into the newest file, and a read finds the same values there, because nothing newer exists. A correct compaction replaces the two oldest files by one in which the newer value of each key wins, which is what a read of those two files returned anyway. So does a Put of the value a read already returns.

    (c) With two keys, TLC reports the action property of PSl10_KV violated after eight states. The figure shows the important ones: Put(k1, v1), Put(k2, v1), Flush, Put(k1, v2), Put(k2, v2), Flush, and then Compact, which leaves only <<(k1 :> v1 @@ k2 :> v1)>>. The mapped store went from both keys at v2 to both at v1 in one step. Each Put changes one key, so no step of the map spec can do that.

    (d) With one key, TLC finds no error, in 21 distinct states. The rollback of k1 from v2 to v1 is the same pair of mapped states as Put(k1, v1), and the map spec lets anyone put any value at any time. The bug was real in both runs; the refinement check could only see it when no abstract step explained it. PSl10_KV says nothing about who writes or which value, so data loss that looks like a write passes. To catch it with one key, put the client into the model, for example a variable recording the last value the client wrote, and require each mapped change to equal it. A weak abstract spec makes refinement easy to pass, and so says less.

    Problem 3●●○Distributed systems

    A replicated log's commit index

    Draws on Refinement mappings, Set operations and quorums, From Paxos Commit to Paxos and Raft and The high-level spec of a channel.

    In Raft-style replication, clients send commands to a leader, which appends them to its log and copies them to followers. An entry counts as committed once a majority of servers store it, and the leader's commit index says how far that goes. The guarantee to clients is an append-only log: committed entries appear one after another and never change.

    ---------------- MODULE PSl10_Log ----------------
EXTENDS Sequences
CONSTANT Vals
VARIABLE log
Init == log = <<>>
Next == \E v \in Vals : log' = Append(log, v)
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_log
==================================================

    The model has one fixed leader and two followers, so a majority is two of three. Its mapping says the abstract log is the leader's log up to the commit index:

    ---------------- MODULE PSl10_RLog ----------------
EXTENDS Naturals, Sequences, FiniteSets
CONSTANTS Vals, Followers, MaxLen
VARIABLES llog, flog, commit
vars == <<llog, flog, commit>>
Init == /\ llog = <<>>                       \* the leader's log
        /\ flog = [f \in Followers |-> <<>>]   \* each follower's log
        /\ commit = 0                         \* the leader's commit index
Request(v) == /\ Len(llog) < MaxLen
              /\ llog' = Append(llog, v)
              /\ UNCHANGED <<flog, commit>>
Replicate(f) == /\ Len(flog[f]) < Len(llog)
                /\ flog' = [flog EXCEPT ![f] =
                              Append(flog[f], llog[Len(flog[f]) + 1])]
                /\ UNCHANGED <<llog, commit>>
\* Entry n is on a majority: the leader plus at least half the followers.
OnMajority(n) == 2 * (1 + Cardinality({f \in Followers : Len(flog[f]) >= n}))
                   > 1 + Cardinality(Followers)
AdvanceCommit == /\ \E n \in (commit + 1)..Len(llog) :
                       /\ OnMajority(n)
                       /\ commit' = n
                 /\ UNCHANGED <<llog, flog>>
Next == \/ \E v \in Vals : Request(v)
        \/ \E f \in Followers : Replicate(f)
        \/ AdvanceCommit
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars

Committed == [i \in 1..commit |-> llog[i]]
L == INSTANCE PSl10_Log WITH log <- Committed
LogSpec == L!Spec
===================================================
    SPECIFICATION Spec
CONSTANTS Vals = {a, b}
          Followers = {f1, f2}
          MaxLen = 3
PROPERTY LogSpec
CHECK_DEADLOCK FALSE
    1. Run it. TLC reports a violation. Is any committed entry lost or changed in the trace? Say exactly which abstract step is missing.
    2. Fix it in two ways: change AdvanceCommit to move the index by one, and, separately, keep the implementation and weaken the abstract spec so one step may append several entries. Check both.
    3. Add a failover step: a new leader that holds only the committed prefix takes over, and uncommitted entries are discarded everywhere. (Real Raft is subtler; this is the part that matters here.) Check the mapping again, and then the mapping log <- llog.

    Under the mapping Committed, what is a Replicate(f) step?

    Hint

    A refinement maps each implementation step to one abstract step or to a stutter. For the weaker spec, say "the new log is longer and keeps every old entry" with a quantifier over 1..Len(log), and use log' \in Seq(Vals) rather than an existential over Seq(Vals), which TLC can't enumerate.

    Solution

    (a) TLC's shortest trace has six states, shown in the figure: two Request(a) steps, two Replicate(f1) steps, and AdvanceCommit setting commit from 0 to 2. Both entries are on a majority, the leader and f1, so committing them is safe, and nothing is lost or changed. But the mapped log went from <<>> to <<a, a>> in one step, and PSl10_Log appends one entry per step. Refinement doesn't let one implementation step stand for two abstract steps. The implementation isn't wrong; the abstract spec's steps are finer than the implementation's.

    (b) First fix, in the implementation (module PSl10_RLogOne):

    AdvanceCommit == /\ commit < Len(llog)
                 /\ OnMajority(commit + 1)
                 /\ commit' = commit + 1
                 /\ UNCHANGED <<llog, flog>>

    Second fix, in the spec. The model keeps the jumping AdvanceCommit and maps to this module instead (PSl10_RLogBatch):

    ---------------- MODULE PSl10_LogBatch ----------------
EXTENDS Naturals, Sequences
CONSTANT Vals
VARIABLE log
Init == log = <<>>
\* One step may append one or more entries; earlier entries never change.
Extend == /\ log' \in Seq(Vals)
          /\ Len(log') > Len(log)
          /\ \A i \in 1..Len(log) : log'[i] = log[i]
Spec == Init /\ [][Extend]_log
=======================================================

    TLC finds no error with either: 1197 states generated and 503 distinct for the one-at-a-time commit, 1425 and 503 for the batch spec. Which fix is right depends on what clients can observe. If a client can watch the committed log grow, the batch spec is honest about what it will see. If the abstract spec is shared with other components that assume one entry at a time, change the implementation.

    (c) The failover step, together with the one-at-a-time commit (module PSl10_RLogFix):

    Prefix(s, n) == [i \in 1..n |-> s[i]]
Failover == /\ Len(llog) > commit
            /\ llog' = Prefix(llog, commit)
            /\ flog' = [f \in Followers |->
                          IF Len(flog[f]) > commit THEN Prefix(flog[f], commit)
                          ELSE flog[f]]
            /\ UNCHANGED commit

    With the Committed mapping, TLC finds no error: 1617 states generated, 503 distinct. Failover discards only entries past commit, so the mapped log doesn't change, and it is a stutter. With log <- llog (module PSl10_RLogLeader), TLC reports a violation in three states: Request(a) makes the leader's log <<a>>, and Failover empties it. Without failover, log <- llog passes too (module PSl10_RLogOneLeader, 503 distinct states), because a single leader's log only grows. That's the real reason the commit index exists: it marks the part of the log that survives a change of leader.

    Problem 4●●●UI design system

    Which list does an optimistic tag input refine?

    Draws on Refinement mappings, Messages, failures, and retries, Liveness and fairness, What it means to implement a spec and Problem set 9.

    A design system ships a tag input, used to put labels on issues. When the user adds a tag, it appears at once, greyed out as pending, and a request goes to the server. If the server accepts, the tag turns solid. If it rejects, for example because the user may not use that label, the tag disappears and a toast explains why. The server's own contract is simple: an issue's tags are only ever added. Messages are a set that only grows, as in lesson 19, so the model allows any delay, reordering and duplicate delivery.

    ---------------- MODULE PSl10_TagSet ----------------
CONSTANT Tags
VARIABLE tags
Init == tags = {}
Add(t) == /\ t \notin tags
          /\ tags' = tags \cup {t}
Next == \E t \in Tags : Add(t)
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_tags
=====================================================
    ---------------- MODULE PSl10_TagList ----------------
CONSTANT Tags
VARIABLES pending, confirmed, server, msgs
vars == <<pending, confirmed, server, msgs>>
Msgs == [type : {"add", "ok", "rejected"}, tag : Tags]
TypeOK == /\ pending \subseteq Tags
          /\ confirmed \subseteq Tags
          /\ server \subseteq Tags
          /\ msgs \subseteq Msgs
Init == /\ pending = {}      \* shown greyed out, waiting for the server
        /\ confirmed = {}    \* shown normally
        /\ server = {}       \* the server's stored tags
        /\ msgs = {}
Sent(t) == \E m \in msgs : m.tag = t
\* The user types a tag; it appears at once, marked pending.
UserAdd(t) == /\ ~Sent(t)
              /\ pending' = pending \cup {t}
              /\ msgs' = msgs \cup {[type |-> "add", tag |-> t]}
              /\ UNCHANGED <<confirmed, server>>
Answered(t) == \E m \in msgs : m.tag = t /\ m.type \in {"ok", "rejected"}
ServerAccept(t) == /\ [type |-> "add", tag |-> t] \in msgs
                   /\ ~Answered(t)
                   /\ server' = server \cup {t}
                   /\ msgs' = msgs \cup {[type |-> "ok", tag |-> t]}
                   /\ UNCHANGED <<pending, confirmed>>
ServerReject(t) == /\ [type |-> "add", tag |-> t] \in msgs
                   /\ ~Answered(t)
                   /\ msgs' = msgs \cup {[type |-> "rejected", tag |-> t]}
                   /\ UNCHANGED <<pending, confirmed, server>>
ClientOk(t) == /\ [type |-> "ok", tag |-> t] \in msgs
               /\ t \in pending
               /\ pending' = pending \ {t}
               /\ confirmed' = confirmed \cup {t}
               /\ UNCHANGED <<server, msgs>>
ClientRollback(t) == /\ [type |-> "rejected", tag |-> t] \in msgs
                     /\ t \in pending
                     /\ pending' = pending \ {t}
                     /\ UNCHANGED <<confirmed, server, msgs>>
Next == \E t \in Tags : \/ UserAdd(t)
                        \/ ServerAccept(t) \/ ServerReject(t)
                        \/ ClientOk(t) \/ ClientRollback(t)
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars
Fairness == \A t \in Tags :
              /\ WF_vars(ServerAccept(t) \/ ServerReject(t))
              /\ WF_vars(ClientOk(t) \/ ClientRollback(t))
FairSpec == Spec /\ Fairness

Shown == pending \cup confirmed
ByShown     == INSTANCE PSl10_TagSet WITH tags <- Shown
ByConfirmed == INSTANCE PSl10_TagSet WITH tags <- confirmed
ByServer    == INSTANCE PSl10_TagSet WITH tags <- server
ShownRefines     == ByShown!Spec
ConfirmedRefines == ByConfirmed!Spec
ServerRefines    == ByServer!Spec
ConfirmedOnServer == confirmed \subseteq server
Settles == \A t \in Tags : (t \in pending) ~> (t \notin pending)
Converges == <>[](Shown = server)
======================================================
    SPECIFICATION FairSpec
CONSTANT Tags = {t1, t2}
INVARIANT TypeOK ConfirmedOnServer
PROPERTY ConfirmedRefines ServerRefines Settles Converges
CHECK_DEADLOCK FALSE
    1. Check the three mappings: what the user sees (ShownRefines), the solid tags (ConfirmedRefines), and the server's tags (ServerRefines). Which ones hold? For any that fails, describe TLC's trace as the user would see it.
    2. Is the failing one a bug in the component? Say which abstract spec the screen does refine, in one sentence.
    3. Problem set 9 asked whether every request is eventually decided. Ask it here: check Settles with Spec instead of FairSpec, and explain the result. Then replace Fairness by two conditions: weak fairness of "the server answers some tag" and of "the client processes some reply". Is that enough here? Would it be enough for a lock that two processes take over and over?
    4. Explain why UserAdd needs the guard ~Sent(t). What could an old rejected message do if the user re-added the same tag?

    Which mapping fails?

    Hint

    Run each mapping in its own model with one PROPERTY line. For (c), the aggregate condition only forces some enabled step. Ask whether any tag can be passed over forever when each tag needs just one answer and one reply.

    Solution

    (a) With the cfg as given, TLC finds no error: ConfirmedRefines, ServerRefines, Settles and Converges all hold, as do TypeOK and ConfirmedOnServer, in 36 distinct states. With PROPERTY ShownRefines, TLC reports the action property of PSl10_TagSet violated in four states: UserAdd(t1), ServerReject(t1), ClientRollback(t1). The user typed t1, saw it greyed out, then saw it vanish, as in the figure. The last step removes t1 from Shown, which no Add step can do.

    (b) It's not a bug. It is the speculative-display contract from the editor example in lesson 33: the screen shows a guess, and a guess can be withdrawn. The screen refines "tags are added, and pending ones may be withdrawn", a different spec with a Withdraw action. What must not happen is a solid tag disappearing, and ConfirmedRefines together with ConfirmedOnServer rules that out. The design-system rule that follows is "only solid tags are promises". So pending tags need a visibly different style, and anything that copies the list, such as an export, should read confirmed.

    (c) With SPECIFICATION Spec, TLC reports Settles violated. Its counterexample has both tags accepted by the server, t2's reply received, and then stuttering forever with t1 still pending, although the ok for t1 is in msgs. TLC also warns that the stuttering counterexample may be caused by a missing fairness constraint. Without fairness, nothing requires the client to process a reply. FairSpec asks for weak fairness of "answer t" and "process the reply to t" for each tag t. That suffices: once t's request is in msgs, answering it stays enabled until it happens, and so does processing the reply while t is pending.

    The aggregate version also suffices here (module PSl10_TagListAgg):

    AggFairness == /\ WF_vars(\E t \in Tags : ServerAccept(t) \/ ServerReject(t))
               /\ WF_vars(\E t \in Tags : ClientOk(t) \/ ClientRollback(t))
AggSpec == Spec /\ AggFairness

    With SPECIFICATION AggSpec, TLC finds that Settles and Converges hold, in the same 36 states. Each tag is answered once and its reply processed once, and each such step disables itself. So "some answer happens" can only pick a different tag each time, and with finitely many tags every one gets its turn. A lock is different: if B can acquire, release and acquire again forever, "some process acquires" is satisfied by B alone, and A may wait forever. Per-item fairness is still the safer habit, because it keeps working if you later add retries that make an item's steps repeat.

    (d) Messages are never removed, so after a rejection [type |-> "rejected", tag |-> t1] stays in msgs. If the user could add t1 again, ClientRollback(t1) would be enabled at once by the old message, and the new attempt would be rolled back before the server saw it. This is the stale-response problem: replies need to identify the request they answer, not just the tag. A real component would put a request id in each message, and the guard would compare ids.

    Beyond the lectures I: Concurrency

    Find the interleaving that breaks the design.

    In lesson 12, one action was one indivisible step, and in lesson 18 TLC tried the resource managers’ steps in every order. Here you use both ideas on purpose: you decide where one step ends, and TLC finds the order that breaks the design.

    An interleaving is one order in which independent actors’ steps can happen. TLC does not simulate CPU instructions. It explores whichever steps you wrote, so choose the step boundaries from the guarantee your system actually has. The diagram shows why that matters: two buyers, one ticket, and a check that happens separately from the reservation. If A or B reserves before the other checks, that path dead-ends safely, as at the top and bottom. If both check first, the middle node, then the sale goes through twice.

    Start with the guarantee you want

    This module makes checking and updating one step, so Reserve is one edge in the graph.

    ---------------- MODULE Inventory ----------------
EXTENDS Naturals, FiniteSets
CONSTANT Buyers
VARIABLES remaining, booked
vars == <<remaining, booked>>
Init == /\ remaining = 1
        /\ booked = {}
Reserve(b) ==
    /\ remaining > 0
    /\ b \notin booked
    /\ remaining' = remaining - 1
    /\ booked' = booked \cup {b}
Next == \E b \in Buyers: Reserve(b)
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars
TypeOK == /\ remaining \in 0..1
          /\ booked \in SUBSET Buyers
Conservation == remaining + Cardinality(booked) = 1
NoOverselling == Cardinality(booked) <= 1
==================================================
    SPECIFICATION Spec
CONSTANT Buyers = {A, B}
INVARIANT TypeOK
INVARIANT Conservation
INVARIANT NoOverselling
CHECK_DEADLOCK FALSE

    TLC finds 3 distinct states and no error. The diagram below is all of them.

    This abstraction promises nothing about a database. It describes the guarantee a design must provide. Whether a real multi-step implementation provides it is the question from lesson 26.

    Now split the step

    Add a per-buyer stage. Check reads the stock and remembers the answer in the stage. Reserve relies on that memory and does not look again.

    Check(b) ==
    /\ pc[b] = "idle"
    /\ remaining > 0
    /\ pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![b] = "checked"]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<remaining, booked>>
Reserve(b) ==
    /\ pc[b] = "checked"
    /\ remaining' = remaining - 1
    /\ booked' = booked \cup {b}
    /\ pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![b] = "done"]

    The invariant is unchanged. TLC reports NoOverselling violated after 4 steps: both buyers check, then both reserve, leaving remaining = -1 and booked = {A, B}. With the invariant removed, the whole graph has the 9 states in the first diagram.

    Predict: if you add remaining > 0 back to Reserve, what happens to the split model?

    The second reservation is disabled, so the double sale goes away. In doing so you moved the real decision back into one atomic step, because the test and the update now happen together in Reserve. The earlier Check no longer decides anything.

    Check before committing

    Buyer A
    Inventory
    Buyer B

    The lab replays one path through each model. It is an educational replay, not TLC.

    Exercise: name an implementation guarantee needed by Reserve.

    The availability test and the successful update must form one indivisible decision. A conditional update can provide this if the database enforces the required concurrency semantics and the application checks whether it succeeded. A transaction boundary alone is not a proof: isolation and retries matter.

    The atomic model passes and the split model fails the same invariant. What changed?

    Concrete architecture: a shopping cart is not a reservation

    Suppose a storefront has one camera left. Ada adds it to a cart, and Ben adds it to another cart. That is not overselling if carts only express interest. Two carts are allowed; two successful reservations of the one unit are not. Naming both concepts “selected” makes the design harder to reason about, so checkout must be the step that decides.

    Represent a reservation as a durable record keyed by request ID. On success, the stock count falls and the reservation appears in the same abstract step. Cancelling is the same move in reverse:

    Cancel(b) ==          \* also models expiry of the hold
    /\ b \in held
    /\ held' = held \ {b}
    /\ remaining' = remaining + 1
    /\ UNCHANGED <<confirmed, paying>>

    The guard blocks cancellation when no hold exists, and the two updates move the unit back. Cancelling the same hold twice is disabled, so stock cannot increase twice.

    Real products add expiry and payment. Then ask whether a delayed payment callback can confirm a hold that has already expired. The TicketHold model tests this with Reserve, StartPayment, Cancel (which also stands for expiry) and LatePayment:

    LatePayment(b) ==
    /\ b \in paying
    /\ b \in held     \* delete this line to get the bug
    /\ confirmed' = confirmed \cup {b}
    /\ held' = held \ {b}
    /\ paying' = paying \ {b}
    /\ UNCHANGED remaining

    With the guard b \in held, TLC finds 16 states and OnePromise holds. Delete that line and it fails in the 5 steps shown below.

    Look at the fourth step: A’s hold is gone and the ticket is back on sale, but A’s payment is still arriving. Confirmation checked only that a payment had started. Rechecking the hold closes this path. If the same buyer can reserve again after expiry, buyer identity is not enough, because an old callback would match the new hold. You would then need a reservation identity or generation.

    Exercise: does adding Cancel preserve the property “once booked, always booked”?
