    No, and that may be intended. Conservation can still hold while bookings are removed. Choose properties that match the lifecycle: “at most one live reservation” is different from “a buyer never loses a reservation.”

    Beyond the lectures I: Concurrency

    Write an algorithm; inspect its translation.

    In lesson 5 you turned a small program into a state machine by hand, with a control variable pc saying what runs next. PlusCal does that translation for you. You still decide what one step is, as you just did in lesson 35.

    PlusCal is an algorithm language written inside a comment in a TLA+ module. Its translator generates ordinary TLA+ after the comment: Init, Next, Spec, and a pc function for processes. The language is convenient for algorithms that read as sequential steps. It does not replace the state machine, and the diagram above is the state machine you get from the source below.

    ---------------- MODULE TicketPC ----------------
EXTENDS Integers, FiniteSets
CONSTANT Buyers
(*--algorithm Ticket
variables remaining = 1, booked = {};
define
    Safe == Cardinality(booked) <= 1
end define;
process Buyer \in Buyers
begin
Reserve:
    if remaining > 0 then
        remaining := remaining - 1;
        booked := booked \cup {self};
    end if;
end process;
end algorithm; *)
=================================================
    SPECIFICATION Spec
CONSTANT Buyers = {A, B}
INVARIANT Safe

    That is the source before translation. To translate, run java -cp tla2tools.jar pcal.trans -nocfg TicketPC.tla or use your editor’s translate command. -nocfg keeps the translator from writing its own config file over yours. The generated text appears between translation markers before the closing line. TLC then finds 5 distinct states and no error.

    self identifies the current process. Each label starts an atomic step, and everything up to the next label runs in that one step. So the if and both assignments under Reserve are one edge in the diagram. Inside a step, := runs in order, so a later statement sees an earlier statement’s value. Do not confuse this with the simultaneous primed equations in raw TLA+.

    Move a label, change the model

    Add one label, Take:, in front of the decrement, and rename the first label Check. The translator now produces two actions for each buyer. This is its real output for that change:

    Check(self) == /\ pc[self] = "Check"
               /\ IF remaining > 0
                     THEN /\ pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![self] = "Take"]
                     ELSE /\ pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![self] = "Done"]
               /\ UNCHANGED << remaining, booked >>
Take(self) == /\ pc[self] = "Take"
              /\ remaining' = remaining - 1
              /\ booked' = (booked \cup {self})
              /\ pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![self] = "Done"]

    The diagram is pc[self] for one buyer. You could have written this translation yourself: it is the same pattern as lesson 5. Between the two actions, the other buyer can run, so TLC now reports Safe violated after 4 steps, the same race as InventorySplit. When reading an error trace, look at pc first. It tells you which labeled step each process is about to run.

    Three more statements cover most algorithms. await P blocks a step until P holds, but does not promise P ever will. either … or … is a choice among alternatives. with x \in S do … picks a value nondeterministically. Each of these translates into guards and existential quantifiers you already know.

    Predict: where does the deadlock go when both buyers finish?

    Nowhere. The translator adds a Terminating action that stutters once every process is at Done, so TLC does not report termination as deadlock. A process stuck on an await is still reported.

    Worked interleaving: two event handlers increment a count

    Consider two workers that each read a shared notification count, compute one more, and write it back. In a single JavaScript event loop, a synchronous increment has no await inside it. But reading the value, awaiting remote work, and later writing the captured value does let another handler intervene. So it gets two labels, and the captured value becomes a per-process variable.

    ---------------- MODULE LostUpdate ----------------
EXTENDS Naturals
CONSTANT Workers
(*--algorithm LostUpdate
variables count = 0;
define
    AllDone == \A w \in Workers: pc[w] = "Done"
    NoLostUpdate == AllDone => count = 2
end define;
process Worker \in Workers
variable local = 0;
begin
Read:
    local := count;
Write:
    count := local + 1;
end process;
end algorithm; *)
===================================================
    SPECIFICATION Spec
CONSTANT Workers = {A, B}
INVARIANT NoLostUpdate

    Read the graph from the left. If one worker gets both of its steps in before the other reads, the top and bottom paths, the count reaches 2. If both read first, the middle node, both write 1. TLC finds the 13 states and reports NoLostUpdate violated.

    For an atomic abstraction, replace the two labels with one, Increment: count := count + 1;. TLC then finds 4 states and no error. This is correct only if the actual operation has that guarantee, such as a synchronous local update or a suitable atomic database update.

    To find a real async boundary, annotate the implementation: what is captured before an await, what can change during the wait, and what is rechecked after it? Captured values become local variables. Each interaction point becomes a label. A familiar callback race is now a state machine.

    Predict: will making the whole process fair repair the lost update?

    No. PlusCal’s fair process asks for the fairness from lesson 29. With it, TLC confirms <>AllDone: both workers do finish. But NoLostUpdate still fails in the same 13-state graph. Fairness rules out stopping early. It removes no order of steps, and this is a safety failure.

    What does adding a label do to a PlusCal model?

    Lamport’s PlusCal tutorial teaches both algorithm structure and model checking.

    Beyond the lectures I: Concurrency

    Model the queue contract.

    lesson 30 used sequences, with Append and Tail, to model message channels. Give a sequence a capacity and you have a queue, a first architecture with ordering, backpressure and boundary cases but no complicated network.

    ---------------- MODULE BoundedFIFO ----------------
EXTENDS Naturals, Sequences
CONSTANTS Values, Capacity
ASSUME Capacity \in Nat /\ Capacity > 0
VARIABLE q
vars == <<q>>
Init == q = <<>>
Enqueue(v) == /\ Len(q) < Capacity
              /\ q' = Append(q,v)
Dequeue == /\ Len(q) > 0
           /\ q' = Tail(q)
Next == (\E v \in Values: Enqueue(v)) \/ Dequeue
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars
TypeOK == /\ q \in Seq(Values)
          /\ Len(q) <= Capacity
===================================================
    SPECIFICATION Spec
CONSTANT Values = {A, B}
CONSTANT Capacity = 2
INVARIANT TypeOK

    Here, duplicate values are distinct entries, since q is a sequence. TLC finds 7 distinct states and no error, and they are the 7 nodes above: 1 + 2 + 4. Seq(Values) contains sequences of every finite length, but the capacity guard bounds the reachable ones. The diagram also shows the two boundaries: from a length-2 node only dequeue leaves, and from ⟨⟩ only enqueue. Capacity blocks insertion, and the empty queue blocks removal.

    TypeOK does not say first-in, first-out

    Nothing in this module would notice a queue that hands out the wrong item, because it has no output. In the diagram, swap the targets of the two middle deq edges and TypeOK still holds. To state the contract, record what went in and what came out. Bound the history so the state space stays finite.

    ---------------- MODULE FIFOOrder ----------------
EXTENDS Naturals, Sequences
CONSTANTS Values, Capacity, MaxSends
VARIABLES q, sent, received
vars == <<q, sent, received>>
Init == q = <<>> /\ sent = <<>> /\ received = <<>>
Enqueue(v) == /\ Len(q) < Capacity
              /\ Len(sent) < MaxSends
              /\ q' = Append(q,v)
              /\ sent' = Append(sent,v)
              /\ UNCHANGED received
Dequeue == /\ Len(q) > 0
           /\ received' = Append(received, Head(q))
           /\ q' = Tail(q)
           /\ UNCHANGED sent
Next == (\E v \in Values: Enqueue(v)) \/ Dequeue
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars
TypeOK == /\ q \in Seq(Values)
          /\ Len(q) <= Capacity
InOrder == received \o q = sent
===================================================
    SPECIFICATION Spec
CONSTANTS Values = {A, B}
          Capacity = 2
          MaxSends = 3
INVARIANT TypeOK
INVARIANT InOrder
CHECK_DEADLOCK FALSE

    InOrder says everything sent is either received already or still queued, in the same order. The operator \o is sequence concatenation. This is close in spirit to the refinement mappings of lesson 33: it relates internal state to what an outside observer can see. TLC finds 41 distinct states and no error.

    Predict: make Dequeue take the last item instead of the first. Which invariant fails?

    Only InOrder. With TypeOK alone, the mutated module passes with 69 distinct states, because length and element types are still correct. With InOrder, TLC reports a violation after 3 steps, shown below.

    Worked architecture: upload processing

    A photo app accepts uploads A and B, then generates thumbnails in the background. Give each upload an immutable job ID. The user-visible contract is that accepted jobs do not disappear. FIFO ordering is a separate scheduling promise. A job moving from the waiting queue to a worker must not be mistaken for a completed upload.

    Claim == /\ Len(waiting) > 0
         /\ active' = active \cup {Head(waiting)}
         /\ waiting' = Tail(waiting)
         /\ UNCHANGED <<accepted, done>>
ExactlyOnePlace ==
    /\ Waiting \cup active \cup done = accepted
    /\ Waiting \cap active = {}
    /\ Waiting \cap done = {}
    /\ active \cap done = {}

    This comes from the complete UploadJobs module with Jobs = {A, B}, which also has Accept and Finish. Claim removes the head and records it as active in one step, and TLC finds 17 distinct states with ExactlyOnePlace holding. The disjointness lines matter: a count alone could hide one missing job and one duplicate.

    Now try the bad implementation, the dashed edge. A is removed from waiting and the worker crashes before recording it as active:

    CrashAfterRemove == /\ Len(waiting) > 0
                    /\ waiting' = Tail(waiting)
                    /\ UNCHANGED <<accepted, active, done>>

    TLC reports the violation in 2 steps: Accept(A), then the crash, leaving accepted = {A} and A nowhere else. A durable claim, or a visibility protocol that permits redelivery, changes the model so this edge no longer exists.

    Do not combine “FIFO” with “completion order” by accident. Two workers can claim A before B while B’s thumbnail finishes first, because Finish takes any active job. If ordered completion is required, add a publication barrier rather than asserting an order the architecture cannot provide.

    Predict: the worker writes A’s thumbnail and crashes before acknowledging A. Where should A go?

    Redelivery is reasonable if processing is idempotent or detects the existing result by job ID. The queue may deliver A again; the user-visible result should still be recorded once. Model claim attempts separately from logical upload identities.

    Why did TypeOK pass on a queue that delivers items out of order?

    Beyond the lectures I: Concurrency

    Separate exclusive access from eventual access.

    lesson 29 separated safety from liveness, and lesson 30 introduced strong fairness. A lock needs all of it: no two owners at once, and waiters eventually served. One can hold without the other, and the second depends on which fairness you assume.

    Begin with an abstract owner variable. Acquire assumes an atomic primitive that claims an unowned lock.

    ---------------- MODULE Lock ----------------
EXTENDS Naturals, FiniteSets
CONSTANTS Processes, NoOwner
ASSUME NoOwner \notin Processes
VARIABLES owner, pc
vars == <<owner, pc>>
Init == /\ owner = NoOwner
        /\ pc = [p \in Processes |-> "outside"]
Request(p) ==
    /\ pc[p] = "outside"
    /\ pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![p] = "waiting"]
    /\ UNCHANGED owner
Acquire(p) ==
    /\ owner = NoOwner
    /\ pc[p] = "waiting"
    /\ owner' = p
    /\ pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![p] = "critical"]
Release(p) ==
    /\ owner = p
    /\ owner' = NoOwner
    /\ pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![p] = "outside"]
Next == \E p \in Processes: Request(p) \/ Acquire(p) \/ Release(p)
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars
MutualExclusion ==
    Cardinality({p \in Processes : pc[p] = "critical"}) <= 1
OwnerAgrees == \A p \in Processes: pc[p] = "critical" => owner = p
\* Three fairness assumptions, weakest first.
ReleaseFair == \A p \in Processes: WF_vars(Release(p))
AggregateWF == ReleaseFair
    /\ WF_vars(\E p \in Processes: Acquire(p))
PerProcessWF == ReleaseFair
    /\ \A p \in Processes: WF_vars(Acquire(p))
PerProcessSF == ReleaseFair
    /\ \A p \in Processes: SF_vars(Acquire(p))
SpecAggregate == Spec /\ AggregateWF
SpecWF == Spec /\ PerProcessWF
SpecSF == Spec /\ PerProcessSF
NoStarvation ==
    \A p \in Processes: (pc[p] = "waiting") ~> (pc[p] = "critical")
=============================================

    With Processes = {A, B}, TLC finds 8 distinct states and both safety invariants hold on Spec. Those are the grid’s 8 nodes. The corner where both are critical has no incoming edge, because Acquire requires owner = NoOwner. The useful invariant is the relation OwnerAgrees: a process in the critical section must be the owner.

    Now the liveness question

    Safety says nothing about the red cycle. A waits; B requests, acquires and releases; B requests again. NoStarvation uses leads-to from lesson 29, so it asks about every waiter. Here are TLC’s answers:

    SpecificationAssumption addedNoStarvation
    SpecAggregateWeak fairness of “some process acquires”Violated
    SpecWFWeak fairness of each process’s AcquireViolated
    SpecSFStrong fairness of each process’s AcquireHolds
    Predict: why is per-process weak fairness not enough here?

    Weak fairness only forces an action that stays enabled continuously. On the red cycle, Acquire(A) is enabled in “A wait, B wait” but disabled in “A wait, B crit”, so it is never continuously enabled and A can be skipped forever. Strong fairness also forces an action that is enabled again and again, which is the case here.

    Strong fairness here is an assumption about the lock. It does not build anything. A real system earns it with a queueing discipline, or with an algorithm that does the work itself.

    Without the primitive

    Suppose the lock is just a shared value, checked in one step and written in the next. This is Look and Take in place of Acquire:

    Look(p) ==
    /\ pc[p] = "outside"
    /\ owner = NoOwner
    /\ pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![p] = "saw-free"]
    /\ UNCHANGED owner
Take(p) ==
    /\ pc[p] = "saw-free"
    /\ owner' = p
    /\ pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![p] = "critical"]

    It is the lesson 35 race again, and TLC reports it after 4 steps. Peterson’s algorithm gets mutual exclusion with only single reads and writes, using a flag for each process and a shared turn. Written in PlusCal from lesson 36:

    ---------------- MODULE Peterson ----------------
EXTENDS Integers
(*--algorithm Peterson
variables flag = [p \in {0, 1} |-> FALSE], turn = 0;
define
    MutualExclusion == ~(pc[0] = "cs" /\ pc[1] = "cs")
    NoStarvation == \A p \in {0, 1}: (pc[p] = "wait") ~> (pc[p] = "cs")
end define;
fair process P \in {0, 1}
begin
ncs:  while TRUE do
setf:   flag[self] := TRUE;
sett:   turn := 1 - self;
wait:   await ~flag[1 - self] \/ turn = self;
cs:     skip;
exit:   flag[self] := FALSE;
      end while;
end process;
end algorithm; *)
=================================================

    TLC finds 42 distinct states; MutualExclusion holds, and NoStarvation holds with just the weak fairness of fair process. The strong fairness that the abstract lock had to assume is unnecessary here, because turn stops one process winning forever. The order of the writes matters. Swap the setf and sett steps and TLC reports a violation after 8 steps with both processes at cs.

    Worked architecture: concurrent checkout

    Two browser requests try to reserve the final concert seat. Request A acquires the lock, reads stock = 1, and pauses. Request B arrives. A lock contract must disable B’s Acquire until A releases, and must not merely discourage it by convention.

    The guard on owner proves nothing about writes that bypass the protocol. In the diagram every arrow to Stock comes from whoever holds the lock, and every stock-changing action in your system must obey that rule.

    Now put A and B on different application servers. A process-local mutex on server 1 does not exclude server 2. Represent that as two owner variables and both requests can enter. Either put ownership in a shared authority with the necessary atomic semantics, or use a storage operation that directly enforces the inventory constraint. The model should describe the shared resource you actually use.

    The failure model comes next. If the owner crashes, owner stays set and everyone waits forever. Clearing it on a timeout is unsafe if the old process can still reach the resource, because a paused process is not a dead one. lesson 46 takes this up with leases and fencing tokens.

    Predict: can we recover from A crashing by unconditionally clearing owner?

    Only under assumptions that ensure A cannot continue writing under its old authority. A delayed or paused process is not necessarily dead. Model the resumed write explicitly; otherwise the recovery action may conceal the violation.

    A lock passes MutualExclusion in TLC. What do you know about starvation?

    Find mutex algorithms in the official example collection.

    Beyond the lectures I: Concurrency

    Problem set 11: decide where one step ends.

    Four concurrency problems. In each one the bug or the fix is a step boundary: a statement that is or isn't atomic, a check separated from its write, a counter published before its data, a lock that expires. You'll write PlusCal, read traces by their pc values, state a queue contract as a refinement, and ask the fairness questions of lecture 9 about a lock.

    PlusCal modules are shown as you write them, before translation. Translate each one with java -cp tla2tools.jar pcal.trans -nocfg File.tla or your editor's command, then run TLC. Every count below is from the translated module, run exactly as shown.

    Problem 1●○○Databases

    Two refunds, one lost

    Draws on PlusCal and program counters, Atomicity and the last ticket and From a program to a state machine.

    A payments service credits refunds to a wallet stored in Postgres. The handler reads the balance, adds the refund in application code, and writes the result back:

    SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 1;          -- returns 100
UPDATE accounts SET balance = 110 WHERE id = 1;     -- 100 + 10, computed in the app

    A customer returns two items and gets two refunds of 10, handled by two requests at the same moment. Support finds the wallet at 110 instead of 120. Each SQL statement is atomic on its own, so each becomes one labeled step, and the value carried between them becomes a process variable:

    ---------------- MODULE PSb1_Wallet ----------------
EXTENDS Naturals, FiniteSets
CONSTANT Clients
(*--algorithm Wallet
variables balance = 100;
define
    AllDone == \A c \in Clients : pc[c] = "Done"
    NoLostUpdate == AllDone => balance = 100 + 10 * Cardinality(Clients)
end define;
process Refund \in Clients
variable local = 0;
begin
Select:  \* SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 1
    local := balance;
Update:  \* UPDATE accounts SET balance = $1 WHERE id = 1, with $1 = local + 10
    balance := local + 10;
end process;
end algorithm; *)
====================================================
    SPECIFICATION Spec
CONSTANT Clients = {A, B}
INVARIANT NoLostUpdate
    1. Translate and run it. Write down TLC's trace as a list of steps, and say at which step the refund was lost.
    2. Replace the two statements by one, UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 10 WHERE id = 1. Write it as one label and check it. Why is one label an honest model of that statement in Postgres?
    3. Keep two statements, but read with SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE, which locks the row until the transaction ends. Model the row lock with a variable holder and a Commit label that releases it. Check it with two clients and with three.

    A teammate keeps a plain SELECT to read the balance, then runs SELECT … FOR UPDATE just before the UPDATE, still writing the value from the first read. Does that fix the lost refund?

    Hint

    For (c), put await holder = "none", holder := self and the read under one label, since SELECT … FOR UPDATE both waits for the lock and returns the row. A label starts a new atomic step, as in lesson 36, so the waiting, locking and reading must not be split.

    Solution

    (a) TLC reports NoLostUpdate violated after five states, shown in the figure: Select(A), Select(B), Update(A), Update(B). The refund is lost at the second Select, when B reads a balance that A is about to change. The write that makes it visible comes two steps later. This is the lesson 36 LostUpdate race, with SQL statements as the steps. Without the invariant, the full graph has 13 distinct states.

    (b) One label:

    ---------------- MODULE PSb1_WalletAtomic ----------------
EXTENDS Naturals, FiniteSets
CONSTANT Clients
(*--algorithm WalletAtomic
variables balance = 100;
define
    AllDone == \A c \in Clients : pc[c] = "Done"
    NoLostUpdate == AllDone => balance = 100 + 10 * Cardinality(Clients)
end define;
process Refund \in Clients
begin
Update:  \* UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 10 WHERE id = 1
    balance := balance + 10;
end process;
end algorithm; *)
==========================================================

    TLC finds 4 distinct states and no error. One label is honest because of what Postgres does with that statement. An UPDATE locks the row it changes. Under the default isolation level, READ COMMITTED, a second UPDATE of the same row waits for the first transaction to finish, then re-evaluates its WHERE clause on the new row version and computes balance + 10 from it. So no other write can come between reading and writing the balance. The label is a claim about the database; it is only true because the database makes it true.

    (c) With the row lock:

    ---------------- MODULE PSb1_WalletLock ----------------
EXTENDS Naturals, FiniteSets
CONSTANT Clients
(*--algorithm WalletLock
variables balance = 100, holder = "none";
define
    AllDone == \A c \in Clients : pc[c] = "Done"
    NoLostUpdate == AllDone => balance = 100 + 10 * Cardinality(Clients)
end define;
process Refund \in Clients
variable local = 0;
begin
Select:  \* SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE
    await holder = "none";
    holder := self;
    local := balance;
Update:  \* UPDATE accounts SET balance = $1 WHERE id = 1
    balance := local + 10;
Commit:  \* COMMIT releases the row lock
    holder := "none";
end process;
end algorithm; *)
========================================================

    TLC finds no error: 13 distinct states with two clients, 46 with three (Clients = {A, B, C}). The lock makes Select wait while another client is between its read and its commit, so every read sees the latest committed balance. Note what the model assumes: every writer of this row uses FOR UPDATE. A plain SELECT doesn't take the lock and isn't blocked by it, which is why the quiz's version still fails (module PSb1_WalletLockLate, violation found).

    Problem 2●●○Databases

    Two passengers in seat 14C

    Draws on Atomicity and the last ticket, PlusCal and program counters and The transaction commit spec.

    An airline's seat picker checks whether a seat is free and then inserts a booking. Two passengers, Ada and Ben, click 14C at the same moment, and both boarding passes say 14C. The team's first answer is a unique constraint on the seat column: the database rejects a second row for 14C, whatever the application does. This problem checks that fix, and then the code around it.

    ---------------- MODULE PSb1_Seat ----------------
EXTENDS Naturals, FiniteSets
CONSTANT Users
(*--algorithm Seat
variables bookings = {}, told = [u \in Users |-> "waiting"];
define
    OneBooking == Cardinality(bookings) <= 1
    Honest == \A u \in Users : told[u] = "confirmed" => u \in bookings
end define;
process User \in Users
variables free = FALSE, inserted = FALSE;
begin
Check:   \* SELECT 1 FROM bookings WHERE seat = '14C'
    free := (bookings = {});
Insert:  \* INSERT INTO bookings (seat, user_id) VALUES ('14C', ...)
    if free then
        bookings := bookings \cup {self};
        inserted := TRUE;
    end if;
Reply:   \* the page the user sees
    told[self] := IF inserted THEN "confirmed" ELSE "taken";
end process;
end algorithm; *)
==================================================
    SPECIFICATION Spec
CONSTANT Users = {A, B}
INVARIANT OneBooking Honest

    told is what each passenger's page says. Honest says no page claims a booking the database doesn't have.

    1. Run it and give TLC's trace in terms of the labels.
    2. Model the unique constraint: the Insert step adds the row only if no row for 14C exists, and otherwise does nothing, leaving inserted false. (In Postgres the insert fails with a unique-violation error, which the application catches.) Check it.
    3. A teammate writes the reply as told[self] := IF free THEN "confirmed" ELSE "taken", since "we already checked the seat was free". Which invariant fails, and what does Ben see?
    4. With the constraint in place, delete the Check label and the free variable entirely. Does anything fail? What was the check for?

    Which invariant fails for the teammate's reply in task (c)?

    Hint

    The constraint makes the test and the insert one indivisible decision, like moving remaining > 0 into Reserve in lesson 35. So the test belongs inside the Insert label. For (c), ask which value Ben's process holds in free when it replies.

    Solution

    (a) TLC reports OneBooking violated after five states: Check(A) and Check(B) both set free to TRUE, then Insert(A) and Insert(B) both add a row, leaving bookings = {A, B}. It is the split check and reserve from lesson 35.

    (b) With the constraint:

    ---------------- MODULE PSb1_SeatUnique ----------------
EXTENDS Naturals, FiniteSets
CONSTANT Users
(*--algorithm SeatUnique
variables bookings = {}, told = [u \in Users |-> "waiting"];
define
    OneBooking == Cardinality(bookings) <= 1
    Honest == \A u \in Users : told[u] = "confirmed" => u \in bookings
end define;
process User \in Users
variables free = FALSE, inserted = FALSE;
begin
Check:
    free := (bookings = {});
Insert:  \* UNIQUE (seat): the INSERT fails if a row for 14C exists
    if free then
        if bookings = {} then
            bookings := bookings \cup {self};
            inserted := TRUE;
        end if;
    end if;
Reply:
    told[self] := IF inserted THEN "confirmed" ELSE "taken";
end process;
end algorithm; *)
========================================================

    TLC finds 32 distinct states and no error. The inner test sits in the same label as the insert, because the database performs it atomically with the insert.

    (c) Honest fails; OneBooking still holds. TLC's trace, shown in the figure: both check, Ada inserts, Ben's insert is rejected so his inserted stays false, and Reply(B) sets told[B] to "confirmed" while bookings = {A}. Ben sees a confirmation and arrives at a seat that is Ada's. The constraint protected the data, not the page. The reply must be based on the result of the step that decides, the insert, never on the check.

    (d) Nothing fails (module PSb1_SeatNoCheck: 13 distinct states, both invariants hold):

    ---------------- MODULE PSb1_SeatNoCheck ----------------
EXTENDS Naturals, FiniteSets
CONSTANT Users
(*--algorithm SeatNoCheck
variables bookings = {}, told = [u \in Users |-> "waiting"];
define
    OneBooking == Cardinality(bookings) <= 1
    Honest == \A u \in Users : told[u] = "confirmed" => u \in bookings
end define;
process User \in Users
variables inserted = FALSE;
begin
Insert:  \* INSERT ... ; the unique constraint rejects a second row
    if bookings = {} then
        bookings := bookings \cup {self};
        inserted := TRUE;
    end if;
Reply:
    told[self] := IF inserted THEN "confirmed" ELSE "taken";
end process;
end algorithm; *)
=========================================================

    Once the insert decides, the check decides nothing. It is still useful for the interface, for example to grey out seats that are already taken, but it is a hint. Postgres also offers INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, which reports zero rows inserted instead of raising an error; either way, the application has to read that result.

    Problem 3●●○Algorithms

    A lock-free ring buffer refines a bounded queue

    Draws on Architecture: bounded FIFO, PlusCal and program counters, Refinement mappings and Architecture: mutual exclusion.

    A logging agent hands records from one producer thread to one consumer thread through a ring buffer: an array of N slots and two counters. tail counts records written and head counts records read, so tail - head records are waiting, and record number i lives in slot i % N. (a % b is the remainder, defined in Naturals.) There is no lock. Only the producer changes tail and only the consumer changes head. When the buffer is full the producer waits, which is the backpressure. The contract is the bounded FIFO queue of lesson 37, written here as its own module:

    ---------------- MODULE PSb1_Queue ----------------
EXTENDS Naturals, Sequences
CONSTANTS Values, Capacity
VARIABLE q
Init == q = <<>>
Enqueue(v) == /\ Len(q) < Capacity
              /\ q' = Append(q, v)
Dequeue == /\ Len(q) > 0
           /\ q' = Tail(q)
Next == (\E v \in Values : Enqueue(v)) \/ Dequeue
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_q
===================================================

    The producer sends 1, 2, …, K, so InOrder can check the order by value. The lines after the algorithm map the slots to the abstract queue.

    ---------------- MODULE PSb1_Ring ----------------
EXTENDS Naturals, Sequences
CONSTANTS N, K      \* N slots; the producer sends 1, 2, ..., K
(*--algorithm Ring
variables buf = [i \in 0..(N - 1) |-> 0], head = 0, tail = 0, got = <<>>;
define
    InOrder == \A i \in 1..Len(got) : got[i] = i
end define;
process Producer = "prod"
variable next = 1;
begin
P1: while next <= K do
P2:   await tail - head < N;        \* full: wait (backpressure)
      buf[tail % N] := next;        \* write the slot
P3:   tail := tail + 1;             \* publish it
      next := next + 1;
    end while;
end process;
process Consumer = "cons"
begin
C1: while Len(got) < K do
C2:   await tail > head;            \* empty: wait
      got := Append(got, buf[head % N]);
C3:   head := head + 1;             \* free the slot
    end while;
end process;
end algorithm; *)
\* Refinement: the occupied slots, oldest first, are the abstract queue.
Queued == [i \in 1..(tail - head) |-> buf[(head + i - 1) % N]]
Q == INSTANCE PSb1_Queue WITH Values <- 1..K, Capacity <- N, q <- Queued
QueueSpec == Q!Spec
==================================================
    SPECIFICATION Spec
CONSTANTS N = 2
          K = 3
INVARIANT InOrder
PROPERTY QueueSpec
    1. Translate and run it. Which labeled steps map to Enqueue, which to Dequeue, and which to stuttering?
    2. Change the full test to await tail - head <= N. Run it with both checks, then with only INVARIANT InOrder. Which check fails first, and why earlier?
    3. Restore the test, and make the producer publish before writing: tail := tail + 1 under P2, then buf[(tail - 1) % N] := next under P3. What does each check report?
    4. Each label is atomic, and the labels of one process run in order. Which of these assumptions does a real CPU not give you for free?

    In task (c), which check fails first?

    Hint

    The mapped queue only covers slots from head to tail - 1. Writing to slot tail % N is outside that range, unless the buffer is already full. For (d), think about what another core sees when one core writes buf and then tail.

    Solution

    (a) TLC finds no error: 96 states generated, 58 distinct. P3 (raise tail) maps to Enqueue(next), since the slot it exposes already holds next. C3 (raise head) maps to Dequeue. P2 writes a slot outside the occupied range, and C2 only copies the head into got, so they map to stuttering, as do the loop tests P1 and C1. This mapping is the one lesson 37 hinted at: InOrder related the queue to an observer's history, and Queued says which part of the array is the queue.

    (b) With both checks, TLC reports the action property of PSb1_Queue violated after nine states: the producer publishes 1 and 2, then, with two records unread, its P2 writes 3 into slot 0. The mapped queue goes from ⟨1, 2⟩ to ⟨3, 2⟩, which no queue step does. With InOrder alone, the trace has eleven states and ends with the consumer receiving 3 first, as in the figure. The refinement check sees the damage when it happens; the invariant sees it only when someone reads the result.

    (c) The refinement check fails after three states: P1, then the early P2 makes tail = 1 while slot 0 still holds 0, so the mapped queue is ⟨0⟩. With InOrder alone, TLC needs five states: the consumer reads slot 0 before the producer writes it, and got = <<0>>. The order of the write and the publish is the whole algorithm.

    (d) The model assumes each process's steps happen in program order as seen by the other process. Compilers and CPUs may reorder the writes to buf and tail, which turns the correct code into the bug in (c). Real ring buffers publish tail with a release store and read it with an acquire load, or use a language's atomic types, so that the order the model assumes is the order other threads see. The label structure is your statement of which orderings the code must guarantee.

    Problem 4●●●Distributed systems

    Guard the wallet with a Redis lock

    Draws on Architecture: mutual exclusion, PlusCal and program counters, Liveness and fairness, Problem 1 of this set and Problem set 9.

    Return to the wallet of Problem 1, but now it lives in a document store with no row locks, and workers on several servers apply refunds to it. The team guards the read-modify-write with a lock in Redis. A worker runs SET wallet:7:lock <worker id> NX, which sets the key only if it doesn't exist, retrying until it succeeds, and later deletes the key. committed counts writes, only so the invariant can say what the balance should be.

    ---------------- MODULE PSb1_RedisLock ----------------
EXTENDS Naturals, FiniteSets
CONSTANT Workers
(*--algorithm RedisLock
variables balance = 100, lock = "none", committed = 0;
define
    NoLostUpdate == balance = 100 + 10 * committed
    Holding == {w \in Workers : pc[w] \in {"Read", "Write", "Release"}}
    MutualExclusion == Cardinality(Holding) <= 1
end define;
fair process Worker \in Workers
variable local = 0;
begin
Acquire:  \* SET wallet:7:lock <worker id> NX
    await lock = "none";
    lock := self;
Read:
    local := balance;
Write:
    balance := local + 10;
    committed := committed + 1;   \* bookkeeping for the check only
Release:  \* DEL wallet:7:lock
    lock := "none";
end process;
end algorithm; *)
=======================================================
    SPECIFICATION Spec
CONSTANT Workers = {A, B}
INVARIANT NoLostUpdate MutualExclusion
PROPERTY Termination
    1. Run it. Then let a worker crash at Release: either lock := "none"; or skip; end either;. What does TLC report, and why isn't it a liveness violation?
    2. Locks that outlive their owner are why Redis locks get an expiry: SET … NX PX 10000 deletes the key after 10 seconds. Drop the crash, and add a process that can expire the lock whenever it is held. Check MutualExclusion, then only NoLostUpdate. Can any fairness assumption remove the violation?
    3. The workers become a background loop: acquire, work, release, forever. In the module below, check NoStarvation with Spec, then with SpecSF. Explain TLC's counterexample, and say what a real lock would need to justify SpecSF.
    ---------------- MODULE PSb1_RedisLockLoop ----------------
CONSTANT Workers
(*--algorithm RedisLockLoop
variable lock = "none";
define
    NoStarvation == \A w \in Workers :
                      (pc[w] = "Acquire") ~> (pc[w] = "Work")
end define;
fair process Worker \in Workers
begin
Loop:
    while TRUE do
Acquire:  \* SET wallet:7:lock <worker id> NX, retried until it succeeds
        await lock = "none";
        lock := self;
Work:
        skip;               \* read and write the balance
Release:
        lock := "none";
    end while;
end process;
end algorithm; *)
\* Strong fairness for each worker's Acquire, on top of fair process.
SpecSF == Spec /\ \A w \in Workers : SF_vars(Acquire(w))
===========================================================

    What does TLC report for the crash in task (a)?

    Hint

    For (b), write the expiry as its own process, process Expiry = "ttl", with a while TRUE loop that awaits a held lock and clears it. For (c), compare the four abstract lock specs in lesson 38: which one is fair process giving you here?

    Solution

    (a) TLC finds no error: 17 distinct states, and Termination holds because of fair process. With the crash (module PSb1_RedisLockCrash), TLC reports Deadlock reached after five states: A acquires, reads, writes, and crashes at Release with the key still set. A is at Done, B waits at Acquire forever, and no step is enabled. That is a safety failure, a reachable state with no way out, so TLC reports it before it looks at any temporal property.

    (b) The expiry process (module PSb1_RedisLockTTL, which also drops fair, since this part checks only safety):

    process Expiry = "ttl"   \* the key's PX timeout runs out
begin
Expire:
    while TRUE do
        await lock # "none";
        lock := "none";
    end while;
end process;

    MutualExclusion fails after four states: A acquires, the lock expires, B acquires, and both are past Acquire. With only NoLostUpdate, TLC reports eight states, the lost update of Problem 1 again: A acquires, the lock expires, A reads 100, B acquires and reads 100, A writes 110, B writes 110. In production, A is a worker paused by garbage collection or a slow network after its lock expired, not a dead one, the case lesson 38 warned about. No fairness assumption helps. Fairness only says some steps must eventually happen; it never forbids an order of steps, and this violation is a finite prefix. The fix has to be in the protocol: the store must reject a write from a worker whose lock has expired. The model also exposes a second problem: A's later Release deletes the key while B holds it. The Redis documentation recommends releasing with a script that deletes the key only if it still holds your own value.

    (c) With Spec, TLC reports NoStarvation violated, with the cycle in the figure: A waits at Acquire while B loops, acquires, works and releases, forever. fair process is weak fairness of each worker's whole step, close to the SpecWF row of lesson 38. A's Acquire is enabled only in the two states where the lock is free, so it is never continuously enabled, and weak fairness never forces it. With SpecSF, which adds strong fairness of each Acquire, TLC finds that NoStarvation holds, in the same 12 distinct states.

    But SpecSF is an assumption about the lock, not something SET NX provides. A retry loop gives no priority to the worker that has waited longest, and if B's retries tend to be faster, A can lose every race. To justify strong fairness, a real lock needs a queue of waiters served in order, or another mechanism that the model would then include as steps.

    Beyond the lectures II: Reasoning at scale

    Find the fact that makes the guarantee inevitable.

    Since lesson 16 you have used invariants like TCConsistent, and TLC checks them by visiting every reachable state. Now ask a stronger question: why does the invariant hold? The answer is usually a larger fact, one that holds even in states no behavior reaches.

    An invariant holds in all reachable states. An inductive invariant Inv also survives every Next step from any state satisfying it, including states Init never reaches. In the diagram, Inv is the blue box: no arrow leaves it. That is the condition that replaces walking an unbounded graph with one local argument. There are three obligations:

    \* Proof obligations, not a standalone module:
Init => Inv
Inv /\ [Next]_vars => Inv'
Inv => Safety

    First establish Inv initially. Then show every allowed step preserves it. Finally show it implies what you wanted. For a state predicate, stuttering preserves truth automatically, so the middle line is often written with Next alone.

    Exercise: what if Inv is so strong that Init does not imply it?

    It cannot establish the intended theorem. A preservation argument about an unreachable region says nothing about your actual initial states. Check the base case before the step case.

    Worked example: money in transit

    An app moves one unit from Alice to Bob through a worker. Debit and Credit are separate actions, as the steps in lesson 35 were.

    ---------------- MODULE Transfer ----------------
EXTENDS Naturals
VARIABLES alice, transit, bob
vars == <<alice, transit, bob>>
Init == alice = 2 /\ transit = 0 /\ bob = 0
Debit == /\ alice = 2           \* one transfer only
         /\ alice' = alice - 1
         /\ transit' = transit + 1
         /\ UNCHANGED bob
Credit == /\ transit > 0
          /\ transit' = transit - 1
          /\ bob' = bob + 1
          /\ UNCHANGED alice
Next == Debit \/ Credit
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars
TypeOK == /\ alice \in 0..2
          /\ transit \in 0..2
          /\ bob \in 0..2
Naive == alice + bob = 2
BobAtMostOne == bob <= 1
Inv == TypeOK /\ alice + transit + bob = 2
\* Start TLC from every state a candidate allows:
IndCandidate == TypeOK /\ BobAtMostOne
=================================================

    The natural first guess fails: TLC reports Naive (alice + bob = 2) violated after one step. The money is not lost, it is just somewhere your invariant was not looking. Inv counts the third place and holds, and the normal check visits only the 3 states in the green box.

    Asking TLC whether a fact is inductive

    TLC can test preservation directly on a finite type. Replace the initial predicate with the candidate, so it starts from every state the candidate allows.

    INIT Inv
NEXT Next
INVARIANT Inv
CHECK_DEADLOCK FALSE

    This run starts from all 6 states in the blue box, and TLC reports no error, so Inv is inductive on this finite set of values. Now try BobAtMostOne. It holds in all 3 reachable states, so as an invariant it passes. Starting from TypeOK /\ BobAtMostOne instead, TLC finds the dashed arrow: from alice = 0, transit = 1, bob = 1, Credit gives bob = 2.

    A counterexample like that one is called a counterexample to induction. It does not mean the system has a bug, because that start state is unreachable. It means your fact is too weak to explain itself, and you must strengthen it or give it up.

    Predict: mutate Credit so it raises bob without lowering transit. And Debit so it lowers alice without raising transit. Does Inv catch both?

    Yes, and differently. TLC’s trace for the bad Credit has total 3, after two steps; for the bad Debit it has total 1, after one. These are different bugs caught by one conservation equation. With several transfers, identify them separately: one scalar transit cannot tell you that one transfer was credited twice and another never.

    Hand-check the argument too. Init gives 2 + 0 + 0 = 2. In Debit, subtracting and adding one cancel. In Credit, the guard transit > 0 keeps the result in type, and they cancel again. Each action moves a unit’s location and keeps the total.

    Back to the ticket

    NoOverselling from lesson 35 looks like the property you want, and it is true. Is it inductive? Start TLC from all states satisfying TypeOK /\ NoOverselling, and it reports a violation from remaining = 1, booked = {B}, then Reserve(A).

    The red edges start where stock and bookings disagree. The missing fact relates the two variables: Conservation, remaining + Cardinality(booked) = 1. Start from TypeOK /\ Conservation and TLC finds 3 states and no error. Because remaining is at least 0, Conservation also implies at most one booking. Relational facts like this one usually do more work than bounding each variable alone.

    This check covers only the values you gave TLC. It can refute a candidate quickly, and a pass is good evidence, but it is not a theorem for all values. lesson 43 builds the proof itself.

    Predict: does this conservation proof establish that Bob eventually receives the money?

    No. The behavior may stay at alice = 1, transit = 1, bob = 0 forever. Credit is possible but not required. Safety says where the money is; reaching the destination needs the fairness of lesson 29.

    Which is true of every inductive invariant that Init implies?

    Using TLC to Check Inductive Invariance explains how finite checks can help develop candidate invariants.

    Beyond the lectures II: Reasoning at scale

    Reuse definitions without hiding assumptions.

    In lesson 26 you read a specification as a formula, and used INSTANCE to compare two of them. Formulas can also be conjoined. That is how you combine components, and it behaves differently from what you might expect from running programs.

    Composition needs a shared step convention

    Writing SpecA /\ SpecB intersects the allowed behaviors. It is not a request to interleave two programs. Here is the experiment behind the diagram, with each component written first as if it owned the whole state:

    ---------------- MODULE Frames ----------------
VARIABLES x, y
vars == <<x, y>>
Init == x = 0 /\ y = 0
\* Each component written as if it owned the whole state:
A == x = 0 /\ x' = 1 /\ y' = y
B == y = 0 /\ y' = 1 /\ x' = x
SpecA == Init /\ [][A]_vars
SpecB == Init /\ [][B]_vars
Conjoined == [A]_vars /\ [B]_vars
Interleaved == A \/ B
\* Each component constrains only its own variable:
OwnX == x = 0 /\ x' = 1
OwnY == y = 0 /\ y' = 1
OwnVars == [OwnX]_x /\ [OwnY]_y
===============================================
    Next-state relationDistinct statesSteps allowed
    Conjoined (what SpecA /\ SpecB means)1Only stuttering
    Interleaved (A \/ B)4The solid arrows
    OwnVars4The solid and dashed arrows

    The first row is the trap: A requires y unchanged and B requires y to change, so no step satisfies both, and all the system can do is stutter. TLC reports no error, because a system that does nothing violates no safety property. For an interleaving composition, write global actions with compatible frames. If you want simultaneous steps, each component must constrain only the variables it owns.

    Assume-guarantee reasoning says a component guarantees G provided its environment satisfies A. Check that the other components establish A. Two components that each assume the other eventually responds may prove nothing useful when combined: circular progress assumptions need an actual argument.

    Predict: is the Conjoined run’s clean TLC result good news?

    No. It found no error in 1 state. A state count far below what you expected is a result to investigate. A liveness property would have failed here.

    Module tools you have not needed yet

    You know EXTENDS and named instances. Substituting parameters lets you reuse a whole model. This puts the queue from lesson 37 into a job system:

    ---------------- MODULE JobQueue ----------------
CONSTANT Jobs
VARIABLE pending
Queue == INSTANCE BoundedFIFO
    WITH Values <- Jobs, Capacity <- 2, q <- pending
Spec == Queue!Spec
QueueSafe == Queue!TypeOK
=================================================

    TLC finds the same 7 states as before, since only the names changed. Queue!TypeOK is the qualified name for a definition in that instance.

    You have also met LET, CHOOSE and RECURSIVE in the lectures. Two more belong beside them. This module runs under TLC, and its ASSUME lines pass:

    ---------------- MODULE LangTools ----------------
EXTENDS Naturals
Outcome(x) == CASE x = 0 -> "empty"
                [] x > 0 -> "ready"
Pick == CHOOSE x \in {"A", "B"}: TRUE
RECURSIVE Fact(_)
Fact(n) == IF n = 0 THEN 1 ELSE n * Fact(n-1)
LOCAL Helper == 41
Exported == Helper + 1
ASSUME Outcome(0) = "empty" /\ Outcome(3) = "ready"
ASSUME Pick = Pick /\ Pick \in {"A", "B"}
ASSUME Fact(4) = 24 /\ Exported = 42
VARIABLE v
Spec == v = Pick /\ [][v' = Pick]_v
Stable == v = Pick
==================================================

    LOCAL keeps a helper from being exported to modules that use this one. It does not make state thread-local. CASE chooses a branch whose guard is true. Do not rely on branch order when guards overlap, and add OTHER if no guard might be true, because otherwise TLC stops with “Attempted to evaluate a CASE with no conditions true”.

    \EE h : F, temporal existential quantification, hides a variable at the level of whole behaviors: a behavior satisfies it if some sequence of values for h makes F true. That differs from the state-level \E. It is how you state a specification with internal variables hidden, but TLC does not accept it (“TLC cannot handle the temporal formula”).

    Predict: does CHOOSE x \in {"A","B"}: TRUE mean TLC will try both at every step?

    No. It denotes one unspecified value, the same every time, which is why Stable holds above and TLC finds 1 state. To explore both, write \E x \in S: Action(x).

    What does SpecA /\ SpecB mean?

    Worked example: compose search, selection, and caching

    A search screen has query text, an asynchronous request, displayed results, and a selected result. You could verify each alone: the service returns matches, the cache stores responses, and selection picks an existing row. The composition can still be wrong when responses arrive out of order.

    ---------------- MODULE SearchUI ----------------
EXTENDS Naturals
CONSTANTS MaxGen, NoSelection
VARIABLES generation, inflight, shownGen, results, selected
vars == <<generation, inflight, shownGen, results, selected>>
Rows(g) == {<<g, 1>>, <<g, 2>>}
Init == /\ generation = 0
        /\ inflight = {}
        /\ shownGen = 0
        /\ results = {}
        /\ selected = NoSelection
Input ==
    /\ generation < MaxGen
    /\ LET g == generation + 1 IN
         /\ generation' = g
         /\ inflight' = inflight \cup {[gen |-> g, rows |-> Rows(g)]}
    /\ UNCHANGED <<shownGen, results, selected>>
ShowResponse(r) ==
    /\ r \in inflight
    /\ r.gen = generation
    /\ shownGen' = r.gen
    /\ results' = r.rows
    /\ selected' = NoSelection
    /\ inflight' = inflight \ {r}
    /\ UNCHANGED generation
DropStale(r) ==
    /\ r \in inflight
    /\ r.gen # generation
    /\ inflight' = inflight \ {r}
    /\ UNCHANGED <<generation, shownGen, results, selected>>
Select(row) ==
    /\ row \in results
    /\ selected' = row
    /\ UNCHANGED <<generation, inflight, shownGen, results>>
Next == \/ Input
        \/ \E r \in inflight: ShowResponse(r) \/ DropStale(r)
        \/ \E row \in results: Select(row)
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars
Status == CASE shownGen = 0 -> "empty"
            [] shownGen = generation -> "ready"
            [] shownGen < generation -> "loading"
SelectionValid == selected = NoSelection \/ selected \in results
SettlesOnLatest ==
    inflight = {} /\ generation > 0 => shownGen = generation
StatusKnown == Status \in {"empty", "ready", "loading"}
=================================================
    SPECIFICATION Spec
CONSTANTS MaxGen = 2
          NoSelection = NoSelection
INVARIANT SelectionValid SettlesOnLatest StatusKnown
CHECK_DEADLOCK FALSE

    TLC finds 16 distinct states and all three invariants hold. Status uses CASE and needs no OTHER because the guards cover every reachable state, which StatusKnown confirms. SettlesOnLatest says that once nothing is in flight, the screen shows the latest generation.

    Two one-line mutations each break a different contract:

    • Delete the guard r.gen = generation, and TLC reports SettlesOnLatest violated after 4 steps: the red arrow in the diagram.
    • Replace selected' = NoSelection with UNCHANGED selected, and SelectionValid fails after 5 steps: the user picks a row from gen 1, gen 2 arrives, and the selection names a row no longer on screen.

    The request component’s guarantee is “every response carries its original generation”. The display relies on that and guarantees it never accepts an obsolete one. The cache must preserve the relevant key too: if results depend on query, tenant, locale and permissions, caching by query alone breaks the composition, even though each lookup is consistent with its own incomplete key.

    If the UI intentionally keeps old results while loading, the "loading" status above says so. That is better than asserting a stricter invariant and then hiding its violations. A policy is part of the model.

    Transfer exercise: why might a query-only cache expose another account’s results?

    Two accounts can issue the same query with different authorized result sets. If account identity or an equivalent authorization scope is missing from the key, one account’s cached response may be reused for the other. Model two accounts, one shared query, and two distinct expected result sets to expose the missing key component.

    Specifying Systems, especially composition, module meaning, and language operators. Keep its published corrections alongside the book.

    Beyond the lectures II: Reasoning at scale

    Reduce the model without removing the question.

    In lesson 18, a symmetry set took three-manager two-phase commit from 288 states to 80. Now you look at what happens as the model grows, and at when a reduction quietly stops testing what you meant to test.

    Here are real TLC runs of the same two-phase commit spec. If each of n independent variables has k values, their product has kⁿ combinations, and per-process state, messages and histories add dimensions quickly. Good modeling is not a contest to reproduce production. It is a search for the smallest model that still permits the failure you suspect.

    Resource managersDistinct statesWith symmetry
    328880
    58,832314
    7296,448920
    81,745,408, in 7 s1,461, in 2 min 9 s

    The last row is a surprise worth noticing. Symmetry cut the states by a factor of over a thousand and made this run slower, because TLC must consider all 8! = 40,320 permutations to recognize that two states are equivalent. Times are from one laptop; yours will differ, but measure them instead of assuming.

    Four reductions with different meanings

    TechniqueWhat changesQuestion to ask
    Smaller constantsChecks a smaller instanceCan the bug require another participant or round?
    AbstractionRemoves distinctionsAre all relevant concrete behaviors represented?
    SymmetryCollapses interchangeable identitiesAre those identities interchangeable in the properties too?
    State and action constraintsLimits explorationWhich paths have been excluded?

    A constraint, written CONSTRAINT P in the config, tells TLC not to explore states where P is false. An invariant is a property you test. A constraint prunes the experiment.

    A distinguished leader, a fixed account, or a process-specific progress formula breaks the symmetry you assumed. Do not combine symmetry with liveness checks unless your tools and reasoning explicitly support it; default to unreduced liveness runs.

    Worked example: a CDN invalidation that loses a race

    A content service publishes a new article version and invalidates cached copies. The origin serves version 2, but a fetch for version 1 began earlier. One key, one edge cache, two versions and one delayed fetch are enough.

    ---------------- MODULE CdnRace ----------------
EXTENDS Naturals
CONSTANT MaxVersion
VARIABLES origin, cached, inflight, floor
vars == <<origin, cached, inflight, floor>>
Init == /\ origin = 1
        /\ cached = 1          \* 0 means no cached copy
        /\ inflight = {}
        /\ floor = 0           \* invalidated through this version
Fetch == /\ origin \notin inflight
         /\ inflight' = inflight \cup {origin}
         /\ UNCHANGED <<origin, cached, floor>>
Publish == /\ origin < MaxVersion
           /\ origin' = origin + 1
           /\ UNCHANGED <<cached, inflight, floor>>
Invalidate == /\ floor < origin - 1
              /\ floor' = origin - 1
              /\ cached' = IF cached <= floor' THEN 0 ELSE cached
              /\ UNCHANGED <<origin, inflight>>
Fill(v) == /\ v \in inflight
           /\ v > floor
           /\ cached' = v
           /\ inflight' = inflight \ {v}
           /\ UNCHANGED <<origin, floor>>
Discard(v) == /\ v \in inflight
              /\ v <= floor
              /\ inflight' = inflight \ {v}
              /\ UNCHANGED <<origin, cached, floor>>
Next == Fetch \/ Publish \/ Invalidate
        \/ \E v \in inflight: Fill(v) \/ Discard(v)
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars
NotResurrected == cached = 0 \/ cached > floor
Fresh == cached = 0 \/ cached = origin
================================================

    Here floor records that everything through that version is invalidated, and Fill rejects anything at or below it. A deletion-only design remembers nothing, so it cannot tell a stale fill from a fresh one. Delete the guard v > floor to get that design, and run these experiments:

    ModelSettingsDistinct statesNotResurrected
    GuardedMaxVersion = 218Holds
    No guardMaxVersion = 2stopped at the errorViolated in 4 steps
    No guardMaxVersion = 12“Holds”
    No guardMaxVersion = 2, CONSTRAINT Fresh2“Holds”

    The two runs in quotation marks are false comfort. With one version nothing can be stale. The constraint case looks more reasonable: Fresh sounds like just the states you care about. But it removes the first state after Publish, so TLC reports “No error has been found” on the buggy design.

    Only 2 states explored, on a model with at least two actions you meant to exercise, is the warning sign. Whenever you add a bound, compare what the run visited with what you expected.

    Exercise: you bound retries to one and a duplicate-charge bug disappears. What next?

    Check whether at least two deliveries are needed to trigger it. Restore that behavior, then reduce some unrelated dimension. A useful reduction preserves the causal path to the property of interest.

    The useful reduction here keeps that path and removes the rest. One key is enough, since a thousand URLs add volume but no new cause. Two versions distinguish stale from fresh. A second edge becomes necessary only when the property concerns divergence between edges. This is a causal argument for the bound, not proof that every other bug fits it. The guarded model at MaxVersion 2, 3, 4 and 5 has 18, 82, 290 and 898 states, so raise it to check your argument, while you can still afford to.

    Measure the right work

    Track distinct states, generated states, search depth and whether the search finished. TLC stores a fingerprint of each visited state, which is a hash, not the state. Two different states could collide, and one would then go unexplored. So it prints an estimate, for example calculated (optimistic): val = 1.3E-13 for the 898-state run. This is why a completed run is a search, not a symbolic proof. Simulation mode (-simulate) samples behaviors and can find bugs in models too large to finish, but a sample with no violation is weaker evidence than a completed search.

    Transfer exercise: can you remove message identities from this model?

    Possibly for the single delayed response, but justify it. If duplicate delivery or retry identity affects whether the cache fills twice, keep enough identity to distinguish those events. Remove fields only after explaining why two states differing solely in that field have equivalent behavior for the property you are checking.

    A state constraint removes every state with a negative balance. What did you prove?

    TLC tools and documentation and the model-checking chapter of Specifying Systems.

    Beyond the lectures II: Reasoning at scale

    Replace a finite search with an explicit argument.

    lesson 8 named TLAPS, the proof system, and lesson 40 gave you the three obligations it needs. A finished TLC run covers the instances you gave it, and lesson 42 showed how little that may be. A proof can cover every instance, provided its assumptions and steps are correct.

    The hard part is usually finding the invariant that carries the design argument, which you did with TLC in the previous lessons. What remains is the structure in the diagram: a claim, split into smaller claims, until each one is small enough to check on its own.

    A worked proof

    Return to Inventory. Let Inv combine TypeOK and Conservation. Initially remaining = 1 and booked is empty. In Reserve(b), the guard ensures b is not already in booked, so adding b raises its cardinality by exactly one. The action lowers remaining by one, preserving the sum, and its positive-stock guard preserves the lower bound. Stuttering preserves both. Inv implies NoOverselling because remaining is nonnegative.

    That is the informal outline. Written as a TLA+ hierarchical proof, the same argument has numbered steps. <1>2 is a top-level step, and its <2> steps are the children that prove it:

    ---------------- MODULE InventoryProof ----------------
EXTENDS Inventory, TLAPS
Inv == /\ TypeOK
       /\ IsFiniteSet(booked)
       /\ Conservation
LEMMA CardEmpty == IsFiniteSet({}) /\ Cardinality({}) = 0
    PROOF OMITTED
LEMMA CardNat == \A S : IsFiniteSet(S) => Cardinality(S) \in Nat
    PROOF OMITTED
LEMMA CardAdd == \A S, x : IsFiniteSet(S) /\ x \notin S =>
    /\ IsFiniteSet(S \cup {x})
    /\ Cardinality(S \cup {x}) = Cardinality(S) + 1
    PROOF OMITTED
THEOREM Safety == Spec => []NoOverselling
<1>1. Init => Inv
    BY CardEmpty DEF Init, Inv, TypeOK, Conservation
<1>2. Inv /\ [Next]_vars => Inv'
    <2> SUFFICES ASSUME Inv, [Next]_vars PROVE Inv'
        OBVIOUS
    <2>1. ASSUME NEW b \in Buyers, Reserve(b) PROVE Inv'
        BY <2>1, CardAdd, CardNat
        DEF Reserve, Inv, TypeOK, Conservation
    <2>2. CASE UNCHANGED vars
        BY <2>2 DEF vars, Inv, TypeOK, Conservation
    <2>3. QED
        BY <2>1, <2>2 DEF Next
<1>3. Inv => NoOverselling
    BY CardNat DEF Inv, TypeOK, Conservation, NoOverselling
<1>4. QED
    BY <1>1, <1>2, <1>3, PTL DEF Spec
=======================================================

    How far this was checked: the module parses under SANY with a stand-in for the TLAPS module, and TLC confirms Inv is inductive for Buyers = {A, B}, with 3 states and NoOverselling holding. It has not been run through TLAPS, so a prover may ask for more detail in some steps. Treat it as the shape of a proof. The three OMITTED lemmas are facts about finite sets that a complete proof must import or prove.

    BY lists the facts a step may use and DEF lists the definitions it may expand. Nothing else is visible, which is the point: every use of an assumption is on the page. PTL names propositional temporal logic, the reasoning that gets from “preserved by every step” to [].

    Exercise: remove b \notin booked from Reserve. Is the one-ticket model enough to expose a bug?

    Not in this one-ticket model. TLC still finds 3 states and no error. Inv plus remaining > 0 implies booked is empty, so the membership guard is redundant here and the proof can recover that fact. With more tickets, the same buyer could reserve twice: adding that buyer again does not increase the cardinality while remaining decreases. The broader conservation proof then needs the guard or a different booking representation. Test assumptions at the size where they become relevant.

    Where TLAPS helps

    TLAPS checks hierarchical proofs by sending each step’s obligation to backend provers. Break large obligations into named claims, and expose the definitions each one needs. An informal outline is not a checked proof. Consult the supported-feature list: the documented system focuses on safety reasoning and does not generally discharge arbitrary temporal liveness arguments.

    Use TLC to attack a candidate invariant before you spend time proving it, as in lesson 40. A finite run can refute a candidate quickly. It cannot prove the unbounded theorem.

    Worked example: prove a cache cannot roll back a version

    An app fetches a product description twice. Version 5 and version 4 are in flight, and the network delivers 5 first. A naive cache that accepts every response replaces the fresh value with the old one.

    ---------------- MODULE CacheVersion ----------------
EXTENDS Naturals
VARIABLES cacheVersion, pending
vars == <<cacheVersion, pending>>
Init == cacheVersion = 3 /\ pending = {4, 5}
Accept(v) == /\ v \in pending
             /\ v >= cacheVersion
             /\ cacheVersion' = v
             /\ pending' = pending \ {v}
Reject(v) == /\ v \in pending
             /\ v < cacheVersion
             /\ pending' = pending \ {v}
             /\ UNCHANGED cacheVersion
Next == \E v \in pending: Accept(v) \/ Reject(v)
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars
Monotonic == [][cacheVersion' >= cacheVersion]_vars
=====================================================

    This time the property is about steps, not states: Monotonic says every step keeps or raises the version. TLC finds 4 distinct states and no error. Delete the guard v >= cacheVersion and it reports the bottom row of the diagram.

    The proof is short. For Accept, the guard gives cacheVersion' >= cacheVersion directly. For Reject and stuttering, cacheVersion is unchanged. An action that resets cacheVersion must join this case split, even if it lives in another component, and this is where a proof tends to find what a design forgot.

    It assumes one key, one monotonically increasing version scheme, and immutable content for a given version. Incomparable version vectors or reused version numbers need a different model.

    What the proof forces you to decide

    Split cacheVersion into what is in memory and what is on disk, with Persist and Restart actions. Now there is a new case to prove, and it fails:

    Restart == /\ volatile # durable
           /\ volatile' = durable
           /\ UNCHANGED <<durable, pending>>

    TLC reports Monotonic violated in 2 steps. You must either persist the accepted version before showing it, weaken the contract to permit rollback after restart, or hold back older data until resynchronization. The proof makes that a design choice instead of a surprise.

    A proof of one property establishes exactly that property. A server could send version 100 with the wrong product’s text and Accept would take it. Add a key-match property and a mapping from version to content if you need them. And checking versions 3 to 5 with TLC can reveal a counterexample, but does not establish the claim for all numbers: the argument above does, because no step of it depends on which numbers they are.

    Transfer exercise: can a cache safely delete its version record on logout?

    It depends on the contract and scope. If the next login begins a new cache epoch with no promised cross-session monotonicity, clearing it may be valid. If old responses can still arrive and populate the new session, include session identity in the acceptance guard; otherwise an old authenticated response can cross the reset boundary.

    What can a proof of Inv establish that a completed TLC run of Buyers = {A, B} cannot?

    TLAPS documentation and tutorial; checking candidate inductive invariants with TLC.

    Beyond the lectures II: Reasoning at scale

    Problem set 12: make the argument, not just the run.

    Four problems about reasoning beyond one TLC run. You'll find the inductive invariant behind a ledger, shrink a connection pool's state space without hiding a bug, compose a client with a rate limiter, and write a hierarchical proof for the locked wallet from Problem set 11. They draw on this chapter's four lessons, and on PlusCal and refinement from the two chapters before it.

    Every module below was checked with TLC exactly as shown, including the inductiveness checks that start from INIT Inv. No proof in this set was checked by a prover: TLAPS wasn't available where these problems were checked, so the proof in Problem 4 was only parsed by SANY, and its invariant checked by TLC.

    Problem 1●○○Databases

    A ledger that never mints money

    Draws on Safety and inductive invariants, The general meaning of implementation and Two-phase commit and records.

    A payments ledger moves money between accounts in two steps, because the accounts may live in different database shards. Debit takes the amount from the sender and marks the transfer debited. Credit later pays the receiver. Auditors care about one promise above all: the ledger never creates money, so the balances never add up to more than the money that was put in. Transfer 1 moves 1 from alice to bob, and transfer 2 moves 2 back.

    ---------------- MODULE PSb2_Ledger ----------------
EXTENDS Naturals
Accounts == {"alice", "bob"}
Xfers == {1, 2}
From == [x \in Xfers |-> IF x = 1 THEN "alice" ELSE "bob"]
To   == [x \in Xfers |-> IF x = 1 THEN "bob" ELSE "alice"]
Amt  == [x \in Xfers |-> IF x = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 2]
Total == 3
VARIABLES bal, status
vars == <<bal, status>>
Init == /\ bal = [a \in Accounts |-> IF a = "alice" THEN 2 ELSE 1]
        /\ status = [x \in Xfers |-> "new"]
Debit(x) == /\ status[x] = "new"
            /\ bal[From[x]] >= Amt[x]
            /\ bal' = [bal EXCEPT ![From[x]] = bal[From[x]] - Amt[x]]
            /\ status' = [status EXCEPT ![x] = "debited"]
Credit(x) == /\ status[x] = "debited"
             /\ bal' = [bal EXCEPT ![To[x]] = bal[To[x]] + Amt[x]]
             /\ status' = [status EXCEPT ![x] = "credited"]
Next == \E x \in Xfers : Debit(x) \/ Credit(x)
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars

RECURSIVE SumOver(_, _)
SumOver(f, S) == IF S = {} THEN 0
                 ELSE LET s == CHOOSE e \in S : TRUE
                      IN  f[s] + SumOver(f, S \ {s})
InFlight == [x \in Xfers |-> IF status[x] = "debited" THEN Amt[x] ELSE 0]

TypeOK == /\ bal \in [Accounts -> 0..Total]
          /\ status \in [Xfers -> {"new", "debited", "credited"}]
NoMint == SumOver(bal, Accounts) <= Total
Conservation == SumOver(bal, Accounts) + SumOver(InFlight, Xfers) = Total
IndNoMint == TypeOK /\ NoMint
IndCons   == TypeOK /\ Conservation
====================================================
    SPECIFICATION Spec
INVARIANT TypeOK NoMint Conservation
CHECK_DEADLOCK FALSE
    1. Run the cfg above. Then check whether NoMint is inductive, starting TLC from every state of IndNoMint. Describe the counterexample, and say whether it is a bug.
    2. Check IndCons the same way. Then argue by hand that Conservation is preserved by Debit(x) and Credit(x), and that it implies NoMint.
    3. Support asks for a Refund(x) action that returns a transfer's amount to its sender and marks it "refunded". Write it with the guard status[x] # "new", check it with the normal cfg and with INIT IndCons, then find the right guard.

    TLC finds a counterexample to induction for IndNoMint. What does it show?

    Hint

    For the inductiveness checks, use a cfg with INIT IndNoMint, NEXT Next, INVARIANT IndNoMint and CHECK_DEADLOCK FALSE, as in lesson 40. NoMint ignores money that has left one account but not arrived in the other. Where is it?

    Solution

    (a) The normal check finds no error in 5 distinct states, the top row of the figure. Starting from IndNoMint, TLC computes 90 initial states and reports a violation after two: from alice = 0, bob = 2 with transfer 2 debited, Credit(2) pays alice 2 and the balances add up to 4. That start state satisfies NoMint (0 + 2 ≤ 3) but is unreachable: transfer 2 has taken 2 from bob, so 4 units exist in all. It isn't a bug. It shows that NoMint doesn't constrain money in flight, so it can't explain why a credit is safe.

    (b) Starting from IndCons, TLC computes 27 initial states and finds no error, so Conservation is inductive for these values. By hand: Debit(x) lowers one balance by Amt[x] and moves x from "new" to "debited", which adds Amt[x] to the in-flight sum. Credit(x) moves x from "debited" to "credited", removing Amt[x] from the in-flight sum, and adds it to a balance. Each step moves money between places, as in Transfer from lesson 40. Since in-flight amounts are never negative, balances plus in-flight equal to 3 implies balances at most 3, which is NoMint. TypeOK needs no separate argument: the guard of Debit keeps balances nonnegative, and Conservation keeps each one at most 3.

    (c) With the guard status[x] # "new" (module PSb2_LedgerRefundBug), the normal check reports NoMint violated after four states: Debit(1), Credit(1), then Refund(1) returns 1 to alice although bob was already paid, and the balances add up to 4. That is a real bug, refunding a completed transfer. Starting from IndCons, TLC also finds a counterexample to induction, with a refund of a credited transfer. The right guard is status[x] = "debited":

    Refund(x) == /\ status[x] = "debited"
             /\ bal' = [bal EXCEPT ![From[x]] = bal[From[x]] + Amt[x]]
             /\ status' = [status EXCEPT ![x] = "refunded"]

    With it (module PSb2_LedgerRefund), the normal check finds 7 distinct states, and the check from IndCons starts from 52 states and finds no error. A refund takes money out of flight and returns it, just as a credit does; Conservation told you which guard to write before any trace did.

    Problem 2●●○Infrastructure

    Shrink a connection pool, and keep the admin

    Draws on State explosion and trustworthy reductions, Paxos Commit: surviving the coordinator, Two-phase commit and records and Sets, functions, and quantifiers.

    An application server keeps a pool of database connections. Clients request one, wait, check one out, and return it, or give up waiting. The pool must never hand one connection to two clients, and a client is busy exactly when it holds one connection. Clients are interchangeable, and so are connections, which makes this a natural place for symmetry.

    ---------------- MODULE PSb2_Pool ----------------
EXTENDS Naturals, FiniteSets, TLC
CONSTANTS Clients, Conns, Free
ASSUME Free \notin Clients
VARIABLES owner, state
vars == <<owner, state>>
Init == /\ owner = [k \in Conns |-> Free]
        /\ state = [c \in Clients |-> "idle"]
Request(c) == /\ state[c] = "idle"
              /\ state' = [state EXCEPT ![c] = "waiting"]
              /\ UNCHANGED owner
Checkout(c, k) == /\ state[c] = "waiting"
                  /\ owner[k] = Free
                  /\ owner' = [owner EXCEPT ![k] = c]
                  /\ state' = [state EXCEPT ![c] = "busy"]
Return(c, k) == /\ owner[k] = c
                /\ owner' = [owner EXCEPT ![k] = Free]
                /\ state' = [state EXCEPT ![c] = "idle"]
Timeout(c) == /\ state[c] = "waiting"     \* gave up waiting for a connection
              /\ state' = [state EXCEPT ![c] = "idle"]
              /\ UNCHANGED owner
Next == \E c \in Clients : \/ Request(c) \/ Timeout(c)
                           \/ \E k \in Conns : Checkout(c, k) \/ Return(c, k)
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars
TypeOK == /\ owner \in [Conns -> Clients \cup {Free}]
          /\ state \in [Clients -> {"idle", "waiting", "busy"}]
\* A client is busy exactly when it holds one connection.
HoldsOne == \A c \in Clients :
              (state[c] = "busy") = (Cardinality({k \in Conns : owner[k] = c}) = 1)
              /\ Cardinality({k \in Conns : owner[k] = c}) <= 1
Sym == Permutations(Clients) \cup Permutations(Conns)
==================================================
    SPECIFICATION Spec
CONSTANTS Clients = {c1, c2, c3}
          Conns = {k1, k2}
          Free = Free
INVARIANT TypeOK HoldsOne
    1. Fill in distinct states for 3 clients and 2 connections, 4 and 2, 5 and 3, and 7 and 3, with and without SYMMETRY Sym. Also note how long the 7-and-3 runs take.
    2. Explain why the symmetry is sound here, using the rule from lesson 22.
    3. The pool now keeps one connection for an admin client that runs health checks: other clients may check out a connection only if at least two are free. Add CONSTANT Admin with ASSUME Admin \in Clients, the guard, and the invariant AdminCanConnect below. Then make the bug of writing >= 1 in place of >= 2, and check the buggy pool with Admin = c1 and 3 clients and 2 connections, with and without SYMMETRY Sym.
    4. Write a symmetry that is sound for the admin pool, and check the buggy pool again.
    FreeConns == {k \in Conns : owner[k] = Free}
Checkout(c, k) == /\ state[c] = "waiting"
                  /\ owner[k] = Free
                  /\ c # Admin => Cardinality(FreeConns) >= 2
                  /\ owner' = [owner EXCEPT ![k] = c]
                  /\ state' = [state EXCEPT ![c] = "busy"]
AdminCanConnect == state[Admin] = "waiting" => FreeConns # {}

    What does TLC report for the buggy admin pool with SYMMETRY Sym?

    Hint

    A symmetry set is sound only if swapping its elements maps behaviors to behaviors and leaves the property's truth unchanged. Look for a constant that names one particular client. For (d), only the clients that are really interchangeable may be permuted.

    Solution

    (a) TLC's counts:

    Clients × connectionsDistinct statesWith SYMMETRY Sym
    3 × 2449
    4 × 212812
    5 × 399218
    7 × 38,86426

    On the machine these were checked on, the 7 × 3 run took about 1 second without symmetry and 17 seconds with it. The reduction is large, but TLC must try 7! × 3! = 30,240 permutations on each state it stores, the same effect lesson 42 showed for two-phase commit. Symmetry pays when states are expensive and identities few.

    (b) No client or connection is named anywhere in the spec or in TypeOK and HoldsOne. They appear only through quantifiers and set operations over Clients and Conns, so swapping two clients, or two connections, turns any behavior into another behavior and doesn't change whether an invariant holds. Free is a separate model value and isn't permuted.

    (c) Without symmetry, the correct admin pool passes in 40 distinct states, and the buggy one fails: TLC reports AdminCanConnect violated after six states, in which c1 (the admin) and c2 request, c2 checks out k1, c3 requests and checks out k2, and the admin is left waiting with nothing free. With SYMMETRY Sym, TLC reports no error in 9 distinct states. Admin breaks the symmetry: swapping c1 and c2 turns a violating state into one that satisfies the invariant, as in the figure. TLC explores only one state of each class, so it can miss the violating member entirely, and here it does. Nothing in TLC's output warns you.

    (d) Leave the admin out of the permutations:

    SymSafe == Permutations(Clients \ {Admin}) \cup Permutations(Conns)

    With SYMMETRY SymSafe, TLC reports the violation in the buggy pool again, and the correct admin pool passes in 15 distinct states. The general rule: any constant that singles out an element, like a leader, an admin or a home region, removes that element from the symmetry set.
