    Problem 3●●○Infrastructure

    Compose a client with a token-bucket rate limiter

    Draws on Modules, composition, and language tools, Refinement mappings, Safety and inductive invariants and Your first spec through TLC.

    An API gateway protects a service with a token bucket. The bucket holds up to Cap tokens and is refilled over time; each admitted request spends one token, and when the bucket is empty the gateway answers 429 Too Many Requests. One team wrote the bucket and another wrote a client, each as its own module:

    ---------------- MODULE PSb2_Bucket ----------------
EXTENDS Naturals
CONSTANTS Cap, MaxRefills
VARIABLES tokens, refills
bvars == <<tokens, refills>>
Init == tokens = Cap /\ refills = 0
Take == /\ tokens > 0
        /\ tokens' = tokens - 1
        /\ UNCHANGED refills
Refill == /\ tokens < Cap
          /\ refills < MaxRefills       \* bounds the model
          /\ tokens' = tokens + 1
          /\ refills' = refills + 1
Empty == tokens = 0
Next == Take \/ Refill
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_bvars
====================================================
    ---------------- MODULE PSb2_Client ----------------
EXTENDS Naturals
CONSTANT MaxReqs
VARIABLES issued, ok, limited
cvars == <<issued, ok, limited>>
Init == issued = 0 /\ ok = 0 /\ limited = 0
Outstanding == issued > ok + limited
Send == /\ ~Outstanding                 \* one request at a time
        /\ issued < MaxReqs
        /\ issued' = issued + 1
        /\ UNCHANGED <<ok, limited>>
GotOk == /\ Outstanding
         /\ ok' = ok + 1
         /\ UNCHANGED <<issued, limited>>
Got429 == /\ Outstanding
          /\ limited' = limited + 1
          /\ UNCHANGED <<issued, ok>>
Next == Send \/ GotOk \/ Got429
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_cvars
====================================================

    The gateway composes them, renaming the client's variables and fixing the constants with INSTANCE … WITH. Admitting a request is a shared step: the client's GotOk and the bucket's Take happen together.

    ---------------- MODULE PSb2_Gateway ----------------
EXTENDS Naturals
VARIABLES reqs, served, throttled, tokens, refills
vars == <<reqs, served, throttled, tokens, refills>>
C == INSTANCE PSb2_Client WITH MaxReqs <- 4, issued <- reqs,
                               ok <- served, limited <- throttled
B == INSTANCE PSb2_Bucket WITH Cap <- 2, MaxRefills <- 1
Init == C!Init /\ B!Init
\* Shared step: the gateway forwards the request and spends a token.
Admit    == C!GotOk /\ B!Take
\* Gateway answers 429 only when the bucket is empty.
Throttle == C!Got429 /\ B!Empty /\ UNCHANGED <<tokens, refills>>
Next == \/ C!Send /\ UNCHANGED <<tokens, refills>>
        \/ Admit
        \/ Throttle
        \/ B!Refill /\ UNCHANGED <<reqs, served, throttled>>
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars
\* Every admitted request spent a token.
TokensAccounted == served + tokens = 2 + refills
=====================================================
    SPECIFICATION Spec
INVARIANT TokensAccounted
CHECK_DEADLOCK FALSE
    1. Run it. Then add ClientContract == C!Spec and BucketContract == B!Spec and check both as properties. Why must they hold for any composition written this way?
    2. Someone suggests composing more simply, with each component stepping its own variables: [C!Next]_<<reqs, served, throttled>> /\ [B!Next]_<<tokens, refills>> as the next-state relation. Check TokensAccounted on that spec and explain the counterexample.
    3. The client's assumption about the gateway is that a 429 means the bucket was really empty. Write that as an action property HonestThrottle, check it, then delete B!Empty from Throttle and check again.

    What is the step in TLC's counterexample for the simpler composition?

    Hint

    TLC accepts only one [][…]_v conjunct in a behavior spec, so write the simpler composition as one next-state relation, like OwnVars in lesson 41. For (c), an action property has the form [][P]_vars, where P may mention primed variables.

    Solution

    The complete module:

    ---------------- MODULE PSb2_Gateway ----------------
EXTENDS Naturals
VARIABLES reqs, served, throttled, tokens, refills
vars == <<reqs, served, throttled, tokens, refills>>
C == INSTANCE PSb2_Client WITH MaxReqs <- 4, issued <- reqs,
                               ok <- served, limited <- throttled
B == INSTANCE PSb2_Bucket WITH Cap <- 2, MaxRefills <- 1
Init == C!Init /\ B!Init
\* Shared step: the gateway forwards the request and spends a token.
Admit    == C!GotOk /\ B!Take
\* Gateway answers 429 only when the bucket is empty.
Throttle == C!Got429 /\ B!Empty /\ UNCHANGED <<tokens, refills>>
Next == \/ C!Send /\ UNCHANGED <<tokens, refills>>
        \/ Admit
        \/ Throttle
        \/ B!Refill /\ UNCHANGED <<reqs, served, throttled>>
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars
\* Every admitted request spent a token.
TokensAccounted == served + tokens = 2 + refills
\* A 429 is sent only when the bucket is empty.
HonestThrottle == [][throttled' > throttled => tokens = 0]_vars
ClientContract == C!Spec
BucketContract == B!Spec
\* The naive composition: conjoin the components, each stepping its own variables.
NaiveNext == [C!Next]_<<reqs, served, throttled>> /\ [B!Next]_<<tokens, refills>>
Naive == Init /\ [][NaiveNext]_vars
=====================================================

    (a) TLC finds no error: 24 states generated, 19 distinct. With PROPERTY HonestThrottle ClientContract BucketContract added (the cfg PSb2_Gateway.cfg), it still finds none. Every disjunct of Next is a step of the client and a step or stutter of the bucket, and the other way round. Send and Throttle leave the bucket's variables unchanged, Refill leaves the client's unchanged, and Admit is a step of both. So each component's spec is implied, by the argument of lesson 26, with the WITH renaming as the refinement mapping.

    (b) With SPECIFICATION Naive, TLC reports TokensAccounted violated after two states: one NaiveNext step in which reqs becomes 1 and tokens becomes 1. The client did Send and the bucket did Take in the same step, and nothing ties a Take to a served request. The conjunction of lesson 41 is still intersection: each conjunct allows its own component's steps, so their intersection allows every combination of them, including simultaneous steps that shouldn't be connected. It also allows GotOk with no Take at all. The fix is to say which steps are shared, as Admit does.

    (c) HonestThrottle == [][throttled' > throttled => tokens = 0]_vars holds for the gateway. Without B!Empty (module PSb2_GatewayLoose), TLC reports HonestThrottle violated after three states: the client sends, and the gateway answers 429 with 2 tokens in the bucket. TokensAccounted still holds, because a throttle spends nothing. This is assume-guarantee reasoning made concrete: the client's correctness argument may assume a 429 means "slow down", and the gateway must guarantee it. Each guarantee needs its own property, because the conservation invariant can't see this one.

    Problem 4●●●Databases

    Prove the locked wallet never loses a refund

    Draws on From model checking to proof, Safety and inductive invariants, PlusCal and program counters and Problem set 11.

    Problem set 11 fixed the lost refund with SELECT … FOR UPDATE and checked it for two and three clients. A proof covers any number. Here is that wallet again, module PSb1_WalletLock: each client locks the row and reads the balance, writes the balance plus 10, and commits, which releases the lock.

    ---------------- MODULE PSb1_WalletLock ----------------
EXTENDS Naturals, FiniteSets
CONSTANT Clients
(*--algorithm WalletLock
variables balance = 100, holder = "none";
define
    AllDone == \A c \in Clients : pc[c] = "Done"
    NoLostUpdate == AllDone => balance = 100 + 10 * Cardinality(Clients)
end define;
process Refund \in Clients
variable local = 0;
begin
Select:  \* SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE
    await holder = "none";
    holder := self;
    local := balance;
Update:  \* UPDATE accounts SET balance = $1 WHERE id = 1
    balance := local + 10;
Commit:  \* COMMIT releases the row lock
    holder := "none";
end process;
end algorithm; *)
========================================================

    The translator produces these actions, with Refund(self) their disjunction and Next the usual (\E self \in Clients : Refund(self)) \/ Terminating:

    Init == (* Global variables *)
        /\ balance = 100
        /\ holder = "none"
        (* Process Refund *)
        /\ local = [self \in Clients |-> 0]
        /\ pc = [self \in ProcSet |-> "Select"]
Select(self) == /\ pc[self] = "Select"
                /\ holder = "none"
                /\ holder' = self
                /\ local' = [local EXCEPT ![self] = balance]
                /\ pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![self] = "Update"]
                /\ UNCHANGED balance
Update(self) == /\ pc[self] = "Update"
                /\ balance' = local[self] + 10
                /\ pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![self] = "Commit"]
                /\ UNCHANGED << holder, local >>
Commit(self) == /\ pc[self] = "Commit"
                /\ holder' = "none"
                /\ pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![self] = "Done"]
                /\ UNCHANGED << balance, local >>

    A candidate inductive invariant, in a module that extends the wallet:

    ---------------- MODULE PSb2_WalletProof ----------------
EXTENDS PSb1_WalletLock, TLAPS
ASSUME ClientsOK == IsFiniteSet(Clients) /\ "none" \notin Clients

Money == Nat
Paid == {c \in Clients : pc[c] \in {"Commit", "Done"}}
TypeOK == /\ balance \in Money
          /\ local \in [Clients -> Money]
          /\ holder \in Clients \cup {"none"}
          /\ pc \in [Clients -> {"Select", "Update", "Commit", "Done"}]
LockHeld  == \A c \in Clients : (pc[c] \in {"Update", "Commit"}) <=> (holder = c)
FreshRead == \A c \in Clients : pc[c] = "Update" => local[c] = balance
Ledger    == balance = 100 + 10 * Cardinality(Paid)
Inv == TypeOK /\ LockHeld /\ FreshRead /\ Ledger
    1. Nat is infinite, so for TLC replace Money by a finite set: add MoneyModel == {0, 100, 110, 120} and the cfg line CONSTANT Money <- MoneyModel. Check that Inv is inductive for two clients, starting from INIT Inv.
    2. Drop FreshRead, and separately LockHeld, and check each weaker candidate the same way. Explain each counterexample to induction.
    3. Write a hierarchical proof of THEOREM Spec => []NoLostUpdate, in the style of lesson 43, with a case for each action. State the facts about Cardinality you need as lemmas with PROOF OMITTED. Make SANY parse it.
    4. Say exactly what your answer to (c) establishes, and what it doesn't.

    Which conjunct of Inv says that the value about to be written was read under the lock?

    Hint

    Only Update changes Paid: it adds self, which wasn't there because pc[self] was "Update". So you need "adding a new element to a finite set raises its cardinality by one" and "a subset of a finite set is finite", plus IsFiniteSet(Clients) as an assumption. For the step case, copy the shape of <1>2 in InventoryProof.

    Solution

    (a) The cfg (PSb2_WalletProof.cfg):

    INIT Inv
NEXT Next
CONSTANT Clients = {A, B}
CONSTANT Money <- MoneyModel
INVARIANT Inv
INVARIANT NoLostUpdate
CHECK_DEADLOCK FALSE

    TLC computes 144 initial states and finds no error, so Inv is inductive for two clients on this finite set of values, and it implies NoLostUpdate in each of them. With three clients and {0, 100, 110, 120, 130}, it finds 2800 states and no error.

    (b) Without FreshRead, TLC starts from a state where A holds the lock at "Update" with local[A] = 0 and the balance 100, and Update(A) writes 10. Nothing in the weaker candidate says A's local value is current. Without LockHeld, TLC starts with both clients at "Update", both holding 100. Update(A) writes 110, and B's FreshRead fails, because B's read is now stale. Both are unreachable states. FreshRead carries the argument about values, and LockHeld is why no one else can make a fresh read stale.

    (c) The proof, in the tree of the figure:

    ---------------- MODULE PSb2_WalletProof ----------------
EXTENDS PSb1_WalletLock, TLAPS
ASSUME ClientsOK == IsFiniteSet(Clients) /\ "none" \notin Clients

Money == Nat
Paid == {c \in Clients : pc[c] \in {"Commit", "Done"}}
TypeOK == /\ balance \in Money
          /\ local \in [Clients -> Money]
          /\ holder \in Clients \cup {"none"}
          /\ pc \in [Clients -> {"Select", "Update", "Commit", "Done"}]
LockHeld  == \A c \in Clients : (pc[c] \in {"Update", "Commit"}) <=> (holder = c)
FreshRead == \A c \in Clients : pc[c] = "Update" => local[c] = balance
Ledger    == balance = 100 + 10 * Cardinality(Paid)
Inv == TypeOK /\ LockHeld /\ FreshRead /\ Ledger

LEMMA CardEmpty == Cardinality({}) = 0
    PROOF OMITTED
LEMMA CardSubset == \A S, T : IsFiniteSet(T) /\ S \subseteq T => IsFiniteSet(S)
    PROOF OMITTED
LEMMA CardAdd == \A S, x : IsFiniteSet(S) /\ x \notin S =>
    Cardinality(S \cup {x}) = Cardinality(S) + 1
    PROOF OMITTED

THEOREM Safety == Spec => []NoLostUpdate
<1>1. Init => Inv
    BY ClientsOK, CardEmpty DEF Init, ProcSet, Inv, TypeOK, Money,
       LockHeld, FreshRead, Ledger, Paid
<1>2. Inv /\ [Next]_vars => Inv'
    <2> SUFFICES ASSUME Inv, [Next]_vars PROVE Inv'
        OBVIOUS
    <2>1. ASSUME NEW self \in Clients, Select(self) PROVE Inv'
        \* holder goes from "none" to self, and local[self] gets balance.
        BY <2>1, ClientsOK DEF Select, Inv, TypeOK, Money, LockHeld,
           FreshRead, Ledger, Paid
    <2>2. ASSUME NEW self \in Clients, Update(self) PROVE Inv'
        \* FreshRead gives balance' = balance + 10, and self joins Paid.
        <3>1. self \notin Paid /\ Paid' = Paid \cup {self}
            BY <2>2 DEF Update, Inv, TypeOK, Paid
        <3>2. IsFiniteSet(Paid)
            BY ClientsOK, CardSubset DEF Paid
        <3>3. Cardinality(Paid') = Cardinality(Paid) + 1
            BY <3>1, <3>2, CardAdd
        <3>4. QED
            BY <2>2, <3>3 DEF Update, Inv, TypeOK, Money, LockHeld,
               FreshRead, Ledger
    <2>3. ASSUME NEW self \in Clients, Commit(self) PROVE Inv'
        \* holder returns to "none"; Commit and Done are both in Paid.
        BY <2>3, ClientsOK DEF Commit, Inv, TypeOK, LockHeld, FreshRead,
           Ledger, Paid
    <2>4. CASE Terminating \/ UNCHANGED vars
        BY <2>4 DEF Terminating, vars, Inv, TypeOK, LockHeld, FreshRead,
           Ledger, Paid
    <2>5. QED
        BY <2>1, <2>2, <2>3, <2>4 DEF Next, Refund
<1>3. Inv => NoLostUpdate
    \* When all are Done, Paid = Clients.
    BY DEF Inv, Ledger, Paid, NoLostUpdate, AllDone
<1>4. QED
    BY <1>1, <1>2, <1>3, PTL DEF Spec

\* For TLC only: a finite stand-in for Money, and the weaker candidates.
MoneyModel == {0, 100, 110, 120}
NoFresh == TypeOK /\ LockHeld /\ Ledger
NoLock  == TypeOK /\ FreshRead /\ Ledger
MoneyModel3 == {0, 100, 110, 120, 130}
=========================================================

    SANY parses this module with no errors, using a stand-in for the TLAPS module that defines PTL, since TLAPS itself wasn't available. The definitions after the comment For TLC only serve the checks in (a) and (b). In <2>2, FreshRead gives balance' = local[self] + 10 = balance + 10, and <3>3 gives one more paid client, so Ledger is preserved. In <2>1, LockHeld and holder = "none" mean no client is at "Update" or "Commit", so the new holder is the only one. In <1>3, when every client is "Done", Paid = Clients.

    (d) What was done: TLC checked that Inv is inductive and implies NoLostUpdate for two and three clients, and SANY checked that the proof is well formed. What was not done: no prover checked any step, so a step may need more facts or definitions than its BY lists, and the three lemmas are omitted. With TLAPS installed, you would run it on this module and add detail wherever a step fails. Even a complete proof would establish only this safety property, under the model's assumptions: that every writer takes the row lock, and that SELECT … FOR UPDATE really is one atomic step that waits, locks and reads. It says nothing about the client finishing, and nothing about a writer that bypasses the lock.

    Beyond the lectures III: Failure-prone systems

    Make retrying safe across a crash.

    A retry is only safe if the effect and the record of that effect cannot be separated by a crash.

    This builds on lesson 19, where a client could not tell a lost request from a lost reply and so had to retry, and on lesson 35, where a check and an action in separate steps let another process slip between them. Now the thing that slips between them is a crash.

    Suppose a worker processes charge request r and records “seen r” so retries can return the earlier result. A durable value survives a crash; a volatile one does not. In each row of the diagram, the arrow labelled “crash, retry” starts from what is left on disk.

    In the top row the charge is on disk with no ID, so the retry charges again. In the middle row the ID is on disk with no charge, so the retry is told the work is done when it is not. Only the bottom row has no gap between the two writes. Step through the top and bottom rows here. This lab is an educational model, not TLC.

    Crash after the effect

    Request roriginal + retry→Durable store

    The contract

    Start with what the system should appear to do, ignoring workers entirely. One atomic step records the request and applies its effect.

    ---------------- MODULE Once ----------------
EXTENDS Naturals
CONSTANT Requests
VARIABLES seen, effects
vars == <<seen,effects>>
Init == /\ seen = {}
        /\ effects = [r \in Requests |-> 0]
Apply(r) ==
    /\ r \notin seen
    /\ seen' = seen \cup {r}
    /\ effects' = [effects EXCEPT ![r] = @ + 1]
Next == \E r \in Requests: Apply(r)
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars
TypeOK == /\ seen \subseteq Requests
          /\ effects \in [Requests -> 0..1]
Consistent == \A r \in Requests:
    (r \in seen) <=> (effects[r] = 1)
=============================================
    SPECIFICATION Spec
CONSTANT Requests = {r1, r2}
INVARIANT TypeOK
INVARIANT Consistent
CHECK_DEADLOCK FALSE

    TLC finds 4 distinct states and 5 generated, with both invariants holding. Duplicate deliveries do not appear here: at this level a repeated request is a stuttering step.

    A worker that can crash

    Now the implementation. effects and seen are durable, so Crash leaves them alone and resets only the volatile pc. Mode selects a design. Begin also models a redelivery, because it can run again whenever the worker is idle. The last two lines use a refinement mapping from lesson 33 to state that this worker should implement Once.

    ---------------- MODULE Worker ----------------
EXTENDS Naturals
CONSTANTS Workers, Mode
ASSUME Mode \in {"EffectFirst", "IdFirst", "Atomic", "CheckThenCommit"}
VARIABLES effects, seen,   \* durable: survive a crash
          pc,              \* volatile: lost in a crash
          replied          \* the client has been told "done"
vars == <<effects, seen, pc, replied>>

Init == /\ effects = 0
        /\ seen = FALSE
        /\ pc = [w \in Workers |-> "idle"]
        /\ replied = FALSE

Go(w, where) == pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![w] = where]

\* A delivery reads the durable ID, then starts the chosen design.
Begin(w) ==
    /\ pc[w] = "idle"
    /\ UNCHANGED replied
    /\ IF seen
       THEN Go(w, "reply") /\ UNCHANGED <<effects, seen>>
       ELSE CASE Mode = "EffectFirst" ->
                   effects' = effects + 1 /\ UNCHANGED seen /\ Go(w, "record")
              [] Mode = "IdFirst" ->
                   seen' = TRUE /\ UNCHANGED effects /\ Go(w, "charge")
              [] Mode = "Atomic" ->
                   effects' = effects + 1 /\ seen' = TRUE /\ Go(w, "reply")
              [] Mode = "CheckThenCommit" ->
                   UNCHANGED <<effects, seen>> /\ Go(w, "commit")

Record(w) == /\ pc[w] = "record" /\ seen' = TRUE
             /\ UNCHANGED <<effects, replied>> /\ Go(w, "reply")
Charge(w) == /\ pc[w] = "charge" /\ effects' = effects + 1
             /\ UNCHANGED <<seen, replied>> /\ Go(w, "reply")
Commit(w) == /\ pc[w] = "commit"
             /\ effects' = effects + 1 /\ seen' = TRUE
             /\ UNCHANGED replied /\ Go(w, "reply")
Reply(w)  == /\ pc[w] = "reply" /\ replied' = TRUE
             /\ UNCHANGED <<effects, seen>> /\ Go(w, "idle")
Crash(w)  == /\ pc[w] # "idle"
             /\ UNCHANGED <<effects, seen, replied>> /\ Go(w, "idle")

Next == \E w \in Workers:
    Begin(w) \/ Record(w) \/ Charge(w) \/ Commit(w) \/ Reply(w) \/ Crash(w)
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars

AtMostOnce  == effects <= 1
ReplyHonest == replied => effects >= 1
Bound       == effects <= 2     \* search limit for the buggy designs

Contract == INSTANCE Once WITH Requests <- {"r"},
                seen <- IF seen THEN {"r"} ELSE {},
                effects <- [r \in {"r"} |-> effects]
Refines == Contract!Spec
================================================

    The two invariants split the problem. AtMostOnce says no duplicate effect. ReplyHonest says the client is never told “done” for work that did not happen. Each is easy to satisfy alone, so check both. The configuration for the safe design:

    SPECIFICATION Spec
CONSTANTS Workers = {w1}
          Mode = "Atomic"
INVARIANT AtMostOnce
INVARIANT ReplyHonest
PROPERTY Refines
CONSTRAINT Bound
CHECK_DEADLOCK FALSE

    Bound is a state constraint from lesson 42. It only keeps the buggy designs finite, since a crash loop could otherwise raise effects forever. Changing Mode and Workers gives these results:

    ModeWorkersTLC result
    EffectFirst1AtMostOnce violated, 4-state trace
    IdFirst1ReplyHonest violated, 5-state trace
    Atomic1Passes, including Refines: 5 distinct states, 8 generated
    CheckThenCommit1Passes the two invariants: 6 distinct states, 10 generated
    CheckThenCommit2AtMostOnce violated, 5-state trace
    Atomic2Passes, including Refines: 9 distinct states, 27 generated

    Trace lengths in these lessons come from TLC with one worker (-workers 1), which searches breadth-first and so reports a shortest trace. With more workers you may get a different trace of the same violation.

    Compare the two grids at the Crash column. It changes the same variable in both. The difference is what seen says afterwards. Checking Refines against EffectFirst also fails, at its very first step: effects changes while seen does not, and Once has no such step.

    Predict: is “record the ID, then charge” safe, since it can never charge twice?

    It is safe for AtMostOnce, and that is the trap. TLC’s trace for IdFirst is Begin, Crash, Begin, Reply: the ID is saved, the worker dies, the retry sees the ID and replies, and effects is still 0. You need both properties: no duplicate effect, and accepted work not silently lost.

    A crash is not the only way in

    The fourth row of the table is the instructive one. With one worker, CheckThenCommit passes, because its commit writes both values at once. Add a second worker and it fails with no crash at all. The diagram draws TLC’s trace.

    Each worker’s commit is atomic, but the check came earlier, so this is the last-ticket race again. In a real store the fix is often a unique key on the request ID, so the second commit fails, or an equivalent compare-and-commit. Translate exactly that guarantee into your atomic boundary. The lesson for modeling: if the deployment has competing workers, a one-worker model can pass while the design is wrong.

    Commit writes the effect and ID atomically, after an earlier read of the ID. What can still go wrong?

    Worked architecture: process an uploaded receipt once

    A receipt-scanning service awards loyalty points after processing an image. Job r42 may be delivered twice. Define the business effect as a durable credit row keyed by r42, and define attempts as separate worker executions. “Exactly once” at the application boundary concerns the credit, not whether a worker ever repeats the computation.

    In the diagram, a crash between OCR and the commit would lose only temporary work. The crash shown comes after the commit, so the acknowledgement is lost and the queue redelivers along the dashed arrow. The worker then finds a saved answer.

    That is why the store keeps a result, not just a flag. A bare seen boolean can suppress a duplicate, but it cannot reconstruct the points awarded. Define a retention policy too: deleting r42’s record while late attempts remain possible reopens the duplicate path.

    If the effect sits at an external payment provider, a local transaction cannot include it. The provider needs compatible request-ID semantics, or you need a different protocol. A transactional outbox commits a local data change together with an intent to publish an event, which makes those two atomic. Downstream consumers still need their own duplicate handling.

    Predict: the points credit is committed locally, but an email is sent before the transaction completes. Is the whole operation atomic?

    No. The email is an external side effect. An outbox can durably record the intention to send alongside the credit, but delivery may repeat unless the email boundary has its own identity or repetition is acceptable. Specify each observable effect separately.

    Beyond the lectures III: Failure-prone systems

    A former owner can still send a write.

    A lease says who should own a resource. Only the resource can stop a former owner’s write from landing.

    This builds on lesson 38, where one holder at a time was a property you could check, and on lesson 19, where messages could be delayed arbitrarily. Put those together and “one holder” is no longer enough: a former holder can have work still on its way.

    A lease grants authority for an interval under assumptions about time. It does not erase a worker’s memory or retract its messages. If A pauses, the coordinator may grant the resource to B, and A may later resume believing it still owns the resource. Follow the red arrow.

    A fencing token is an ordered number issued with each grant. The resource remembers the last token it accepted and refuses lower ones. Here is the same order of events with that rule.

    The difference between the two charts is one comparison in the last two rows. Notice where it lives. The coordinator’s lease table cannot reject a write already in flight; only the resource sees that write.

    The model

    In this module a token stands for its holder. AcceptWrite(t) can run for any token ever granted, because to the resource a paused holder and a delayed message look identical. Tokens come from a single counter, so two holders cannot share one and nobody can invent a larger one. Those are requirements on the real issuing authority.

    ---------------- MODULE Fencing ----------------
EXTENDS Naturals
CONSTANTS MaxToken, Fenced
ASSUME Fenced \in BOOLEAN
VARIABLES issued,        \* highest token the authority has granted
          fence,         \* token of the last write the resource accepted
          staleAccepted  \* history: did it accept a superseded token?
vars == <<issued, fence, staleAccepted>>

Init == /\ issued = 0
        /\ fence = 0
        /\ staleAccepted = FALSE

Grant == /\ issued < MaxToken
         /\ issued' = issued + 1
         /\ UNCHANGED <<fence, staleAccepted>>

\* Any token ever granted can still try to write: its holder may have
\* paused, or its message may have been delayed.
AcceptWrite(t) ==
    /\ t \in 1..issued
    /\ Fenced => t >= fence
    /\ fence' = t
    /\ staleAccepted' = (staleAccepted \/ t < issued)
    /\ UNCHANGED issued

Next == Grant \/ \E t \in 1..MaxToken: AcceptWrite(t)
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars

TypeOK == /\ issued \in 0..MaxToken
          /\ fence \in 0..MaxToken
          /\ staleAccepted \in BOOLEAN
FenceNeverRegresses == [][fence' >= fence]_fence
RevokedAtGrant == ~staleAccepted
================================================
    SPECIFICATION Spec
CONSTANTS MaxToken = 3
          Fenced = TRUE
INVARIANT TypeOK
PROPERTY FenceNeverRegresses
CHECK_DEADLOCK FALSE

    FenceNeverRegresses is an action property, not an invariant, because “did not go down” compares two states. A state predicate such as fence >= 0 would pass in every design and prove nothing. With Fenced = TRUE, TLC finds no error: 15 distinct states, 34 generated. With Fenced = FALSE the property fails on the trace in the first chart: Grant, Grant, AcceptWrite(2), AcceptWrite(1).

    What fencing does not promise

    Predict: B holds token 2, but its write has not reached storage. Can storage still accept A’s token 1?

    Yes. Add INVARIANT RevokedAtGrant with Fenced = TRUE and TLC reports a violation: Grant, Grant, AcceptWrite(1). Storage has never seen token 2.

    So state the requirement precisely. Rejecting tokens below the highest accepted token is weaker than revoking A at the instant a new lease is issued. The stronger meaning needs another mechanism, such as installing the new epoch at the resource as part of the grant, or stronger timing assumptions.

    What does the fence rule in this module guarantee?

    Introduce time explicitly

    Notice that the module has no clock. Fencing does not need one, because tokens are logical epochs. A lease model does. Untimed TLA+ does not secretly advance a clock, so add a variable such as now, a Tick action, expiration fields, and guards. Decide whether clocks are shared or local, how drift is bounded, whether processes can pause, and whether time must keep advancing. If now may stop forever, an eventual-expiration property can fail.

    For a finite experiment, bound time or use a justified abstraction of “before expiry” and “after expiry.” Avoid wrapping timestamps modulo a small bound when ordering matters: the wrap can invent or hide stale-token bugs.

    Worked example: a mobile session after logout

    A mobile app starts uploading a profile change under session epoch 12. The user logs out, and the server revokes that session by advancing its epoch to 13. The old upload reaches the server afterward. Deleting the token from the phone does not recall the request.

    Here the server’s test is equality with the current epoch, not “at least the last accepted,” because the server itself performs the revocation. That closes the gap from the previous section. The module has one request and one revocation, so you can see every step. Split chooses whether the comparison and the write are one step or two.

    ---------------- MODULE Session ----------------
CONSTANT Split
ASSUME Split \in BOOLEAN
VARIABLES sessionEpoch, profile, pc,
          acceptedEpoch, epochAtAcceptance
vars == <<sessionEpoch, profile, pc, acceptedEpoch, epochAtAcceptance>>

Req == [epoch |-> 12, value |-> "new"]   \* the delayed upload

Init == /\ sessionEpoch = 12
        /\ profile = "old"
        /\ pc = "sent"
        /\ acceptedEpoch = 0
        /\ epochAtAcceptance = 0

Revoke == /\ sessionEpoch = 12
          /\ sessionEpoch' = 13
          /\ UNCHANGED <<profile, pc, acceptedEpoch, epochAtAcceptance>>

Install == /\ profile' = Req.value
           /\ acceptedEpoch' = Req.epoch
           /\ epochAtAcceptance' = sessionEpoch
           /\ pc' = "done"
           /\ UNCHANGED sessionEpoch

\* One step: compare and write inside the same boundary.
Accept == /\ ~Split /\ pc = "sent"
          /\ IF Req.epoch = sessionEpoch
             THEN Install
             ELSE /\ pc' = "rejected"
                  /\ UNCHANGED <<sessionEpoch, profile,
                                 acceptedEpoch, epochAtAcceptance>>

\* Two steps: the check's result can outlive the authority it saw.
Check == /\ Split /\ pc = "sent"
         /\ pc' = IF Req.epoch = sessionEpoch THEN "checked" ELSE "rejected"
         /\ UNCHANGED <<sessionEpoch, profile,
                        acceptedEpoch, epochAtAcceptance>>
Write == /\ pc = "checked" /\ Install

Next == Revoke \/ Accept \/ Check \/ Write
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars
AcceptedWithCurrentAuthority == acceptedEpoch = epochAtAcceptance
================================================
    SPECIFICATION Spec
CONSTANT Split = FALSE
INVARIANT AcceptedWithCurrentAuthority
CHECK_DEADLOCK FALSE

    The two recorded epochs describe the last acceptance event. Do not instead require every past request’s epoch to equal today’s sessionEpoch: a legitimate past write does not become invalid when the user later logs out.

    With Split = FALSE, TLC finds no error: 5 distinct states, 5 generated. With Split = TRUE, it fails.

    Read the grid from the left. The check was correct when performed, and its result outlived the authority it represented. This is the stale-check structure of lesson 35, applied to authorization. A fix must make the acceptance boundary enforce current authority, or deliberately document weaker revocation.

    In a real app, include the user, tenant, and session in the credential’s scope. An epoch comparison does not authenticate a request or prevent cross-account access. Likewise, if a cached token validation stays valid for five minutes, immediate revocation is not your contract, and the model’s time and cache assumptions must say so.

    Transfer exercise: where should a background photo upload be rejected after workspace switching?

    First ask whether it is still authorized for the original workspace. Switching the visible UI is not necessarily revocation. If the product promises cancellation, model an upload or session generation checked by the receiving service at acceptance. Always preserve the original workspace identity in the request, rather than interpreting it using whichever workspace is currently selected.

    Specifying Systems, chapter 9, develops explicit real-time specifications. Compare your lease model with an untimed fencing model before combining them.

    Beyond the lectures III: Failure-prone systems

    Two safe configurations can have an unsafe handoff.

    Quorum overlap protects you inside one membership. Changing the membership needs its own argument.

    This builds on lesson 21, where any two majorities of one set had to intersect, and on lesson 23, where that intersection carried decisions forward. Here the proof’s premise stops being true, because the two quorums come from different sets.

    Suppose the old cluster is {A,B,C} and the new cluster is {C,D,E}. Each uses majorities of two.

    The diagram shows the problem: the configurations share C, yet the quorums {A,B} and {C,D} share nothing. A proof that every pair of quorums intersects within one configuration says nothing about this pair.

    The joint rule, and what it does not do

    Joint consensus requires decisions during the transition to satisfy both old and new quorum rules. For this pair the smallest such sets are {A,C,D}, {A,C,E}, {B,C,D}, {B,C,E}, and {A,B,D,E}. Each contains a majority of Old, so each intersects any earlier old quorum.

    That overlap, shown in the diagram at A, blocks a conflicting decision during the transition. It does nothing after the switch, when New is on its own. A joint phase with no further rule still fails, as you will see below. The bridge is the transition protocol: when old-only decisions stop, and what the new majority must hold before it takes over.

    A model of the handoff

    This module tracks one decision. A node stores at most one value. Decide is the acknowledgement, under whatever rule the current phase uses. Copy is state transfer: it brings a new node up to the decided state as it is at that moment. Copying is separate from voting authority, because a caught-up replica does not vote until the phase says so.

    ---------------- MODULE Reconfig ----------------
EXTENDS Naturals, FiniteSets
CONSTANT Mode
ASSUME Mode \in {"Direct", "CopyOnly", "JointNoEvidence", "Joint", "OldLingers"}
Old == {"A", "B", "C"}
New == {"C", "D", "E"}
Nodes == Old \cup New
Values == {"X", "Y"}
VARIABLES phase,     \* "old", "joint", or "new"
          val,       \* val[n]: the value node n has durably stored
          decided,   \* values acknowledged as decided
          copied     \* new nodes that have run the state copy
vars == <<phase, val, decided, copied>>

Init == /\ phase = "old"
        /\ val = [n \in Nodes |-> "none"]
        /\ decided = {}
        /\ copied = {}

Holding(v) == {n \in Nodes : val[n] = v}
Majority(s, c) == Cardinality(s \cap c) * 2 > Cardinality(c)
JointAck(s) == Majority(s, Old) /\ Majority(s, New)

\* The rule this phase uses to acknowledge a decision.
CanDecide(v) ==
    \/ phase = "old" /\ Majority(Holding(v), Old)
    \/ phase = "joint" /\ JointAck(Holding(v))
    \/ phase = "new" /\ Majority(Holding(v), New)
    \/ Mode = "OldLingers" /\ Majority(Holding(v), Old)

Voters == CASE phase = "old" -> Old
            [] phase = "joint" -> Nodes
            [] phase = "new" ->
                 IF Mode = "OldLingers" THEN Nodes ELSE New

Store(n, v) == /\ n \in Voters
               /\ val[n] = "none"
               /\ val' = [val EXCEPT ![n] = v]
               /\ UNCHANGED <<phase, decided, copied>>

Decide(v) == /\ CanDecide(v)
             /\ decided' = decided \cup {v}
             /\ UNCHANGED <<phase, val, copied>>

\* Copy the decided state, as it is right now, to a new node.
Copy(n) == /\ n \in New
           /\ copied' = copied \cup {n}
           /\ val' = IF decided = {} THEN val
                     ELSE [val EXCEPT ![n] = CHOOSE v \in decided : TRUE]
           /\ UNCHANGED <<phase, decided>>

UsesJoint == Mode \in {"JointNoEvidence", "Joint", "OldLingers"}

EnterJoint == /\ UsesJoint /\ phase = "old"
              /\ phase' = "joint"
              /\ UNCHANGED <<val, decided, copied>>

\* What must be true before the new configuration takes over.
ReadyToActivate ==
    CASE Mode = "Direct" -> phase = "old"
      [] Mode = "CopyOnly" -> phase = "old" /\ Majority(copied, New)
      [] Mode = "JointNoEvidence" -> phase = "joint"
      [] Mode \in {"Joint", "OldLingers"} ->
           /\ phase = "joint"
           /\ \A v \in decided : Majority(Holding(v), New)

Activate == /\ ReadyToActivate
            /\ phase' = "new"
            /\ UNCHANGED <<val, decided, copied>>

Next == \/ \E n \in Nodes, v \in Values : Store(n, v)
        \/ \E v \in Values : Decide(v)
        \/ \E n \in New : Copy(n)
        \/ EnterJoint \/ Activate
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars

TypeOK == /\ phase \in {"old", "joint", "new"}
          /\ val \in [Nodes -> Values \cup {"none"}]
          /\ decided \subseteq Values
          /\ copied \subseteq New
Agreement == Cardinality(decided) <= 1
================================================
    SPECIFICATION Spec
CONSTANT Mode = "Joint"
INVARIANT TypeOK
INVARIANT Agreement
CHECK_DEADLOCK FALSE

    Agreement is the global property: it spans configurations, rather than being checked inside each one. Each Mode removes one part of the handoff.

    ModeWhat it doesTLC result
    DirectSwitches with no copy and no joint phaseViolated, 8-state trace
    CopyOnlyWaits for a new majority to run the copy, while old quorums keep decidingViolated, 10-state trace
    JointNoEvidenceUses the joint phase, then activates without the evidence guardViolated, 9-state trace
    OldLingersKeeps every guard, but the old rule still counts after the phase changesViolated, 9-state trace
    JointStops old-only decisions, then requires the evidence guardPasses: 6372 distinct states, 39293 generated

    Read the Direct grid by rows. X is decided while A and B hold it. Then the phase flips, and C and D, a majority of New that has never heard of X, decide Y.

    The other three failures each match a slogan you may have heard. CopyOnly is “wait until copying finishes”: in TLC’s trace, C runs the copy before anything is decided and keeps its Y, X is decided next, D copies X, and the switch goes ahead because two nodes have “copied.” C and E then decide Y. JointNoEvidence is “use joint consensus” with no statement of what the switch requires. OldLingers is “raise the epoch” while old servers still accept old-epoch work. Each is a real action, so TLC can refute it.

    Know the limits. The model has one decision, no crashes, and no delayed messages beyond what OldLingers stands for. A value that was stored but never acknowledged may be discarded. It is a study model of the handoff, not of any particular protocol.

    Exercise: why is “add one node at a time” not a full specification?

    It leaves unanswered when the change becomes authoritative, which voters count, how state is transferred, what a leader persists, and how concurrent or interrupted changes recover. A slogan can guide design; an action relation must define the handoff.

    Old and new memberships share one node. Must their chosen majorities intersect?

    Worked example: moving an inventory shard

    A shopping service moves one stock record from {A,B,C} to {C,D,E}. All old replicas know there are three units. The new replicas are copied from an earlier snapshot. The team changes a routing configuration so that new clients use the new cluster, while some old clients keep cached routes.

    Follow the chart from the top: copy stock = 3 to D and E; A and B acknowledge r1 for one unit; routing switches; D and E acknowledge r2 for three units from their copy. This is CopyOnly in business terms. Read X as r1 and Y as r2: two acknowledgements that cannot both stand, because together they promise four units out of three. The old route was not merely inefficient. It kept decision authority during a handoff that lost evidence.

    Checking each cluster’s local stock misses this, so the property must be global: total acknowledged quantity never exceeds three. The evidence rule must connect to what future decisions actually read. It cannot mean that some isolated new node has the record. Activate asks for a majority of New because that is the set every later new quorum must intersect.

    A complete design says when the authoritative configuration changes, how that decision is persisted, how new authority learns all committed state, and where stale authority is rejected. Inject a crash between each pair of those steps as a next experiment. A client’s routing cache can affect availability and placement, but it must not decide whether an obsolete server may still commit.

    Transfer exercise: does reducing the DNS cache TTL solve the unsafe handoff?

    No. It shortens some clients’ stale-routing period but does not prove all stale requests disappear. Safety should follow from server-side authority and evidence rules even when an old route is used. A route refresh or redirect can then restore progress under the appropriate network assumptions.

    For one concrete protocol, study membership changes in the extended Raft paper and compare them with its log and election rules.

    Beyond the lectures III: Failure-prone systems

    Problem set 13: failures that outlive the step that caused them.

    These problems practice the third Beyond part: durable and volatile state across a crash, leases and fencing tokens, and changing a cluster's membership. They draw on Architecture: durable idempotent worker, Architecture: leases, fencing, and time and Architecture: changing membership, and reach back to Messages, failures, and retries, Set operations and quorums, Liveness and fairness and Safety and inductive invariants.

    Every module below is complete and was checked with TLC exactly as shown, so your state counts should match if your copy is identical. When a problem asks for the length of a trace, run TLC with one worker (-workers 1) so that its breadth-first search reports a shortest one. Each trace length counts the initial state.

    Problem 1●○○Payments

    An idempotency key that doesn't stop a double debit

    Draws on Architecture: durable idempotent worker, Atomicity and the last ticket and Problem set 11.

    A wallet service stores balances in Postgres and exposes POST /debit. Following the convention of many payment APIs, the mobile app sends an Idempotency-Key header and, after a timeout, retries with the same key. The handler looks like this:

    const prior = await db.query("SELECT response FROM idem WHERE key = $1", [key]);
if (prior.rows.length) return prior.rows[0].response;
await db.query("INSERT INTO ledger (account, amount) VALUES ($1, $2)", [acct, -amt]);
await db.query("INSERT INTO idem (key, response) VALUES ($1, 'ok')", [key]);
return "ok";

    Each statement commits on its own. Support finds customers debited twice for one purchase, always during deploys, when a handler process can be killed mid-request. The module below models one key. ledger and stored are durable; each handler's pc is volatile, so Crash resets it. Receive can run whenever a handler is idle, so it stands for the first attempt and for every retry. Mode selects a design: NoTx is the code above, KeyThenDebit swaps the two INSERTs, TxAfterCheck wraps both INSERTs in one transaction after the SELECT, and KeyFirstTx runs one transaction that begins by inserting the key, which is the primary key of idem.

    ---------------- MODULE PSb3_Wallet ----------------
EXTENDS Naturals
CONSTANTS Handlers, Mode
ASSUME Mode \in {"NoTx", "KeyThenDebit", "TxAfterCheck", "KeyFirstTx"}
VARIABLES ledger,   \* durable: debit rows written for key k
          stored,   \* durable: does the idem row for k exist?
          pc,       \* pc[h]: volatile position of handler h
          replied   \* the client has received "ok"
vars == <<ledger, stored, pc, replied>>

Init == /\ ledger = 0
        /\ stored = FALSE
        /\ pc = [h \in Handlers |-> "idle"]
        /\ replied = FALSE

Go(h, where) == pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![h] = where]

\* An attempt (the first try or a retry with the same key) reaches h.
Receive(h) == /\ pc[h] = "idle"
              /\ Go(h, "select")
              /\ UNCHANGED <<ledger, stored, replied>>

\* SELECT response FROM idem WHERE key = k
Select(h) == /\ pc[h] = "select" /\ Mode # "KeyFirstTx"
             /\ Go(h, IF stored THEN "reply" ELSE "write")
             /\ UNCHANGED <<ledger, stored, replied>>

\* NoTx: two autocommitted INSERTs.
Debit(h)   == /\ pc[h] = "write" /\ Mode = "NoTx"
              /\ ledger' = ledger + 1
              /\ Go(h, "key")
              /\ UNCHANGED <<stored, replied>>
SaveKey(h) == /\ pc[h] = "key"
              /\ stored' = TRUE
              /\ Go(h, "reply")
              /\ UNCHANGED <<ledger, replied>>

\* KeyThenDebit: the same two INSERTs, in the other order.
KeyFirst(h)  == /\ pc[h] = "write" /\ Mode = "KeyThenDebit"
                /\ stored' = TRUE
                /\ Go(h, "debit")
                /\ UNCHANGED <<ledger, replied>>
DebitLast(h) == /\ pc[h] = "debit"
                /\ ledger' = ledger + 1
                /\ Go(h, "reply")
                /\ UNCHANGED <<stored, replied>>

\* TxAfterCheck: both INSERTs in one transaction, after the SELECT.
Commit(h) == /\ pc[h] = "write" /\ Mode = "TxAfterCheck"
             /\ ledger' = ledger + 1
             /\ stored' = TRUE
             /\ Go(h, "reply")
             /\ UNCHANGED replied

\* KeyFirstTx: BEGIN; INSERT INTO idem (k is its primary key);
\* INSERT INTO ledger; COMMIT. If k already exists the INSERT fails,
\* nothing is written, and the handler returns the stored response.
KeyTx(h) == /\ pc[h] = "select" /\ Mode = "KeyFirstTx"
            /\ IF stored THEN UNCHANGED <<ledger, stored>>
                         ELSE /\ ledger' = ledger + 1
                              /\ stored' = TRUE
            /\ Go(h, "reply")
            /\ UNCHANGED replied

Reply(h) == /\ pc[h] = "reply"
            /\ replied' = TRUE
            /\ Go(h, "idle")
            /\ UNCHANGED <<ledger, stored>>

\* The process dies: its position is lost, the database is not.
Crash(h) == /\ pc[h] # "idle"
            /\ Go(h, "idle")
            /\ UNCHANGED <<ledger, stored, replied>>

Next == \E h \in Handlers :
          \/ Receive(h) \/ Select(h) \/ Debit(h) \/ SaveKey(h)
          \/ KeyFirst(h) \/ DebitLast(h)
          \/ Commit(h) \/ KeyTx(h) \/ Reply(h) \/ Crash(h)
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars

AtMostOnce    == ledger <= 1
OkMeansDebited == replied => ledger >= 1
Bound         == ledger <= 2      \* keeps the buggy designs finite
====================================================
    SPECIFICATION Spec
CONSTANTS Handlers = {h1}
          Mode = "NoTx"
INVARIANT AtMostOnce
INVARIANT OkMeansDebited
CONSTRAINT Bound
CHECK_DEADLOCK FALSE
    1. Run NoTx with one handler. Which invariant fails? Match each step of TLC's trace to a line of the handler code.
    2. A teammate proposes KeyThenDebit: "if the key is saved first, a retry can never debit again." Predict which invariant fails, then run it.
    3. Run TxAfterCheck with Handlers = {h1} and then with {h1, h2}. Explain the difference. What real event does a second handler stand for?
    4. Run KeyFirstTx with two handlers. Explain why one KeyTx step is a fair model of a Postgres transaction even though two of them can run at the same time.

    Run NoTx with two handlers. Does TLC's shortest double debit need a crash?

    Hint

    Look at what is durable at the moment of the crash, as in the three-row diagram of Architecture: durable idempotent worker: the debit, the key, both or neither. For task 3, a second handler can be the retry arriving while the first attempt is still running, not only after a crash.

    Solution
    ModeHandlersTLC result
    NoTx1AtMostOnce violated, 8-state trace
    NoTx2AtMostOnce violated, 7-state trace, no crash
    KeyThenDebit1OkMeansDebited violated, 8-state trace
    KeyThenDebit2OkMeansDebited violated, 7-state trace, no crash
    TxAfterCheck1No error: 9 distinct states
    TxAfterCheck2AtMostOnce violated, 7-state trace, no crash
    KeyFirstTx1No error: 8 distinct states
    KeyFirstTx2No error: 22 distinct states

    1. AtMostOnce fails. The trace is Receive(h1) (the request arrives), Select(h1) (no key), Debit(h1) (the ledger INSERT commits), Crash(h1) (the deploy kills the process before the second INSERT), then the retry: Receive(h1), Select(h1) finds no key, Debit(h1) and ledger = 2. The diagram draws it. The key exists to remember the debit, but the two are written by separate commits, so a crash can separate them.

    2. OkMeansDebited fails, and AtMostOnce never does. With one handler: KeyFirst(h1) saves the key, Crash(h1), then the retry's Select finds the key and Reply tells the client "ok" with ledger = 0. The customer is told they paid and the merchant ships for free. This is the ID-first trap from Architecture: durable idempotent worker, and it is why the module checks two invariants: each design can pass one by failing the other.

    3. One handler passes, two fail without any crash: both run Select while no key exists, then both Commit. A second handler is what a client timeout produces. The app gives up after ten seconds and retries, while the first attempt is still waiting on a slow query. A transaction makes the two INSERTs atomic, but the SELECT ran earlier, outside it. That is the stale check of Atomicity and the last ticket.

    4. KeyFirstTx passes with two handlers. The fix:

    BEGIN;
INSERT INTO idem (key, response) VALUES ($1, 'ok');   -- key is the primary key
INSERT INTO ledger (account, amount) VALUES ($2, $3);
COMMIT;
-- on unique_violation: ROLLBACK, then SELECT the stored response and return it

    Postgres enforces the unique index across concurrent transactions. If a second transaction inserts a key that an uncommitted transaction has already inserted, it waits; if the first commits, the second fails with a unique violation and writes nothing. So the outcome is always as if one whole transaction ran before the other, and a single atomic step models it. The check is no longer a separate read: the database performs it as part of the write. A crash at any point either rolls back both rows or leaves both.

    This works because the debit is a row in the same database. If the effect were a charge at an external card network, no local transaction could include it, and you would need the provider's own idempotency contract, as Architecture: durable idempotent worker says.

    Problem 2●●○Infrastructure

    A garbage-collection pause outlives a lease

    Draws on Architecture: leases, fencing, and time, Messages, failures, and retries, Architecture: bounded FIFO and Problem set 11.

    A nightly compaction job rewrites a table's data file in object storage. Two instances run for availability, and only the one holding a lease from a lock service may write. Each instance checks that its lease is still valid just before writing. One night instance c1 checks its lease, then stops for a long stop-the-world garbage-collection pause. Its lease expires, c2 gets the lease and writes, and then c1 wakes up and sends its write anyway. The file ends up with c1's stale data on top of c2's.

    The module adds time explicitly, as Architecture: leases, fencing, and time recommends: now is the lock service's clock and Tick advances it. A lease lasts LeaseLen ticks. The pause is simply that any number of Tick steps may happen between Check(c) and Send(c). Writes travel over a network modeled as a set, so they can be delayed and reordered. Storage keeps log, the sequence of tokens whose writes it applied, so the property is an ordinary invariant. Fenced turns on the storage-side token check.

    ---------------- MODULE PSb3_Lease ----------------
EXTENDS Naturals, Sequences
CONSTANTS Clients, LeaseLen, MaxTime, Fenced, CheckAndSend
ASSUME Fenced \in BOOLEAN /\ CheckAndSend \in BOOLEAN /\ LeaseLen >= 1
VARIABLES now,      \* the lock service's clock
          holder,   \* the client the service granted the lease to
          expires,  \* the time at which that lease ends
          issued,   \* the highest fencing token issued so far
          token,    \* token[c]: the token client c received
          pc,       \* pc[c]: "idle", "checked" or "sent"
          net,      \* tokens of writes still on the network
          fence,    \* the highest token storage has accepted
          log       \* tokens of the writes storage accepted, in order
vars == <<now, holder, expires, issued, token, pc, net, fence, log>>
Tokens == 1..(MaxTime + 1)  \* at most one grant per tick, plus one at time 0

Init == /\ now = 0
        /\ holder = "none"
        /\ expires = 0
        /\ issued = 0
        /\ token = [c \in Clients |-> 0]
        /\ pc = [c \in Clients |-> "idle"]
        /\ net = {}
        /\ fence = 0
        /\ log = <<>>

Tick == /\ now < MaxTime
        /\ now' = now + 1
        /\ UNCHANGED <<holder, expires, issued, token, pc, net, fence, log>>

\* The service grants a lease when there is none or it has expired.
\* (Renewal is left out: a client never takes over its own lease.)
Acquire(c) == /\ holder = "none" \/ now >= expires
              /\ holder # c
              /\ pc[c] # "checked"
              /\ holder' = c
              /\ expires' = now + LeaseLen
              /\ issued' = issued + 1
              /\ token' = [token EXCEPT ![c] = issued + 1]
              /\ pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![c] = "idle"]
              /\ UNCHANGED <<now, net, fence, log>>

\* The client checks that its lease is still valid ...
Check(c) == /\ ~CheckAndSend
            /\ pc[c] = "idle" /\ holder = c /\ now < expires
            /\ pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![c] = "checked"]
            /\ UNCHANGED <<now, holder, expires, issued, token, net, fence, log>>
\* ... and later (after a pause of any length) sends its write.
Send(c) == /\ pc[c] = "checked"
           /\ net' = net \cup {token[c]}
           /\ pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![c] = "sent"]
           /\ UNCHANGED <<now, holder, expires, issued, token, fence, log>>
\* The variant with no gap between the check and the send.
CheckSend(c) == /\ CheckAndSend
                /\ pc[c] = "idle" /\ holder = c /\ now < expires
                /\ net' = net \cup {token[c]}
                /\ pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![c] = "sent"]
                /\ UNCHANGED <<now, holder, expires, issued, token, fence, log>>

\* Storage receives a write. With fencing it refuses old tokens.
Deliver(t) == /\ t \in net
              /\ net' = net \ {t}
              /\ IF Fenced /\ t < fence
                    THEN UNCHANGED <<fence, log>>
                    ELSE /\ log' = Append(log, t)
                         /\ fence' = IF t > fence THEN t ELSE fence
              /\ UNCHANGED <<now, holder, expires, issued, token, pc>>

Next == \/ Tick
        \/ \E c \in Clients : Acquire(c) \/ Check(c) \/ Send(c) \/ CheckSend(c)
        \/ \E t \in Tokens : Deliver(t)
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars

\* Storage never applies an older lease's write after a newer one.
WritesInLeaseOrder ==
    \A i, j \in 1..Len(log) : i < j => log[i] <= log[j]
====================================================
    SPECIFICATION Spec
CONSTANTS Clients = {c1, c2}
          LeaseLen = 2
          MaxTime = 3
          Fenced = FALSE
          CheckAndSend = FALSE
INVARIANT WritesInLeaseOrder
CHECK_DEADLOCK FALSE
    1. Run the configuration above (Fenced = FALSE, CheckAndSend = FALSE). Write out TLC's trace. Where is the pause, and at what time did c1's lease expire?
    2. Someone proposes removing the pause window: check the lease and send the write in one step (CheckAndSend = TRUE). Predict whether that fixes the bug, then run it. What takes the pause's place in the trace?
    3. Set Fenced = TRUE and run both values of CheckAndSend. Report the distinct states.
    4. Architecture: leases, fencing, and time stated "the fence never goes down" as an action property. Why can WritesInLeaseOrder be an invariant here?

    With Fenced = TRUE, c2 holds token 2 but has not written yet. Can storage still accept c1's write with token 1?

    Hint

    A check that was true when it ran tells you nothing about the moment the write lands. Ask where the write is between the check and the moment storage applies it. For task 4, look at which variable remembers the past.

    Solution

    1. WritesInLeaseOrder fails with an 11-state trace. Acquire(c1) at time 0 gives token 1 and expires = 2. Tick to 1, then Check(c1): the lease is valid, since 1 < 2. Tick to 2: the lease has now expired, and c1 has not written. That gap is the pause. Send(c1) puts token 1 on the network. Acquire(c2) gives token 2, c2 checks and sends, and storage applies Deliver(2) and then Deliver(1): log = <<2, 1>>. The diagram draws this.

    2. It still fails, now with a 9-state trace: Acquire(c1), Tick, CheckSend(c1), Tick, Acquire(c2), CheckSend(c2), Deliver(2), Deliver(1). The write leaves c1 while the lease is valid, but it waits in net while time passes. To storage, a paused process and a slow message look the same, which is the point Architecture: leases, fencing, and time makes. No client-side check can close a gap that lies after the client.

    3. No error in either run: 186 distinct states with CheckAndSend = FALSE and 124 with TRUE. Storage drops token 1 because its fence is already 2.

    4. log is a history variable: it records every accepted write, in order. "Never accepted a lower token after a higher one" is then a fact about the current value of log, so a state predicate can express it. The fence alone forgets the past, so with only fence you need an action property that compares two states. Both work. The history version gives a trace that ends with the evidence on screen.

    The model still leaves things out: the clocks of c1 and c2 do not appear, because the lock service's clock decides expiry, and renewals are omitted. Fencing makes those questions matter less for safety: the order of writes no longer depends on any clock being right.

    Problem 3●●○Distributed databases

    Grow a three-node cluster to five

    Draws on Architecture: changing membership, Set operations and quorums, Sets, functions, and quantifiers and Problem set 7.

    A configuration store runs on nodes A, B and C and decides with majority quorums. Load is growing and the team wants five nodes. One engineer edits the member list from three to five in one step. Another says that is unsafe and proposes two steps, adding D and then E, "because the old and new majorities of each step overlap". Before arguing, measure. The first module checks quorum overlap between two fixed memberships, using Init as a search over pairs of quorums.

    ---------------- MODULE PSb3_Quorums ----------------
EXTENDS Naturals, FiniteSets
CONSTANTS Old, New
Majorities(S) == {Q \in SUBSET S : 2 * Cardinality(Q) > Cardinality(S)}
VARIABLES q1, q2   \* an old-configuration quorum and a new one
InitAll == /\ q1 \in Majorities(Old)
           /\ q2 \in Majorities(New)
InitDisjoint == InitAll /\ q1 \cap q2 = {}
Next == UNCHANGED <<q1, q2>>     \* only the initial states matter
Overlap == q1 \cap q2 # {}
=====================================================
    INIT InitAll
NEXT Next
CONSTANTS Old = {"A", "B", "C"}
          New = {"A", "B", "C", "D", "E"}
INVARIANT Overlap

    The second module tracks one decision across a sequence of memberships, in the style of Architecture: changing membership's Reconfig. A node stores at most one value, a value is decided when a majority of the active configuration stores it, and Activate moves to the next configuration in Configs. Guarded adds one condition to Activate.

    ---------------- MODULE PSb3_Grow ----------------
EXTENDS Naturals, Sequences, FiniteSets
CONSTANTS Plan, Guarded
ASSUME Plan \in {"3to4", "3to5", "3to4to5"} /\ Guarded \in BOOLEAN
C3 == {"A", "B", "C"}
C4 == {"A", "B", "C", "D"}
C5 == {"A", "B", "C", "D", "E"}
Configs == CASE Plan = "3to4"    -> <<C3, C4>>
             [] Plan = "3to5"    -> <<C3, C5>>
             [] Plan = "3to4to5" -> <<C3, C4, C5>>
Nodes == C5
Values == {"X", "Y"}
VARIABLES cfg,      \* index of the active configuration in Configs
          val,      \* val[n]: the value node n has durably stored
          decided   \* values acknowledged as decided
vars == <<cfg, val, decided>>

Init == /\ cfg = 1
        /\ val = [n \in Nodes |-> "none"]
        /\ decided = {}

Majority(S, c) == 2 * Cardinality(S \cap c) > Cardinality(c)
Holding(v) == {n \in Nodes : val[n] = v}

Store(n, v) == /\ n \in Configs[cfg]
               /\ val[n] = "none"
               /\ val' = [val EXCEPT ![n] = v]
               /\ UNCHANGED <<cfg, decided>>

Decide(v) == /\ Majority(Holding(v), Configs[cfg])
             /\ decided' = decided \cup {v}
             /\ UNCHANGED <<cfg, val>>

\* Switch to the next configuration. Guarded: only once a majority of
\* the next configuration already stores every decided value.
Activate == /\ cfg < Len(Configs)
            /\ Guarded => \A v \in decided :
                             Majority(Holding(v), Configs[cfg + 1])
            /\ cfg' = cfg + 1
            /\ UNCHANGED <<val, decided>>

Next == \/ \E n \in Nodes, v \in Values : Store(n, v)
        \/ \E v \in Values : Decide(v)
        \/ Activate
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars
Agreement == Cardinality(decided) <= 1
==================================================
    SPECIFICATION Spec
CONSTANTS Plan = "3to4to5"
          Guarded = FALSE
INVARIANT Agreement
CHECK_DEADLOCK FALSE
    1. By hand, find a majority of {A, B, C} and a majority of {A, B, C, D, E} that share no node. Can you do the same for {A, B, C} and {A, B, C, D}?
    2. Run PSb3_Quorums as shown, then with New = {A, B, C, D}. Then replace INIT InitAll with INIT InitDisjoint and drop the invariant: the number of distinct states is the number of disjoint pairs. Report it for both memberships.
    3. Run PSb3_Grow with each Plan and Guarded = FALSE. Which plans fail? For "3to4to5", say which nodes decided X, which decided Y, and in which configurations.
    4. Set Guarded = TRUE and rerun all three. Say in one sentence what the guard requires, and why it repairs the chain of two safe-looking steps.

    In the "3to4to5" plan every consecutive pair of memberships has overlapping majorities. Why can it still decide two values?

    Hint

    Overlap is a fact about two particular quorums. In task 3, ask which two quorums actually decided, not which configurations are adjacent. For task 4, a decided value must be present wherever the next configuration's quorums can look.

    Solution

    1. {A, B} is a majority of three, and {C, D, E} is a majority of five; they are disjoint. For four nodes a majority has 3 members, and 2 + 3 > 4 means any old majority of 2 and new majority of 3 must share a node among the four, so no disjoint pair exists.

    2. With five nodes TLC reports Overlap violated by an initial state, q1 = {"A", "B"} and q2 = {"C", "D", "E"}. With four, no error on 20 distinct states, which is every pair: 4 majorities of {A, B, C} times 5 of {A, B, C, D}. With InitDisjoint, five nodes give 3 distinct states and four give 0.

    PlanGuarded = FALSEGuarded = TRUE
    "3to4"No error, 164 distinct statesNo error, 140
    "3to5"Agreement violated, 9-state traceNo error, 386
    "3to4to5"Agreement violated, 10-state traceNo error, 485

    3. In the chain, A and B store X and C stores Y. X is decided in configuration 1 by {A, B}. Activate moves to {A, B, C, D}; D stores Y, so Y has 2 of 4, not a majority, and nothing is wrong yet. Activate again; E stores Y, and in configuration 3 Y holds C, D, E: 3 of 5, decided. The diagram shows that {A, B} and {C, D, E} miss each other. Each step's majorities did overlap. But the overlap argument from Set operations and quorums only protects a decision if the quorum that made it intersects the quorum that might contradict it. Here those quorums are two configurations apart.

    4. The guard says: switch to the next configuration only when a majority of it already stores every decided value. Then any quorum of the new configuration meets a node that holds X, and that node can never store Y. Applied at each step, the evidence is carried forward one configuration at a time, which repairs the chain. Raft's single-server changes rely on a similar fact supplied by the log. A change starts only after the previous configuration entry is committed in its configuration, and a log is ordered, so a majority that stores that entry also stores every entry before it. "Add one node at a time" is safe only together with that rule, which is the exercise in Architecture: changing membership made concrete.

    Problem 4●●●Microservices

    Ship every order once: the transactional outbox

    Synthesis. Draws on Architecture: durable idempotent worker, Messages, failures, and retries, Liveness and fairness, Safety and inductive invariants and Problem set 6.

    A checkout service writes orders to Postgres. A shipping service prints a label for each order it hears about through a message broker. The first version commits the order and then publishes an OrderPlaced event, and some orders never ship: the process died between the commit and the publish. This is a dual write, two systems updated by separate steps. The team switches to a transactional outbox. The order and an outbox row are inserted in one transaction, and a relay process reads outbox rows, publishes them, and deletes them afterward. The broker delivers at least once. The shipping service deduplicates by inserting the order ID into a processed table in the same transaction that creates the label.

    The broker is modeled as a set that Consume never removes from, as in Messages, failures, and retries. That covers redelivery, the same idea you used for at-least-once delivery in Problem set 6. MaxCrashes bounds how many process crashes can happen. Shipped is the liveness requirement: every committed order eventually gets a label.

    ---------------- MODULE PSb3_Outbox ----------------
EXTENDS Naturals
CONSTANTS Orders, Mode, Dedup, MaxCrashes
ASSUME Mode \in {"DualWrite", "Outbox"} /\ Dedup \in BOOLEAN
VARIABLES orders,     \* order service DB: committed orders
          outbox,     \* order service DB: outbox rows not yet relayed
          handler,    \* handler[o]: "new", "publish" or "done" (volatile)
          relay,      \* the relay's in-memory work: "idle" or an order
          broker,     \* orders whose event the broker holds
          processed,  \* shipping DB: orders recorded as handled
          labels,     \* labels[o]: shipping labels printed for o
          crashes     \* crashes so far
vars == <<orders, outbox, handler, relay, broker,
          processed, labels, crashes>>

Init == /\ orders = {}
        /\ outbox = {}
        /\ handler = [o \in Orders |-> "new"]
        /\ relay = "idle"
        /\ broker = {}
        /\ processed = {}
        /\ labels = [o \in Orders |-> 0]
        /\ crashes = 0

\* The checkout handler commits the order. In Outbox mode the same
\* transaction inserts the outbox row.
Place(o) == /\ handler[o] = "new"
            /\ orders' = orders \cup {o}
            /\ IF Mode = "Outbox"
                  THEN outbox' = outbox \cup {o} /\ handler' = [handler EXCEPT ![o] = "done"]
                  ELSE UNCHANGED outbox /\ handler' = [handler EXCEPT ![o] = "publish"]
            /\ UNCHANGED <<relay, broker, processed, labels, crashes>>

\* DualWrite: after the commit, the handler publishes to the broker.
Publish(o) == /\ handler[o] = "publish"
              /\ broker' = broker \cup {o}
              /\ handler' = [handler EXCEPT ![o] = "done"]
              /\ UNCHANGED <<orders, outbox, relay, processed, labels, crashes>>

\* Outbox: a relay publishes a row, then deletes it in a second step.
RelayPublish(o) == /\ relay = "idle" /\ o \in outbox
                   /\ broker' = broker \cup {o}
                   /\ relay' = o
                   /\ UNCHANGED <<orders, outbox, handler, processed, labels, crashes>>
RelayDelete == /\ relay # "idle"
               /\ outbox' = outbox \ {relay}
               /\ relay' = "idle"
               /\ UNCHANGED <<orders, handler, broker, processed, labels, crashes>>

\* A process crash loses in-memory state; databases and broker survive.
Crash == /\ crashes < MaxCrashes
         /\ crashes' = crashes + 1
         /\ \/ \E o \in Orders : /\ handler[o] = "publish"
                                 /\ handler' = [handler EXCEPT ![o] = "done"]
                                 /\ UNCHANGED relay
            \/ /\ relay # "idle"
               /\ relay' = "idle"
               /\ UNCHANGED handler
         /\ UNCHANGED <<orders, outbox, broker, processed, labels>>

\* The broker delivers at least once: an event stays available, so the
\* consumer can receive it again. With Dedup, printing the label and
\* recording the order happen in one shipping-DB transaction.
Consume(o) == /\ o \in broker
              /\ Dedup => o \notin processed
              /\ labels[o] < 2
              /\ labels' = [labels EXCEPT ![o] = @ + 1]
              /\ processed' = processed \cup {o}
              /\ UNCHANGED <<orders, outbox, handler, relay, broker, crashes>>

Next == \/ \E o \in Orders : Place(o) \/ Publish(o) \/ RelayPublish(o) \/ Consume(o)
        \/ RelayDelete \/ Crash
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars
Fairness == /\ \A o \in Orders : WF_vars(Publish(o)) /\ WF_vars(RelayPublish(o))
                                 /\ WF_vars(Consume(o))
            /\ WF_vars(RelayDelete)
FairSpec == Spec /\ Fairness

OneLabel == \A o \in Orders : labels[o] <= 1
NoLostEvent == \A o \in orders :
    o \in outbox \/ o \in broker \/ handler[o] = "publish"
Shipped == \A o \in Orders : (o \in orders) ~> (labels[o] >= 1)
====================================================
    SPECIFICATION FairSpec
CONSTANTS Orders = {o1, o2}
Mode = "Outbox"
Dedup = TRUE
MaxCrashes = 1
INVARIANT OneLabel
INVARIANT NoLostEvent
PROPERTY Shipped
CHECK_DEADLOCK FALSE
    1. Run Mode = "DualWrite", Dedup = TRUE with PROPERTY Shipped. Read TLC's counterexample, including its last line. Then check the same design with INVARIANT NoLostEvent instead, and compare the two traces.
    2. Run Mode = "Outbox", Dedup = FALSE with both invariants. Which fails? A relay crash between publish and delete is the obvious source of duplicates. Is it in TLC's trace? Explain.
    3. Run the configuration shown, with the outbox and deduplication. Report the distinct states.
    4. Remove one conjunct of Fairness at a time and rerun Shipped. Which conjunct can go? For the others, describe the behavior TLC reports.
    5. Why must crashes be bounded for Shipped to hold, and what would you assume about a real relay instead?

    Which conjunct of Fairness can you remove from the outbox design and still have Shipped?

    Hint

    A liveness failure ends in a state the system can stay in forever. Ask what fact about that state already shows the order is lost: that fact is a safety property you can check much sooner. For task 2, adding an element to a set that already contains it changes nothing.

    Solution

    1. Shipped is violated: Place(o1), Crash (the handler dies before publishing), Place(o2), Publish(o2), Consume(o2), then "Stuttering". The behavior stays forever in a state where o1 is committed and nothing will ever ship it. Fairness cannot help, because no action that could deliver o1 is enabled. NoLostEvent says every committed order is in the outbox, in the broker, or about to be published by a live handler. It fails after 3 states: Place(o1), Crash. This is the method of Safety and inductive invariants: find the state fact that explains why the good thing will happen. A violation of it is found sooner, reads more easily, and needs no fairness.

    2. OneLabel fails with Place(o1), RelayPublish(o1), Consume(o1), Consume(o1). No crash is needed. The broker never forgets an event, so any delivered event can be delivered again. A relay crash would republish o1, but adding o1 to broker again changes nothing, because duplicate sends and redeliveries look the same in a set model. That is why the model needs no separate duplicate action, and why the consumer, not the relay, must be idempotent. NoLostEvent holds: the outbox fixed the lost event.

    3. No error, 84 distinct states, with OneLabel, NoLostEvent and Shipped all holding.

    4. The fairness of Publish(o) can go: that action belongs to the dual-write design and is never enabled here. The run still finds 84 states and no error. Without WF_vars(RelayDelete), TLC's counterexample ends with the relay holding o2 forever after a republish, so RelayPublish(o1) is never enabled and o1 is never published. Without fairness on Consume, a crash makes the relay publish o2 twice and then everything stops, with o1's event sitting in the broker unconsumed. Each fairness condition is a claim about a real process: the relay keeps polling, and the consumer keeps reading.

    5. If the relay could crash after every publish, forever, then RelayDelete would never happen, and o2 would block o1 indefinitely. Real systems assume that crashes eventually stop long enough for progress, or that a supervisor restarts the relay and it eventually completes a cycle. MaxCrashes is a finite stand-in for "finitely many crashes"; it is an assumption, not a fact about the relay. Notice too where exactly-once holds. Labels are at most once because the label row and the processed row commit together. If printing were an external call, you would be back in Problem 1.

    Beyond the lectures IV: Applied models

    Keep an old response from replacing a newer choice.

    A search screen can show the wrong results even when every request succeeds. Model which response is allowed to change the current view.

    This builds on lesson 19, where messages arrive in any order, and on lesson 46, where a resource refused superseded work. Here the resource is your screen, and the token is a request ID.

    The concrete bug

    A user searches for cats, then dogs. The cats request is slow; dogs returns first. A handler that displays every successful response shows dogs, then replaces it with cats.

    The HTTP responses in the chart are individually correct. The screen is wrong because it has forgotten which request represents the user’s current choice. A debounce reduces how often requests start, but it does not establish response ordering.

    State the contract

    Use a fresh increasing request ID whenever a search begins. latest records that ID, and pending contains requests whose responses can still arrive. The UI is a tagged record: idle has no request, loading identifies the current request, and ready contains its request and result. These variants rule out combinations such as idle = TRUE with resultsLoading = TRUE.

    The property is precise: whenever the UI is ready, it shows the result of latest. Compare the same delivery order with and without the guard.

    The two grids differ in one cell. We also clear the old view on Start on purpose. A product that keeps previous results while loading needs a different contract, such as a separate displayedRequest field and an explicit “updating” state.

    Choose the response order

    User choice→Screen

    A complete bounded model

    Save as AppState.tla for the real tools. There are two possible requests with fixed results. Start issues them in order, but Deliver may select either pending response. Errors, cancellation, and duplicated responses are omitted to isolate the stale-response race.

    ---------------- MODULE AppState ----------------
EXTENDS Naturals
VARIABLES latest, pending, ui
vars == <<latest,pending,ui>>
Requests == 1..2
Query == [r \in Requests |->
             IF r = 1 THEN "cats" ELSE "dogs"]
UIStates ==
    [tag : {"idle"}]
    \cup [tag : {"loading"}, request : Requests]
    \cup [tag : {"ready"}, request : Requests,
          value : {"cats", "dogs"}]

Init == /\ latest = 0
        /\ pending = {}
        /\ ui = [tag |-> "idle"]
Start ==
    /\ latest < 2
    /\ LET r == latest + 1 IN
           /\ latest' = r
           /\ pending' = pending \cup {r}
           /\ ui' = [tag |-> "loading", request |-> r]
Deliver(r) ==
    /\ r \in pending
    /\ pending' = pending \ {r}
    /\ UNCHANGED latest
    /\ ui' = IF r = latest
              THEN [tag |-> "ready", request |-> r,
                    value |-> Query[r]]
              ELSE ui
Next == Start \/ (\E r \in Requests: Deliver(r))
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars
FairSpec == Spec /\ (\A r \in Requests: WF_vars(Deliver(r)))

TypeOK == /\ latest \in 0..2
          /\ pending \subseteq 1..latest
          /\ ui \in UIStates
CurrentView ==
    IF ui.tag = "ready"
    THEN /\ ui.request = latest
         /\ ui.value = Query[latest]
    ELSE TRUE
Settles == (ui.tag = "loading") ~> (ui.tag = "ready")
=================================================

    Start’s LET names the new request number; all three primed equations describe the same step. Deliver always removes the arriving request from pending but updates ui only if the ID still equals latest. CurrentView reads the tagged record’s fields only when they exist.

    SPECIFICATION FairSpec
INVARIANT TypeOK
INVARIANT CurrentView
PROPERTY Settles
CHECK_DEADLOCK FALSE

    TLC completes with 7 distinct states and 9 generated, with both invariants and Settles holding. That is small enough to draw completely.

    Follow the two dashed arrows: they are the only places where a stale response arrives. Each changes pending and leaves ui alone. Settles uses fairness from lesson 29: each pending Deliver stays enabled until executed, and only two Start steps exist, so a current request cannot be postponed forever. Real applications cannot promise this over a permanently failed network; add error and timeout outcomes for their progress contract.

    Make the bug appear

    Replace the entire IF expression in Deliver with the ready record, unconditionally. Check TypeOK and CurrentView under Spec.

    Predict: does TLC need dogs to arrive first to break the view?
